Tom insists he is innocent, but his protective veneer gradually cracks. He eventually admits a past stained by violence to his wife and son, and later to the police. Long ago, he and a close friend carried out a calculated killing and a daring robbery against mobsters, a brutal act carried out in retaliation for a family member’s murder. The friend’s arrogance, flaunting his share of the loot, betrays them to the mob, who seize him for vengeance. Tom narrowly escapes a similar fate and flees, seeking a fresh start under a new identity. A turning point comes when their lawyer arrives, revealing that the police never read Tom his rights, rendering his confession unusable in court. Yet as the McKenna clan rides toward the father’s former hometown to confront related legal concerns, the mob learns of Tom’s detention and begins plotting a retaliatory strike, one that will unfold with a terrifying shock.

Igraine lives in an old castle with her family, magicians who possess powerful books of magic. Her older brother Albert is following in the family line, but Igraine plans to be a knight one day, even though she feels there is not much adventure to be had at home these days. Her ancestors, though, had warded off many attempts to steal the books of magic. On her 12th birthday, Igraine's parents give her a magical suit of armor, but in the process, they are turned into pigs by mistake. Matters get worse when the next-door Baroness's castle is taken over by Osmond the Greedy, who wants to take the magical books so he can overthrow the king. Igraine and her brother must find a way to defend the castle from Osmond's siege while keeping their parents' condition secret and searching for the missing ingredient for their restoration to human form. Albert handles the castle's magical defenses while Igraine leaves to find the missing ingredient. She finds the ingredient and some assistance, in the form of the Sorrowful Knight of the Mount of Tears, who not only agrees to help her return home but also begins teaching her about the rules of chivalry, and eventually helps Igraine and her family end the siege.

;Act 1 Following a brief courtship, Elyot and Sybil are honeymooning at a hotel in Deauville, although her curiosity about his first marriage is not helping his romantic mood. In the adjoining suite, Amanda and Victor are starting their new life together, although he cannot stop thinking of the cruelty Amanda's ex-husband displayed towards her. Elyot and Amanda, following a volatile three-year-long marriage, have been divorced for the past five years, but they now discover that they are sharing a terrace while on their honeymoons with their new and younger spouses. Elyot and Amanda separately beg their new mates to leave the hotel with them immediately, but both new spouses refuse to cooperate and each storms off to dine alone. Realising they still love each other and regret having divorced, Elyot and Amanda abandon their mates and run off together to her flat in Paris. ;Act 2 After dinner at the Paris flat several days later, Elyot and Amanda use their code word "Sollocks" to stop their arguments from getting out of hand. They kiss passionately, but the harmony cannot last: while Elyot and Amanda cannot live without each other, neither can they live with each other. They argue violently and try to outwit each other, just as they had done during their stormy marriage. Their ongoing argument escalates to the point of physical abuse, as Amanda breaks a record over Elyot's head, and he retaliates by slapping her face. They seem to be trapped in a repeating cycle of love and hate as their private passions and jealousies consume them. At the height of their biggest fight, Sybil and Victor walk in. ;Act 3 The next morning, Amanda tries to sneak away early, but is surprised to find Sybil and Victor there. As they talk, Elyot comes in, and he and Amanda start bickering again. It has been decided that neither of the new spouses will grant a divorce for a year, to give Amanda and Elyot time to confirm if this is really what they want. As tempers rise, Sybil and Victor begin to bicker with each other, defending their respective spouses. Amanda and Elyot realise that Sybil and Victor are as suited to each other as they are, forgive one another and sneak out, leaving the younger two together. As Elyot and Amanda tiptoe out, Victor and Sybil have reached the point of mutual violence.

Cugel is easily persuaded by the merchant Fianosther to attempt the burglary of the manse of Iucounu the Laughing Magician. Trapped and caught, he agrees that in exchange for his freedom he will undertake the recovery of a small hemisphere of violet glass, an Eye of the Overworld, to match one already in the wizard's possession. A small sentient alien entity of barbs and hooks, named Firx, is attached to his liver to encourage his "unremitting loyalty, zeal and singleness of purpose," and Iucounu uses a spell to transport Cugel via flying demon to the remote Land of Cutz. There, Cugel finds two villages, one occupied by wearers of the violet lenses, the other by peasants who work on behalf of the lens-wearers, in hopes of being promoted to their ranks. The lenses cause their wearers to see, not their squalid surroundings, but the Overworld, a vastly superior version of reality where a hut is a palace, gruel is a magnificent feast, etc. — "seeing the world through rose-colored glasses" on a grand scale. Cugel gains an Eye by trickery, and escapes from Cutz. He then undertakes an arduous trek back to Iucounu, cursing the magician the entire way; this forms the principal part of the book. After many pitfalls, setbacks, and harrowing escapes, including the eviction of Firx from his system, Cugel returns to Iucounu's manse, where he finds the wizard's volition has been captured by a twin to Firx. Cugel manages to extirpate the alien, subdue the magician, and enjoy the easy life in the manse, until he tries to banish Iucounu and Fianosther (who himself has come to pilfer from Cugel) with the same spell that the magician had used on him. But Cugel's tongue slips in uttering the incantation, and the flying demon seizes him instead, delivering him to the same spot as before. Author Michael Shea wrote an authorized sequel, A Quest for Simbilis (DAW Books, NY, 1974). Vance's own Cugel sequel was published as Cugel's Saga in 1983.

A young Conan Finds himself drawn into schemes aimed at dethroning the ruler of Khauran. After rescuing Lady Khashtris from an assault by thieves from Shadizar and a cadre of treacherous accomplices, Conan agrees to serve as her bodyguard in exchange for freedom from the mirror that has trapped his soul since his encounter with Hissar Zul. The plan hinges on a release by someone of noble birth, and Khashtris convinces him that Queen Ialamis—the sister she longs to appeal to—will grant his liberation. Unbeknownst to Conan, Khashtris, and the Queen, the Queen’s latest lover, Sergianus, is in fact Sabaninus, the aged Duke of Korveka. Korveka governs a Kothian province seeking to annex Khauran, and his true identity is masked by a disguise. The disguise falls away when the Queen shatters the mirror that contains Conan’s soul; as his spirit re-enters his body, Conan recognizes the Duke’s true nature. Together with Lady Khashtris and her steadfast bodyguard Shubal, Conan sets out to expose the Duke and safeguard Khauran. It is also noted that Ialamis is the mother of Salome and Taramis, figures who appear prominently in Howard’s Conan story, “A Witch Shall Be Born.”

A scientific expedition from Earth reaches the Crab Nebula only to collide with another spaceship pursuing the same objective: an alien vessel that bears humanoid traits, differing in some details (notably that it communicates by microwaves instead of sound). Yet the two crews reveal many commonalities, including a shared sense of humor, and soon establish a working means of dialogue. Despite their rapport, both sides fear the other could be sent home with knowledge that might enable its destruction. Months slip by with a stalemate persisting between the ships. In a breakthrough, a junior human scientist proposes a risky plan: exchange the vessels and, crucially, erase all records of each crew’s homeworld so that neither side can identify or pursue the other. Thus the proposal would let both groups return home without annihilating one another. This story, First Contact, was selected in 1970 by the Science Fiction Writers of America as one of the finest pre-Nebula Award short stories, leading to its inclusion in The Science Fiction Hall of Fame Volume One, 1929-1964.

A psychiatric patient has lost his way and arrives at the country of Kappa. He is treated as a special guest and talks with Kappas of many occupations. Geeru, a radical capitalist, states that the unemployed labourers of Kappas are killed and their flesh is provided for food. The patient is astonished but Geeru argues that because the Japanese women in the poorest class are obliged to survive by prostitution, the patient's opposition is sentimental. Kappa's national characteristics are materialism and nihilistic realism. The babies of Kappa control their destiny. While in the womb, the fetus can refuse life as a Kappa, and be aborted. The Maggu, the sceptical philosopher Kappa committed suicide and appears as a ghost through the person of Tokku, a poet. Maggu is concerned about his fame after his death, although he admires the writers and philosophers who has died by suicide such as Heinrich von Kleist and Otto Weininger. At last the patient is due to return to the real human world, but muses that Kappa was clean and superior to human society and becomes a misanthrope.

The Hardy Boys come to France for a vacation. When the brothers spot The Gray Man in Manhattan, they learn about an investigation he is working on regarding a terrorist organization in France. While the Gray Man does not want the brothers involved because they are too young and the case is too dangerous, the Hardys secretly work to get themselves in the center of the investigation and soon they find themselves undercover in France as a couple of gun dealers who are into the punk rock scene, complete with dyed hair and grungy clothes. They get caught up in a company called Renyard and Company, which secretly sells guns and other illegal things to people. They are almost killed in a machine when a lady known as Denise helps them escape. The book has an interesting storyline in which almost everybody is betraying each other - Renyard and Company, Denise and many other people. The Hardy Boys are also captured by the French special police known as the Sûreté. They eventually escape by beating everybody up. Soon when the book is about to end, they are chased by the Chairman of Renyard & Company and his other partners. The people try to kill them but Denise saves them at the right moment. The case is then solved by the Hardy Boys and they return back to USA.

Mma Ramotswe is asked to investigate a cook who is being blackmailed, and a doctor whose nurse believes he is doing something illegal. She discovers the identity of the blackmailer, who is a newspaper agony aunt abusing the confidences of her correspondents, and forces her to stop. The doctor is selling generic drugs at the full cost to his patients, and she causes him to be reported. During the investigation she becomes more aware of her excess weight and its health risks and even tries to diet, but decides the most important thing is to be herself and happy. Mr Polopetsi, the new employee, is happy in his work but still struggles with poverty and hostility from relatives due to his spell in prison. He wants to help Mma Ramotswe, his mentor, with detective work, and when superstitious fears disturb staff at the Mokolodi Nature Reserve, it is he who discovers the cause: an injured ground-hornbill, believed to bring ill luck. He removes it, but it dies, and he fears he has lost Mma Ramotswe's trust, but is relieved and grateful when she shows faith in him after all. Mma Makutsi fears her engagement to Phuti Radiphuti is over after a misunderstanding about feminism, but all is explained and, in the process, Mr J.L.B.Matekoni gains a comfortable new chair which will make him happy too. She begins to appreciate how her fortunes will change with her marriage, and indulges her passion for impractical shoes with a new blue pair, even though they do not fit very well.

Oliver Russell, a man with a desire for power, is fated to rise to the highest office, that of President of the United States. Leslie Stewart, his betrayed fiancée, is a woman dedicated to the single purpose of bringing Oliver Russell to ruin. After amassing her own media empire and marshaling all her forces against him, she stands poised to destroy Russell on the eve of his most dazzling triumph. Thinking only of preventing Oliver from winning the Presidency for a second term, little does she know that she is about to fall into her own trap. When Oliver returns from Paris married to Jan, Leslie vows to avenge him. However she keeps her thoughts concealed. This makes Todd Davis, Jan's father, introduce her to one of his friends, who owns a newspaper. A brief introduction followed by marriage sees Leslie manage her husband's empire. With his falling health and subsequent death, Leslie becomes the sole owner of his properties. In spite of all the other businesses, Leslie takes an immense liking for the media empire, with which she intends to destroy Oliver. During this part, Dana Evans, who stars in Sheldon's other novel "Sky is Falling," appears as an inquisitive reporter who adopts a boy from war torn Sarajevo. In the meantime, Oliver becomes the president, but during his first term there occur a series of deaths, all due to toxicity of Liquid Ecstasy, a dangerous aphrodisiac that Leslie connects to him. When she is convinced it is Oliver who is behind these murders, she goes on to publish the news of his arrest before it is confirmed. Dana Evans then unmasks the real culprit, while the president reveals a shocking secret. The book ends with the proposal of a peace pact, brokered by President Russell, among the Arab nations, while Leslie is left wondering if she has gone a bit too far.

The tale centers on Horton, an elephant who is persuaded by Mayzie, a carefree and unreliable bird, to sit on her egg while she takes a brief “break.” That break proves to be Mayzie’s permanent move to Palm Beach. The sight of an elephant perched in a tree instantly causes a stir: Horton endures exposure to the elements, is ridiculed by his jungle peers, is captured by hunters, endures a brutal voyage at sea, and finally lands in a traveling circus. Yet Horton never abandons the nest; he remains steadfast because he believes in keeping his word, proclaiming, “I meant what I said and I said what I meant, And an elephant’s faithful, one hundred per cent!” The circus eventually tours near Mayzie’s Palm Beach home, and she returns to the show when the egg is expected to hatch, demanding its return without offering Horton any compensation. When the egg finally hatches, the offspring is a hybrid—a cross between Horton and Mayzie—an “elephant-bird.” Horton and the baby are joyfully restored to the jungle, a reward for his perseverance, while Mayzie faces consequences for her laziness, ending up empty-handed.

The novel The Snake’s Skin is about entire universe, where the space is complete and united. The scene takes place at the entire planet: the West and the East; Russia, Europe and finally Robakidze’s motherland – Georgia. Here one may also find an imaginary world of American billionaire living in his villa at Mediterranean Sea along with various prominent artists. There is only one tense in the The Snake’s Skin – present, but it includes past and future as well. The main thing is reality, but myths and legends are part of this reality. The way of thinking is not only particularly human, but at the same time metaphysical and idealistic. The personages of the novel do not live in the particular time period, or represent persons with concrete nationality. The author describes generalized citizen of the world that gets transformed into a particular person or in other words, returns to his roots (actual father, motherland), oneself, and the God. This is an adventure of Archibald Mekeshi’s soul taking place throughout the centuries.

Biagio, the younger brother, narrates the tale of Cosimo Piovasco di Rondò, a twelve-year-old whose defiant act sets the course of events. In Ombrosa, a broad woodland realm within Liguria near the French coast, the brothers belong to a noble eighteenth‑century clan and live on an estate that stretches through dense forests. Italy remains fragmented, and the Ligurian Coast has no rightful monarch to govern it. After refusing Battista’s snail dinner, Cosimo climbs a tree and vows never to descend. He has had enough—enough of family expectations, propriety, the future title of Baron, and all things rooted to the ground. At first, Biagio offers aid and occasional assistance, yet Cosimo gradually becomes self-reliant. Ironically, the more he distances himself to gain a fresh perspective, the more he ends up aiding the world beneath him. A turning point arrives with his romance for Viola, a young woman whose presence reshapes the destinies of Cosimo, Viola, Biagio, and Ombrosa’s entire community.

In 1998, Travis Boyette abducted, raped, and buried Nikki Yarber, a teenage high school student from Slone, Texas, in a shallow grave near Joplin, Missouri—about six hours away. He calmly watches as Donté Drumm, a Black high school football player with no connection to the crime, is arrested, tried, and convicted. Despite his innocence, Drumm receives a death sentence and remains on death row for nine years at the time of the events described. While Drumm endures imprisonment, attorney Robbie Flak fights to overturn his conviction and a backlash among Black Americans erupts, sparking a tense law-and-order climate. Meanwhile, Boyette has fled to Kansas, where he has lived since then, and his health has been failing due to a brain tumor that has worsened over nine years. As Drumm’s scheduled execution nears in 2007, Boyette, reflecting on his ruined life, resolves to do the right thing: he confesses. A priest, Reverend Keith Schroeder, accompanies him back to Slone to reveal the truth. Even after Boyette’s public confession, the state proceeds with Drumm’s execution by lethal injection. Only then does Boyette disclose Nikki’s burial site, and DNA testing later confirms marks of rape and assault on her remains.

The Discworld part of the book begins when a new experimental power source for the Unseen University is commissioned in the university's squash court. The new "reactor" is capable of splitting the thaum (the basic particle of magic), in homage to the Chicago Pile-1 nuclear reactor, which was housed in a rackets court at the University of Chicago. However, the wizards' new reactor produces vastly more magical energy than planned and threatens to explode, destroying the University, the Discworld, and the entire universe. The university's thinking engine, Hex, decides to divert all the magic into creating a space containing nothing — no matter, no energy, no reality, and, importantly, no magic. The Dean sticks his fingers in the space and "twiddles" them, inadvertently creating the universe. The wizards soon discover that they can move things around in the universe, using Hex. They call it the Roundworld (the Earth), because in it, matter seems to accrete into balls in space (instead of discs on the backs of turtles). They decide to appoint Rincewind, whom they dragged out of bed in the early hours of the morning, the Egregious Professor of Cruel and Unusual Geography, and send him down (against his will) to investigate this strange world. The wizards create a series of balls of matter in space, and give one of them a Moon (accidentally). This stabilizes the ball enough that, over a score of millennia (the wizards can skip over vast periods of Roundworld time, allowing them to view the history of the universe in less than a month), blobs of life emerge, ready to begin evolving into more complex forms. The book also features a fictional crab civilization and the dinosaurs (both of which are wiped out by comets/asteroids colliding with the earth), before jumping ahead to when an advanced civilization (presumably humans) has evacuated the earth due to an impending natural disaster.

Rose Trelawny, the beloved melodrama heroine at Barridge Wells Theatre—a nod to Sadler’s Wells—abandons the stage to wed her sweetheart, Arthur Gower, for the sake of his conventional family. The marriage proves stifling: Arthur’s grandfather, Sir William, and his great-aunt, Lady Tralfagar, are bored by Rose’s boisterous, uninhibited nature. She flings herself back to the theater, leaving Arthur behind, yet the “real world” bluntly erodes her talent for melodrama, and she cannot recapture the vibrancy that once made her a star. Meanwhile, Arthur has taken a covert path, fleeing to pursue acting at the Bristol Old Vic. The narrative shifts toward resolution when Rose meets Sir William again, reigniting his memory of admiring the renowned actor Edmund Kean as a youth. In a bid to nurture realism on the stage, Sir William offers support to Rose’s friend Tom Wrench, who longs to produce plays in a more naturalistic vein than the prevalent melodramas. Tom stages a production with Rose as the lead, and her newly found gravity aligns perfectly with his vision. Behind the scenes, Tom quietly arranges for Arthur to assume the leading male role as well, culminating in the lovers’ reunion on the stage.

The book opens in the autumn of 1558, just after the death of Mary I, and bells are heralding the fact that Mary's half-sister, Elizabeth, is now queen. The book is told from four main perspectives: Elizabeth I's; William Cecil's, the queen's main advisor; Robert Dudley, the queen's favourite; and Amy Robsart's, who is Robert Dudley's wife. Robert Dudley returns to court upon Elizabeth's coronation, and Amy hopes that his ambitions will not get him into trouble. During Mary's reign, Dudley was kept in the Tower of London, his father and brother were executed, and another brother died in Calais. However, her hopes for the quiet life soon die, as Elizabeth and Robert become closer and more intimate. Elizabeth has inherited a bankrupt and rebellious country, in turmoil as a result of the previous two monarch's reigns. Her advisor, William Cecil, warns that she will only survive if she marries a strong prince, but the only man that Elizabeth desires is her childhood friend, and married man, Robert Dudley. Robert is sure that he can reclaim his destiny at Elizabeth's side. And as queen and courtier fall in love, Dudley begins to contemplate the impossible - setting aside his loving wife to marry the young Elizabeth...

The story is about Mr. Mixie Dough, who "lives away up in the sky in a place called "Behind-The-Clouds-Town". But unhappiness creeps over the town because the King Misty "cannot get a Happiness cake for his little boy's birthday." Mr. Mixie Dough, along with all of the other bakers, compete in making a "Happiness birthday cake" for the King's son's birthday. Many bakers offer their cakes to the King only to find that he is not happy with the result. That is until Mr. Mixie Dough presents his cake. The King smiled after the very first bite and announced "SIR Mixie Dough, the baker man... shall be made Royal Baker to the King and shall bake us a Happiness cake every day." There are short sing-songs throughout the story and a recipe for the Happiness Cake. Much of the book is made up of full-page drawings of colorful Goofs preparing and baking the Happiness cake for King Misty. Pictographs appear between words (such as a drawing of clouds after the word clouds; a silhouette of Mr. Mixie Dough). There is no UPC, nor is there an ISBN printed on the book. Mr. Mixie Dough is now a rare collector's item that has been sold for $100-$750, depending on condition.

A witch, Jenny Waynest, and lord, John Aversin, who live in the Northlands are approached by a young southern noble, Gareth, who requests they slay a dragon in the capital city of Bel to the south. The pair agree on the condition the king send troops to the north to fend off bandits. On arriving, it is revealed that Gareth is not a mere noble, but the prince of the realm seeking aid against the wishes of his father. The dragon is revealed as Morkeleb the Black, an ancient and powerful dragon, inhabiting the caverns of the gnomes. In addition, the sorceress Zyerne is revealed to hold the king in her power, dominating him with the goal of capturing the power of the Stone in the heart of the gnomish Deep. John is persuaded to kill Morkeleb, with Jenny's assistance, but is himself wounded and Jenny is forced to save the dragon's life in exchange for that of John's. In saving Morkeleb's life, Jenny's weak powers are much augmented, allowing her to confront Zyerne but also tempting her to transform into a dragon and abandon the concerns of humanity. Zyrene enters the Deep, attempting to claim its magic, but is defeated when the Stone is destroyed by John, Jenny and Morkeleb. Jenny accepts Morkeleb's offer to transform into a dragon, but later returns to the North, unable to live without her humanity.

Set during the reign of King Charles II, the narrative follows Quaker leader Rowland Ellis and his journey from Wales to founding a Welsh settlement in Pennsylvania after religious persecution drove him abroad. A sequel, Y Rhandir Mwyn (The Gentle Region), continues the tale. Ellis becomes a Quaker under a neighbor’s influence, though his wife remains outside the faith. After her death, he weds a sympathetic cousin. A servant he has dismissed betrays him to the authorities, claiming to have seen a hidden chamber in Ellis’s house filled with Catholic worship objects. Yet the title The Secret Room signals more than this alleged secret: it also points to the private chamber within the heart where the inner light resides. Ellis and his fellow Quakers are jailed and illegally sentenced to death, but the king personally intervenes to secure their release. Despite this reprieve, they opt to leave Wales and seek a livelihood in America. cy:Y Stafell Ddirgel

Two protagonists closely resemble Farmer’s beloved archetypes, Tarzan and Doc Savage, though their names are altered to Lord Grandrith and Doc Caliban. They are clearly inspired by those legendary figures yet remain distinct characters. The half-brothers share the same father, the infamous Victorian-era serial killer Jack the Ripper, and suffer a terrible malady tied to a potent elixir that grants them near-immortality. At the outset, they discover a shocking constraint: they cannot engage in sexual activity unless it occurs amid violence, and their orgasms accompany the taking of lives. By the conclusion, Grandrith and Caliban will have confronted each other nude, fighting with fists, claws, and teeth, each bearing exaggerated erections. The opening scene finds Grandrith under attack from three fronts— Kenyan troops, Albanian mercenaries, and Caliban himself, who believes Grandrith murdered Caliban’s cousin and beloved partner. Complicating matters, both Caliban and Grandrith have been summoned for their annual appearance before The Nine, a formidable cabal of near-immortals who grant them perpetual life in exchange for unwavering obedience. In the end, the pair uncover a shared adversary within The Nine: a master controller who orchestrates global events and has manipulated their lives—and even the preceding clash between them. United, Grandrith and Caliban pledge to topple The Nine, a conflict their saga will chronicle in the interwoven sequels Lord of the Trees and The Mad Goblin.

Beginning with the run-up to Germany and Britain going to war, the book contrasts with Massie’s earlier work, which concluded at the war’s onset. It canvasses the era’s pivotal naval strategies and battles of World War I, from the Battle of Coronel—where Admiral Maximilian von Spee’s German squadron decimated a weaker British force commanded by Admiral Sir Christopher Cradock—to the Falklands engagement, where Spee’s fleet was decisively defeated by a superior British squadron. The narrative proceeds through the Dogger Bank clash in 1915, then follows naval operations within the Dardanelles Campaign, before presenting a thorough, multi-chapter treatment of the Battle of Jutland and its consequences. Additional chapters examine German submarine warfare and the sequence of events that drew the United States into the war. Prominent figures featured include British Admirals John Jellicoe and David Beatty, as well as German admirals Franz von Hipper and Reinhard Scheer. The volume concludes with the scuttling of the German High Seas Fleet in Scapa Flow, and it is supplemented by numerous maps and photographs.”

The tale unfolds as Ender earns the role of Dragon Army’s commander at Battle School, an academy aimed at molding young pupils into military leaders for an upcoming interstellar conflict against an unnamed foe. In Battle Room, where gravity is null, cohorts of students engage in simulated warfare, organized into squads called “toons.” Ender’s exceptional leadership quickly makes Dragon Army dominant, despite teachers continually stacking obstacles in their path. After achieving nineteen straight victories, Ender learns his unit will be disbanded; his toons will rise as commanders in their own right, and he himself will be sent to Command School for further training. There he encounters Mazer Rackham, a seasoned veteran who introduces him to a space-battle simulator. With time, many of his former toon leaders rejoin him as his subordinates. As they grow accustomed to the simulator, they participate in a sequence of battles that Mazer characterizes as mock confrontations against a computer-ruled adversary. Ender’s squad repeatedly triumphs, ultimately destroying a planet that the hostile fleet appears to shield. When the ordeal ends, the exhausted Ender is told by Mazer that the battles were not simulations at all: the commands issued by the children were being transmitted to a real fleet, and Ender has just annihilated the enemy’s home world, thereby ending the war.

Thirty-five-year-old Michiel (Michael) Steyn returns to the family farm in South Africa for his mother’s funeral, marking his first trip back in fifteen years since he fled in 1987 to escape a scandal tied to his service as a naval officer. Of mixed Afrikaans and English heritage, Steyn has become a United States citizen and now shares a life with his partner, Kamil Cassis, who is of Palestinian and Jewish heritage, on the edge of San Francisco’s Castro district. The novel centers on South African themes—racism, guilt, accountability, and the fragility of forgiveness—while its finale pushes readers toward an international lens, notably through foreshadowing US foreign and domestic policy in the George W. Bush era. Kings of the Water also recalls an older incarnation of a marginal figure from Embrace and nods to the extended fishing sequence in The Smell of Apples, thereby inviting readers to interpret all three works in a connected dialogue.

The narrator returns after a brief visit a few summers prior, to the small coastal town of Dunnet, Maine, in order to finish writing her book. Upon arriving she settles in with Mrs. Todd, a local elderly apothecary or herbalist. The narrator begins to work for Mrs. Todd when Mrs. Todd goes out, but this distracts the narrator from her writing. She rents an empty schoolhouse, so she can concentrate on her writing. After a funeral, Captain Littlepage, an 80-year-old retired sailor, comes to the schoolhouse to visit the narrator because he knows Mrs. Todd. He tells a story about his time on the sea and she is noticeably bored so he begins to leave. She sees that she has offended him with her display of boredom, so she covers her tracks by asking him to tell her more of his story. The Captain's story cannot compare to the stories that Mrs. Todd, Mrs. Todd's brother and mother, and residents of Dunnet tell of their lives in Dunnet. The narrator's friendship with Mrs. Todd strengthens over the course of the summer, and the narrator's appreciation of the Maine coastal town increases each day.

Eleven-year-old Josie travels to upstate New York to live with her great-aunt after her mother abandons her father for no clear reason. There, she encounters Jared, her 25-year-old cousin who is training to become a minister. Josie’s stay proves to be deeply distressing: she endures physical and psychological abuse from both her mother and great-aunt, and she faces relentless bullying at school. Rejected by her mother, she yearns for affection and turns toward Jared for solace. But his intentions are cruel in disguise; he feigns care to manipulate her into self-harm, into drinking her own blood, and into viewing explicit material, subjecting her to his verbal torment. Soon his sexual abuse begins, which Josie mistakes for genuine love even as she recognizes the wrongdoing. Her realization grows about her mother’s incapacity for love, traced to her mother’s enduring lack of admiration for Josie’s father and other men. After an extended stay, Josie’s mental state deteriorates, likely due to her illicit relationship with Jared. In a pivotal moment by a creek, the two initiate sexual activity; Jared then cuts his chest with a stone, Josie licks the bleeding wound, and he dies from blood loss. This constitutes the novella’s climax. Ultimately, Josie escapes the mansion, breaking free from Jared’s imprisonment.

In Remix Lawrence Lessig, a Harvard law professor and a respected voice in what he deems the "copyright wars", describes the disjuncture between the availability and relative simplicity of remix technologies and copyright law. Lessig insists that copyright law as it stands now is antiquated for digital media since every "time you use a creative work in a digital context, the technology is making a copy" (98). Thus, amateur use and appropriation of digital technology is under unprecedented control that previously extended only to professional use. Lessig insists that knowledge and manipulation of multi-media technologies is the current generation's form of "literacy"- what reading and writing was to the previous. It is the vernacular of today. The children growing up in a world where these technologies permeate their daily life are unable to comprehend why "remixing" is illegal. Lessig insists that amateur appropriation in the digital age cannot be stopped but only 'criminalized'. Thus most corrosive outcome of this tension is that generations of children are growing up doing what they know is "illegal" and that notion has societal implications that extend far beyond copyright wars. The book is now available as a free download under one of the Creative Commons' licenses.

David Innes and his captive, a member of the reptilian Mahar race from Pellucidar’s inner world, return from the surface aboard the Iron Mole, a vehicle devised by his loyal comrade Abner Perry. They surface at an unknown Pellucidaran location, where David frees his captive. He designates the area Greenwich and, armed with the tools from the surface, begins a deliberate program of exploration and cartography of the uncharted realm while seeking his missing allies—Abner, Ghak, and Dian the Beautiful. Soon a new ally appears: Ja the Mezop from the island realm of Anoroc, whom David befriends. Later, he locates Abner and learns that, in his absence, human resistance against the Mahars has faltered. During a formal exchange with the Mahars, David negotiates for information about Dian, his beloved, and about Hooja the Sly One, his foe. In return for the coveted Great Secret of Mahar reproduction— the book David previously stole and hid—the Mahars offer what they know. Determined, David resolves to retrieve the secret, only to discover that Hooja has already reached it and claimed Dian as his reward from the Mahars. Now David must pursue and defeat the wily adversary before resuming the struggle for human independence. In the end, this goal is achieved; aided by the surface-world resources he brought, David and Abner unite the human tribes into an Empire of Pellucidar, annihilating Mahar cities and replacing them with a new human civilization.

The novel is set at the start of the twentieth century and deals with the orphaned boy Álfgrímur, his adoptive grandparents, and the small, tolerant community of misfits and eccentrics they gather around them at Brekkukot, their cottage on the outskirts of Reykjavík. As Álfgrímur begins to encounter the minor politicians, businessmen and social-climbers of the growing town of Reykjavík he starts to question his future as a fisherman's grandson, and is increasingly fascinated by Garðar Hólm, the celebrated Icelandic "world singer" whose sporadic returns to Iceland encourage Álfgrímur to pursue his own personal goals of self-expression. He discovers the true value of his boyhood experiences only as he sets out on a path that will take him away from them forever. The boy's name, Álfgrímur, is explained in the book as a compound of Álf (elf) and grímur (a poetic word for 'night') meaning 'he who spends the night with the elves'. The original name of the book in Icelandic is 'Brekkukotsannáll' (Annals of Brekkukot). de:Das Fischkonzert is:Brekkukotsannáll

La Vendetta recounts the tragic end of Ginevra Piombo, the daughter of proud Corsican newcomers, who falls in love with another Corsican, Luigi Porta. When it becomes clear that Luigi survived a massacre in which the rest of his family perished in a bloody vendetta against Ginevra’s kin, Bartolomeo, Ginevra’s father, resolves to complete the vengeance by killing him. Yet Ginevra resists her father’s demands, and she and Luigi wed. In the years that follow, the couple’s life is marked by misery, hunger, and poverty, while Ginevra’s affluent father will not lift a finger to help; his only plausible action is to refrain from murdering Luigi. Ginevra bears a child, but both mother and infant die on the very day Monsieur Piombo finally relents and contemplates aiding the destitute pair. Before he can act, Luigi confronts him and offers the hair of his deceased daughter. “Dead! Our two families were doomed to annihilate one another. Here is all that remains of her,” he declares, placing Ginevra’s long black tresses on the table. The news shatters Ginevra’s parents as if struck by lightning. Luigi departs. “He has spared me a shot, for he is dead,” says Bartolomeo, slowly, staring at the ground beneath him.

John Ashbery summarizes Locus Solus thus in his introduction to Michel Foucault's Death and the Labyrinth: "A prominent scientist and inventor, Martial Canterel, has invited a group of colleagues to visit the park of his country estate, Locus Solus. As the group tours the estate, Canterel shows them inventions of ever-increasing complexity and strangeness. Again, exposition is invariably followed by explanation, the cold hysteria of the former giving way to the innumerable ramifications of the latter. After an aerial pile driver which is constructing a mosaic of teeth and a huge glass diamond filled with water in which float a dancing girl, a hairless cat named Khóng-dek-lèn, and the preserved head of Danton, we come to the central and longest passage: a description of eight curious tableaux vivants taking place inside an enormous glass cage. We learn that the actors are actually dead people whom Canterel has revived with 'resurrectine', a fluid of his invention which if injected into a fresh corpse causes it continually to act out the most important incident of its life." As well as Dutch, Italian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish translations, there have been three English translations of the work in question, published by the University of California Press (Berkeley) (1970), Calder and Boyers (London) (1970) and Calder (2008), and all based on Rupert Copeland Cunningham's scholarship and transcription.

One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) is the story of seven generations of the Buendía Family in the town of Macondo. The founding patriarch of Macondo, José Arcadio Buendía, and Úrsula, his wife (and first cousin), leave Riohacha, Colombia, to find a better life and a new home. One night of their emigration journey, whilst camping on a riverbank, José Arcadio Buendía dreams of "Macondo", a city of mirrors that reflected the world in and about it. Upon awakening, he decides to found Macondo at the river side; after days of wandering the jungle, José Arcadio Buendía's founding of Macondo is utopic. Founding patriarch José Arcadio Buendía believes Macondo to be surrounded by water, and from that island, he invents the world according to his perceptions. Soon after its foundation, Macondo becomes a town frequented by unusual and extraordinary events that involve the generations of the Buendía family, who are unable or unwilling to escape their periodic (mostly) self-inflicted misfortunes. Ultimately, a hurricane destroys Macondo, the city of mirrors; just the cyclical turmoil inherent to Macondo. At the end of the story, a Buendía man deciphers an encrypted cipher that generations of Buendía family men had failed to decipher. The secret message informed the recipient of every fortune and misfortune lived by the Buendía Family generations.

Long ago in China lived a family with five brothers who resembled each other very closely. They each possessed a special talent. One can swallow the sea; one has an iron neck; one can stretch his legs; one can survive fire; and the last can hold his breath forever. When one of the brothers, a somehow very successful fisherman, agrees to let a young boy accompany him on his fishing trip, trouble results. This brother holds the entire sea in his mouth so that the boy can retrieve fish and treasures. When the man can no longer hold in the sea, he frantically signals to the boy, but the boy ignores him and drowns when the man releases the water. The man is accused of murder and sentenced to death. However, one by one, his four brothers assume his place when subjected to execution, and each uses his own superhuman ability to survive (one cannot be beheaded, one cannot be drowned, one cannot be burned, and one cannot be smothered). At the end of the story, a judge decides that the brother accused of murder must have been innocent, since he could not be executed, and the five brothers return home.

Jade is going to Paris with her grandmother. She meets a boy - Flynn Jackson - in the train to Brighton. They become friends. Flynn lives in Dunchester, so Jade can see him. They fall in love with each other quickly. Jade is trying to help Tansy with Andy, who doesn't talk to her. She sends text messages, which are supposed to be from Tansy. Cleo is still in love with Angus. But he only pretends to be interested with her. He shows his parents that he's normal by "going out" with Cleo. The girl sings with his and Kyle's band on the music festival. But they don't win the price. Cleo breaks up with Angus, because she is upset of being not exactly his girlfriend. She could also see that, Angus is more interested in Kyle. Holly's parents want to sell their house. The buyers are Walker family - Angus and his parents. Unfortunately, before selling a house there is a fire in it that burns the whole house. Holly saved her nephew from sthe burning house, but she had to stay at the hospital, because she had burns on her legs. She still is afraid of the fire and sometimes she has panic attack. Tansy's private life is complicated. Andy doesn't talk to her and she doesn't know why. Then she discovers that he went to a party and he got drunk. He also was kissing Melanie, who is Tansy's rival. Luckily, he explains her everything and they are together again.

At the start of the novel, Sophie finds herself dumped by her current boyfriend Lou, then immediately falls into a new relationship with Dylan, a boy considered the height of masculine beauty by her friends. As they date, Sophie discovers she does not really love or even like Dylan all that much and ends their relationship in favor of not actually liking his personality. She then forms a secret romance with an internet chat-room boy named Chaz. Before she meets Chaz in person, Sophie discovers he is a pervert and ends the relationship quickly. Now on her own, in real life, she encounters an outcast classmate, Robin Murphy, at the local art museum and is astonished to realize that while he is not physically attractive or liked by her friends, she falls in love with him. The book ends with Sophie choosing to sit with Robin in the cafeteria instead of her friends, knowing that revealing her secret relationship to her friends and classmates would be okay. The companion book What My Girlfriend Doesn't Know, written from the perspective of Sophie's boyfriend Robin (Murphy), was published in 2007.

Dennis narrates Frisk, recalling a destabilized youth. At thirteen, in 1969, he was habitually allowed to peruse pornographic magazines, and snuff imagery imprinted itself on him—though he later discovers those photographs were forged. He realizes that Henry, then seventeen, had been the boy depicted as thirteen or fourteen in the images. Dennis, who identifies as gay and uses drugs, is devastated when his partner Julian leaves for France. He then becomes involved with Julian’s younger brother, Kevin. The psychologically troubled Kevin soon enters Dennis’s orbit, and Dennis—now eighteen—pulls him into drug use and enters a sexual relationship with him. In 1989, Dennis writes to Julian describing a spree of sadistic killings he began in Amsterdam; the letter’s content is explicit, detailing torture and deliberate cruelty. Dennis subsequently encounters two Germans, confesses his actions to them, and they ally to carry out a succession of random, motiveless murders. Among the serial killer’s more recent victims is an eleven-year-old boy, whom they torture, mutilate, and slaughter at Dennis’s windmill conversion home, merely two weeks before the letter’s origin. Julian, accompanied by Kevin, travels to Amsterdam to verify whether the murders described in the correspondence are real or a malignant fantasy.

1878 in The town of Fort Weakling, Texas, is "terrorized" by the notorious outlaw Billy the Kid - or rather, the citizens cower in fear of the things Billy, a bullying type, could (supposedly) do to them. When Lucky Luke, who happens to pass by, does not succeed in bringing in Billy through the local justice, he decides to teach the citizens that desperados are not as bad as they pretend to be by playing the role of a desperado himself, with the help of the only courageous person in the town, the local newspaper editor. And so, much to Billy's increasing consternation, the townspeople begin to view him no longer as their primal terror, but as the one who will free them of this new "menace". This ends in the situation depicted on the cover: Lucky Luke giving Billy a sound spanking before ferrying him to jail. As a result of his unusual action, the people of Fort Weakling find the courage of fending off desperado incursions with nothing more than a smile and cool wits - as Jesse James is quick to discover.

Max sets off for a friend’s house, only to find the friend absent and confronted by the friend’s overprotective mother, who insists on guiding him home. He views her behavior as irrational and bolts away on his bike toward the edge of the woods, glimpsing a glimpse of his personal struggles. Later, he constructs a snow fort in the backyard, complete with a flag and shelves stacked with snowballs. When Claire, his sister, and her friends step outside while the boys in the group chew tobacco, a fierce snowball exchange erupts. After a few hits, Max darts back to his fort, certain he’s secure. The others quickly locate him, drawn by the flag and the fort’s vulnerability. One boy leaps onto the structure, causing it to buckle and trapping Max beneath the debris. He emerges in tears, while Claire does nothing to help. Consumed by fury, Max ascends to Claire’s room and douses it with water, ruining several of her possessions. Later, their mother returns from work to find Max hiding in bed, remorseful for his actions. Reluctantly, he admits what he did to Claire’s room, and, exhausted and exasperated, the trio cleans up the wreck together."

An Open Swimmer unfolds in three parts as a coming‑of‑age tale centered on Jerra Nilsam, a late‑teenager. Much of the narrative follows a camping excursion he takes with his childhood friend Sean. During that trip, the pair encounter an old man who lives in a shack by the beach near their campground. As events unfold, it becomes clear that this man previously killed his wife in a similar shack on a neighboring shore by setting the place ablaze with her inside. The novel is threaded with numerous subplots—delivered in brief, spontaneous paragraphs and dialogue among unnamed figures that presumably include Jerra. After returning home and drifting apart from Sean, Jerra goes back to the campsite alone. While he sleeps in his van, a violent storm rages, toppled a large tree onto the Kombi, and the storm subsides with Jerra waking up in the old man’s hut, having been rescued by the same man. In the closing moment, Jerra reappears at his Kombi, opens the fuel tank, and casts a lit match inside before fleeing.

Émilie de Fontaine, after repeatedly spurning several suitors on the pretext that they lacked French peerage, finds herself drawn to a mysterious young man who quietly attends the village dance in Sceaux. Although he bears an elegant air and aristocratic demeanor, he never reveals his name and appears to care only for his ailing sister, rather than for Émilie. Yet he does respond to Émilie’s attention, and he accepts her father, the Comte de Fontaine’s invitation. Soon Émilie and the stranger fall in love. Worried for his daughter, the Comte investigates the enigmatic youth and uncovers him on Rue du Sentier—disguised as a simple cloth merchant. The revelation shatters Émilie, who, angry and desperate, marries a 70-year-old uncle to gain the title of Vice Admiral, becoming the Comte de Kergarouët. Years later, Émilie learns that Maximilien is no clothier at all but Vicomte de Longueville, now a Peer of France. Finally the young man explains why he kept a store: to provide for his family, sacrificing himself for his sick sister and for a brother who had left the country.

Ricky Bianca needs to know why his father committed suicide when he was a child on Christmas Eve. Unfortunately, his father at the time was fighting the Mafia from controlling the funeral industry. The Mafia sent a friend to deliver a letter on that holy night and after reading the letter, he blew his brains out. The letter was never found and no one but the head Don, Salvatore Biganti, knows what it contained. When Ricky heard the blast, he ran to his father's aid only to see him on the floor bleeding profusely from his temple. He knelt in a pool of blood and held his father's head, unsuccessfully trying to stop the bleeding. Subsequently, Ricky has no recollection of the event but suffers from wild nightmarish hallucinations. His mother soon thereafter died in an upstate sanitarium of severe depressive catatonia. His aunt in Connecticut raises him and after twenty years he decides to return to New York as a Funeral Director, back to the industry that holds the secret. His Psychology Professor friend at college advised him to get the answers his mind so desperately needs, before his hallucinogenic demons devour him. His innocence is lost as this cryptic industry leads him through a maze of deceit, greed and evil. Subsequently, he gets caught in an intricate spider’s web of organized crime, secret cults and unspeakable atrocities. The truth is, the known is worse than the unknown and it sends him spiraling down into a hell of fiendish demons and worse nightmares.

In 1994, Moss was an 18-year-old college student at UNLV. While studying for his honors thesis, he established relationships with John Wayne Gacy, Richard Ramirez, Henry Lee Lucas, Jeffrey Dahmer, and Charles Manson. He obtained samples of correspondence from and interviews with these men. Moss researched what would interest his subject the most and then cast himself in the role of disciple, admirer, surrogate, or potential victim. In his book he mentioned that he was interested in a career with the FBI; he reasoned that gaining the trust of a serial killer, possibly learning more about their stated crimes or unsolved murders, was a way to distinguish himself as a job candidate. Moss forged the strongest relationship with Gacy; letters led to regular Sunday morning phone calls, during which Gacy trumpeted his innocence even as he gave Moss a guided tour of his world. In the book, Moss tells the story of his correspondence and eventual meeting with Gacy shortly before Gacy was executed. According to the viewpoint informing the title of this book, Moss became Gacy's "last victim" after a face to face meeting in prison, in essence being overpowered by a manipulative, depraved sociopath. Moss felt that this misadventure allowed him to understand how a killer's mind works in not only controlling the vulnerable but also in terms of how to break them. Jason Moss committed suicide in June 2006

The book starts where Exile left off, with Ben returning to Jacen aboard the Sith Meditation Sphere he found on Ziost. The novel follows Jacen as he manipulates politics, introducing a new law that allows him to rewrite other laws. Using this and Cal Omas' betrayal to the Galactic Alliance as leverage, he and Admiral Niathal stage a bloodless coup, arresting Omas and installing themselves as joint Chiefs of State. At the same time, Jacen sends Ben to assassinate Dur Gejjen, throwing the Corellian-led Confederation into chaos. Meanwhile, Boba Fett and Mirta Gev are still in search of a cure to Fett's illness after finding Kad Skirata, the son of a clone. In exchange for the promise of making the Mandalorians a united people, he cures Boba, giving him another thirty or so years to live. Ben overhears a conversation between Lumiya and Jacen and, horrified, confesses all to his mother, Mara Jade Skywalker. Mara, livid with Jacen for attempting to turn Ben to the dark side, sets out to kill him. This backfires, however, as Jacen kills Mara as his final sacrifice. This sacrifice kills Ben's love for Jacen, making the prophecy complete. Thinking that Lumiya killed Mara, Luke hunts her down and kills her. Ben then reveals that Mara's killer could not have been Lumiya, since Ben was with her at the time. At the end of the book, Jacen Solo assumes his Sith name: Darth Caedus.

Paul Rayment, a man of late middle-age, loses part of a leg after his bicycle is hit by a car driven by a reckless young man. He becomes reclusive and retreats to his flat where he is cared for by a succession of nurses. None suit him until Marijana, with whom he shares a European childhood (hers in Croatia, his in France), comes along. Paul's feelings for Marijana, and for her teenage son Drago, become more complex. When Paul offers to finance Drago's education, Marijana's husband becomes suspicious of Paul's relationship with Marijana, which causes trouble in their family and culminates in Drago fighting with his father and moving in with Paul. It is not until the famed author Elizabeth Costello shows up unexpectedly and uninvited at Paul's doorstep that he confronts his feelings for Marijana and his resentment at the state of his life following his bicycle accident. Costello's sudden presence in his life confounds Paul, who believes she is merely using him as a character in her next novel. The book can be read as a metafictional discourse on the inter-relationship between the literary author and the characters, and with reality.

A group of migrant laborers from three continents flees their English strawberry fields to traverse England in pursuit of diverse dreams of a better future. The narrative follows workers from Eastern Europe, China, Malaysia, and Africa who have gathered in Kent to harvest berries bound for supermarkets, eventually living in two small caravans—one for men and one for women. Each is seeking a better life, and, in their own ways, seeking love as well, having arrived in England—some legally, some illegally—to pursue those aims. Their overseer is Farmer Leapish, a ruddy-faced man who treats everyone equally except Yola, a Polish woman who leads the crew and indulges him with flirtations in exchange for a bit of extra on the side. Their arrangement remains discreet, and the atmosphere in this tranquil vale seems harmonious until a fateful evening when Leapish’s wife stumbles upon him with Yola and, in retaliation, rams him with her red sports car. After the police are summoned, the migrant workers (along with a dog named Dog) hurry into one of the trailer homes and abandon their idyllic refuge, embarking on a wide-ranging journey across England.

Richard Bolitho first arrives at a Portsmouth inn popular with midshipmen, where he meets Martyn Dancer. A lieutenant from the Gorgon later escorts them. The ship sets course for West Africa, and soon comes upon an abandoned Merchantman, the City of Athens. Inside the vessel, Dancer and Bolitho find it pillaged and its crew slain. The officers quickly conclude that pirates were responsible, and Captain Conway informs them that the Admiralty has dispatched the Gorgon to investigate the disappearances plaguing the region. With the captured City of Athens in tow, the Gorgon steers toward a coastal fort ringed by perilous reefs and shoals. Near the fort, two other ships are spotted in the harbor, but the fort opens fire, sinking the City of Athens. Night falls as the Gorgon retreats, planning a daring night raid to seize the raiding ship. Dancer and Bolitho undertake the mission, commanded by the fourth lieutenant, Mr. Tregorren, whose resentment toward Bolitho’s noble lineage fuels his mistreatment. Their assault succeeds in capturing the vessel, and they also seize a Slave Dhow during the escape, aided by the Gorgon. Under the ruse of pilots’ fleet members, the ships raid the pirates’ base at the castle, using the guise to overwhelm the stronghold.

The year is 1934, and Nick, stuck writing scripts for a film company without notable success, receives an invitation from his colleague Chips Lovell to attend a party hosted by Lady Molly Jeavons. There, he learns that Widmerpool is set to wed Mildred Haycock, a woman who is twice widowed and regarded by some as notorious—or even a bit mad, in Nick’s view. The luncheon with Widmerpool and the ambush of questions from Widmerpool’s future in‑laws quickly become a recurring motif for Nick throughout the novel. At the same gathering, the familiar Alfred Tolland makes another appearance. A chance encounter with Quiggin at a cinema showing Man of Aran leads to an unexpected and enigmatic invitation to spend a weekend out in the country. It turns out Quiggin and Mona Templer are staying in a cottage lent by Erridge, Lord Warminster and the eccentric head of the Tolland clan. While there, the group visits Thrubworth Park, the Tolland ancestral home, for a modest but eventful dinner. As the meal nears its end, two Tolland sisters, Susan and Isobel, arrive. Later, Nick crosses paths with Lady Molly’s husband, Ted Jeavons, in a Soho pub, and the pair head to Umfraville’s nightclub, where they encounter Widmerpool—whose jaundice has flared up again—along with Mrs. Haycock and Templer. In the autumn of 1934, Jenkins becomes engaged to Isobel. Erridge, intent on personally observing conditions, travels to China amid Japanese military offensives, while Mona accompanies him, leaving Quiggin behind. Widmerpool’s engagement to Mildred Haycock ends in a ridiculous—and, for most men, crushing—disappointment, yet Widmerpool remains unfazed. Adapted, in part, from material published by the Anthony Powell Society with their consent.”

Set in the early 1980s, Liza Normal pursues a string of theater and commercial auditions driven by her mother Peppy, who dresses the child in strapless evening gowns, heavy makeup, and long false eyelashes. Repeated humiliations follow as the family endures ongoing degradation after opening a dinner theater in Marin County, California. In the first half of the novel, Liza must perform in a dilapidated firehouse that doubles as both theater and home, attend school where she endures constant ridicule and abuse, and at one point, suffers rape. Subsequently, Liza enters several developmental phases. She first gravitates toward a punk-rock persona, adopting the style of Wendy O. Williams of the Plasmatics. Her trajectory leads her to relationships with a drug dealer, and she experiences addiction during her tenure at “Elf House,” a commune of hippies who fetishize elves and speak in “Quenya,” the High Elven language from Tolkien. During this period, while employed by Centaur Productions—a company that crafts and distributes Slash fiction—Liza devises an alter ego, Venal de Minus. She transforms this persona into a phone-sex phenomenon and a Las Vegas stage act, thereby achieving a fresh form of success that reinterprets the theater ambitions her mother initially hoped to realize.

Set in Krynn not long after Takhisis’s demise at the end of the War of Souls, Amber and Ashes unfolds as magic returns and the gods reemerge, each jostling for dominance. The war left nations displaced and power realigned across Ansalon, and a mysterious warrior-woman named Mina, haunted by failure and the loss of her goddess, makes a perilous pact with a seductive evil. A vampiric cult spreads its influence through the fragile world, while unlikely champions—a wandering monk and a kender who can speak with the dead—rise to confront the source of this rising darkness. The tale opens with Chemosh speaking to himself in an abandoned temple, outlining his ambition to dominate the pantheon and to command living beings rather than corpses. Soon afterward, Mina and Galdar appear. Mina, mourning Takhisis’s death and near suicide, is rescued from despair by Chemosh, who binds her to himself as lover. It is at this moment that the scheme to forge the Beloved of Chemosh takes root.

An alliance forms between a human family and an alien, a tentacled being capable of thriving in the transformed air. To cope, people shelter behind sealed habitats with oxygen-generating plants or rely on specialized breathing gear. Mutations have turned some of Earth's native life into forms suited to the new atmosphere. Because the hostile environment erodes metals, technology gravitates toward ceramics and glass. Mistrust toward the alien presence runs high among some humans, who even blame them for the atmospheric shift, as the aliens appear to be better adapted to it. During a near-fatal confrontation, the family is ambushed by a faction that has captured another alien. In a moment of biochemically shared memories, the two extraterrestrials merge into a single personality spread across two bodies. This union furnishes them with the expertise and know-how that enable the humans to break free. In the end, the aliens disclose their true nature: they are largely explorers or scientists passing through vast regions for millennia. Over time, atmospheres “mature” when nitrogen exhausts the remaining oxygen, a process driven by the natural evolution of bacteria that use gold as a catalyst. It remains implied, though never openly stated, that human gold mining may have sparked this cascade.

Blankets follows Craig Thompson through adolescence into early adulthood, tracing his childhood bond with a younger brother and the tensions surrounding his Christian faith and first romantic awakening. Though the narrative unfolds in roughly chronological order, Thompson intersperses flashbacks to align late-teen experiences with earlier memories, creating a dialogue between youth and past. Central themes emerge: first love, sexuality in youth and adulthood, spirituality, sibling ties, and coming of age. The story opens with Thompson's childhood in Wisconsin, where a sibling dynamic—marked by typical disputes yet deeply intimate—helps him endure verbal and physical abuse from zealously religious parents and harassment from school bullies. During the preteen years, his appearance and home life leave him feeling like an outsider. As he grows into his teenage years, fitting in remains challenging until a winter Bible camp introduces him to a group of peers he believes he belongs with. Among them is Raina, an alluring and engaging girl who captures his attention; their bond grows rapidly, and they arrange to spend two weeks together at Raina’s home in Michigan. There, Thompson meets Raina’s family: her separated parents, her adopted siblings Ben and Laura, her birth sister, and her infant niece Sarah. Laura’s mental disability and Sarah’s frequent neglect by her parents place a heavy burden on Raina, who internally resolves to look after both children. While Raina forms a deep connection with Craig during his visit, she eventually decides she cannot shoulder another dependent and ends the relationship after he leaves. In the aftermath, Craig destroys most of Raina’s gifts and mementos—save for a quilt she made for him—stores them in the attic, and moves away to start anew. Away from his family, Thompson confronts and reevaluates his religious beliefs and spiritual sense of self. Years later, he returns to his childhood home transformed, renewing bonds with his family and strengthening those ties. The narrative closes on a note of reconciliation, with Thompson finding peace in his relationships and in himself.

Jade travels to Paris with her grandmother, while a chance encounter on the Brighton-bound train introduces her to Flynn Jackson. He’s a Dunchester local, which makes it easy for Jade to see him, and their connection blooms rapidly into love. Meanwhile, Jade tries to help Tansy by reaching out to Andy—who won’t speak to Tansy—sending messages that are meant to be from Tansy herself. Cleo remains in love with Angus, though he only pretends to reciprocate; he acts normal by taking Cleo out and showing his parents a facade of normalcy. At the music festival, Cleo joins Angus and Kyle’s band to perform, yet they fail to win the prize. Frustrated by what she perceives as a superficial boyfriend, Cleo ends things with Angus, noting his greater interest in Kyle. Holly faces another upheaval as her parents decide to sell the house. The prospective buyers turn out to be the Walker family—Angus and his parents. Tragedy strikes before the sale when a fire engulfs the house; Holly heroically saves her nephew but sustains burns to her legs, leaving her hospitalized and plagued by lingering fire-related fears and occasional panic attacks. Tansy’s love life also takes a turbulent turn: Andy’s silence toward her remains unexplained until she learns he attended a party, got drunk, and kissed Melanie, Tansy’s rival. Eventually, Andy confesses, clearing the air, and the two reconcile and stay together.

In Oppenheimer’s account, the origin of modern humans traces to Africa, where both the emergence of Homo sapiens and the onset of modern behavior occurred before any Out of Africa displacement. He argues there was a single migratory event out of Africa that seeded populations across the globe. From the Horn of Africa, anatomically modern humans are said to have crossed the Red Sea and then advanced along the southern coastal corridor in Asia. Consequently, he disputes the alternative hypothesis proposed by Lahr and Foley (1994) of a separate northern out-of-Africa route through the Nile and into the Levant. The text also supports the idea that modern humans inhabited South Asia during the time of the Toba catastrophe. To describe genetic lineages, Oppenheimer employs well-known biblical names for the most recent common ancestors inferred from mitochondrial DNA and the Y chromosome, while other paternal lines are labeled Cain, Abel, and Seth. Mitochondrial haplogroups are frequently named with female identifiers drawn from regions where those groups are common—for instance, haplogroup M is called Manju because it is prevalent in India, and haplogroup N is called Nasreen as it predominates in Arabia.

Set in a vaguely futuristic society dominated by The Game—a brutal fusion of rock music and violence performed by the Markers under The Keepers’ control—the play follows Hoss as he battles to be the top Marker. Facing rival Gypsies who flout official rules, he begins to doubt himself. In Act I, his eagerness to go out clashes with Star-Man’s astrology-based cautions. News arrives that Mojo Root Force threatens his Las Vegas turf in a questionable maneuver, and when a Gypsy from Vegas is en route to attack, Hoss reaches out to old ally Little Willard for help. Discovering that Willard has committed suicide from the pressure of his status compounds Hoss’s insecurities and his sense that the old order is ending. He tries to shore up his courage by challenging the Gypsy to a shiv duel, which marks a shift in tone. Act II opens with the duel’s format altered to a verbal contest supervised by a referee. Hoss and Crow engage in psychological games, with Crow mimicking Hoss’s gait and mannerisms while Hoss taunts him with the voice of a seasoned Western gunslinger. A later turn, in which Hoss adopts the persona of a Delta bluesman, seems to give him an edge, yet Crow exposes a persistent fear that he might shatter. After the referee is killed, a desperate Hoss pleads with Crow to teach him the new technique. In the end, he chooses to perform one final act of authenticity by taking his own life, a moment Crow approves. The curtain falls with Crow occupying Hoss’s throne as Becky swiftly shifts her allegiance.

The narrative centers in part on the disappearance of a master copy of a film cartridge named Infinite Jest, which the novel also calls the Entertainment or the samizdat. Viewership of the film is so compulsive that spectators become inert, caring only to watch more of it. This cartridge represents James O. Incandenza’s final film, completed during a sobriety period demanded by the lead actress, Joelle, and ending with his microwave suicide. Meanwhile, Quebec separatists seek to obtain a redistributable master to fund terrorist acts against the United States. The USOUS, determined to stop the widespread release and the potential upheaval of the Organization of North American Nations, aims to intercept the master copy. At The Ennet House Drug and Alcohol Recovery House, Joelle and later Hal undergo treatment for substance abuse, and Marathe visits the center in search of information about the Entertainment’s master copy, thereby weaving the various threads of the story together.

Miranda is sixteen and concerned with being sensible, while Cassandra, nine years and eleven months, likes and believes in magical things. Miranda is outnumbered in this family, because Professor Aisling lectures on mythology and legends at his university, and believes in mysterious and magical things too. But some of the members of the university think that it is nonsense to teach about myths and legends, because magical and mysterious things cannot be dissected, weighed and measured. One member in particular, Mr. Bilgewallow, takes delight in tormenting Professor Aisling, who wishes, and dreams, of a ship that would take him to the worlds where he might find the creatures of legend. One evening, his wish comes true. As he and his daughters walk along the river, they come across a curious little ship, with a crew of dwarfs and gremlins. One of the dwarfs introduces himself as Malachi, Captain of H.M.S. Basset. He says that it is Professor Aisling's ship, conjured from his wishes and ready to sail on the "tides of inspiration." Aisling is astonished and delighted, and he and Cassandra waste no time in going aboard. Miranda needs a bit more coaxing. The Aislings set sail on a magical voyage where they meet a number of creatures from mythology that join them on board the ship. Included among these are the Harpies, who take over the galley, the Manticore, the Sphinx, the Minotaur and a dryad, complete with tree. Disaster strikes when Aisling becomes distracted by the potential of bringing back measurable proof for Bilgewallow and his ilk. He also insists on bringing the lovely but deadly Medusa on board, with predictable results for one of the crew. But through the help of his daughters and Medusa, he recovers his belief and his balance, as all of them must unite against the evil trolls who pursue him.

Maigret investigates the circumstances when a homeless tramp is recovered from the Seine, after being attacked and badly wounded. The tramp proves to be a former doctor, known to fellow tramps as 'The Doc', who abandoned his family twenty years previously to work in Gabon, but returned to Paris to live rough, mainly under various bridges. Thanks to Madame Maigret's sister, who lives in Mulhouse, Maigret learns more of the family background. His wife, estranged but not divorced, is persuaded to visit him in hospital, but displays no affection or interest in a reconciliation. The tramp, identified as François Keller, was rescued by Jef van Houtte, a Belgian barge owner, and whilst in hospital, refuses to talk. But Maigret suspects that Keller knows his attacker and is keeping quiet for a good reason. He also believes that the Belgian is not telling him the whole story. Under intense interrogation, van Houtte eventually confesses that many years ago he was responsible for the death by drowning of his father-in-law and that Keller was a witness. But Keller still won't say anything, and Maigret is forced to release the Belgian for lack of evidence. Keller returns to his life on the streets.

The plot opens in the year 2021.India is ruled by a dictator Jeeva. In his rule, population is kept under control, old people are allowed to live only up to particular age and are killed when they cross the limit, each and every one should have names with two letters only alloted by Government, every Citizen of the country must strictly adhere to the rule of Jeeva and admire,adore him, everywhere and anywhere lies Robots, people are identified only with their social security numbers and all the details are fed and controlled by Master Computer at Capital City. On a New Year eve, Nila, a homemaker lady is very delighted for having Government permission letter to have a boy baby from Population Control Board. She intimates the news to her husband Sibi. While Government, allots a home space of Nila's residence for a man Ravi and his pet Jeano. Jeano is a Robotic pet which could speak. As per government rule, home space should not be alloted for more than three people. So Nila's husband leaves to verify about Ravi's allotment but not returns back to home. Nila, to find him, uses his social security number but wonders to get an answer that there is no existence of such a person. She tries to find him but in vain. What happened to Sibi? What is the role of Ravi in Sibi's disappearance? How Nila finds her husband and a shocking truth about Jeeva and his dictatorship with the help of Jeano? The rest of story moves with the answers to these questions.

Two boys, prompted by a newspaper mystery promising two young builders for a spaceship, cobble together a craft from scraps of tin and wood and present it to the advertiser. The man behind the ad is Mr. Bass, a reclusive scientist who spends most of his days in an observatory, largely unseen by the townsfolk. He unveils to the boys a hidden Earth satellite—the eponymous planet—that can only be viewed through a special filter he devised. After giving them a self-made fuel to power their vessel, he instructs them to sail toward the mushroom planet, contingent on obtaining their parents’ consent. A crucial stipulation is that a mascot accompany them on the journey; at the last moment they seize a hen for this role, and launch into orbit. They awaken on a lush, mossy world dotted with enormous mushrooms, the mushroom planet. Soon they encounter its inhabitants—small, large-headed beings with a hint of green skin who happen to be cousins of Mr. Bass. These residents reveal that their world is in crisis and its people are dying off. The boys later meet the planet’s ruler, Great Ta, and help to resolve the predicament faced by the natives, then return to Earth. The root of the mushroom people’s trouble is a sulfur shortage, which the hens’ eggs—rich in sulfur—help to alleviate, providing a solution to their crisis.

_ The book concerns an elephant named Horton, who is convinced by Mayzie (a lazy, irresponsible bird) to sit on her egg while she takes a short "break", which in actuality ends up being Mayzie's permanent relocation to Palm Beach. Naturally, the absurd sight of an elephant sitting atop a tree makes quite a scene – Horton is exposed to the elements, laughed at by his jungle friends, captured by hunters, forced to endure a terrible sea voyage, and finally placed in a traveling circus. However, despite his hardships and Mayzie's clear intent not to return, Horton refuses to leave the nest through all of these, because he insists on keeping his word ("I meant what I said and I said what I meant, And an elephant's faithful, one hundred per cent!") The traveling circus ends up visiting near Mayzie's new Palm Beach residence; she returns to the circus once the egg is due to hatch, and demands its return without offering any reward for Horton. However, when the egg hatches, the creature that emerges is an "elephant-bird" cross between Horton and Mayzie, and Horton and the baby are returned happily to the jungle, rewarding Horton for his persistence, while Mayzie is punished for her laziness by ending up with nothing.

Scully Christopher Crockett La Cruz is an actor, fortune seeker and adventurer from the long isolated orbital technocratic democracies of Circumluna and the Bubbles Congeries. He lands in what he believes to be Canada to reclaim family mining interests only to discover that Canada is now North Texas and what is left of civilization in North America is ruled by primitive, backslapping, bigger than life anti-intellectual "good ole boys" convinced of their own moral superiority. In the tortured version of history known to the giant hormone-boosted Anglo-Saxon inhabitants who rule a diminutive Mexican underclass, the original Texas, or Texas, had actually secretly ruled the pre-nuclear war United States since 1845. Texas escaped the nuclear destruction of the rest of the United States because of the foresight of Lyndon the First. An enormous bunker then known as the Houston Carlsbad Caverns-Denver-Kansas City-Little Rock Pentagram and now referred to simply as the Texas Bunker had saved the heartland during a war that destroyed both American coasts, Europe, Russia, China, and Africa. Texas then conquered the rest of the continent, although Hawaii and Cuba remain stubbornly "unconquered".

When Bill, an impoverished Cambridge student, is even unable to pay for his mother's funeral, his thoughts turn to crime.
