However, a friend warns him that "To have no money is to join the aristocracy, Bill. When the day comes for you to have it, you will have left the aristocracy, never to return." Another central character, Helen, an undergraduate reading English literature, lacks stability in her life and finds her main solace in poetry and particularly in the romantic medieval work of Tennyson. Her obsession with The Lady of Shalott, and her identification with the lady of the poem, bring her to a fatal ending. Helen has been seduced by the medieval romances of the Victorian era but does not wish to be seduced by Bill. Lance, a scientist, hopes to save the world, but the effect of his experiments on Helen is less positive. Meanwhile, 'the Cambridge rapist' is at large. "This is the world of bedsitter girls, of Auden and Betjeman and Brian Patten." By buying a Donald Duck mask for bank robbing purposes, Bill unwittingly identifies himself with the rapist. In the course of a week during the University's Michaelmas term, the tensions and interplay between the leading characters lead not only to bank robbery, but also to ritual castration, transvestism, and a fatal car crash. "From the Whipple Museum to the University Arms Hotel, intellectuals and tourists turned pale. What could have caused it, this catastrophic sound?" The novel includes many quotations, not only from Tennyson but also from Thomas Hood, William Thackeray, and W. H. Auden.

Lieutenant Bret Taylor married his wife after knowing her only over a single overnight drinking binge while on shore leave during the war. His ship is bombed out of the water and he returns home to find his wife freshly murdered in the home he bought but had never seen. The shock of the two events sends him into a mental lapse, and he's in an asylum. The woman who loves him, a successful screenwriter, calls in a specialist who jogs his memory—and his sense of duty. Taylor hits the streets of Los Angeles, digging through his wife's lies and lovers in an attempt to avenge her murder. The book is a psychological thriller, with the main action being the unraveling of the story within Taylor's mind. The reader is denied information that other major characters obviously have throughout the whole novel, and is meanwhile treated to long passages of theories from the main character. The limited number of characters keeps the possible solutions to a minimum and the book is perhaps more straightforward than what makes a good mystery. Alfred A. Knopf, Jr., who functioned as an editing publisher, asked for revisions in what he considered a slow-paced novel. Macdonald cut '10,000 good words' and concentrated the action into four days. The 1985 movie Deadly Companion (or Double Negative) was based on this novel.

Two interwoven narratives unfold in the novel. One chronicles the romance between Nacib Saad, a respectable Syrian-born tavern keeper, and Gabriela, a naive yet captivating migrant worker from the rural interior. The other tracks the clash between Cacao’s aging power brokers—the Bastos clan at the helm—and the modernization currents embodied by Mundinho Falcão, a wealthy youth from Rio de Janeiro. Read together, the work offers an unusual, enchanting love story while also painting the political and social dynamics of 1920s Brazil, delivering a lightly satirical meditation on Latin American quests for “modernity.” It additionally exalts Bahia’s local culture and pleasures. Adaptations followed: Brazilian TV series aired in 1960, 1976, and 2012, and Bruno Barreto directed a 1983 feature film. In that movie, Sonia Braga played Gabriela and Marcello Mastroianni portrayed Nacib, with an original score by Antonio Carlos Jobim.

The story is set in the reign of King Charles II of England and follows the experiences of Quaker leader Rowland Ellis who founded a Welsh colony in Pennsylvania after being forced to leave Wales because of religious persecution. A sequel, Y Rhandir Mwyn (The Gentle Region), continues the story. Rowland Ellis becomes a Quaker as a result of the influence of a neighbour, but his wife does not share his religious beliefs. Following her death, he marries a sympathetic cousin. He is betrayed to the authorities by a servant he has dismissed, who describes a "secret room" he claims to have seen in the house, containing objects of Catholic worship. However, this is not the main reason why the novel is named "The Secret Room", as it also refers to the secret room within one's heart where the inner light is found. Ellis and his fellow Quakers are imprisoned and illegally condemned to death, but are released following the direct intervention of the king. Nevertheless, they decide to leave Wales for a better life in America. cy:Y Stafell Ddirgel

A kindly, elderly grandfather narrates a tale to his grandchildren about the town of Chewandswallow, where weather arrives three times daily—at breakfast, lunch, and dinner—and it always brings food and drinks. Rain consists of juice and soup, the snow is ice cream, and the wind delivers hamburgers. With this odd climate, grocery stores become unnecessary. Yet the weather soon deteriorates, initially raining unpleasant things like pea-soup fog, soggy green beans, and Brussels sprout cakes. Quickly the situation escalates into a catastrophe as portions of food grow enormous, and the island faces a deluge of edibles that bury buildings, crush homes, and block roads. In an effort to escape before total destruction, the people fashion boats from stale bread and pizza. They flee Chewandswallow and eventually reach a new town, where they must endure life in a world where the sky no longer provides sustenance.

The villain is a middle-class small businessman named John Wright who decides to assassinate the President of the United States. He spends his life savings to carry out the theft of a U.S. Army shipment of the two precursor chemicals that form a deadly nerve gas codenamed VZ when combined. The ingredients for the nerve gas VZ were intended to be detonated in downtown San Diego, corresponding with the arrival of the President to attend a Republican party conference taking place there. This nerve gas had no safe antidote, and it kills in two to three minutes after being inhaled or touched. This nerve gas is contained inside two "Alacran" (a combustible plastic) tanks, and plastic explosives are wrapped around the containers, so that when after the nerve gas is released, the containers explode, rendering the scene of the crime untraceable. This plan is thwarted by John Graves, a State Department agent who has been tailing Wright, who deduced the neferious plan, and the stopped it just two minutes before the timers set to release the nerve gas hit zero.

Kylar Stern has rejected the assassin's life. In the wake of the Godking's violent coup, both his master and his closest friend are dead. His friend was Logan Gyre, heir to Cenaria's throne, but few of the ruling class survive to mourn his loss. So Kylar is starting over: new city, new companions, and new profession. But when he learns that Logan might be alive, trapped and in hiding, Kylar faces an impossible choice: he could give up the way of shadows forever, and find peace with his young family. Or he could succumb to his flair for destruction, the years of training, to save his friend and his country - and lose all he holds precious. Godking Garoth Ursuul has assumed power in Cenaria and is manipulating the futures and destinies of all who live there. Many nobles, led by self proclaimed Queen Terah Graesin, have left the city in ruins to the Khalidorans. Attempting to leave behind the life of shadows that ruined his master, Kylar flees to Caernarvon and an idealic life with Elene. But darkness finds Kylar along the road to the light as friends return for one last job and Kylar learns more about who Durzo and ultimately Kylar are. Kylar has become a titanic force with a foot in the light and in the dark, but which will our twilight hero choose?

The narrative picks up from where 1632 left off, but quickly shifts its focus toward the intricate politics surrounding the newly formed United States and Cardinal Richelieu’s bid to neutralize the technological edge that Gustavus Adolphus and his Confederated Principalities of Europe enjoy. Richelieu overturns France’s foreign policy, molding it into a strategic alliance aimed directly at the NUS and Gustavus, under the banner of the League of Ostend. In response, Mike Stearns dispatches emissaries seeking allies; some of these agents were already secret members of the Ostend League and later reveal themselves during the Battle of Four Fleets. The Dutch Republic teeters on collapse as one of Stearns’s envoys chooses to remain behind, becoming ensnared in the Siege of Amsterdam. As a result, the timeline detours markedly from actual 17th-century history, aided by rumors of a town from the future that usher in spies, emissaries, and a flood of encyclopedias and history textbooks into European courts. A recurring motif throughout the series concerns leaders from the down-time trying to alter or accelerate their histories, while the everyday actions of Grantville’s people and the decisions of its leaders trigger deeper societal and political transformations.

The work outlines Augustine's sinful youth and his conversion to Christianity. It is widely seen as the first Western autobiography ever written, and was an influential model for Christian writers throughout the following 1000 years of the Middle Ages. It is not a complete autobiography, as it was written in his early 40s, and he lived long afterwards, producing another important work (City of God); it does, nonetheless, provide an unbroken record of his development of thought and is the most complete record of any single person from the 4th and 5th centuries. It is a significant theological work. In the work St. Augustine writes about how much he regrets having led a sinful and immoral life. He discusses his regrets for following the Manichaean religion and believing in astrology. He writes about Nebridius's role in helping to persuade him that astrology was not only incorrect but evil, and St. Ambrose's role in his conversion to Christianity. The first nine books are autobiographical and the last four are commentary. He shows intense sorrow for his sexual sins, and writes on the importance of sexual morality. The books were written as prayers to God, thus the title, based on the Psalms of David; and it begins with "For Thou has made us for thyself and our hearts are restless till they rest in Thee" . The work is thought to be divisible into books which symbolize various aspects of the Trinity and trinitarian belief.

Bernard, a former Catholic priest now living secularly, escorts his reluctant father, Jack, to Hawaii at the urging of his dying aunt Ursula. Shortly after they arrive, a car strikes Jack, sending him to the hospital. While he tends to Jack at the hospital and then balances time at Ursula’s nursing home, Bernard gradually uncovers the family’s hidden past. Ursula, long cast as the selfish outcast, reveals that she was sexually abused by her eldest brother Sean, a figure the family idolized for his wartime heroism. The revelation explains how the trauma wrecked Ursula’s marriage and life, and she urges Jack to offer forgiveness—aware that he knew about the abuse but remained silent. Amid these revelations, Bernard begins a cautious romance with Yolande Miller, the woman who drove the car that struck his father. His own sexual awakening unfolds in tandem with Ursula’s battle with illness. The storytelling shifts among multiple formats: third-person narration, Bernard’s diary, a lengthy letter Bernard writes to Yolande, and a collection of postcards and notes sent from Hawaii by characters they encounter on the plane journey from England. The narrative closes with a final letter from Yolande to Bernard.

Three men—Lu Decheng, Yu Dongyue, and Yu Zhijian—travel to Beijing in 1989 with a shared act of defiance: they vandalize Mao Zedong’s portrait in Tiananmen Square. All three are Southern Chinese friends who seek to voice their discontent with the Chinese Communist Party. The narrative centers on Decheng, whose activist spark drives the book. As the tale unfolds, his frustrations radiate through his personal life and through the people around him, tracing threads from Cultural Revolution–era education reforms to the protests of 1989. Zhijian, also an activist and participant in the graffiti, explains the motive behind their act: to push student leadership to challenge the regime’s legitimacy and, by extension, its authority that enforces martial law. The novel traces the experiences that shape Decheng’s choice, beginning with his unwillingness to cry on cue beside classmates after Mao’s death and continuing through lessons about the CCP’s brutality imparted by his grandmother. After the vandalism, the trio receives prison sentences; during Decheng’s confinement his wife leaves him in divorce. Years later, back in Liuyang, Hunan, he remarries. The narrative alternates chapters, gliding between Decheng’s prison years and earlier memories of adolescence. The ending returns to the moments just before the act of defacing Mao’s portrait.

Set aboard the Sky pirate vessel The Galerider, the tale follows Wind Jackal as he seeks vengeance against his former quartermaster, Turbot Smeal, whom he blames for burning Western Quays in Undertown and for devastating much of Wind Jackal’s family. Simultaneously, Undertown’s Leagues prepare to wage war on the sky pirates. Along the voyage, The Galerider’s crew confront a series of perilous traps as Wind Jackal presses on with his search for Smeal. Though the crew is initially perplexed, the truth gradually unfolds: the man posing as Turbot Smeal is a counterfeit, driven by envy and far more dangerous. By the end, only Wind Jackal, Quint, Tem Barkwater, and Spillins the Oakelf remain from the original squad. They stumble upon a wrecked skyship where a skullpelt-masked stranger claims to be Turbot Smeal. A duel ensues between Wind Jackal and the impostor, resulting in Wind Jackal’s death. The mystery is clarified when the masked man is revealed to be Thaw Daggerslash, one of the crew members. The narrative culminates with a dramatic skyborne confrontation between the Leagues of Undertown and the Sky Pirates, culminating in the Leagues’ launch of the Bringer of Doom during the climactic sequence. The ultimate truth of the story is disclosed at the end. All told, the tale centers on betrayal, warfare among aerial factions, and a final, spectacular clash in the heavens.

Timofey Pavlovich Pnin, the novel’s central figure, is a Russian-born professor who resides in America. In his fifties, a refugee from both Communist Russia and what he calls the “Hitler war,” he serves as an assistant professor of Russian at Waindell College, a fictional institution inspired by places Nabokov taught—perhaps Wellesley or Cornell. Pnin has established himself at Waindell in an unsettled, untenured, yet largely respectable academic life, marked by a string of tragicomic blunders, setbacks, and the challenge of adapting to American society and language. The cast includes his departmental supervisor, other professors and campus staff, his landlord, his ex-wife, and her son. The narrative is delivered by an apparently unreliable first-person observer who identifies himself as “Vladimir Vladimirovich N—,” a persona that echoes Nabokov himself, reflecting shared interests such as lepidoptery and a history as a landed-gentry Russian émigré. The novel closes with Pnin, unemployed and unmoored, fleeing Waindell College toward an unspecified fate.

Suicide Circle: The Complete Edition tells in four different chapters the story behind a fictional mass suicide that takes place on the Shinjuku Station in 2002, on which 54 high school girls throw themselves in front of a train. This event unleashes in Japan—and soon after, in the world—a chain of suicides that seems endless. Police officers try to stop it and understand why this is happening, and after several events they find a connection between the suicides and a website that belongs to a mysterious organization called Family Circle. Through this website, Family Circle enrolls young people and incite them to run away from home to serve the Circle "family rentals", a service that the organization provides to families who lost relatives to suicide. Parallel to this, alongside the police's quest, the book also follows the story of one of Family Circle's new members that witnessed the mass suicide, Noriko Shimabara, and how her own family slowly falls apart to the suicide wave, while her father tries to "rescue" her from the Circle. In the end, all the pieces come together as the true meaning behind the website is revealed.

On Christmas Eve, Ricky Bianca confronts the haunting question of why his father chose to end his life. At the time, his father was opposing mob influence over the funeral trade, a conflict that ran deep. A man loyal to the Mafia arrived with a letter on the sacred night, and after reading it, Ricky’s father shot himself in the head. The document disappeared, and only the Crime Family’s capo di tutti capi, Salvatore Biganti, knows its contents. When the blast rang out, Ricky hurried to help, finding his father collapsed and bleeding from a fatal wound near the temple. He knelt amid the crimson slick, trying in vain to staunch the bleeding as he cradled his father’s head. The aftermath left Ricky with no memory of the moment, yet plagued by violent, surreal nightmares. His mother soon died in an upstate sanitarium, overcome by severe depressive catatonia. His aunt in Connecticut raised him, and after two decades he returns to New York to work as a Funeral Director, drawn back into the very world that guards its secrets. A college psychology professor, a friend, urges him to uncover the truths his mind desperately seeks before the hallucinatory torment consumes him. Darkness closes in as the industry’s web of deceit, greed, and malevolence ensnares him, stripping away his innocence. He becomes entangled in a perilous lattice of organized crime, secret cults, and unspeakable horrors. In the end, what is known proves more terrifying than what remains hidden, driving him into a personal hell of fiendish nightmares and monstrous visions.

The plot focuses on three key events that happen mostly simultaneously. The first is the occupation of Coruscant and the trouble the Empire left behind with its crippling bio-attack on the planet. The virus used in the attack is the Krytos virus, a biological weapon developed by General Evir Derricote and released under the orders of Imperial leader Ysanne Isard. Humans are apparently immune, while all other species are vulnerable. This, combined with Imperial Intelligence officer Kirtan Loor's terrorist activities while taking orders from the Palpatine Counterinsurgency Front, leaves Coruscant and the New Republic in a state of emergency. The second event is the treason trial of Rogue Squadron executive officer Tycho Celchu, who is suspected of murdering Rogue Squadron pilot Corran Horn, who was captured during the invasion. Finally, Corran Horn is being held prisoner in her Lusankya prison facility. His attempts to escape lead him to uncover the secret of Rogue Squadron's mole, and it becomes a race against time to save the innocent and reveal the true traitor.

The play is set in a vaguely described science fiction future dominated by "The Game," a conflation of rock music and violence played by "Markers" under the direction of "The Keepers." Hoss has struggled to become the top Marker, only to find himself doubting his own abilities in the face of opposition from "Gypsies" who operate outside of the official rules. Act 1: Eager to make an outing, Hoss is frustrated when the Star-Man advises him against it on the basis of his astrology. Hoss learns that his rival, Mojo Root Force, has encroached upon his territory in Las Vegas in a move of questionable legality. After getting word that a Gypsy from Vegas is on his way to attack him, Hoss calls an old friend, Little Willard, for backup, only to find that Willard has committed suicide due to his inability to cope with his status. These successive revelations exacerbate Hoss's self-doubt and his belief that the old way is dying, and he attempts to perk up his confidence by challenging the Gypsy to a shiv fight. Act II: Before the duel (which has been changed from a shiv fight to battle of words under the guidance of an official referee) Hoss and Crow attempt to psych each other out. While Crow learns to imitate Hoss's walk and style, Hoss intimidates Crow by taking on the voice of an old Western gunslinger. Despite an ostensibly effective second round in which he takes on the voice of a Delta bluesman, Hoss loses the battle when Crow exposes Hoss's "Fear that he's crackin' busted in two." After killing the Ref, a desperate Hoss begs Crow to teach him the new style. Ultimately, however, he decides to commit his last authentic act by killing himself, for which Crow commends him. The play ends with Crow assuming his place on Hoss' throne, with Becky quickly shifting her loyalty.

Two central figures stand as protagonists while two serve as antagonists. The leading characters are Koot Hoomie “Kootie” Parganas, an eleven-year-old boy, and Pete “Teet” Sullivan, a man in his early forties. The story unfolds largely in Los Angeles during 1992 and touches on the U.S. presidential election. The principal antagonists are Sherman Oaks and Loretta deLarava. In common with Tim Powers’ Fault Line sequence, Last Call looms as a thematic touchstone, with immortality as the driving pursuit. While Oaks’ exact age remains unspecified, deLarava is 76, though she frequently appears younger; both sustain themselves by ingesting ghosts. A magical system governs the ghosts—how they are captured and consumed, their behavior, and even a clandestine market where bottled phantoms are traded. When ready to be consumed, these entities go by the names “smokes” or “cigars.” The chase for ghosts fuels the plot. Kootie has unknowingly swallowed the ghost of Thomas Edison, but puberty has not yet arrived, so he cannot digest it. In the ghost’s undigested form, Edison’s apparition assists Kootie, and his formidable personality makes him highly coveted by both sides seeking ingestion. Loretta deLarava also pursues the ghost of Pete Sullivan’s father; capturing Pete would bring her closer to locating Arthur Patrick “Apie” Sullivan’s ghost. Sullivan is aided by a former psychiatrist, Angelica Anthem Elizalde. Loretta’s objectives extend to pursuing Solomon Shadroe, who is the former Nicky Bradshaw and, incidentally, a son of Arthur Patrick “Apie” Sullivan as a godson. Shadroe/Bradshaw once played “Spooky” on a fictional TV sitcom titled “Ghost of a Chance.”

Harding’s Pleasure & Profit volume offers a mosaic of real outdoor experiences drawn from Eldred Nathaniel Woodcock’s memory. Spanning fifty years from 1855 to 1905, Woodcock recounts camping, hunting, trapping, and fishing across Northern Pennsylvania and beyond. Frequently, his tales center on a memorable companion—often called his “Pard”—along with other locals from Potter County, Pennsylvania. Many of the wild settings where he camped have since become state parks and forests. Written in plain, accessible language, the narratives cover deer and bear hunting, bear trapping, hunting for wildcats, foxes, martens, mink, and muskrat, as well as encounters with porcupines and skunks. He also shares mishaps experienced by himself and his partners, and routine camp-life episodes. Beyond storytelling, Woodcock offers his viewpoints on state game laws, bounties, and the necessity of conservation. The book additionally provides practical guidance on cabin construction, campfire skills, staying warm, locating beehives, setting traps and deadfalls, using baits, skinning and stretching fur, tracking game, and selecting guns and ammunition.

Taylor Rusk is a star college quarterback and a can't-miss prospect in The League. Through various illegal means, North Texas is awarded an expansion franchise. As expected, the expansion Texas Pistols draft Rusk number one. The Pistols have a five-year plan to turn the team into champions, and getting Taylor Rusk ready is the key. But Rusk is on to the corruption and refuses to be a victim. With his college coach at the helm and "old league" legends mentoring him, Taylor Rusk plays The League's game until it's time for him to make his most daring move to bring it down. But along the way, Rusk is betrayed. One teammate, a chronic con man, becomes the Pistols' general manager and ultimately betrays him. Another teammate suffers a devastating knee injury. However, the surgery is botched. Rusk sees him get tossed aside and, due largely to steroid abuse, he murders his family and commits suicide. Five years later, the Texas Pistols are world champions, but Taylor Rusk has little time to celebrate. He's got to save the life of another victim: the woman he's fallen in love with — who's also the mother of his son. They ultimately take control of the Texas Pistols for him.

Trelawny of the 'Wells tells the story of Rose Trelawny, a popular star of melodrama plays at the Barridge Wells Theatre (a thinly disguised Sadler's Wells Theatre). Rose gives up the stage when she decides to marry her sweetheart, Arthur Gower, in order to please his conservative family. She finds life with Arthur's grandfather and great-aunt, Sir William and Lady Tralfagar, unbearably dull and they detest her loud and unrestrained personality. Rose runs back to the theatre, abandoning Arthur. But her experience of the 'real world' has killed her talent for melodrama, and she cannot recapture the liveliness that had made her a star. Meanwhile, Arthur has secretly run away to become an actor at the Bristol Old Vic. The problem is solved when Rose encounters Sir William again, and she reawakens his memory of admiring the great actor Edmund Kean as a young man. Sir William offers to help Rose's friend Tom Wrench, an aspiring playwright who dreams of staging plays in a more realist style than the melodramas that dominate the stage. Tom stages the play with Rose as the star, and her newfound seriousness fits his style perfectly. Tom secretly arranges for Arthur to play the leading male role, and the lovers are reunited on stage.

The work unfolds in three major segments—preceded by a short prologue and bookended by interludes and an epilogue—each centering on the silver tiassa statue and the figure of Khaavren from House Tiassa, yet each one narrates a different tale. The opening portion, titled Tag, recounts events from Vlad Taltos’s early career as a prominent Jhereg, told in his characteristic first-person voice. In this part, Vlad is approached by the Viscount of Adrilhanka, a rogue highwayman, who seeks Vlad’s help to foil a plot by the Empire to recover pilfered funds. Jumping to a later moment in the chronology, the second section, Whitecrest, follows several characters after Vlad has fallen out with the Jhereg: most prominently, the Countess of Whitecrest—Khaavren’s wife and the Viscount’s mother—and Vlad’s former wife, Cawti. Here, news of an impending Jenoine invasion surfaces, though the threat might be a feint designed to lure Vlad into the open. The final segment, Special Tasks, represents the most recent timeline and adopts the voice of Paarfi, the fictional author shaping the Khaavren Romances. Its focus is largely on Khaavren as he investigates an attempt on Vlad’s life.

The book unfolds in two sections. In the first, it attempts a comprehensive appraisal of modern capitalist civilization, charting what the Invisible Committee call seven dimensions of alienation: the self, social relationships, labor, the economy, urban life, the environment, and the collapse of civilization itself. In the second section, it shifts toward offering a roadmap for revolutionary struggle, grounded in forming communes or affinity-group-style cells operating as an underground network. This clandestine cadre would grow beyond mainstream politics and strike at moments of crisis—political, social, or environmental—to advance an anti-capitalist insurrection. The envisioned uprising centers on local popular empowerment, direct disruption of economic processes, and the dismantling of police power. The text points to the late-2000s financial crisis and environmental decay as signs of capitalism in decline, and it also situates examples such as Argentina’s 1999–2002 crisis and the piquetero movement, the 2005 riots and 2006 student protests in France, the 2006 Oaxaca upheaval, and the grassroots relief efforts in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina as demonstrations of the fractures in contemporary social order capable of triggering partial insurrectionary conditions.

The novel was written in 1914. It is set a few years previous and is divided into three parts. In the first part, Sensei and I, the narrator, a guileless university student, befriends an older man, Sensei (most of the characters' real names are not given). Sensei lives as a recluse, interacting only with his wife and the narrator, and occasional unseen visitors, but still maintaining a distance between himself and them. He regularly visits the grave of a friend, but for the moment refuses to tell the narrator any details of his earlier life. In the second part, My Parents and I, the narrator graduates and returns to his home in the country to await his father's death. As his father lies dying, the narrator receives a letter from Sensei which is recounted in the third part of the novel, Sensei and His Testament. Sensei reveals that in his own university days he was cheated out of most of his fortune by his uncle. As a result he moved to Tokyo and began living with a widow and her daughter, with whom he fell in love. Later he convinced his childhood friend (known only as K), who was in dire straits, to move in with him. Gradually K recovered, but also fell in love with the landlady's daughter. K confessed this love to Sensei, who was shocked, and later full of jealousy. Sensei then proposed marriage, and shortly after, K committed suicide. Sensei, who had lost his faith in humanity after being cheated by his uncle, was horrified to find the same dark impulses lurking in his own heart, and felt a heavy guilt for the death of his friend. In the present, 1912, Sensei is prompted by the suicide of General Nogi Maresuke (following the death of the Meiji Emperor) to take his own life, writing the letter to his only friend to explain his decision.

The three main characters are Sandry, a Lord of Tep's Town, Sandry's cousin Regapisk, also a Lord, and Burning Tower, a daughter of Whandall, the main character of the previous book. Regapisk is an incompetent Lord and his family arrange for him to be shanghaied to become an oarsman on a coastal ship. Sandry and Burning Tower are romantically linked throughout the book. Large flightless birds attack trading caravans, but Sandry fights them off. He is sent by the Lords with the caravan, of which Burning Tower is also a part, to discover the source of the birds. They travel to the southern city of Condigeo and then to Crescent City, defeating terror bird attacks along the way. In Crescent City, they are joined by Regapisk, who has escaped from his ship. The three of them travel on to the high-magic city of Aztlan, where Regapisk redeems himself. The authors researched Aztec culture for the book, and many aspects of the culture depicted in the book are based on that research. This is explained in a brief note at the end of the book. Also mentioned is that within the described timeline, the terror birds continued to exist until long after humans spread through the Americas; this is based on the North American phorusrhacid Titanis walleri (but see McFadden et al. 2007).

The tales of Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser center on two charming yet thieving rogues as they wander the fantasy realm of Nehwon. In Swords Against Death, their adventures begin with shedding Lankhmar’s dust in the wake of their first loves’ deaths, only to discover that choosing not to return cannot truly be a solution ("The Circle Curse"). What follows is a loose sequence of exploits from their travels: a treasure-seeking expedition inside a dwelling protected by uncanny defenses ("The Jewels in the Forest"), another confrontation with the Thieves’ Guild blamed for the deaths of their beloveds ("Thieves’ House"), a spellbound voyage to a distant realm ("The Bleak Shore"), an encounter with a lone, beast-haunted wanderer ("The Howling Tower"), a perilous sojourn to a Nehwonan Atlantis-like site ("The Sunken Land"), a clash with a murderous priesthood ("The Seven Black Priests"), a magical plague menacing Lankhmar ("Claws from the Night"), and at last a farewell to their lost loves in the Shadowland ("The Price of Pain-Ease"). The collection closes with an investigation of a mysterious shop that defies ordinary expectations, titled Bazaar of the Bizarre.

Toward the close of World War I, in 1918, the tale centers on Paul Peachy, a timid Milwaukee railway worker who moonlights as an amateur actor. After realizing his wife no longer loves him, he signs up as a private in the U.S. Army and sails to the French front. In the brutal melee of war he finds brief comfort in companionship, yet soon falls into German hands in No Man’s Land. His only hope of surviving hinges on impersonating a renowned enemy spy, a skill within his reach as a native speaker of German. Assuming the persona of the sophisticated operative Harry Stroller, Peachy earns the top brass’s admiration and enters a luxury world he had never imagined. The role also uncovers latent courage and resourcefulness, pushing him toward bolder ruses as his German hosts grow increasingly mistrustful. Amid this web of illusion, Peachy encounters Annie, a striking French courtesan who seems to see through his elaborate disguise. The narrative builds to an ending filled with twists and deft plotting.

During World War II, at a secret Nazi submarine base, containers crafted entirely from looted wartime gold were hidden away. The treasure was not the solid-gold chests, but the cargo they carried - an artifact so lethal that whoever possessed "Pandora's Boxes" held the power to unleash hell upon earth.... In the unforgiving wastes of Greenland, geologist Philip Mercer uncovers a long - abandoned U.S. Army base buried under the ice - and a long-dead body still hot with radiation. Before Mercer and his colleague, the seductive Dr. Anika Klein, can investigate further, a flash fire engulfs the base, and they are ordered to evacuate. But their plane is forced to land when a bomb is discovered on board, and they must seek shelter from the murderous weather in a hidden ice cavern. That's where they learn the startling truth. A powerful German corporation has launched an operation to destroy evidence of its Nazi past. But one of the corporate mercenaries knows what's inside the Pandora boxes, and he plans to hold the entire world hostage - unless Mercer can find a way to stop him....

Three months after the events of Peter and the Starcatchers, the narrative shifts to a new pursuit. Slank returns to the island, bringing additional Others—including Lord Ombra—with the aim of reclaiming the trunk of starstuff that vanished in the previous book. Discovering that the trunk has been carried back to England by the Starcatchers, Slank and his party head for London. Peter, worried for Molly’s safety, disguises himself on their vessel with Tinker Bell’s assistance. In London, Peter struggles to locate Molly. After a string of uncomfortable run-ins with beggars, traders, and the police, he finally obtains directions to Lord Aster’s residence from J. M. Barrie and makes his way there. He rescues Molly from Lord Ombra just in time. Yet Molly’s mother, Louise Aster, has been abducted by the Others, forcing the children to seek out Lord Aster, who is guarding the starstuff. Back on the island, the pirates hunt the Lost Boys, capturing them to bait Peter—unaware that he is not present. Ultimately, Peter retrieves Molly, and she brings him to her former best friend’s home, where she introduces him to George. The two instantly become close friends.

In Adventure in Australia, the Count of Champignac, accompanied by a young professor, Walker Donahue, thinks he has made an extraordinary discovery in Australia, namely an immense indigenous monolith in the surroundings of a mining village. He asks Spirou and Fantasio to join them. Thus, the two go to the Australia, accompanied by Seccotine, which was essential. When they arrive, Donahue informs them that the Count was killed by miners. After investigation, they discover that the Count did not die but the heroes find him in bad shape, face to face with Sam, a gangster who grows rich by holding prospectors to ransom. Sam ends up dying when his truck explodes because of a bottle of nitroglycerin. Thanks to the aboriginals, of which they were allies, Spirou, Donahue and the Count put in rout Sam's men who are trying to eliminate Fantasio and Seccotine. Finally, the monolith is discovered and the aboriginals make an agreement to share resources with the prospectors, who are grateful to them for getting rid of Sam.

Anastasia Krupnik's little brother, Sam, wants fangs more than anything in the world. But there is one big problem. Sam's mother, Mrs. Krupnik, has fangphobia and forbids Sam even to touch his plastic vampire fangs in the house. How can she not see how cool fangs really are? Sure, they make it hard to eat hot dogs, but they make him look disgusting - and Sam loves to look disgusting. So Sam decides to run away to Alaska, where "fanged" walruses lie around in a pile and sharp teeth are generally accepted. He packs his mittens and bear in his father's Harvard University gym bag and sets off, but just down the block, Lowell Watson, the mailman, reminds him he will need food for Alaska. Neighbor Gertrude Stein's homemade chocolate chip cookies are just the thing. And how can he leave without saying goodbye to the Sheehans' baby, Kelly? He needs a glass of water, and there really isn't any reason to hurry to Alaska ... In See You Around, Sam!, Lois Lowry continues to give Anastasia's brother a voice of his own. As the quirky characters on his block welcome him into their homes one by one, he discovers the true meaning of community.

Jonathan Dark (Jandar), an earthman mysteriously landed on Callisto, the Jovian moon, has already rescued Princess Darloona of Shondakar from the Sky Pirates of Zandahar. Yet her deliverance proves short-lived as she is seized again by the Black Legion, the mercenary force that once seized her city and forced her people into exile. In Shondakar, Jandar unexpectedly earns the Legion’s goodwill by saving its leader’s son—the very alliance the commander intends to cement by arranging Darloona’s marriage. With permission to operate behind enemy lines, Jandar surveys the city’s defenses, focusing on the subterranean tunnel network. He disrupts the wedding by coordinating a Ku Thad infiltration through those tunnels, catching the occupiers off guard. The mastermind behind Darloona’s woes—a supposed priest named Oola—falls, revealed as a secret Mind Wizard plotting domination over all of Thanator. Chaos erupts as Sky Pirates stage an assault, and though the Ku Thad ultimately prevail against both adversaries, Prince Thuton of Zandahar manages to flee, taking Darloona back to captivity—the fate Jandar had previously liberated her from in the prior volume. It ends with the situation reset to square one.

Detective Inspector John Rebus finds the body of an overdosed drug addict in an Edinburgh squat, laid out cross-like on the floor, between two burned-down candles, with a five-pointed star painted on the wall above. Some of his colleagues are inclined to categorise it as the routine death of a "junkie", but Rebus is perturbed by some unusual facts of the case: a full package of heroin in the dead man's room, and some mysterious bruises on his face and body. Rebus takes seriously a death which looks more like a murder every day, and he begins to investigate the true circumstances of the death. As part of his investigation, Rebus finds the young woman named Tracy who knew the dead man and heard his terrifying last words: "Hide! Hide!" It emerges that the dead man was a photographer who took and hid some sensitive photos in a specialist private members' club - Hyde's - where highly-connected people in society watch illegal boxing. Rebus is able to arrest Hyde's owner and several high profile members, but to his outrage and disgust all the prisoners die suspicious deaths: the powers-that-be are covering it up to prevent scandal. Shortly after Rankin moved to London, there was a real-life case of male prostitutes bribing lawyers and judges, similar to some parts of the book: "questions were asked in parliament" and two lawyers began to investigate the police investigation. "To everyone's surprise, this inquiry found that the allegations were false. Police officers involved in the case found themselves demoted..."

In a damp little house among the buttercups at the pond’s edge lives Jeremy Fisher, a frog who enjoys the feel of wet feet. His home and pantry run slick with water, yet he never minds—a sign of his habit of getting his feet wet, and no one scolds him for it. One rainy day, Jeremy decides to try his luck at fishing. If he reels in more than five minnows, he’ll host a dinner for his friends. He dons a Macintosh, slides on shiny goloshes, grabs his rod and basket, and sets off with mighty hops toward the lily-pad boat storage. He paddles to a spot he knows holds plenty of minnows, then plants himself cross-legged on a lily pad and lays out his gear. His float is a diminutive, endearing red bobber, while his rod is simply a stalk of grass and the line a strand of horsehair. An hour passes with no bites. He takes a break to enjoy a butterfly sandwich for lunch. A water beetle brushes his toe, and the rustling of rats among the reeds drives him to relocate to a safer area. He drops the line again and is rewarded at once with a nibble, but it’s not a minnow; it’s Jack Sharp, a stickleback. The fish escapes, though Jeremy’s fingers are pricked by Jack’s spines in the process. A school of small fish surfaces and mockingly gawks at him. Sucking his sore fingers, Jeremy endures until a trout suddenly rises, snaps him up, and he cries out in pain. The trout dives, leaving the Mac in its mouthful of spit and Jeremy’s goloshes swallowed instead. He shoots back to the surface, bobbing like a cork as bubbles escape a soda bottle, and swims toward the pond’s edge. Clambering up the bank, he makes his way home across the meadow, resolved to give up fishing. In the closing pages, Jeremy mends his fingers with sticking plaster and welcomes three visitors: Sir Isaac Newton, a newt, and Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise, a salad-eating tortoise. Isaac wears a black-and-gold waistcoat, while Ptolemy carries a salad in a string bag. For dinner, Jeremy has prepared roasted grasshopper with ladybird sauce, a scene the narrator calls a “frog treat,” though he suspects it must have been unpleasant.

The primary focus of Democracy in America is an analysis of why republican representative democracy has succeeded in the United States while failing in so many other places. Tocqueville seeks to apply the functional aspects of democracy in America to what he sees as the failings of democracy in his native France. Tocqueville speculates on the future of democracy in the United States, discussing possible threats to democracy and possible dangers of democracy. These include his belief that democracy has a tendency to degenerate into "soft despotism" as well as the risk of developing a tyranny of the majority. He observes that the strong role religion played in the United States was due to its separation from the government, a separation all parties found agreeable. He contrasts this to France where there was what he perceived to be an unhealthy antagonism between democrats and the religious, which he relates to the connection between church and state. Insightful analysis of political society was supplemented in the second volume by description of civil society as a sphere of private and civilian affairs. Tocqueville's views on America took a darker turn after 1840, however, as made evident in Aurelian Craiutu's Tocqueville on America after 1840: Letters and Other Writings.

Heartless blends steampunk aesthetics with urban fantasy, set in an alternate Victorian England where vampires and werewolves are embraced by society, often among the upper class. The narrative follows Alexia Tarabotti, known as the Lady Maccon, a soulless woman whose lack of a supernatural pulse renders her immune to the powers of beings of that world. In interviews, the author indicated that while Changeless and Blameless—the second and third books in the series—are tightly connected, Heartless stands more on its own, recalling the self-contained feel of Soulless, the series’ inaugural entry. The book was published in 2011 by Orbit Books, with the USA paperback released on June 28, 2011 (ISBN 0-316-12719-1) and the UK paperback following on July 7, 2011 (ISBN 0-356-50009-8). On September 22, 2010, the author announced the manuscript was 99% complete, with a final draft due to the publisher by November 1, 2010. Orbit Books unveiled the cover on February 1, 2011, and issued a revised version in late March 2011. As with the series’ first three novels, Lauren Panepinto designed the cover, featuring model Donna Ricci; Ricci’s original photographs for the cover were shot by Pixie Vision Productions. Although the author’s website lists translations into German, Italian, Spanish, and other languages as forthcoming, no publication dates have yet been announced for Heartless’ non-English editions.

Morgarath, the angry, evil ,exiled lord of the bleak, barren Mountains of Rain and Night, has been waiting for fifteen years in his dark realm, carefully planning his revenge against the Kingdom of Araluen. His former fief, known as Gorlan, was long ago brought to ruin as a result of his unsuccessful rebellion against King Duncan. Now he silently plots to rebel again, rallying creatures known as Wargals to his side. Wargals have little will of their own, and are easy to control, therefore being suitable as soldiers in Morgarath’s army. Now, after the fifteen years, Morgarath prepares to unleash his power and attempt to take the Kingdom once more. In Araluen, in the fief Redmont, a special day has come for Will, called Choosing Day, where he becomes an apprentice to a craftmaster. Although Will's first choice was Battleschool, he becomes apprenticed to Halt of the Rangers. Rangers are the intelligence group of the country and specialize in long range weapons and the art of staying unseen. Will is trained in these skills as he prepares for the annual Ranger meeting called the Gathering which is where his skills will be tested. At the Gathering the Rangers receive a report that the Kalkara, vicious creatures under the control of Morgarath, have killed important Araluen figures. Halt leaves to track down the Kalkara while Will rides for help. The Baron, Sir Rodney, and several others head out to slay the Kalkara and to save Halt. Finding where Halt is battling the Kalkara, Sir Rodney and the Baron manage to slay one, but are badly injured by the other. Suddenly, the last Kalkara is killed by Will with a flaming arrow that burns it because of its highly flammable fur. Back at his fief, Will is considered a hero and receives his bronze oakleaf medal which identifies him as a Rangers Apprentice. On the other hand, Araluen is preparing for a battle with Lord Morgarath.

Igraine shares a home with her family in an ancient castle, where magicians guard potent books of magic. While her elder brother Albert follows the family path, Igraine dreams of becoming a knight, despite sensing little excitement awaiting them at home. Though their lineage has long repelled countless attempts to seize the magical tomes, trouble erupts on Igraine’s twelfth birthday when her parents gift her a suit of enchanted armor, inadvertently turning them into pigs. The situation worsens as Osmond the Greedy seizes control of the neighboring baroness’s fortress, intent on capturing the magical books to topple the king. With their parents’ condition concealed, Igraine and Albert must defend the castle against Osmond’s siege while their search for the missing ingredient to restore their parents continues. Albert takes charge of the castle’s magical defenses, and Igraine ventures out in search of the required component. Her quest yields the needed ingredient and unexpected aid: the Sorrowful Knight of the Mount of Tears. This knight agrees to assist in the family’s return to humanity and begins instructing Igraine in the codes of chivalry, ultimately helping to end the siege and restore peace to their home.

Set against the backdrop of the Tiberium Wars, the narrative unfolds through multiple perspectives and up-close glimpses of key figures, including Kane, Lieutenant Sandra Telfair, General Jack Granger, and W3N reporter Cassandra Blair, who are either depicted or referenced throughout. The opening chapter centers on a high-stakes summit aboard the Philadelphia space station, bringing together nearly every top GDI director and official, as well as Dr. Mobius, GDI’s premier scientist from the original Command & Conquer. In a devastating turn, Nod launches a nuclear strike after disabling the station’s defenses at Goddard Space Center, annihilating everyone aboard. As Kane’s broadcasts are dispersed to a global audience, his chilling pronouncement marks the chapter’s conclusion: “Rejoice, children of Nod, the blood of your oppressors will flow…” The novel then follows the exploits of GDI’s 22nd Infantry Division, commanded by Michael McNeil, whose unit is lauded as heroic in the wake of their missions, even as the world’s fate shifts under the influence of Tiberium. A key scene transports readers to Atlanta, a Yellow Zone partially afflicted by Tiberium yet still under GDI control, observed through the eyes of W3N correspondent Annabella Wu. Throughout the work, the narrative toggles between Ricardo Vega’s and Annabella Wu’s experiences amid the ongoing conflict, weaving their stories together against the broader war-torn landscape.

The story starts off with Chinese Cinderella being pursued by a mysterious woman wearing black. CC falls and ends up in a hospital recovering from a nasty fall. There she sees a famous Chinese painting called 'Along The River AT Qing Ming'. Chinese Cinderella is suffering from sudden and random bouts of unconsciousness she is haunted by vivid dreams that seem very strange yet somehow very familiar. A tale and adventure emrges of friendship, wealth, poverty, eunuchs and an emperor who loved art. Chinese Cinderella recalls a life eight hundred years ago during the Song Dynasty. After a fall, CC is whisked away to a hospital. As she drifts in and out of consciousness, she is haunted by vivid dreams that seem strange—yet somehow familiar. Thus begins CC’s emotional journey back to a privileged life lived eight hundred years ago during the Song dynasty. CC was the daughter of a wealthy and influential man, but she finds herself drawn to a poor orphan boy with a startling ability to capture the beauty of the natural world. As the relationship between these two young people deepens, the transforming power of art and romantic love comes into conflict with the immovable rules of Chinese society.

The narrative follows the consequences of Jesus’ crucifixion through the eyes of the Roman tribune Marcellus Gallio and his Greek slave Demetrius. To remove Marcellus from Rome, Prince Gaius dispatches him to command the garrison at Minoa, a southern Palestinian port. In Jerusalem at Passover, Marcellus witnesses the crucifixion of Jesus and is unsettled by what he perceives as Jesus’ innocence. During the event, Marcellus and other soldiers gamble on who will receive Jesus’ seamless robe; he wins and entrusts Demetrius with the priceless garment. After the crucifixion, Marcellus attends a banquet with Pontius Pilate, where a drunken centurion pressures him to wear the robe. He complies, but the experience drives him toward a breakdown, and he returns to Rome in a deteriorated state. Sent away to Athens for recovery, Marcellus eventually succumbs to Demetrius’s insistence and touches the robe again, which then restores his peace of mind. Reinvigorated by the sense that the robe holds some intrinsic power, Marcellus travels back to Judea, retracing Jesus’ steps and meeting many whose lives were touched by Him. Through these encounters, Demetrius and, later, Marcellus are drawn to Jesus as followers. Upon returning to Rome, Marcellus must report his revelations to the emperor, Tiberius. He frees Demetrius, who escapes, yet because of his unwavering Christian faith both Marcellus and his new wife Diana are executed by the subsequent emperor, Caligula. In the end, Marcellus arranges for the robe to be entrusted to “The Big Fisherman.”

On the fictional world of Pern, the narrative reveals how locals uncover the unique powers of watch-whers, distant kin to dragons. These creatures later serve in the mines as early warnings for gas pockets and as rescuers to locate miners trapped after collapses. The tale unfolds years before the 3rd Pass at Camp Natalon, a mining settlement, where a young boy named Kindan is introduced. His father owns a watch-wher named Dask. A cave-in traps Kindan’s family and Dask, leaving him an orphan who is taken in by Master Harper Zist. Zist trains him to perform as an entertainer and to operate as a spy—skills Harpers cultivate. Through this upbringing, Kindan discovers the camp’s factional split between Natalon’s supporters and those loyal to his uncle Tarik. At the same time, the camp lacks a watch-wher, and several minor accidents threaten to slow production. Despite Tarik’s protests, Natalon arranges a bold exchange: a full winter’s worth of coal in return for an opportunity for Kindan to petition a queen watch-wher for an egg. Kindan succeeds and faces the daunting task of rearing a nocturnal creature. With no manuals available on how to raise or train watch-whers, he is left improvising, though the enigmatic Nuella offers crucial help. Together, they cultivate Kisk, and in doing so, uncover extensive insights about this species. This knowledge becomes essential as the plot advances, for Kisk’s gifts ultimately save many lives, including Natalon’s own leadership, near the novel’s end.”

Telling the tale of a man from schooldays to middle age, the narrative traces his life arc. Born to a north German merchant father and an Italian artist mother, Tonio inherits a blend of traits from both families. In childhood, he grapples with mixed emotions toward the bourgeois world around him, feeling a sense of superiority in his own insights while at the same time coveting the carefree vitality they seem to possess. This inner tension persists as he grows older, even after he attains fame as a writer and settles in southern Germany. He concludes that true artistry requires a break with ordinary life. The conflict remains unresolved until Tonio journeys north, back to his hometown, where a wrongful arrest as an escaped criminal starkly underscores his belief that the artist stands apart from respectable society. Critics like Erich Heller, who personally knew Thomas Mann, summarized Tonio Kröger’s central message as the artist living as an exile from reality, a view aligned with Goethe’s Torquato Tasso and Grillparzer’s Sappho as companions in theme. Yet, paradoxically, Heller had already, in his own youth, identified the core motif of Tonio Kröger as the intoxication and entanglement of a passionate heart—one fated to give its feelings form and expression through art.

Kwang Meng, an 18-year-old recent secondary-school graduate, frames the narrative as a young working adult navigating a dull clerical job. His life runs parallel to the divergent paths chosen by two old school friends: Hock Lai, who pursues a white-collar climb up the corporate ladder, and Portia (Nadarajah), who plans to study in the United Kingdom. A romance with a local bar girl named Lucy at Paradise Bar blossoms for a time, but their different social worlds compel Lucy to end things. In an effort to help, Hock Lai tries to arrange a match between Kwang Meng and one of his female acquaintances, Anne. Meanwhile, the neighborhood pair Boon Teik and Mei-I, both teachers, become part of Kwang Meng’s circle, and he envisions them as an ideal couple. Hock Lai marries Cecilia, the daughter of one of Singapore’s wealthy tycoons. Throughout the story, Kwang Meng remains largely passive, preferring to observe his surroundings and seek solace in sea swimming, smoking, and drinking. The novel closes with a personal upheaval as his father suffers a stroke, forcing the son to shoulder the family’s burdens moving forward.

The twenty-first century sees positronic-brain technology spawn robot laborers and reshape life on Earth. Yet for the Martin family, their household robot NDR-113—who comes to be known as Andrew—is more than a mere servant. He evolves into a trusted friend, confidant, and integral family member. The narrative unfolds through Andrew’s (later Andrew Martin) point of view, a departure from U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men’s typical leasing model. Early interactions with the Martins are awkward, highlighting his social unpreparedness, though he handles inanimate objects and animals with greater ease. As he develops, he exhibits distinctly human-like qualities—creativity, emotion, and self-awareness. Assigned to tasks beyond routine domestic labor, he is allowed to explore creativity, even earning a fortune by selling his own creations. He pursues legal recognition of his personhood by gradually replacing his robotic components with organic ones, framing the change as a transformation from machine to human. The Martins of successive generations assist him, yet each generation hesitates to fully affirm his humanity. In The Positronic Man, Asimovian robotics—as sketched in I, Robot and linked to Andrew’s story—provides background for these events and hints at influence on later fiction. No further robots are developed within Andrew’s lineage, and there is a shift toward centralized processing and centralized robot control to prevent the emergence of more self-aware beings like him. Only when Andrew permits his positronic brain to decay—choosing to relinquish his immortality—is he recognized as human. This culmination occurs on the robot’s two-hundredth anniversary, which also gives the novella and its film their title.

Set in the World of Greyhawk, the Forgotten Temple of Tharizdun unfolds as the PCs trail a raiding band of norkers from their cavern hideouts and stumble upon the temple along the way. To reach the norker lair, the adventurers must push through perilous mountain passes. A gnomish community motivates and guides the party to make the journey, and once they break their way inside, they begin a thorough investigation of the temple’s chambers, populated by ordinary beasts as well as unfamiliar denizens drawn from the Fiend Folio. As they explore, several chambers reveal former sites of Tharizdun’s cultic rites, exposing the explorers to the lingering madness and peril that accompany glimpses of the imprisoned deity’s worshipers. Progress hinges on performing elements of those worship rites, which entails venturing into an underground sub-temple and magically unlocking an inner sanctum known as the Black Cyst. Reaching this point, the characters face a grim likelihood: they may go insane, be slain, or become inescapably trapped within the subterranean precincts.

In this sequel, Becker Drane is drawn into a fresh assignment. The climax of the previous volume, The Glitch in Sleep, revealed that 50 trays of Frozen Moments had been stolen, enabling the construction of a Time Bomb capable of catastrophic harm to The World. When reports surface that the Time Bomb has been located inside the Department of Time, Lucien Chiappa is dispatched to Fix it. The device explodes, forcing Becker to intervene by reuniting its two halves so that Essence—the liquid that accelerates aging—cannot seep into the World. To fix this Second, Becker must reunite both fragments, preventing further Essence leakage. The first half lies hidden in a basement, while the second half is trapped by Tide, the faction that created the bomb and intends to overturn the existing order of the Seems to forge a new world. A legendary Fixer once presumed dead, Tom Jackal, appears to aid Becker. He succeeds in seizing the Second and reassembling it, yet the Essence saturates their Sleeves, causing Tom to age. Tom dies from overexposure, but his action saves the World. In a final turn, Becker violates the Golden Rule by meeting Jenifer Kaley, whose Case File—documents about her private life—was handed to Becker after the mission. The epilogue reveals a Time Being, a formidable founder of the Seems, agreeing to align with The Tide.

In the twenty-first century the creation of the positronic brain leads to the development of robot laborers and revolutionizes life on Earth. Yet to the Martin family, their household robot NDR-113 is more than a mechanical servant. "Andrew" has become a trusted friend, a confidant, and a member of the Martin family. The story is told from the perspective of Andrew (later known as Andrew Martin), an NDR-series robot owned by the Martin family, a departure from the usual practice by U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men of leasing robots. Andrew's initial experiences with the Martin family are replete with awkward moments which demonstrate his lack of socialization. However, he is much better with inanimate objects and animals and begins to display sentient characteristics (such as creativity; emotion; self-awareness) traditionally the province of humans. He is taken off his mundane household duties, for which he was intended, and allowed to pursue his creativity, making a fortune by selling his creations. Andrew seeks legal protection stemming from his initial creative output and eventual full recognition as a human, by gradually replacing his robotic components with organic ones, and citing the process as a transformation from robot to human. Succeeding generations of the Martin family assist him in his quest for humanity, but each is limited to what degree they are prepared to acknowledge Andrew's humanity. In The Positronic Man, the trends of fictional robotics in Asimov's Robot series (as outlined in the book I, Robot) are detailed as background events, with an indication that they are influenced by Andrew's story. No more robots in Andrew's line are developed. There is also a movement towards centralized processing, including centralized control of robots, which would avoid any more self-reflecting robots such as Andrew. Only when Andrew allows his positronic brain to "decay," thereby willfully abandoning his immortality, is he declared a human being. This event takes place on the two-hundredth anniversary of his creation, hence the title of the novella and film.

Moominpappa recounts his remarkable life in an autobiography, narrating it first to his son Moomintroll and then to Moomintroll’s companions, Sniff and Snufkin. The tale begins with him as an orphan, growing tired of the dull routine at the orphanage and disliking its stern headmistress Hemulen. After deciding to leave, he befriends Hodgkin, and the two later encounter Joxter (Snufkin’s father) and the Muddler (Sniff’s father). United, they construct a living-quarters boat and set out to sea, deceiving the colossal Edward the Booble into aiding their departure. Edward’s rage flares when he discovers the ruse, yet the group sails on. They rescue a Hemulen from a Groke’s predation, though the rescued Hemulen proves bossy, prompting the travelers to abandon her with the Niblings. A lone Nibling secretly joins the voyage, remaining aboard as they journey onward. Their travels lead them to a distant land where they meet the Mymble family; the Mymble’s daughter befriends them, and together they attend Daddy Jones’ hundredth birthday celebration, where everyone wins prizes. They later settle into new homes on a remote island, but are unsettled by a spectral inhabitant. After striking a deal with the ghost, they form a friendship. Meanwhile, Hodgkins engineers Amphibian—a hybrid vessel capable of both land and sea travel—for Daddy Jones. On its inaugural trip, a gigantic fish attacks, but Edward the Booble rescues them by squashing the sea monster. In a separate thread, the Muddler marries the Fuzzy, and Moominpappa rescues another Moomin—this one with her handbag—from the sea, who turns out to be Moominmamma. The narrative concludes, aligning chronologically with The Moomins and the Great Flood.

Jean-Jacques Pauvert published Story of O in French, a narrative centered on female submission. It follows a Parisian fashion photographer known as O, who endures bondage, blindfolds, chains, whipping, branding, piercings, and wearing a mask, while being conditioned to remain constantly available for oral, vaginal, and anal sex. Throughout the ordeal, O’s prior permission is obtained for every act, and requests for consent are continually sought. The tale opens as her lover René takes her to the Roissy château, where she is trained to serve the men of an elite circle. After this initial phase, René entrusts O to Sir Stephen as a demonstration of their bond and his generosity, hoping she will learn to serve someone she does not love and who does not love her. During the training, O falls for Sir Stephen and comes to believe he loves her in return. While her superficial friend and former lover Jacqueline recoils from O’s chains and scars, O herself embraces pride in her role as a willing slave. In summer, Sir Stephen relocates O to Samois, a secluded mansion long used for women’s advanced training and body modification related to submission. There, she consents to branding and a labia piercing, receiving rings bearing Sir Stephen’s initials and insignia. The story culminates with O, naked save for an owl-like mask, appearing before a large audience that regards her solely as an object.

Set roughly four to five years after the events of Hip Hop High School, Homeboyz follows 17-year-old Dixon Theodore Anderson, known as Teddy. A bright, dual-tuned youth—both a hacker and a bodybuilder—he faces his neighborhood’s gang-ruled chaos, a reality that claims his sister Tina in crossfire. In the wake of her death, Teddy seeks vengeance, but his efforts falter and land him behind bars. He spends time in a California juvenile facility as his case moves through the courts, being treated as a gang figure during confinement. Released eventually, he enters house arrest and enters a probation program that redesigns his days. Five of those days each week are devoted to mentoring Micah, a younger boy he is supposed to guide. The tutoring proves tough because Micah longs for a gang life too, yet the relationship gradually teaches Teddy about love and the possibility of change in others. The narrative also recounts Teddy’s confrontation with Tina’s killer: not a member of his own 0-1-0 faction, but from a rival gang. After a fierce struggle, Teddy emerges victorious, though the antagonist ends up jailed and dies there.

Two boys, Hashi and Kiku, endure a haunting ordeal: abandoned by their mothers as infants and left inside coin lockers at a Tokyo train station in the summer of 1972. Fostered later by the Cherryfield Orphanage in Yokohama, Kiku’s robust, athletic nature often shields Hashi, who is small and frequently harassed. The Kuwayama family—headed by a wife who is Zainichi Korean—adopts them and moves to an island off Kyushu. At sixteen, their paths diverge and they confront a decaying, neon-lit Tokyo called Toxitown. Hashi, whose voice exerts a peculiar, almost hypnotic influence, rises as a bisexual rock star under the guidance of an eccentric producer named D. Meanwhile, Kiku becomes a pole vaulter; with his girlfriend Anemone, a model who has repurposed her condo into a crocodile-filled swamp, he hunts for a substance called DATURA to fuel his vendetta against the city. Their quest for Hashi’s birth mother leads them to a woman who is revealed to be Kiku’s mother, a discovery that triggers grave and far-reaching consequences for all involved.

Critique of Dialectical Reason marks a later phase in Sartre’s thought, where he no longer equates Marxism with the Soviet Union or French Communism, yet moves closer to self-identifying as a Marxist. It presents a revision of Existentialism and positions Marxism as a premier contemporary philosophy, one that can only be faulted from a reactionary pre-Marxist perspective. Sartre contends that while the free combination of multiple human projects might, in principle, yield a Communist society, such an outcome is not guaranteed. Conscious human acts are not mere projections of freedom that generate human temporality, but rather movements toward totalization, with their meaning co-determined by existing social conditions. Consequently, individuals are neither absolutely free to determine the meaning of their actions nor wholly enslaved by their circumstances. Social life is not solely a series of acts rooted in freedom; it also comprises a sedimentation of history that constrains us and a struggle with nature that imposes further barriers, causing social relations to be dominated by scarcity. Every satisfaction of a need can provoke antagonism and hinder mutual recognition as human beings. Scarcity robs people of the ability to choose particular options and diminishes their humanity. Communism, in Sartre’s view, will restore both individual freedom and the capacity to acknowledge the freedom of others.

A crew of migrant workers from three continents are forced to flee their English strawberry field for a journey across all of England in pursuit of their various dreams of a better future. The story centres on a group of migrant workers who hail from Eastern Europe, China, Malaysia and Africa and have come to Kent to harvest strawberries for delivery to the supermarkets, and end up living in two small caravans, a men's caravan and a women's caravan. They are all seeking a better life (and in their different ways they are also, of course, looking for love) and they've come to England, some legally, some illegally, to find it. They are supervised by Farmer Leapish, a red-faced man who treats everyone equally except for the Polish woman named Yola, the boss of the crew, who favors him with her charms in exchange for something a little extra on the side. But the two are discreet, and all is harmonious in this cozy vale – until the evening when Farmer Leaping's wife comes upon him and Yola and in retaliation she runs him down in her red sports car. By the time the police arrive the migrant workers (and a dog called Dog) have piled into one of the trailer homes and quickly leave their arcadia, thus setting off on a journey across the length and breadth of England.

The book is highly critical of Richard Fuld, Henry Paulson, and the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act, a 1999 act of Congress signed by former United States President Bill Clinton that repealed portions of the Glass–Steagall Act of 1933. The book contains an account of how McDonald, after attending the University of Massachusetts Amherst, selling pork chops, and self-teaching himself the material required to pass the General Securities Representative Exam, went on to develop the website ConvertBond.com, which was later purchased by Morgan Stanley. The author's stated expertise, in the convertible bond market, was what allowed him to create the website ConvertBond.com during the dot-com bubble, and successfully sell it to Morgan Stanley before the Internet bubble burst. It was while he was working at Morgan Stanley that McDonald was offered a job as vice-president at Lehman Brothers. The book characterizes Richard Fuld as being out of touch, smug, and a ruthless CEO with a short temper and a penchant for rage. The book sarcastically refers to Fuld as "his majesty," "god-like," and a "spiritual leader." McDonald believes that the United States government should have saved Lehman Brothers, and that Dick Fuld falsely believed that the United States government would save the company after having a meeting with Henry Paulson in the spring of 2008, which led him to engage in unnecessarily risky behavior and reject an offer of $18 per share from the Korea Development Bank as late as August 2008.

In the small fishing village of Shora, Lina Sendak stands out as one of six schoolchildren. When she pens an essay about why storks are missing from their town, the teacher urges the class to investigate for themselves. Their inquiry reveals that the rooftops are so steep that storks cannot find space to nest on the sharp ridges; the solution they propose is to place wagon wheels along the roof ridges to create nesting sites. Locating a wagon wheel in the tiny community proves challenging, and along the way the children encounter a troupe of intriguing personalities. The narrative, though simple, carries a powerful message: curiosity and questioning can set things in motion, turning dreams into reality. The six students are Lina (the sole girl at the small school), Jella (the tallest), Auka (an average boy), Eelka (a stout, awkward child), and the inseparable twins, Pier and Dirk. Their efforts are supported by their teacher, Grandmother Sibble III, the legless Janus, the elderly Douwa, and the enigmatic “tin man.” Additional figures include the children's fathers, all of whom are fishermen, Lina’s aunt in Nes, Evert who lives opposite her aunt, Lina and Auka’s younger siblings Linda and Jan, Jana, Janus’s wife, and the children's mothers. The dedication proclaims, “To my nieces, Shirley and Beverly, and their flying fingers.”

Life is a memoir covering Keith Richards's life, starting with his childhood in Dartford, Kent, through to his success with the Rolling Stones and his current life in Connecticut. His interest in music was triggered by his mother, Doris, who played records by Sarah Vaughan, Billy Eckstine and Louis Armstrong, and his maternal grandfather, Augustus Theodore Dupree, a former big band player, who encouraged him to take up the guitar. In his teens he met up with Mick Jagger, who he had known in primary school, and discovered that they both shared a love of blues music. In the early 1960s Richards moved into a London flat, shared with Jagger and Brian Jones. Together with Bill Wyman, Ian Stewart and Charlie Watts, the Rolling Stones were founded in 1962, playing gigs at Ealing Jazz Club and the Crawdaddy Club. The book chronicles Richards's career with the Stones since 1962, following their rise from playing small club gigs to stadium concerts, Richards's drug habits, his arrests and convictions. His relationships with a number of women, including Anita Pallenberg, Marianne Faithfull, Ronnie Spector and Patti Hansen, whom he married in 1983, are covered in detail. The often difficult partnership between Richards and Jagger is referred to throughout the work and coverage of this has caused much media interest. Throughout the work, much attention is given to Richards' love of music, his style of playing and chord construction. His non-Stones projects, such as the X-Pensive Winos and recording with the Wingless Angels in Jamaica, as well as collaborations with Chuck Berry and Gram Parsons amongst others are covered in some detail.

The action starts in Sacramento in 1867. The Cascabels are a French family of circus artists who spent several years touring the United States and plan to return home. Their savings get stolen so the family cannot afford the ship ticket. Instead, César Cascabel decides to travel overland, via Alaska and Bering Straits, through Siberia and Central Russia with their horse drawn Carriage, the Belle-Roulotte (the Fair Rambler). They don't expect dangers to happen. On their way, they rescue at the Alaskan border, with the help of native girl Kayette, a Russian political fugitive, count Narkine, whom they bring along so that he can see again his father in Russia. Count Narkine adopts Kayette as his daughter. In Sitka, the group witnesses the transfer of Alaska to the United States. On their way from Port Clarence the travellers unfortunately end up on a floating iceberg that drifts to the Lyakhovsky Islands in Arctic Ocean. There they are captured by the natives. Other troubles, including political ones, occur but Cascabels manage to get through Ural to Perm and then, easily, to France. The Wylies, a well-to-do but uneducated Scottish family, are concerned about their daughter, Maggie, a plain young woman who they fear, will remain a spinster. One night the Wylies discover that a serious young university student, John Shand, has been breaking into their home so that he can read books from their large library. Shand is penniless and cannot afford to buy books for his law school education. Maggie Wylie and John Shand come to an understanding: that her family will fund his education if, at the end of five years, he agrees to marry her. John honours his commitment to Maggie, marrying her although he does not love her. Recognising her husband's ambition to become a Member of Parliament, Maggie quietly uses her intelligence and her connections behind the scenes to get John elected. She continues to foster his career, never allowing him to see that she is the power behind his rise to fame. Eventually John begins to believe that his wife is too plain for a man of his stature and position, and he takes up with Lady Sybil Lazenby, a beautiful, refined and high-born young Englishwoman. Maggie is prepared to let her husband go, if Sybil can help him more than she herself can. However, when Shand is preparing a speech that will make or break his career, he finds that Sybil is no help to him, and he realises that Maggie is his inspiration.

The book opens with a fictional historical overview/flashback to events of Homer's famous Odyssey, but alters the original plot. In the present day, Dirk Pitt, his son Dirk Pitt, Jr., his daughter Summer Pitt, and friend Al Giordino are involved in the search for the source of a brownish contamination in the ocean's waters, which leads to a diabolical plot that they must unravel and ultimately topple. As this is occurring, discoveries relating to the "true" tale of the Odyssey are made. The villain is the mysterious Specter, a huge man who disguises his identity by wearing sunglasses, a hat, and a scarf over his face. The book also features a significant event between Dirk Pitt and Congresswoman Loren Smith. He and Al retire from their life of daredevilry and settle down. Pitt asks for the hand of Loren who also steps down. Pitt assumes the responsibility of head of NUMA as Admiral Sandecker accepts the Vice Presidency. This marks a change in Dirk Pitt Sr. series, as confirmed by his next novel, which features Dirk Pitt Jr. as the primary protagonist.
