As with every Dirk Pitt novel, this one features a classic car, in this case a Marmon V-16 Town Car. A custom-built 1952 Meteor DeSoto hot rod modified with a engine is briefly mentioned.

The novel describes a world set in the year 2048 after a catastrophe which has fractured the United States into several nations. The protagonists live in San Francisco and have evolved in the direction of Ecotopia, reverting to a sustainable economy, using wind power, local agriculture, and the like. San Francisco is presented as a mostly pagan city where the streets have been torn up for gardens and streams, no one starves or is homeless, and the city's defense council consists primarily of nine elderly women who "listen and dream". The novel describes "a utopia where women are leading societies but are doing so with the consent of men." To the south, though, an overtly-theocratic Christian fundamentalist nation has evolved and plans to wage war against the San Franciscans. The novel explores the events before and during the ensuing struggle between the two nations, pitting utopia and dystopia against each other. The basic premise resembles that of Pat Murphy's earlier novel The City, Not Long After. The story is primarily told from the points of view of 98-year-old Maya, her nominal granddaughter Madrone, and her grandson Bird. Through these and other characters, the story explores many elements from ecofeminism and ecotopian fiction.

The novel unfolds around a case of mistaken identity involving two identical twins, a scenario Jin Yong later notes evokes Shakespearean echoes such as Twelfth Night and The Comedy of Errors. The narrator-protagonist calls himself Gouzazhong, a term meaning “mongrel dog” or bastard, and begins as a penniless youth roaming Kaifeng in search of his lost mother. His path crosses a brawl among wulin fighters, where he encounters the Shi family and members of the Snowy Mountain Sect. An accident separates him from Kaifeng and places him under the care of a martial artist named Xie Yanke, who brings him to a secluded home atop Motian Cliff. There, Yanke, though frequently irritated by Gouzazhong, decides to mentor him in martial arts. For six years Gouzazhong trains in qi cultivation under Yanke’s guidance; what he does not realize is that Yanke harbors a hidden, malicious plan—teaching him the wrong methods to ensure internal wounds and eventual death. Meanwhile, Shi Potian, the leader of the Changle Sect (whose true name is Shi Zhongyu), vanishes without explanation. Much of the narrative follows the tangled consequences of Gouzhazhong’s mistaken identity: not only sect members with ulterior motives, but also Shi Zhongyu’s parents, his beloved Ding Dang, and the Snowy Mountain Sect all misrecognize him as Shi Zhongyu. Although the pair share striking resemblance, their dispositions are poles apart: Gouzhazhong remains straightforward, sincere, and quick-witted, whereas Shi Zhongyu is infamous for being lewd and calculating. Through these events, Gouzhazhong attains formidable martial prowess. Pursued by Snowy Mountain Sect adherents who suspect him of molesting A’xiu—the granddaughter of their sect leader—Gouzazhong ends up forming a relationship with A’xiu after a series of episodes in which misunderstandings are gradually resolved. The climax arrives when leaders from various factions are compelled to travel to a secluded island by two enigmatic, highly skilled messengers to partake in Laba congee for the festival. The tale then pivots toward a startling finale, offering revelations about Gouzhazhong’s true parentage and uncovering further secrets revealed on the island.

The story of twelve-year-old Cosimo Piovasco di Rondò is narrated by his younger brother, Biagio. Set in Liguria near the French Riviera, the two brothers belong to a noble 18th century family whose estate is located in the vast forest landscapes of Ombrosa. The regions of Italy have not yet united and the Ligurian Coast is not ruled by a legitimate king. In a rebellious fit after refusing to eat a dinner of snails prepared by Battista, his sadistic sister, Cosimo climbs up a tree and decides never to come down again. He has literally had enough: enough of family and decorum, his proper role as a future Baron, and of everything on the ground. Initially helped and sometimes cared for by Biagio, the young Baron eventually becomes self-sufficient but finds that the more he distances himself from others in order to see them from a new point of view, the more he helps everyone on the earth. His love for a young woman named Viola changes the course of the lives of everyone: Cosimo, Viola, Biagio, and the community of Ombrosa.

Set in 2048, the novel follows a world fractured into multiple nations after a devastating catastrophe. Its protagonists inhabit San Francisco, where society has steered toward Ecotopia: a sustainable economy built on wind energy, local farming, and related practices. The city itself is depicted as largely pagan, with streets torn up to create gardens and streams, and with no hunger or homelessness. Its defense council is dominated by nine elderly women who “listen and dream.” A key line describes a utopia in which women lead societies with the consent of men. South of San Francisco, a theocratic Christian fundamentalist state has emerged, openly preparing for war against the coastal city. The narrative traces the events before and during the conflict between these two realms, framing a clash of utopia and dystopia. The premise echoes Pat Murphy’s earlier work, The City, Not Long After. Narration is centered primarily on Maya, age 98, along with her nominal granddaughter Madrone and her grandson Bird, among other voices. Through these characters and others, the novel delves into themes of ecofeminism and ecotopian fiction, exploring their intersections and implications.

Forged in the Fire is an epic love story in which love prevails over all. When Will is sent to prison during the plague, Susanna has no way of knowing whether her beloved is alive or not. Will gets sent to jail with two of his friends for starting a fight in the streets. Whilst in jail both his friends are infested with the plague and Will becomes deathly ill. Both of his companions die but Will is bailed out by a man called Edmund who is extremely wealthy and a friend of Nat, who during the story is always at Will's side. When Susanna finally finds out where Will is located she travels at once to London. There she finds Will happy and healthy in Edmund's home with his eldest daughter. This is the one and only blow to their love but is soon overcome. The two get married in the sight of God at a Quaker meeting. The London fire is the next huge thing to happen. The city is destroyed bit by bit, and now that Susanna is with a child she and Will must leave. But Will refuses to leave until he has finished his work, so he sends Susanna, with friends, to make it out of the city and into a farm where she is to camp for many nights. Finally Will with Nat manage to get out of the city and they are reunited at last. Will also makes up with his father who has never much cared for Will and Susanna's love. He gives them some money and they live happily ever after. A few years later they have a son and life happily goes on.

Mr. and Mrs. Lane invited the delightful Frenchwoman Annette Reynaud to their brownstone for a family dinner, unaware that she was a jewel thief going by the alias Michelle. Richard Duffy, Mrs. Lane’s younger brother, happened to know Michelle from a previous life and privately cautioned her against targeting his sister’s home. She insisted she was retired and had come to the United States to escape those who required her to work for them. Not long after, however, she spoke to him in a cryptic phone call, hinting she was in danger but unable to speak plainly. The hints—“nice,” “park,” and “au revoir”—led Richard and his nephew Stephen Lane to travel to Nice. They checked into Hotel Parc and, using binoculars, observed Michelle aboard a yacht named Au Revoir. In a staged, chance meeting, Richard uncovered that Michelle was being forced to carry out a diamond heist for a gang, and she hoped to learn the mastermind’s name to bargain with the police. They even prepared counterfeit gems to replace the real stones during the theft. With few options left, Richard and Stephen resolved to shadow Michelle, hoping not to reveal themselves in the process. Their sole ally was Inspector Armand Duval, a police officer who agreed to entertain their wild tale because he already suspected a gang of thieves operating nearby and had evidence of stolen precious stones. The criminals were likened to a hydra: the police had only captured the petty thieves so far and had no clue who their mastermind was.

70 years after the events of Rendezvous with Rama, a second Raman vessel enters our solar system. Its arrival is expected and an expedition is sent to unlock more of Rama's mysteries, but the crew are unprepared both for what they find and for the conflicts that arise between them. Rama II brings new characters into a new story and is mostly unrelated to the original and largely serves to set up its own sequels. It ends with three of the twelve astronauts stranded inside Rama as it travels out of the solar system, Nicole des Jardins Wakefield, Richard Wakefield and Michael O'Toole. Unlike Rendezvous with Rama, which depicted a utopian future and focused almost entirely on the hard science fiction elements regarding the scientific wonders of the alien spacecraft, Rama II and its sequels deconstruct Clarke's vision of human colonies throughout the solar system through a global economic crisis that forced their almost total deactivation. Then follows a very different storytelling that brings forward contemporary issues like abortion, racism, drug abuse and organized crime.

Emily Windsnap, a girl aboard the boat The King of the Sea with her mother, Mary Penelope, repeatedly asks for swimming lessons until her water-phobic mother finally consents. After a string of startling events, Emily learns she is half mermaid and half human, with her legs transforming into a tail when she is in water and returning to legs upon leaving it. She befriends a fellow mermaid named Shona, and the two become close companions. Together, they uncover that Emily’s father is imprisoned for having wed a human, while Mary is under a spell that makes her forget everything. The two girls devise a plan to rescue Jake Windsnap, Emily’s father, though they remain unsure how. When an opportunity arises to execute her “daydream” plan, Emily guides their houseboat close to the prison. Mary, in pursuit, regains memories of her husband and Emily’s father. Neptune intercepts them, and they are taken to trial. There, Emily persuades Neptune, appealing to the family’s shared love, to release them. Neptune agrees to free the Windsnaps on one condition: they must relocate to a desolate island.

The Pinhoe family works hard to conceal their magical activities, hoping to avoid intervention by the Big Man, Chrestomanci, who pursues those who misuse magic. Marianne suspects Gammer, the clan matriarch, isn’t truly mad, though she isn’t entirely certain. She believes Gammer is behind the plagues afflicting the Farleighs, a related clan that also wishes to stay off the Big Man’s radar. Though the Farleighs and Pinhoes once faced the world together, it appears Gammer has ignited a conflict, threatening to unravel their secrecy for good. Meanwhile, at the Castle, Cat comes into possession of a horse and encounters Jason—the bootboy from Chrestomanci’s youth—and helps him and his new wife locate a home. They finally decide on Woods House, Gammer’s former residence. During a tour, Marianne shows Cat an ancient egg stored in the attic, one sealed with powerful “Don’t Notice” spells. That egg will inevitably draw the Big Man’s attention to the Pinhoe clan, a development that Gammer and the rest seek to avoid at all costs.

The story tells how the people of the fictional planet Pern discover the special abilities of the watch-whers or whers, a distant relative of the dragons. Subsequently, these beasts are used in mines to warn miners of gas pockets and also to locate stranded miners, should there be a cave-in. The story begins some years before the 3rd Pass in Camp Natalon, a mining camp. There, the reader is introduced to a young boy Kindan, whose father owns a watch-wher called Dask. During a mining cave-in, Kindan loses his entire family as well as Dask, and is adopted by the Master Harper Zist, who begins to train him to be both an entertainer and a spy, something that Harpers do. This is how Kindan learns that the camp is divided into two parties, Natalon's and his uncle, Tarik's. Meanwhile, the camp is without a watch-wher and minor accidents keep delaying the work. Despite the protests from Tarik and his group, Natalon decides to trade an entire winter's worth of coal for a chance for Kindan to ask a queen watch-wher for an egg. He succeeds and begins the difficult task of raising a nocturnal animal. As no records exist on how to raise or train the watch-wher, Kindan has no clue but is luckily aided by the mysterious Nuella. Together, they train Kisk and, in the process, learn a great deal about this species. This proves to be vital as, towards the end of the novel, Kisk's abilities will save many lives, including that of the camp leader, Natalon.

Jonathan Dark (Jandar), earthman mysteriously transported to the Jovian moon of Callisto (or Thanator), has succeeded in rescuing Princess Darloona of Shondakar from the Sky Pirates of Zandahar, only to see her fall into the hands of the Black Legion, the mercenary force that had previously occupied her native city and driven her and her followers into exile. Journeying to Shondakar, Jandar improbably finds himself in the Legion's good graces after saving the son of its leader, the very man that leader intends to have Darloona wed in order to cement his control of the city. Having essentially been given a free hand to spy on the enemy, Jandar scouts out the city's defenses and weaknesses, particularly its underground tunnel system. He disrupts the wedding as Darloona's Ku Thad people infiltrate Shondakar through the tunnels and take the occupiers by surprise. Jandar kills the mastermind behind the princess's misfortunes, the supposed priest Oola, who is secretly one of the Mind Wizards conspiring to take over all of Thanator. But during the battle the Sky Pirates invade, and while the Ku Thad are ultimately victorious over both foes, Prince Thuton of Zandahar escapes, carrying Darloona back to the captivity from which Jandar sprung her in the previous volume. Back to square one...

Though published as three volumes, the Deed of Paksenarrion was written as one continuous narrative. Some readers have highlighted parallels to Dungeons & Dragons: notably, Brewersbridge in Moon’s tale resembles Hommlet from The Temple of Elemental Evil, and the faith of Gird mirrors Saint Cuthbert’s worship in Greyhawk. Yet such motifs appear across many strands of high fantasy and are not exclusive to any single fictional universe. The tale centers on the adult life of Paksenarrion Dorthansdotter, nicknamed Paks, who hails from Three Firs. Set in a medieval-style realm inhabited by humans, dwarves, gnomes, and elves, the story opens with an 18-year-old Paks, headstrong and dissatisfied with an arranged marriage arranged by her father, who leaves Three Firs to enlist in a mercenary company. Through trials and travels she gradually discovers that she possesses paladin gifts, though in a way that deviates from conventional expectations.

In an Edinburgh squat, Detective Inspector John Rebus discovers a man’s body, an overdose victim laid out crosswise between two extinguished candles, a five-pointed star painted above on the wall. While some colleagues dismiss it as a routine junkie death, Rebus notes odd details that unsettle him: a complete heroin packet in the deceased’s room and peculiar bruising on his face and body. He treats the apparent murder as a real possibility and delves into the true circumstances behind the death. During his inquiry, Rebus encounters a young woman named Tracy, who knew the victim and heard his chilling last words: “Hide! Hide!” It turns out the man was a photographer who had snapped and concealed sensitive photographs at Hyde’s, a private club catering to an elite circle that also hosts illegal boxing. Rebus ultimately secures the arrest of Hyde’s proprietor and several prominent members, but, to his horror, they all die under dubious circumstances. The authorities are actively concealing the truth to avert a scandal. Soon after Rankin’s own relocation to London, a parallel real-world incident emerged: male prostitutes had bribed lawyers and judges. Parliament was prompted to investigate, and two lawyers began probing the police inquiry. In an unexpected turn, the inquiry concluded the allegations were unfounded, resulting in demotions for officers involved in the case.

Mary Lou Finney is less than excited about her assignment to keep a journal over the summer. She also has to read The Odyssey, which she often relates to her own story. Then her cousin Carl Ray comes to stay with her family, under the pretense of looking for a job, which he eventually finds at Mr. Furtz's hardware store. Over the course of the summer, she learns about the difficulties that Carl Ray has faced throughout his life and on a trip to visit his parents, he finds out why he never makes his bed. She also hangs out with her best friend Beth Ann and becomes Alex Cheevey's girlfriend. As Mary Lou's story unfolds, she examines both her struggles with her family and her own sense of self. Sharon Creech stated that the inspiration for this story was an occasion when, "I'd been living overseas (England and Switzerland) for about ten years, and I was sadly missing my family back in the States. I thought I'd write a story about normal family chaos and that's how this began, with me trying to remember what it was like growing up in my family. Writing the story was a way for me to feel as if my family were with me, right there in our little cottage in England.".

Dalgliesh visits Saint Anselm's in a semi-official capacity to follow up the death of a student some time previously - his father was not satisfied with the verdict. Whilst there, a visiting Archdeacon is murdered. Dalgliesh is assigned the investigation, summoning D I Miskin and D I Tarrant from London to assist, as well as local officers. Initial suspicion falls on one of the fathers who run and teach at the college, as the archdeacon was known to be recommending the closure of the college. Two more murders follow and after all present have been questioned, several skeletons are brought out the cupboard - including the fact that one of the students is unknowingly the son of one of the lay lecturers and that through his Mother, he will inherit the property, should it be closed and sold. Forensic evidence clinches the case against the lecturer and he confesses. The college is closed and the student inherits the proceeds. In this novel, Dalgliesh meets and begins a relationship with Dr Emma Lavenham, a visiting teacher from Cambridge.

In the story, 17-year-old Peter Collins McPhee (nicknamed P.C. because he loves playing computer games) is called by his Uncle Cliff to solve a mystery in Australia. The brother of a young Aboriginal girl named Maruul has gone suddenly missing while searching for their tribe's treasure, told of in a riddle. She says there was a terrible screeching sound, and a boat came near just as her brother disappeared. but P.C. finds that there is a killer creature living in the depths of the reef. The creature attacks and kills his uncle. The two kids go to Wally Wallygong, an Aboriginal fishing shop owner, who explains the riddle. Afterwards, they all go to the reef location of the creature and pretend to be attacked by snakes. The strange ship that has been passing by takes them on board. They attempt to escape and are almost killed. They find out that the captain of the ship, a geologist, has had the treasure—an encarved opal wall—all along, and was making the screeching noise mechanically, which signaled the creature to attack. She also plans to destroy the treasure. P.C. tricks the creature into eating the captain, and Maruul returns to her village with the treasure. The village buys long-needed resources with the treasure.

Steven Masters, the main character, is a pampered 23-year-old and the sole heir to the planet’s wealthiest man. During a party, while intoxicated, he declares a desire to join a distant space mission bound for Mittend, a life-bearing world 30 light-years from Earth. When told he does not qualify, he reacts with indignation and launches a campaign to secure a seat on the expedition. Funds from his father enable him to obtain a berth, and six weeks later he lands on Mittend. The planet closely resembles Earth, boasting a breathable atmosphere. Once ashore, he strays from the group and encounters the indigenous people. They are naked and primitive but possess a collectivist intellect called “Mother.” As soon as they glimpse Steven, they pursue him; upon capturing and touching him, his consciousness is transferred into the body of a 38-year-old bar waiter back on Earth. In a twist, the bar waiter’s mind takes over Steven’s body on Mittend. It later emerges that the bar waiter had previously worked for Steven as a butler; he blames Steven for a crime he did not commit and got him fired. Right after the transfer, Steven experiences severe psychological shock, and the bar must call an ambulance. He spends several days hospitalized while doctors sedate him. News of his mind swap spreads, and the disappearance of the expedition amplifies the sensation surrounding his story. During his hospital stay, Masters Senior, his father, visits and later departs, insisting that the person lying in the hospital bed is not Steven. After leaving, a bartender arrives to pick him up and drive him to work, where he spends the day performing his duties.

In a small Canadian fishing village unfolds the tale of Primrose Squarp, an eleven-year-old girl whose life centers around a quirky restaurant and an unresolved loss. After a typhoon swallows her parents, Primrose refuses to concede they are gone and skips their memorial. Instead, she clings to the belief that they survived, while her guardianship sprawls between an elderly neighbor, Miss Perfidy, and a distracted Uncle Jack. Amid the upheaval, the one constant remains her fondness for the Girl on the Red Swing, a diner where every dish arrives on a waffle. The restaurant’s proprietor, Kate Bowzer, takes Primrose under her wing, teaching her to cook with a notebook full of cited recipes. Kate’s patient support never wavers, even when Primrose’s odd misadventures—such as unintentionally setting the class guinea pig ablaze—arise. The girl’s situation shifts again when custody moves from Uncle Jack to an older couple; though she forms attachments to them, a string of accidents, including the loss of a toe, complicates her life. As neighbors watch with growing concern, Primrose’s eccentricities turn her into a town curiosity, yet she clings to the hope of reuniting her family and achieving some sense of normalcy. In a surprising turn, her parents eventually return, stunning everyone in the village.

The tale opens as Des Grieux, accompanied by his mother, attends a concert where he experiences uncanny, suggestive visions during a piano performance by the alluring Teleny, a Hungarian virtuoso. Drawn to him, Des Grieux becomes consumed by a mysterious, telepathic bond that seems both sexual and emotional, a mixture of fascination, admiration, and longing that soon morphs into jealousy. Aware that Teleny attracts many suitors before they become involved, Des Grieux and the elder musician finally meet and exchange accounts of their inexplicable connection, which quickly blossoms into an intense affair. Torn between love and desire for a man, Des Grieux briefly pursues a relationship with a household servant; this doomed pursuit indirectly precipitates the servant’s death. Shaken, he resolves to embrace his feelings and allows Teleny to introduce him to a clandestine circle of men drawn to other men’s desires. Their bond survives a coercive blackmail attempt and the emotional turmoil that follows, until Teleny announces a temporary departure, supposedly for a concert engagement. In this absence, Des Grieux visits Teleny’s apartment only to discover him in bed with Des Grieux’s mother, who had offered to settle Teleny’s debts in exchange for sexual favors. The scene shatters them, and Des Grieux sinks into despair, nearly ending his life in a hospital isolation. After his release, he seeks out Teleny, only to learn that his lover has stabbed himself in a gesture of remorse as he bleeds to death. Des Grieux forgives him; they reaffirm their love, but Teleny dies in the end.

Ninette Dupond, a dancer with the Paris Opera Ballet, is promoted to lead after Mademoiselle Jean-Marie Augustine is injured. Although her acclaimed performance earns praise, she is dismissed when her liaison with Augustine’s patron is noticed. Facing poverty and desperation, Ninette encounters a talking tomcat named Thomas who can communicate telepathically. The cat persuades her to flee to England and pursue premier-dancer status there. With little choice, Ninette accepts, even though she doubts magic. During their journey, Thomas teaches her English, explains the basics of the magical world, and persuades her to adopt the alias Nina Tchereslavsky, a Russian ballerina. Thomas also convinces Nigel Barret, owner of a music hall and an Elemental Master of Air, to hire Ninette as the star of his show. Drawing on fairy-tale stratagems, Nigel and his collaborators—Arthur, who leads the orchestra, and Wolf, a parrot claimed to be Mozart’s reincarnation—stage a production inspired by Nina’s supposed shipwreck off a Blackpool beach. They provide Ninette with a comfortable apartment and a maid, Alsie McKenzie, who, while non-magical, possesses the Sensitivity gift that allows perceiving elemental beings. Rehearsals proceed, and Ninette continues to perform some dance numbers onstage. To ensure the project’s success, Nigel enlists Jonathon Hightower, an Elemental Master of Fire and a seasoned stage magician, both to contribute to the show and to investigate whether the shipwreck was in fact an attack on Nina. The danger escalates when the real Nina Tchereslavsky learns of Ninette’s impersonation. The peril is amplified by the truth that the authentic Nina is a troll capable of absorbing identities and memories. Previously, the troll had assumed a young poet’s guise, seduced the real Nina, exhausted her memories with its elemental powers, and replaced her.

Although it opens like a memoir or autobiography, the book quickly shifts into a collage of fragmented episodes detailing Thompson’s exploits, forming a kind of Gonzo biography. The narrative follows an uneven timeline, with many events out of chronological order, yet a thread of continuity runs through the work. Notably, the “Witness” segments—concerned with Gail Palmer’s lawsuit against him—recur in roughly the same vicinity in each section. Beyond these larger strands, numerous passages stand alone, linked only by shared people or locales mentioned across sections. The events that most closely intersect Thompson’s life are, chronologically or thematically, among the following: an early incident in which the FBI attempts to arrest a nine-year-old Thompson for an act that allegedly damaged a federal mailbox; the recurring “Witness” episodes; episodes involving Thompson’s exploits at or around the Mitchell Brothers O’Farrell Theatre in San Francisco, a notorious porn venue where he asserts he worked throughout the mid-1980s; and a possibly fictionalized account of how he met his assistant and future wife, Anita.

Twelve-year-old Heidi resides in Reno, Nevada, living with her mentally challenged mother and their neighbor, Bernadette. Her mother speaks only twenty-three words, one of which remains a mystery—“soof”—a term no one can define. Bernadette, meanwhile, suffers from severe agoraphobia and dares not venture outside. To provide for everyone, Heidi shoulders responsibilities far beyond her years. When she uncovers photographs of her mother at a Christmas party in New York, Heidi resolves to travel there, driven by a desire to learn more about her family’s past and to uncover the meaning of the circulating word—soof—after hearing her mother mutter it repeatedly. Bernadette, anxious about Heidi’s departure, grants permission only if she promises to phone every night. On her journey to Liberty, New York, Heidi befriends Georgia Sweet, a warm and inquisitive woman she meets aboard the bus. Upon arriving at Hilltop Home, Heidi feels unwelcome in Thurman Hill’s presence. Overcome with sadness, Ruby welcomes Heidi into her own home and, with her husband Roy, begins to investigate. Through their sleuthing, Heidi discovers Thurman Hill is her grandfather, Elliot is her father, and her grandmother’s name is Diana. She finally learns the true meaning of her mother’s enigmatic word—soof—which turns out to be Heidi’s nickname for Sophia Demuth. The story closes with the death of Heidi’s mother.

One of Harding's Pleasure & Profit Books. A collection of real life outdoor stories based on the experiences of the author, Eldred Nathaniel Woodcock. Writing from memory, Mr. Woodcock tells of incidents that happened during the fifty years (1855–1905) he spent camping, hunting, trapping and fishing in the wilderness of Northern Pennsylvania and several other states. Most of E. N. Woodcock's stories feature an interesting partner (who he sometimes refers to as "Pard"), and other local people who lived in the Potter County, Pennsylvania area. Many of the wild places where he made his camps are now State Parks and Forests. E. N. Woodcock tells his stories in plain language, about deer and bear hunting; trapping bear, wild cat, fox, marten, mink and muskrat; run-ins with porcupines and skunks; mishaps that happened to himself and his partners; and the everyday occurrences of camp life. He gives his opinion of state game laws and bounties, and his views on the need for conservation. The book also includes practical information on building cabins, camp fires and cooking, staying warm, finding bee hives, trap sets, building deadfalls, using baits, skinning, stretching and drying fur, tracking game, and types of guns and ammunition.

Carthoris is madly in love with Thuvia. This love was foreshadowed at the end of the previous novel. Unfortunately Thuvia is promised to Kulan Tith, Jeddak of Kaol. On Barsoom nothing can break an engagement between a man and woman except death, although the new suitor may not cause that death. Thus it is that Thuvia will have none of him. This situation leaves Carthoris in a predicament. As Thuvia suffers the common Burroughsian heroine's fate of being kidnapped and in need of rescue, Carthoris' goal is abetted by circumstances. Thus he sets out to find the love of his life. His craft is sabotaged and he finds himself deep in the undiscovered south of Barsoom, in the ruins of ancient Aanthor. Thuvia's kidnappers, the Dusar, have taken her there as well, and Carthoris is just in time to spot Thuvia and her kidnappers under assault by a green man of the hordes of Torquas. Carthoris leaps to her rescue in the style of his father. The rescue takes Carthoris and his love to ancient Lothar, home of an ancient fair-skinned human race gifted with the ability to create lifelike phantasms from pure thought. They habitually use large numbers of phantom bowmen paired with real and phantom banths (Barsoomian lions) to defend themselves from the hordes of Torquas. The kidnapping of Thuvia is done in such a way that Carthoris is blamed. This ignites a war between the red nations of Barsoom. Carthoris must try to be back in time with Thuvia to stop the war from breaking loose. Carthoris wonders if his love will ever be requited by the promised Thuvia.

Adelia “Dee” Cunnane, an Irishwoman, becomes entwined with American Travis Grant as their story unfolds. With no means and little choice, Dee sails to the United States to stay with her uncle Paddy, who manages a vast horse farm. Her affection for animals shines through, earning her a position beside Paddy. A quick temper makes Dee prone to clashes with Travis, the farm’s affluent owner, and their disputes frequently give way to heated, undeniable passion. At one perilous moment, Travis saves Dee from an attempted assault. When Paddy collapses from a heart attack, he grows fixated on his own fragility and on what lies ahead for Dee, insisting that Travis assume responsibility for her. The men reach a private agreement: a provisional marriage of convenience, formalized in Paddy’s hospital room. As events unfold, happiness dwindles for both, and neither is willing to admit true feelings. Even after their marriage is consummated, Dee and Travis seem more assured about each other, yet their deeper emotions remain unspoken. The dynamic shifts when Margot, Travis’s sophisticated ex-lover, returns to the neighborhood and begins to prey on Dee’s insecurities, threatening the union. Dee flees, and Travis pursues. In a frank moment together, they acknowledge their love and commit to making the marriage work.

Elsha is a teenager living in a bleak, cold future where world-wide cloud cover has permanently blocked out the sun. Humans have split into two classes - the Chosen and the Quelled, of which Elsha is the latter. The Quelled are doomed to spend their lives in servitude to the Chosen, mining "firestones" - the only means of warmth on the planet. The Firelord is the leader of the Chosen, said to be a great and powerful man. A rebellious girl, Elsha causes trouble for herself - even going so far as being considered for execution - until she is met by a Chosen man named Amasai, Steward of the Firelord, and given the highest position available to a woman - Handmaiden to the Firelord. On her journeys with the Firelord, Elsha meets Teraj, later revealed to be the Firelord's son, with whom Elsha forms a romantic relationship. Elsha uses her unlikely position to fight the stigma and oppression of her people, eventually inheriting the title for herself after the Firelord's unexpected death and changing the course of the planet's history for the better. It is implied Elsha marries Teraj. *Out of Print*

Harvard law professor Lawrence Lessig, renowned for his stance in the so-called “copyright wars,” highlights a growing mismatch between the ease and ubiquity of remix technologies and the outdated tenor of copyright law. He argues that current copyright regimes cannot keep pace with digital media, since every act of reusing a creative work in a digital setting inherently produces a copy (p. 98). Consequently, amateur creators now face control over digital manipulation that once applied mainly to professionals. Lessig further frames multimedia fluency as the era’s literacy—analogous to reading and writing in earlier times—suggesting it is the vernacular through which today’s society communicates. Children immersed in technologies that saturate daily life struggle to grasp why remixing should be illegal. He contends that, in the digital age, unauthorized reuse by amateurs cannot be halted, only criminalized. A troubling corollary is that generations of youngsters may grow up convinced that what they do is illegal, a belief with consequences for society that reach beyond the realm of copyright battles. The work is available as a free download under a Creative Commons license.

Diamond is the central figure of this tale, a remarkably gentle boy whose presence brightens every place he Goes. He combats sorrow and darkness, becoming a beacon of calm for his family. One night, as sleep eludes him, he repeatedly seals a hole in the wall of the attic—his bedroom—to keep the wind out. In time, though, he discovers that this act prevents the North Wind from peering through her window. A bond forms between them, and she allows him to ride upon her back, whisking him away on several escapades. While the North Wind performs good deeds and aids others, she also enacts actions that seem harsh. In one mission she is ordered to sink a ship. Yet every action that appears grim culminates in a blessing. The North Wind embodies Pain and Death at the behest of divine intention, guiding toward something ultimately beneficial. During their journeys, she transports Diamond to the land she calls home—an ideal realm devoid of pain and death. But what he reaches is only a shadow of that country, a distant reflection tucked away at the edge of the North Wind’s realm. The true country remains accessible only after his death. In the book’s conclusion, Diamond passes away, finally allowed to glimpse the country in its fullness.

Set towards the end of WWI, in 1918, it tells the story of a shy young railway employee and amateur actor from Milwaukee, named Paul Peachy. Having realised that his wife no longer loves him, Paul enlists as a private in the U.S. Army and boards ship for the trenches of France. Peachy finds temporary solace in friendship amid horrors of war, but is soon captured by the enemy Germans in No Man's Land. His only chance of survival is to impersonate one of the enemy's most famous spies (as a child of immigrants, he is a fluent German speaker). As the urbane and accomplished spy Harry Stroller, Peachy is feted as a hero by the German top brass and gains access to a previously unimagined world of sumptuous living. But his new role also reveals inner reserves of courage and ingenuity he never knew he possessed, as the mounting suspicions of his German hosts force Peachy into ever more outrageous deceptions. In this atmosphere of smoke and mirrors, Paul Peachy falls in love with Annie, a beautiful French courtesan, who seems to see through his artful disguise. The ending is a surprise of twists and clever plotting.

In the prologue, Watarai leads his squad, the Cobalt Knights, into a zone barred to ordinary players. They attempt to erase a stray AI resembling a young girl in a red dress, but their effort fails and she escapes. Chapter one introduces Albireo, who sneaks into the dungeon’s lowest floor and encounters the Vagrant AI. Via text chat, she reveals her name as Lycoris. The dungeon’s final treasure is an item labeled “eciov.cyl,” which Albiero trades to Lycoris at her request. Within the game, Lycoris gains a voice. She then teleports them without warning to Albireo’s home, where a massive monster outbreak is underway. A novice player named Hokuto pleads with Albireo for help; he must assist, compelled by circumstance, and receives an item named “rae.cyl,” which is also given to Lycoris. Hokuto manipulates Albireo into allowing her onto his empty friends list and eventually into forming a two-person party. This arrangement lets Hokuto see Lycoris. Orca and Balmung later approach Albireo, asking him to join the effort to resolve the “One Sin,” a supposedly unbeatable event, but he declines. Although he cannot log out of The World, he continues his real life as usual, unlike later .hack characters who fall into comas. Returning to the “One Sin” location, Albireo reunites with Hokuto there, witnessing Orca and Balmung defeat the boss. After its fall, an angel appears, its body trailing feathers. Lycoris asks Albireo to locate a red feather, which turns out to be “eye.cyl,” restoring her sight. Lycoris then escorts them to another zone, where she enters a phantom spring and Albireo acquires “yromem.cyl.” Back in the prologue area, Albireo gives Lycoris the item, enabling her to recover her memories and recognize Albireo as Watarai, the Cobalt Knight who first attempted to delete her. Watarai had aimed to complete the event to erase the previously fragmented Lycoris. Lycoris informs him of Morganna Mode Gone and of her origin as a failed Aura prototype, revealing the final fragment of herself stored in Albireo’s spear: “etaf.cyl.” In the end, she chooses to delete herself, stabbing herself onto Albireo’s spear.

The late 21st century seems like a good time to be alive. Earth is at peace. Humans now command self-replicating machines that create engineering marvels on enormous scales. Artificial habitats dot the solar system. Anti-matter driven Valkyrie rockets carry explorers to the stars at nearly the speed of light. All seems well. Then, from the uncaring black of space come swarms of relativistic missiles. Though they are merely boulder-sized hunks of metal, they move fast enough to hit with the force of many nuclear arsenals. They are impossible to track and impossible to stop. Humanity is all but wiped out by the horrific bombardment. (To read a discussion of relativistic weapons and an excerpt of the attack, see Atomic Rockets: Relativistic Weapons). A handful of survivors desperately struggle to escape the alien mop-up fleet. They hide close to the sun, inside asteroids, beneath the crusts of moons, within ice rings, and in the fathomless depths of interstellar space. But most are hunted down and slaughtered. The last man and woman on Earth are captured as zoo specimens. In the belly of an alien starship, a squid-like being relates to them the pitiless logic behind human-kind's execution: the moment we learned to travel at relativistic speeds was the moment we had the power to do to them what they did to us first. The attack was nothing personal. Humanity was simply too dangerous a neighbor to have around.

Set in Eskibahçe, a small, fictional southwestern coastal Anatolian village, the narrative unfolds across the 1900s, through World War I and the rise of Turkish nationalism. Midway through the tale, the Battle of Gallipoli interrupts the story. Though invented, Eskibahçe draws heavily on Kayaköy (Turkish: Levissi Λεβισσι), a real village near Fethiye whose ruins endure today. Once a flourishing Greek settlement with more than a thousand houses, two churches, fourteen chapels, and two schools, Kayaköy was emptied in 1923 as part of a large, government-coordinated population exchange between Turkey and Greece after the Turkish War of Independence, sending Greek residents back to Greece along with many Greeks across the country. For centuries, Turks and Greeks coexisted in the region: Turks tended fields in the Kaya valley while Greeks conducted crafts and trades on the hillsides. The Greek presence there is centuries-old, and Kayaköy—known as Karmylassos in Greek—had remained inhabited since at least the 13th century. Since then it has stood vacant and decaying, the only sounds the mountain breeze and sea mist threading through empty streets. Attempts to repopulate the village by deporting Turks from Greece failed, and by the 1950s the rooftops of all houses were removed. Some characters from this story also appear in the author’s earlier work Captain Corelli’s Mandolin. The book furnishes a vivid, unflinching portrait of trench life during World War I, detailing its terrors with striking immediacy.

In a remote California desert town of Hard Pan, population 43, Lucky—a ten-year-old girl—navigates life with two friends: Lincoln, a budding knot-tyer whose mother envisions him as future president, and Miles, a five-year-old whose favorite book is Are You My Mother? by P.D. Eastman. After Lucky’s mother dies two years earlier from electrocution, their father asks Brigitte, his first ex-wife from France, to come to the United States and care for Lucky. Fearing Brigitte might be tired of guardianship and their Hard Pan existence, Lucky becomes anxious when she spots Brigitte’s suitcase and passport left out, picturing an imminent return to France. To cope, she leans on a notion she overhears at a local 12-step meeting—her “Higher Power.” Acting on three perceived signs, she decides to run away, taking her dog HMS Beagle along as storms and sand whip across the landscape. Outside town, Miles is found lost and injured in the storm, and Lucky insists on bringing him with them. The two seek shelter in the dugouts beside an abandoned mine and wait for the weather to pass while Lincoln soon joins them, explaining that the rest of the town has begun a search party and will arrive shortly. Before leaving the shelter, Lucky conducts a small memorial for her mother, casting ashes to the wind with the townspeople present. Back home, Brigitte confronts Lucky with the truth: the papers found in Brigitte’s suitcase were part of a legal adoption, and Brigitte reveals her plan to open a restaurant in Hard Pan.

Dalgliesh undertakes a semi-official visit to Saint Anselm’s to review a student’s death that occurred some time earlier, prompted by the father’s dissatisfaction with the verdict. While there, a visiting Archdeacon is killed, and Dalgliesh takes charge of the ensuing inquiry, enlisting support from London detectives Miskin and Tarrant in addition to local officers. Early leads point to a college father who runs and teaches there, since the archdeacon had been urging the institution’s closure. As the investigation unfolds, two more murders occur. After questioning everyone present, a series of hidden truths comes to light: one student is unknowingly the son of a lay lecturer, and through his mother he stands to inherit the college’s assets if it is ever shut and sold. Forensic analysis seals the lecturer’s guilt, and he admits to the crime. The college is subsequently closed, with the inheritance passing to the student. Amid these events, Dalgliesh begins a romance with Dr Emma Lavenham, a visiting lecturer from Cambridge.

The narrative begins in autumn 1558, soon after Mary I’s death, with bells announcing that Elizabeth, Mary’s half-sister, has ascended to the throne. The tale unfolds through four principal viewpoints: Elizabeth I herself, her chief advisor William Cecil, Robert Dudley—Elizabeth’s favored confidant—and Amy Robsart, Dudley’s wife. Dudley returns to court at Elizabeth’s coronation, while Amy hopes his ambitions won’t jeopardize him. Under Mary’s reign, Dudley spent time in the Tower of London; his father and brother were executed, and another brother perished in Calais. Yet Amy’s optimism for a tranquil life proves short-lived as Elizabeth and Dudley grow nearer and more intimate. Elizabeth inherits a bankrupt, discontented realm already unsettled by the precedents set by the two previous monarchs. Cecil warns that Elizabeth’s survival hinges on marrying a powerful prince, yet her heart longs for her childhood friend—now a married man—Robert Dudley. Dudley believes he can reclaim his fate by standing beside Elizabeth. As the queen and her courtier fall in love, Dudley begins to confront a nearly impossible idea: abandoning his wife to wed the young queen.

The novel posits the existence of parallel worlds, some home to intelligent non-human species and others inhabited by English-speaking humans. Before the events unfold, one reality is overtaken by a malevolent force called Shadow. In the World of Shadow, magic flourishes and warriors clash with swords and sorcery within a classic high-fantasy setting. While scattered resistances survive, Shadow’s dominance leaves that world nearly subjugated by evil. A separate realm, the Galactic Empire, soon learns it is being invaded by Shadow’s minions and declares war. This Empire, a science-fiction relic of a bygone era akin to Flash Gordon or Buck Rogers, spans numerous planets colonized by advanced technology, with telepaths serving in its armed forces. Once hostilities begin, Empire telepaths establish contact with the World of Shadow; in turn, Shadow’s inhabitants sustain contact with the Empire through magical means. Mutual enmity notwithstanding, genuine alliance proves elusive due to vast cultural gaps. The Empire views Shadow’s people as brutish barbarians with little wartime utility, while Shadow’s inhabitants regard the Empire’s fascist regime as possibly the lesser evil. Eight years pass without meaningful cooperation from either side. Then the telepaths uncover a third, unnamed reality—modern-day Earth. Separately, both worlds dispatch diplomatic missions to Montgomery County, Maryland, where locals briefly dismiss them as either lunatics or a film crew. Eventually, a few open their minds and accept the travelers’ truth, agreeing to journey to the World of Shadow to confirm their sanity. Soon after their arrival, Shadow launches an assault, forcing the group to flee through a portal into the Galactic Empire to survive. Stranded across realities with scant hope of rescue, strangers from three different worlds must relinquish their differences and join forces if they intend to endure.

In 1994, an 18-year-old college student at UNLV named Moss embarked on his honors thesis research, which brought him into contact with notorious figures such as John Wayne Gacy, Richard Ramirez, Henry Lee Lucas, Jeffrey Dahmer, and Charles Manson. He collected samples of their correspondence and conducted interviews with them, then crafted his role to fit as a devoted follower, admirer, stand-in, or potential prey. Moss’s inquiry focused on what would captivate his subjects the most, guiding his strategic posture in the interactions. He even entertained a distant objective of a career with the FBI, arguing that earning a serial killer’s trust and probing their crimes or unsolved murders could bolster his job prospects. Among these connections, his rapport with Gacy grew the strongest. The correspondence escalated into regular Sunday-morning phone conversations, during which Gacy proclaimed his innocence while giving Moss a virtual tour of his worldview. Moss recounts in his book how his correspondence culminated in a face-to-face meeting with Gacy shortly before the killer’s execution. Interpreting the book’s title, Moss portrays himself as Gacy’s “last victim”–a prisoner of manipulation by a depraved sociopath once they met in person. This unsettling experience, Moss argues, taught him how a killer can coerce the vulnerable and... potentially exploit them as well. Moss ultimately took his own life in June 2006.

Five centuries after Earthfall’s end, Harmony’s lone original colonist remains: Shedemei, now donning the Cloak of the Starmaster, a conduit to the Oversoul. Centuries pass, and Nafai and Elemak’s lineages have built cities and towns, yet the old feud between the brothers lingers unforgotten. Yet the Oversoul still has not fulfilled its mission: locating the Keeper of Earth, the central intelligence capable of repairing the damaged counterpart at Harmony. The Keeper’s influence resumes spreading, and following the dreams, Shedemei chooses to return to Earth. This final Homecoming volume shifts away from the style and plot of the preceding four installments. All prior characters except Shedemei lie dead. The old Nafai–Elemak rivalry persists through their descendants, but it plays a secondary role here. The narrative centers on the struggles of Nafai’s followers’ descendants. Leading the action are the king of Darakemba, the empire founded by the Nafaris, his offspring and advisers, and the high priest of Darakemba with his progeny and converts, who drive the principal events of the tale.

In The Pirates of Silence, Fantasio gets an assignment from Le Moustique to write a story about Incognito City, a highly modernized city inhabited by wealthy celebrities and where security is tight and photography strictly forbidden. Fantasio gets around this by hiding miniature cameras in everyday items such as his pipe. But before he and Spirou leave, the Marsupilami surprisingly appears at their home, having somehow traveled alone from the Count's mansion in Champignac. Unable to reach the Count by phone, they drive to Incognito City and have an unpleasant traffic encounter with Juan Corto Dos Orejas, leaving them with a bad impression and a small object found on the ground. Further encounters with thugs and suspicious events slowly expose a fiendish plot, involving the kidnapping of the Count of Champignac. In The Quick Super, Fantasio sets out to test-drive a "Quick" (a large car manufactured by Genial Motors) for the week-end, in order to write a review for Spirou Méchanique. There are mysterious elements however, as all previously test-driven Quicks have ended up stolen, and this one is no exception. As the events unfold, old acquaintances from Circus Zabaglione (from Les voleurs du Marsupilami) reappear.

Japhy’s affinity for a pared-down lifestyle and Zen practice so profoundly shaped Kerouac that it colors the narrative on the eve of On the Road’s sudden fame, as Ray Smith’s tale unfolds around him. The plot oscillates between Smith and Ryder’s urban escapades—three-day parties and Buddhist Yab-Yum rituals—and the serene, almost sublime imagery Kerouac pursues in his search for transcendence. As the book nears its end, Kerouac shifts to a solitary voice, taking a post as a fire lookout on Desolation Peak by Hozomeen Mountain, in the landscape that would soon be designated North Cascades National Park (see Desolation Angels). These threads mark The Dharma Bums as a pivotal hinge, anticipating the consciousness-quest writings of 1960s figures such as Timothy Leary and Ken Kesey. A segment depicts Smith, Ryder, and Henry Morley (a stand-in for Kerouac’s real friend John Montgomery) scaling Matterhorn Peak in California, recounting Kerouac’s first foray into this mountaineering mode. That episode would fuel his resolve to spend the ensuing summer serving as a U.S. Forest Service fire lookout on Washington’s Desolation Peak. The novel also recounts the legendary 1955 Six Gallery reading, where Allen Ginsberg unveiled his poem “Howl” (renamed “Wail” within the book), alongside performances by Snyder, Kenneth Rexroth, Michael McClure, and Philip Whalen.

Algarve renews an assault in the south of Unkerlant toward the Mamming Hills, which is Unkerlant's source of cinnabar, leading to the mammoth Battle of Sulingen. Kaunian refugees begin showing up in Zuwayza, which takes them in; other Kaunians get away from a caravan in Valmiera and come to the attention of Skarnu and his friends (who had blown up the caravan to disrupt the Algarvians) or are set loose in a Lagoan raid on a camp in Valmiera. Leofsig is killed by Sidroc, who joins the Plegmund's Brigade. Istvan and his squad accidentally eat goat stew in a raid on a camp in Unkerlant's western forest and are purified by their captain. The Algarvians kill Kaunians in the Land of the Ice People in an attempt to use magic against the Lagoans, but the magic from the killed Kaunians slaughters the Algarvian army instead, and Algarve is forced to withdraw from the continent completely, leaving it to the Lagoans. The wear on the Algarvians is showing as they start to rely more on Sibians, Forthwegians, and the unreliable Yaninans to keep up the fight against Unkerlant. The Battle of Sulingen is won by the Unkerlanters that winter, with Trasone dying in the very last scene in the book. Algarve is on the way to losing the war. The Naantali Project starts, and the Kuusamans take Obuda.

The novel is written in the first-person, continuing the aesthetic of Ellis' earlier Less Than Zero, and is told from the points of view of multiple characters. The main narrators are three students: Paul, Sean, and Lauren. A number of other characters also provide first-hand accounts throughout the story, which takes place at the fictional Camden College, a liberal arts school on the East Coast of the United States. The three main characters (who rarely attend class) end up in a love triangle within a sequence of drug runs, "Dress to Get Screwed", and "End of the World" parties. The story begins midway through a sentence (the first word being 'and') in order to give the effect that it begins somewhere closer to the middle, rather than at a true beginning (in medias res). Another interpretation is that the story has neither a beginning nor an ending, signifying the endless cycle of debauchery in which the characters of the novel engage. This is sometimes mistaken by readers as a typographical error or the result of a missing page, but was purposely done by Ellis. The novel ends in a similar fashion, with the last sentence cut off before it ends.

The protagonist of the novel is Benedykt Gierosławski, a Polish mathematician and notorious gambler, collaborating with Alfred Tarski on his work on many-valued logics. The Ministry of Winter's officials visit Gierosławski and make him embark on a Transsiberian journey to find his lost father, who is said to be able to communicate with Lute. During his journey Gieroslawski finds out that he is caught in a political intrigue, brought about by rivalry between two palace factions, liedniacy (conservatives and Siberian entrepreneurs backing the idea of "frozen Russia") and ottiepelnicy (mostly revolutionaries aiming for a literal and political "thaw"), supported also by the Tsar. He also meets Nikola Tesla in disguise, who has conceived a technology for manipulating and eventually destroying the Ice and has been hired by the Tsar to relieve Russia from the Winter. During the journey and upon his arrival in Irkutsk Gierosławski discovers that various political forces, including Followers of St. Marcyn, a sect worshiping the Ice led by Rasputin, followers of Nikolai Fyodorovich Fyodorov, who strive for assuring human immortality, and Siberian industrial potentates, are interested in his person and that Józef Piłsudski, in this reality leading a group of Sybiraks and Siberian separatists fighting for Polish independence, may possess knowledge about his father.

Blair Maynard, a divorced journalist in New York City, decides to write a story about the unexplained disappearance of yachts and other small boats in the Caribbean, hoping to debunk theories about the Bermuda Triangle. He has weekend custody of his preteen son Justin, and decides to mix a vacation with work, taking his son along. They fly from Miami to the Turks and Caicos island chain but, while on fishing trip, are captured by a band of pirates. The pirates have, amazingly, remained undetected since the establishment of their pirate enclave by Jean-David Nau, the notorious buccaneer L'Olonnais, in 1671 (in reality, however, L'Olonnais is known to have died four years earlier). The pirates have a constitution of sorts, called the Covenant, and have a cruel but workable society. They raise any children they capture to ensure the survival of the colony, but kill anyone over the age of thirteen. In short order, Justin is virtually brainwashed and groomed to lead the pirate band, much to Maynard's horror. Maynard tries repeatedly to escape, and finally attracts the attention of the passing United States Coast Guard cutter New Hope. The pirates attack and capture it, but Maynard is able to use a machine gun aboard to kill most of the pirates and to win Justin's and his own freedom.

Hillary Van Wetter sits on death row for killing a corrupt local sheriff, Thurmond Call, who had earlier bludgeoned Wetter’s handcuffed cousin to death. While imprisoned, Wetter is courted by Charlotte Bless, a woman who has never met him but is hopelessly enamored and determined to secure his freedom and wed him. Bless radiates intense sexual magnetism, intensifying every encounter. She seeks Wetter’s exoneration by roping in two sensationalist Miami reporters: Yardley Acheman, ambitious and hungry for a scandal, and Ward James, earnest and idealistic, a hometown boy returning to the place of Wetter’s confinement who harbors conflicted feelings. Convinced that a redneck-justice narrative could win a Pulitzer, they believe Wetter’s innocence can be proven through risky journalism. Yet the reporters bend the rules—skimming facts, glossing over minor contradictions, and exploiting the story, even bedding Charlotte. With their backing, Wetter is freed and the duo earns the Pulitzer. Soon, however, the public’s perception shifts: Wetter proves not to be the victim the journalists portrayed. After marrying Charlotte, he murders her, and overwhelmed by remorse, Ward ends his own life.

Kirn’s novel follows Justin Cobb, a Minnesota teenager whose family endures a wide range of dysfunction. His father, Mike, is a washed-up college football star whose militaristic, emotionless demeanor mirrors his old coach. Audrey, his mother and a nurse, wrestles with accepting how reduced her life has become. Joel, the younger brother, does his best to blend in and appear normal. At 14, pressured to quit thumb-sucking, Justin seeks help from unorthodox dentist Perry Lyman, who attempts hypnosis to cure the habit, with limited success: the thumb-sucking stops, yet new problematic behaviors emerge in its place. Justin begins acting strangely, and his school identifies him as having attention deficit disorder, resulting in a prescription for Ritalin. The medication provides temporary relief, but it merely glosses over deeper issues that beset Justin and his family. When he stops taking Ritalin, he turns to drugs (marijuana), sex, and religion to cope. Eventually, weary of this life, Justin returns to Lyman, who reminds him that everyone has flaws; the aim isn’t to fix them, but to live with them. Armed with that perspective, Justin is sent to serve as a Mormon missionary in New York and, once again, finds himself thumb-sucking, at the cost of the drugs and sex. This coming-of-age story probes the raw emotions of adolescence while exploring broader themes of identity and existentialism. ru:Дурная привычка (фильм)

The story begins in a prison in Occupied France during World War II. It is decreed that one in every ten prisoners is to be executed; lots are drawn to decide who will die. One of the men chosen is a rich lawyer. He offers all his money to anyone who will take his place. One man agrees. Upon his release from prison the lawyer must face the consequences of his actions. The story comprises four parts. In Part I, set in prison, the occupying German guards issue a decimation order to the thirty inmates. One of the three chosen by drawing lots is a rich lawyer named Chavel. Chavel becomes hysterical and desperately offers his entire wealth to any man willing to die in his place. A young man, known as Janvier, accepts his offer and is executed. In Part II, the war is over and Chavel is alive and free, but virtually destitute. He returns to the house he sold for his life and finds it occupied by Janvier’s mother and sister, Thérèse. Assuming the false name Charlot, he becomes their servant. Part III sees the arrival of an impostor, named Carosse, who claims to be Chavel. Carosse attempts to denounce Charlot, win the favour of Thérèse and stake a claim on the property. Finally in Part IV, Charlot, having fallen in love with Thérèse, must save her from Carosse, as a means of redemption from his earlier cowardice.

Raised amid the serene splendor of the Summer Country, Princess Guenevere has known a sheltered, serene existence until a sudden, brutal death strikes down Queen Maire, plunging the realm toward anarchy. The miraculous arrival of Arthur, rightful heir of the Pendragon line, enables Guenevere to claim the throne her mother once held. Captivated by the bold and sensuous princess, Arthur proposes marriage to unite their lands while permitting Guenevere to govern in her own right. Their union creates the largest, most formidable kingdom across the isles. Yet Arthur’s Golden Age begins to falter when he reconnects with his mother and his long-lost half-sisters, Morgause and Morgan. Before Arthur’s birth, their father, the ruthless King Uther, banished the king’s wife’s daughters—Morgause into a cruel marriage and Morgan to a distant convent—setting the stage for centuries of grievance. Each sister has motive to avenge herself, but only one will unleash the deadliest assaults against the King and Queen, wielding sorcery to shatter all Guenevere cherishes. When the Queen withdraws to Avalon, even her union with Arthur comes under peril. Amid the ensuing turmoil, a young knight arrives at Arthur’s court, pledging service to the Queen. Guenevere’s fidelity to Arthur wavers, and she falls for Lancelot, a passion that threatens to topple Camelot.

During a post-concert cleanup in Yorkshire in 1969, volunteers uncover a young woman’s corpse wrapped in a sleeping bag, brutally slain. The case is assigned to Detective Stanley Chadwick, a hardened Second World War veteran whose rigid, conventional outlook clashes with the era’s rebellious, long-haired hippies, their marijuana, and the thrum of rock and roll. Determined to solve the murder, Chadwick suspects the victim had ties to the rising psychedelic folk-tinged group, the Mad Hatters. In the present day, Inspector Alan Banks probes the killing of a freelance music journalist who was writing a feature on the Mad Hatters for MOJO magazine. This isn’t the first brush with tragedy for the band, now aging rock icons; Banks must root through history to uncover the hornet’s nest provoked by the journalist’s report and how it all connects to the murder.”

The tale centers on Vikraman, the son of a fictional Chola king named Parthiban, and his attempt to throw off Pallava suzerainty under Narasimhavarman. The Cholas are portrayed as vassals, yearning to reclaim the bygone imperial glory that they believe has faded with their loss of sovereignty. Parthiban passes this longing to Vikraman, urging him to restore the dynasty’s former prominence. Refusing Pallava taxes triggers a Pallava assault on the Cholas. In the ensuing conflict, Parthiban falls, and a mysterious monk on the battlefield vows to ensure Vikraman fulfills his father’s dream. As time passes, Vikraman matures with plans to strike back at Narasimhavarman. His uncle, Marappa Bhupathi, betrays him, leading to Vikraman’s arrest and exile from India by the Pallavas. The narrative then follows his return, driven by a desire to reunite with his mother and the enigmatic beauty he had glimpsed before exile. Tragically, he learns his mother has vanished—indeed kidnapped by the ruthless Kapalikas, a tribe practicing human sacrifice. He also discovers that Kundhavi, the woman he loves, is the daughter of his arch-enemy Narasimhavarman. The climax reveals the monk’s true identity as the Pallava king Narasimhavarman and marks the establishment of an independent Chola realm under Vikraman at Uraiyur. In the finale, Vikraman weds Kundhavi.

Nana Saheb, adopted son of Bajirao II—the final Maratha Peshwa—and rightful heir to the office of the Maratha prime minister, was reared in extraordinary wealth. Though his father’s authority had already been stripped by the British, Nana Saheb grew up as a Brahmin prince and later carried himself with urbanity and refinement. After Bajirao II’s death, the British refused to acknowledge Nana Saheb’s title yet allowed him to remain in a comfortable exile at Bithoor. Though cordial toward many British people—some of whom were close friends—Nana Saheb could not accept their domination and the exploitation of India. With the outbreak of the 1857 mutiny in May, he found himself compelled into a leadership role. What followed was a protracted, ultimately futile conflict marked by brutal acts on both sides. Eventually, Nana Saheb fled to Nepal, where he obtained a wary sanctuary. He departed with an Englishwoman he had rescued and with whom he had fallen in love. Decades later, he returned to India briefly before seeking refuge once more, this time in Istanbul, the city where he would compose and deposit his memoirs.

Oliver Russell longs for power and seems destined to ascend to the presidency. His fiancée, Leslie Stewart, betrayed, dedicates herself to the sole aim of ruining him. After building her own media empire and mobilizing every resource against him, she stands ready to crush Russell just as he reaches the peak of triumph. Yet her plan backfires, for she is unaware that she herself is stepping into a trap. Upon Oliver’s return from Paris, he is married to Jan, and Leslie swears vengeance—but keeps her thoughts tightly guarded. This secrecy draws Todd Davis, Jan’s father, to introduce her to a friend who owns a newspaper. A brief acquaintance leads to marriage, and Leslie comes to run her husband’s business empire. As his health declines and death follows, Leslie becomes the sole proprietor of his holdings. Despite other ventures, the allure of the media empire grips her, and she schemes to use it against Oliver. In the midst of these developments, Dana Evans—the heroine from Sheldon’s other novel Sky is Falling—appears as an keen investigative reporter who adopts a boy from war-torn Sarajevo. Meanwhile, Oliver ascends to the presidency, but his first term is marred by a string of deaths linked to Liquid Ecstasy, a dangerous aphrodisiac. Leslie’s conviction that Oliver is behind the killings drives her to publish word of his arrest before it’s confirmed. Dana Evans ultimately exposes the true culprit, and the president reveals a startling secret. The novel closes with Oliver proposing a peace pact brokered by his administration among Arab nations, leaving Leslie to ponder whether her vendetta has gone too far.

At the outset, Blacky frets over the looming grand final and the weight of his new role as the team’s primary ruck. His formidable opponent is the unstoppable Thumper, and to shield himself he conceives the Thumper tackle—a defensive ploy that parades as a tackle but is, in truth, a clever dodge. The after-party of the game brings a different kind of pressure: the coach’s son receives the Best On Ground award, a choice he believes should have gone to Dumby Red, the team’s brightest star. Shortly thereafter, news breaks that Dumby and his two brothers were shot dead during a robbery at a Public Bar, a catastrophe that splinters Blacky’s emotional world. The winter that follows sees him avoiding responsibility in a mirror of his earlier tactics. By the next summer, however, he grasps the necessity of taking a stand, and he finally does. His brothers and sisters rally beside him, and the novel closes with Blacky at peace with himself, content in his bond with his siblings, and confident that he can face future challenges that morning may bring.

Mary Lou Finney isn’t thrilled about spending her summer keeping a journal, and the assignment is coupled with reading The Odyssey, a text she often ties to her own experiences. When her cousin Carl Ray comes to stay, ostensibly to search for work, his eventual employment at Mr. Furtz’s hardware store becomes a turning point in the story. Throughout the season, Mary Lou learns about the hardships Carl Ray has endured and discovers why he never makes his bed during a trip to visit his parents. Her social world expands as she spends time with her best friend Beth Ann and begins dating Alex Cheevey. As events unfold, Mary Lou confronts tensions within her family and reflects on her evolving sense of self. Sharon Creech has said that the novel drew its spark from a time when she lived abroad in England and Switzerland for about a decade, missing her relatives back in the United States. She recalls wanting to write about ordinary family chaos as a way to feel close to home, which she began by trying to remember what growing up in her family was like. Writing the story, she explained, helped her imagine her family right there with her in their small cottage in England.

Pauline Hannum, a strikingly young and beautiful daughter of the recently deceased Major Hannum, who also appears as a performer in his circus, visits The Magic Shop owned by The Great Merlini. She shows an unusually high willingness to pay well above the normal price to receive a “Headless Lady” illusion instantly. Moved by Merlini’s fascination with circuses, Merlini and his writer friend Ross Harte embark on an inquiry into her demand. Their investigation quickly uncovers evidence that Major Hannum’s death was likely murder, and that the culprit may still have urgent, dangerous business tied to a real headless lady whose head has vanished. Joined by a new ally, detective-writer Stuart Towne, Merlini and Harte uncover a raft of revealing backstage details about the circus world—such as why the orchestra’s playing of Suppé’s Light Cavalry March is considered bad luck, what the mummified remains of John Wilkes Booth are made of, and a method for forging fingerprints without loops or whorls. To solve the case, Merlini must wield his magical prowess to break out of an apparently escape-proof jail, gather the suspects, and disclose the murderer in a climactic, twist-filled finale.”

Lyman Ward narrates a century after the fact. Lyman interprets the story at times and leaves gaps that he points out at other times. Some of the disappointments of his life, including his divorce, color his interpretation of his grandparents' story. Toward the end of the novel, he gives up on his original ambition of writing a complete biography of his grandmother. Stegner's use of Mary Hallock Foote's historical letters gives the novel's locations—Leadville, New Almaden, Idaho, and Mexico—an authentic feel; the letters also add vividness to the Wards' struggles with the environment, shady businessmen, and politicians. Lyman's position in the contemporary culture of the late sixties provides another historical dimension to the story. Foils for this plot line include Lyman's adult son, a Berkeley-trained sociologist who sees little value in history, and a neighbor's daughter who helps transcribe Lyman's tape-recorded notes while she is home on summer break from UC Berkeley, where she has been active in the "hippie" counterculture movement.

The vast lake, Lake Agassiz, covered much of North Dakota, Manitoba and Minnesota during prehistoric times. The story begins when farmer Tom Lasker and his son, Will, uncover a seemingly brand new yacht. Found on a landlocked farm, it draws tourists to the area. Max Collingswood, a friend of Tom's, tries to help discover the origins of the boat. Collingswood enlists April Cannon, a worker at a chemical lab who discovers that the yacht is made of an unknown material. In fact, it is a fiberglass-like material with an impossible atomic number (161). Collingswood and Cannon discover something else on a nearby ridge which is part of a Sioux reservation. The Sioux assist in its excavation and examination. It turns out to a green glassy roundhouse-like structure, made from the same material. Eventually, they gain access to it, revealing a dock for the sailboat, but no entrance for it. The discovery that the structure contains the means to access other sites not on Earth sets off a struggle between the Government and the Reservation for control of it.

In Calcutta, Protima, Inspector Ghote’s wife, has inherited wealth and a grand house, a development that unsettles Ghote because it forces him to abandon Mumbai and leave policing behind. Soon after arriving, the couple finds their new residence dilapidated and besieged by hostile squatters. A nearby wetlands area is slated for a housing project, and it happens to provide the only access route to the proposed development. Their solicitor, A. K. Dutt-Daster, who manages the will, urges a quick sale and a return to their former life, but Ghote suspects there is corruption at play. His inquiry uncovers a sprawling network of graft that climbs the social and political ladder of Calcutta. Along the way, he engages with a clerk who, though easily bribable, becomes a liability after he acquires incriminating documents from Dutt-Daster’s files and is murdered. Ghote is assaulted beneath The Great Banyan tree in the Indian Botanical Gardens, and crosses paths with a crusading newspaper editor who chooses his battles with care, a hardened and corrupt police inspector, and a powerful businessman who views bribery as acceptable. The odds—anchored by influential adversaries—press in from all sides, and the elderly couple’s position looks increasingly untenable. In the end, Ghote is compelled to pay a substantial bribe to ensure their escape from Calcutta with their freedom and lives. As he contemplates the inevitability of corruption and bribery in life, Ghote contends that such realities do not justify surrendering to them.

When Mr. and Mrs. Lane invited charming French woman Annette Reynaud to their brownstone for dinner with the family, they had no idea that she was a jewel burglar whose real name was Michelle, and that Mrs. Lane's younger brother Richard Duffy had known Michelle from his past. Richard privately warned Michelle from having any ideas about his sister's home, but she assured him she was retired, having come to USA to get away from those who demanded she work for them. Shortly afterwards though, he got a strange phone call from her hinting she was in trouble but could not speak freely. The clues she gave in her talk were 'nice', 'park' and 'au revoir'. That got Richard and his nephew Stephen Lane to fly to Nice, booked into a Hotel Parc and saw from binoculars that Michelle was on board a yacht named Au Revoir. Faking a chance meeting, Richard learned that Michelle was being compelled to stage a diamond heist for a gang, whose mastermind's name she was hoping to learn to trade with the police. They even got ready imitations for Michelle to replace the real stones during the heist. With no other recourse available, Richard and Stephen could only keep a close watch on Michelle while trying not to be discovered. Their only ally was the police inspector Armand Duval, who was only prepared to take a chance on their crazy story because there was really a gang of thieves operating in the area, having stolen some very precious stones. The gang was likened to a hydra, and so far, the police only managed to get hold of the lowly footpads but had no inkling about the mastermind.

There are two main protagonists and two main antagonists. The protagonists are Koot Hoomie "Kootie" Parganas and Pete "Teet" Sullivan. Kootie is an eleven-year old boy and Sullivan is a man in his early 40's. The novel takes place mostly in Los Angeles in the year 1992, and there are references to the United States presidential election. The main antagonists are Sherman Oaks and Loretta deLarava. As in Last Call, the previous novel of Tim Powers' Fault Line series, a prominent theme is the quest for immortality. Oaks' age is unknown, deLarava's age is 76 (but she often appears to be younger); both have been prolonging their lives by ingesting ghosts. There is a magical system surrounding these ghosts - their behavior, how they are ingested, how to catch them so that they may be ingested, and even a mysterious market where the bottled ghosts are bought and sold. In their ready-to-be digested state, they are known as "smokes" or "cigars". The narrative is propelled by this chase for ghosts. Koot Hoomie Parganas has unwittingly ingested the ghost of Thomas Edison. However, because Kootie hasn't yet reached puberty, he isn't able to digest it. In its undigested state, the ghost of Edison functions as a helper to Kootie. Because of Edison's powerful personality, this ghost is particularly sought after by both antagonists who wish to ingest it themselves. In addition, Loretta deLarava is pursuing the ghost of Pete Sullivan's father.
