If Loretta deLarava manages to capture Pete Sullivan, it will help her to locate Pete Sullivan's father's ghost, Arthur Patrick "Apie" Sullivan. Pete Sullivan has his own helper, a former psychiatrist named Angelica Anthem Elizalde. Loretta deLarava also pursues Solomon Shadroe. Shadroe is the former Nicky Bradshaw. Shadroe/Bradshaw is also a son of Arthur Patrick "Apie" Sullivan, albeit a godson. Shadroe/Bradshaw played "Spooky" in a fictional situation comedy called "Ghost of a Chance".

The book harshly critiques Richard Fuld, Henry Paulson, and the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act of 1999, the Congressional measure signed by Bill Clinton that repealed parts of the Glass–Steagall Act of 1933. It recounts how, after completing his studies at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, McDonald sold pork chops, taught himself the material needed to pass the General Securities Representative Exam, and then built ConvertBond.com, a site eventually acquired by Morgan Stanley. The author credits his expertise in the convertible-bond market as the driving force behind launching ConvertBond.com during the dot-com boom and his successful sale to Morgan Stanley before the market bubble burst. While employed at Morgan Stanley, McDonald received an offer to serve as vice president at Lehman Brothers. The narration depicts Richard Fuld as detached, arrogant, and a harsh, hot-tempered, ruthless chief executive with a tendency toward anger, whom the book mockingly labels as “his majesty,” “god-like,” and a “spiritual leader.” McDonald contends that the U.S. government should have rescued Lehman Brothers, and that Fuld wrongly assumed federal intervention would come after a spring 2008 meeting with Henry Paulson, a miscalculation that spurred him to take on unnecessary risk and to reject an $18-per-share proposal from the Korea Development Bank as late as August 2008.

The two main characters are thinly-veiled versions of two of Farmer's favorite characters, Tarzan and Doc Savage. Called "Lord Grandrith" and "Doc Caliban", respectively, the two are recognizable as the iconic characters, but still unique. The two, half-brothers with the same father (the infamous Victorian era serial killer, Jack the Ripper) share a horrible affliction thanks to the powerful elixir that gives them near-eternal life. At the start of the novel they have discovered that they can no longer engage in sexual activity except during acts of violence (their penises become erect only during an act of violence) and they ejaculate after taking lives. By the end of the novel, Grandrith and Caliban will have grappled with each other in the nude, punching, clawing and biting, each of them sporting massive erections. The novel begins with Grandrith under attack by three parties: the Kenyan army, a group of Albanian mercenaries, and Doc Caliban who believes that Grandrith has killed Caliban's cousin and one true love. In addition, both Caliban and Grandrith have been summoned for their annual appear before The Nine, a powerful group of near immortals, who have given them both the secret of immortality in return for their obedience. However, Caliban and Grandrith ultimately find a common enemy among the Nine that is revealed to be controlling the world, and to have been manipulating their own lives, and indeed, the entire preceding battle between the two. The two iconic warriors vow to defeat the Nine together—that tale is told in the intertwining sequels, Lord of the Trees and The Mad Goblin.

A psychiatric patient, having wandered off course, finds himself in the land of Kappa. There, he is welcomed as a distinguished guest and engages in conversations with Kappas from various professions. Geeru, a radical capitalist, declares that Kappa’s unemployed workers are slain and their flesh is repurposed as sustenance. The patient is stunned, yet Geeru argues that the patient’s objections are merely sentimental, noting that the poorest Japanese women are forced into prostitution simply to survive. Kappa’s national character is framed as a blend of materialism and nihilistic realism, and the babies of Kappa supposedly determine their own fates. In the womb, a fetus may reject life as a Kappa and be aborted. The Maggu—an introspective Kappa who commits suicide—haunts the living as a ghost inhabiting Tokku, a poet. Maggu worries about posthumous fame, even as he admires writers and philosophers who died by suicide, such as Heinrich von Kleist and Otto Weininger. Eventually the patient is set to return to the human world, but he reflects that Kappa remains pristine and superior to human society, leading him to become misanthropic.

It is Christmastime. A living lump of coal falls off a barbecue grill. He wishes for a miracle to happen. The lump of coal is artistic and wants to be an artist. He goes in search of something. First, he finds an art gallery that, he believes, shows art by lumps of coal. But when he comes in, he sadly discovers the art is by humans who use lumps of coal. He then finds a Korean restaurant called Mr. Wong's Korean Restaurant and Secretarial School, but he goes in and discovers that all things used must be 100% Korean (although the owner does not use a Korean name or proper Korean spices). The lump of coal continues down the street and runs into a man dressed like Santa Claus. The lump of coal tells the man about his problem, and the man gets an idea. He suggests he put the lump of coal in Jasper (his bratty son)'s stocking. The son finds it and is ecstatic; he has wanted to make art with coal. So he makes portraits and he and the lump of coal become rich. They move to Korea and open an actual genuine Korean restaurant and have a gallery of their art.

Set in Swinging London, the novel describes one day in the life of Adam Appleby, who lives in constant fear that his wife might be pregnant again with a fourth child. As Catholics, they are denied any form of contraception and have to play "Vatican roulette" instead. Adam and Barbara have three children: Clare, Dominic, and Edward; their friends ask if they intend working through the whole alphabet. In the course of only one busy day, several chances to make some money present themselves to Adam. For example, he is offered the opportunity to edit a deceased scholar's unpublished manuscripts; however, when he eventually has a look at them, he feels uncomfortable realizing that the man's writings are worthless drivel. Also, at the house in Bayswater where he is supposed to get the papers, Adam has to cope with an assortment of weird characters ranging from butchers to a young virgin intent on seducing him. Lodge's novel makes extensive use of pastiche, incorporating passages where both the motifs and the styles of writing used by various authors are imitated. For instance, there is a Kafkaesque scene where Adam has to renew his reading-room ticket. The final chapter of the novel is a monologue by Adam's wife in the style of Molly Bloom's soliloquy in Ulysses. This use of different styles mirrors James Joyce's Ulysses, a work also about a single day. When Lodge's novel first came out, quite a number of reviewers and critics, not appreciating the literary allusions, found fault with Lodge for his inhomogeneous writing.

The story concerns Lancelot who has survived to the present day by means of magic. He must help Morgana le Fay confront Merlin, who is half-mad and attempting to meddle in the affairs of the world. Lancelot has remained alive since the fall of Camelot, having the appearance of an elderly man but retaining his strength and fighting skills. He has spent his long life seeking the Holy Grail, believing that his immortality is punishment for his sins, and that finding the Grail will end his curse. Lancelot instead learns from Morgana le Fay that Merlin is responsible for his condition. Merlin has slept for centuries, but is about to awaken, and intends for Lancelot to be his champion and protector. Morgana warns Lancelot that Merlin will cause great harm in his misguided attempts to right the wrongs of the modern world, and that he must be stopped. Lancelot finds Merlin and rejuvenates him from his centuries-long sleep with a magic elixir. Lancelot tries to persuade Merlin to desist from his plans, and Merlin removes the spell of immortality. Anticipating Merlin, Lancelot drinks the remainder of the elixir to restore his own youth. Merlin summons a "hollow knight" (a suit of armor animated by a spirit) to kill Lancelot. Morgana defeats Merlin, and Lancelot vanquishes the spirit, but is mortally wounded. As Lancelot dies, he finally sees a vision of the Holy Grail.

Democracy in America centers on explaining why republican representative government has thrived in the United States yet faltered in numerous other contexts. Tocqueville aims to transpose the functional strengths of American democracy onto the perceived shortcomings of democracy in his homeland, France. He then speculates about the future trajectory of American democracy, outlining potential threats and perils it may face. Among these concerns are his warnings that democracy can slide into “soft despotism” and that a tyranny of the majority could emerge. He notes that religion assumes a robust, influential role in the United States precisely because it remains separate from government—a separation that all political factions endorse. By contrast, he sees in France a corrosive tension between democrats and religion, a tension he links to the intertwining of church and state. In Volume II, Tocqueville enriches his political analysis with a portrayal of civil society as a realm of private and nonstate life. His outlook on America darkens after 1840, a shift that is documented by Aurelian Craiutu in Tocqueville on America after 1840: Letters and Other Writings.”

At the outset, Tamis, a sorceress, gazes into the future and realizes that only a mixed-blood Spartan named Parmenion can assist her. Parmenion—a half-blood Spartan whose mother hails from Macedon—is a gifted runner and a strategic mind, yet he is scorned by the young Spartan nobles. After killing a rival in a duel to defend a love, he is forced to flee to Thebes. There he begins a new life as a professional runner and becomes entangled with Theban rebels seeking to dislodge the Spartan garrison entrenched in the city’s heart. This involvement sparks a protracted war between the two polities, culminating in Parmenion’s decisive rout of the Spartan army and the destruction of the Spartan legend. Years later, he has become a celebrated mercenary general, earning victories across Asia. He then receives an invitation to help rebuild the Macedonian army under Philip II of Macedon. The tale subsequently traces the rise of Macedon under Philip II and the birth of Alexander the Great. fr:Le Lion de Macédoine pl:Lew Macedonii

A looming global crisis becomes evident to the Maasai when ominous, otherworldly beings known as shetani begin to emerge from a separate dimension they call the Out Of, the place from which all beings originally originate. These malevolent entities manipulate tensions between major powers, seeking to ignite conflict and even war. Without intervention, the gateway between worlds could rupture and an infinite tide of shetani would overrun the Earth, annihilating all life. To avert disaster, Maasai elder Olkeloki travels to Washington, D.C., to brief the U.S. President and solicit aid. There he meets two unlikely allies: Joshua Oak, a disillusioned FBI agent, and Merry Sharrow, a reserved call-center employee unsettled by her own life. Believing they are pivotal in the struggle, Olkeloki convinces them to accompany him back to Africa, where Maasai warriors strive to suppress the intruding beings. In time, Olkeloki leads Oak and Merry into the Out Of itself, and with their assistance he conducts a ritual that closes the dimensional breach, even though it costs him his supernatural powers. The trio returns to the ordinary world to find the shetani’s schemes thwarted and the political crisis easing. In addition, Oak and Merry discover a personal bond they had been seeking throughout the ordeal.

High above a troubled China where beasts contend with machines for dominance, a delicate network of hot-air balloons known as the Sky Village floats. When Mei Long, twelve, learns her mother has been kidnapped, her father sends her to live among strangers in the sky, amid mounting danger. Across the world, thirteen-year-old Rom Saint-Pierre fights to endure in a Las Vegas overrun by beast-controlled forces. After his younger sister is abducted by two demonic beings, Rom must pursue them into a shadowy subterranean realm. There he becomes drawn into gladiator-style arena combat, where battles between mechanical-beast demons entertain a chaotic gambling community. Although Mei and Rom have never met, they exchange through connected journals—books that mysteriously enable their communication. The journals also disclose that both carry the enigmatic and terrifying Kaimira gene, fusing beastly and mek attributes in their very DNA. This intricately plotted novel, the first in a five-book series, follows Mei and Rom as they confront the powers bent on destroying them and summon the courage to marshal the conflicting forces within. Their only hope for survival—and for saving those they love—depends on it.

In the Alberta wilderness, far from civilization, a remote setting frames the action. The world mirrors ours in many ways, yet rumors and signs of werewolves and other supernatural oddities linger as faint but acknowledged possibilities. The story begins with Cheyenne “Chey” Clarke leaping from a plane and landing amid the rugged terrain, carrying a substantial array of hiking gear that she promptly loses in the harsh environment. A violent encounter soon follows: a werewolf—clearly more than a mere wolf—attacks, but Chey fights it off, sustaining only a scratch that nevertheless curses her with lycanthropy. As she roams the wilds, she encounters the elusive Dzo, who then introduces her to Monty Powell, a werewolf and possibly the same creature that attacked her. It becomes clear, during their interaction, that Chey had already come with a hidden mission to find the werewolf and is collaborating with external backers who want him eliminated. After a botched assassination attempt on Powell, Chey is left under the guardianship of those backers, serving as bait to draw Powell in, while her own future—whether she remains useful to them or faces a different fate—hangs in the balance.

As volunteers clean up after a huge outdoor rock concert in Yorkshire in 1969, they discover the body of a young woman wrapped in a sleeping bag. She has been brutally murdered. The detective assigned to the case, Stanley Chadwick, is a hard-headed, strait-laced veteran of the Second World War. He could not have less in common with - or less regard for - young, disrespectful, long-haired hippies, smoking marijuana and listening to the pulsing sounds of rock and roll. But he has a murder to solve, and it looks as if the victim was somehow associated with the up-and-coming psychedelic pastoral band the Mad Hatters. In the present, Inspector Alan Banks is investigating the murder of a freelance music journalist who was working on a feature about the Mad Hatters for MOJO magazine. This is not the first time that the Mad Hatters, now aging rock superstars, have been brushed by tragedy. Banks finds he has to delve into the past to find out exactly what hornets' nest the journalist inadvertently stirred up.

The narrative centers on Josef, a grandfather who recounts events in the first person. After returning from Soviet captivity at war’s end, he discovers his wife Katharina entangled in an affair. Throughout the tale, he pursues reconciliation with her, and his efforts bear fruit as she descends into madness and increasingly seeks him out. The lineage unfolds across generations, exposing strained, damaged souls and a string of murders, including his son’s death by suicide. A pivotal moment reveals Josef’s wartime order to execute a Russian commissar, carried out under the grim, punitive logic of the Commissar Order, without room for mercy. In a needless act, he then kills another crouching figure who is already dead. Later, Katharina’s mental turmoil is explained: the “visitors” she imagines inhabiting their apartment are really deceased family members. They reappear in the narrative as a quasi-ghostly troupe on a fictional plane, while the living protagonists seem to be real. The reader discerns this reversal as the actual kin begin to die. In the conclusion, the storyteller’s perspective shifts to reveal that the narrator himself is, in truth, the spirits of the slain boys.

The book opens with Richard Bolitho arriving at an inn frequented by Midshipmen in Portsmouth. There he meets another midshipman Martyn Dancer. They are retrieved by a lieutenant from the Gorgon. The ship sails towards West Africa, where they encounter an empty Merchantman, the City of Athens. Dancer and Bolitho are sent aboard the ship, and discover that the ship has been pillaged and the crew killed. The officers soon deduce that the ship was raided by Pirates and Captain Conway announces that the Admiralty had dispatched them to investigate the disappearance of ships in the region. In company with the captured City of Athens, the Gorgon approaches a coastal fort surrounded by treacherous reefs and shoals. Upon approaching the fort, they see that two ships are in the nearby harbour, however the fort opens fire and destroys the City of Athens. The Gorgon withdraws and returns during the dark of the night to cut out the ship. Dancer and Bolitho are sent on the mission, commanded by the 4th lieutenant, Mr. Tregorren, who holds a grudge and mistreats Bolitho over Bolitho's prestigious heritage. They succeed at taking the ship, and also capture a Slave Dhow in the escape with the help of the Gorgon. The ships, under the guise at being members of the pilot fleet raid the castle from which the pirates had been using as a base.

Summer settles over Lake Eden, Minnesota, and excitement runs high for the family reunion that Hannah’s partner, Lisa, has organized. Unexpectedly, Uncle Gus returns after a thirty-year absence, arriving with lavish jewelry, stylish outfits, and a new car, instantly becoming the focal point of the gathering. The responsibility of supplying the treats falls to Hannah Swensen, owner of The Cookie Jar bakery, who serves up one of her specialties—carrot cake—that proves especially popular. Gus admires the cake and requests another tray, but the next day, during the family reunion photo session, one person is conspicuously missing. Hannah searches for Gus and discovers him at the pavilion bar, near two pieces of carrot cake, dead from an ice-pick stabbing. The mystery falls squarely on Hannah to unravel. With Grandpa Jack showing signs of Alzheimer’s, suspicion initially points toward him as the killer, but Hannah believes he is innocent and sets out to clear him. The story also includes recipes.

When people and dogs vanish suddenly and eerie screams pierce the night, the notion of vengeful spirits begins to seem plausible. These peculiar events draw Frank and Joe Hardy to the Pocono Mountains to assist their father’s friend, a retired police captain, in unraveling the mystery of Black Hollow. Upon reaching Captain Thomas Maguire’s cabin at the hollow’s rim with Chet Morton, they learn he has vanished. In the surrounding woods, only scant clues remain: a flashlight stamped with the initials T.M., scraps of bright plaid fabric, and two freshly fired shotgun shells. Despite Chet’s warnings after a night of unnerving, terrifying cries, the brothers resolve to locate the captain. Neighbors insist the bloodcurdling sounds belong to a legendary witch haunting Black Hollow in pursuit of vengeance. In a twist, it is a small puppy that helps the boys uncover an unusual and startling chain of events, linking a mute boy, a reclusive hermit, and a fearless trainer of pumas.

Told through the perspectives of the novel’s central figures, the narrative centers on Jacob Hunt, an eighteen-year-old with Asperger’s syndrome, a high-functioning form of autism. He lives with his mother and brother, Emma and Theo Hunt, and thrives only when daily routines are meticulously planned; any disruption or surprise unsettles him. His fixation on forensic analysis dominates his life, shaping much of the plot. The story begins with Jacob arranging a staged crime scene for his mother to investigate, effectively making himself the victim of the scenario. His relentless attention to detail and need for structure frequently exhaust Emma and provoke Theo’s anger. When counselor Jess Ogilvy, who helps Jacob navigate social situations, is found dead, suspicion quickly falls on him. After the first suspect, Mark Maguire, is detained and released, Detective Rich Matson requests Emma’s permission to interview Jacob. Following Jacob’s confession that he moved Jess’s corpse, he is arrested and charged with murder, and the case moves to trial. During proceedings, prosecutor Helen Sharp emphasizes how closely Jacob’s Asperger’s symptoms resemble traits often associated with guilt, challenging the reliability of behavioral cues. The prosecution also points to physical and documentary evidence they claim links Jacob to the crime—his fingerprints at the scene, a crime-scene evaluation in his notebook that mirrors Jess’s, and a backpack belonging to Jess retrieved from her home. On the witness stand, Jacob claims that he found Jess dead in her bathroom, bleeding from a head wound. He admits to having cleaned Jess, dressing her, and moving her outside, then tidying the original crime scene and fabricating a fresh one intended to mislead investigators. He explains this was driven by the realization that the death, though it began as an accident, resulted from Theo’s presence in the house and an encounter with Jess; after witnessing her naked in the shower, Theo fled, and Jess slipped and died. In the end, the court accepts that Jess’s death was indeed an accident, resolving the case as a fatal mishap rather than a deliberate murder."

Toby Flower, a reserved and withdrawn teenager who has grown his hair long and adopted a burnous, becomes a source of deep distress for his editor father and novelist mother after his expulsion from school for drug use. In their attempts to help, Charlie and Maggie Flower project their own ambitions onto him, clinging to the dream of a university future despite Toby’s clear disinterest in more schooling. Eventually, the suffocating environment drives Toby to leave home for London, where he rents a basement flat and stops communicating with his parents. The Flowers, at a loss, seek help from a psychiatrist friend who arranges for Toby to be hospitalized and treated for mental illness. In the capital, Toby encounters Hermia, the somewhat unattractive young daughter of the psychiatrist, and they begin a romance that leads to pregnancy. Unknowingly, their parents’ plot to press Hermia into an abortion severs the last remaining link Toby has with them. Responding to the rupture, Toby brings Hermia from her parents’ house, and the couple takes up residence with Toby’s maternal grandmother, a frail elderly woman who has quietly supported their needs all along.

Lenny is a recently released ex-convict. Despite his imposing size, he was gang raped repeatedly while incarcerated and struggles to find his manhood on the outside. Daisy, his alcoholic girlfriend, craves a “real” life with a “real” man and abandons him at a seedy pre-Giuliani Times Square bar in pursuit of some cheap Chinese takeout. At the bar is Skank, a former failed actor turned junkie, who is trying to outlast the rain storm and get a buyback from the long-missing Irish bartender as he begins to go through withdrawals. Also at the bar is Sammy, an old, dying guilt-ridden drunk who exists somewhere between reality and the afterlife. DeMaris, a seventeen-year-old gun-brandishing single mother, wants to learn to turn tricks. She enlists the aid of Chickie, Skank’s girlfriend, a young crackhead hooker who plays Go Fish with the simple-minded day bartender Charlie, who thinks he’s a Jedi warrior and who buys meals for Chickie because he loves her and because he lives for the day they can go out someday, “just as friends.” The owner of the bar is Jake. The place was his father’s before him, and after thirty years, he longs for the chance to leave “this sewer” for a re-invented life in Florida. The real-estate boom, “gentrification” and the emergence of Disney in Times Square affords him that opportunity. Unaware that their last piece of home is about to be pulled out from under them, the bar patrons struggle on. Their sense of humor, their misguided hopes and dreams, and their lack of self-pity are badges that are tattooed to their souls. They will all, before the end, demand and take the chance to face head on their complicated and sad truths.

Arthur Zouch, a portrait painter who dubs himself a “superman,” arrives at Passenger Court ostensibly to paint Mary, the younger Passenger daughter. Yet his visit is driven as much by a hunger for social advancement, financial gain, and sexual satisfaction as by artistic purpose. At the manor, he discovers openings for all three motives, but encounters unforeseen resistance in Vernon Passenger—another self-styled “superman”—who stands in his way. Nearby, the Fosdicks—the Major and his sons, Torquil and Jasper—maintain a long-running feud with the Passengers. Their quarrels are as likely to be tempered by superior manners and proper etiquette as by fiery tempers and sharp disputes. A local young woman named Joanna Brandon adds further complication to several characters’ lives; Powell’s portrayal of her is perhaps the novel’s most delicately drawn female figure. Spanning ten chapters, the narrative builds toward an unavoidable denouement, even as it withholds the exact means by which the book’s title foreshadowing will come to pass. The intertwined plots—sometimes reminiscent of Lear’s arc for the neighboring clans—converge on a double climax, from which only one self-styled “superman” can emerge.

Set against Sydney’s western suburbs, the novel follows Jamie Towfeek, a teenager yearning to become her authentic self. From the moment she dyes her hair blonde and trims away clues about her identity, Jamie fights a life she despises: her dark hair, her father’s rigid curfew rules, and her legal name, Jamilah Towfeek. For three years she has concealed her Lebanese Muslim roots from everyone at school, finding refuge only in correspondence with her email friend John, where she can truly be herself. But trouble is mounting. The most popular boy at school is drawn to Jamie, yet he would never accept her if he learned the truth about who she is. Timothy, the school’s quiet loner, occupies her thoughts in a way she can’t explain. And John, it turns out, has a sizeable secret of his own. The tension intensifies as the upcoming school formal looms, with Jamie’s band—the Muslim school’s musicians—slated to perform at the event. Attending now hinges on unveiling her real identity. Who is she really: Jamie or Jamilah? Interwoven within Jamie’s story are other strands. Her older sister Shereen is an outspoken human-rights and anti-war protester, while their father urges caution and conformity. As Jamie grows closer to her friend Amy, she becomes increasingly aware of Amy’s own growing secrecy. Amy is the first person Jamie admits she is Muslim to, and their bond deepens into a close friendship that ultimately eclipses their former circle, leaving Liz and the discriminatory crowd at school behind.

The story is set in Eskibahçe, a small fictional village in southwestern coastal Anatolia during the 1900s, spanning World War I and the era of Turkish nationalism. The Battle of Gallipoli takes place halfway through the novel. Although fiction, the setting of Eskibahçe is based upon Kayaköy (Greek: Levissi Λεβισσι) village near Fethiye, the ruins of which still exist today. Once a thriving Greek village, this town of over one thousand houses, two churches, fourteen chapels, and two schools, was completely deserted in 1923 when the Greek inhabitants living there, along with a vast number of Greeks living throughout Turkey were deported to Greece through a massive government mandated population exchange between the two countries following the Turkish war of independence. Historically, Turks and Greeks had lived together in this region for centuries, the Turks as farmers in the Kaya valley and the Greeks living on the hillside dealing in crafts and trades. A Greek presence in this region goes back for centuries. Since then, the village of Kayakoy, as it is called in Turkish, or Karmylassos, as it was called in Greek, which had been continually inhabited since at least the 13th century, has stood empty and crumbling, with only the breeze from the mountains and mist from the sea blowing through its empty houses and streets. Attempts by the Turkish government to get Turks deported from Greece to inhabit the village failed, and eventually, in the 1950s, the roofs of all the houses were removed. Some of its characters are also present in the author's earlier novel Captain Corelli's Mandolin. The book includes a vivid and detailed description of the horrors of life in the trenches during World War I.

Guadalupe "Lupe" Guardado is a middle-aged Salvadoran woman who lives near Chalatenango, El Salvador. During the day she is required to do what she can to support her family, while her husband works for a wealthy landowner. Her husband José has become involved in rebellion against the economic conditions and became a leader in the Christian farmers organization. Fearing persecution for his opposition, José regularly stays "in the hills" after work and sees his family little. The Guardado's son Justino was killed by the "authorities" prior to the events in the novel, and their son-in-law Helio has "disappeared." Guadalupe's granddaughter Adolfina relays the protest at a cathedral, as well as a massacre of students on a bus. At the end of the novel, the authorities bring a beaten man to Guadalupe and Adolfina who had said the name "Adolfina" after being severely beaten. Adolfina does not recognize the man, but Guadalupe recognizes her husband José. On his previous advice, she denies knowing him, and he is taken away.

The novel depicts the inward journey of Mrs. Curren, an old classics professor. She lives in the Cape Town of the Apartheid era, where she is slowly dying of cancer. She has been philosophically opposed to the Apartheid regime her entire life, but has never taken an active stance against it. Now, at the end of her life, she finally comes face-to-face with the horrors of the system - she witnesses the burning of a black township and the killing of her servant's son, as well as the shooting by security forces of a young black activist whom she shelters in her house. Against a backdrop of violence by whites and blacks alike, Mrs. Curren remembers her past and her daughter, who left South Africa because of the situation in the country: the book is framed as an extended letter from the mother to her daughter in America. As the story progresses, she constructs a relationship of a different kind with Vercueil, an old homeless man who happens to be sleeping in her driveway, as well as finally becoming truly aware of Florence, her black live-in servant. Coetzee brings together important themes in this book: aging, the confessor as hero, narrative representation, the meaning of freedom, and the position of the white liberal in Apartheid South Africa. * ISBN 0-14-027565-7 ca:L'edat de ferro eu:Age of Iron (Coetzee) fa:عصر آهن (رمان) it:Età di ferro

Martin Clarke is celebrating his acquisition and refurbishment of an old stately home by inviting a number of guests to stay for the weekend. The house has an unsettling history; two decades ago, the butler, a frail man of over 80 years, was killed when he uncharacteristically decided to swing back and forth from the chandelier, which then fell and killed him. Another report features a chair which leaps off the wall at the viewer. Clarke's guests have been selected as a cross-section of "ordinary, skeptical human beings" and have been invited to investigate the rumours of ghostly hauntings. The weekend begins when, as the guests are entering the home, one woman screams and claims that something has clutched at her ankle—something "with fingers". The host immediately tells the story of a former owner of the home whose death was met with such suspicion of witchcraft from the servants that the body lay as it fell for days, and the servants reported that something seemed to clutch at their ankles. The weekend is off to a spooky start but proceeds spectacularly when three witnesses agree that a gun jumped off the wall and killed a seated guest, with no hand holding it. Famous crime-solver and debunker of impossible crimes Gideon Fell is called in to explain matters and does so in a way that leads to a spectacular and fiery finish.

During the Cretaceous Period, a Tyrannosaurus poised to swallow a smaller captured dino is interrupted when an alien-crafted flying saucer lands, piloted by Vorb. He enlists the T. rex and several other dinos for a trial of a special “vitamin” he has developed; once ingested, it renders them sapient. Vorb then abducts the group aboard his craft and transports them to the present day, depositing them in New York City as it is celebrating the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The dinos attempt to blend in by posing as inflatable balloons, but Rex misidentifies a genuine dino balloon as his ally Allosaurus. The deception collapses after he accidentally pops the true Allosaurus balloon, triggering a panic among the crowd and prompting the dinos to flee. Soon after, police arrive to detain them, but Dr. Bleeb, a benevolent curator from the American Museum of Natural History, hides them by arranging for them to appear as life-size model dinosaurs. The authorities, satisfied, depart in search of the others, and the curator lets the group stay the night. That night, she reads them a bedtime story about a trilobite who dreamed of walking on land, while the dinos watch the city from the window, uncertain about what lies ahead. ru:Мы вернулись! История динозавра

Set in the 27th century, the world described in the novel mirrors the culture depicted in the concluding chapter of Accelerando, “Survivor.” Humanity has dispersed across the galaxy, leveraging wormhole technology copied from alien routers to form a mosaic of distinct societies and polities. Robin, a male human, is recovering from memory-erasure surgery at a rehabilitation center. Although his memories of former lives are erased, he privately suspects he endured traumatic events as a participant in wars that preceded the present era. Fearing assassination by unknown adversaries, he agrees to join a radical, isolated social experiment designed to resurrect the forgotten Dark Ages of the late 20th and early 21st centuries. When he is sent to the polity hosting the program, he learns he has been given the body of a woman, Reeve. As the experiment unfolds, she grows wary that not everything is as it seems and that the founders are embroiled in a profoundly sinister plot. Gradually she comes to doubt the simplicity of her assigned role, prompting episodes of questioning and resistance within the program. Within the novel’s universe, “glasshouse” signifies a military penitentiary. The polity that dominates much of the narrative once operated as a high-security facility for war criminals. The term evokes mid-19th-century Glasshouse facilities with glass-roofed detention barracks in Aldershot, UK. Stross also uses Glasshouse to symbolize a panopticon—a prison designed so that guards standing at the center can observe every action of the prisoners, while the inmates can never be sure if they are being watched. Philosophical inquiries by Michel Foucault on surveillance and internalized social norms inform this concept, a notion Stross exploits in the novel to explore conformity through perpetual gaze.

Joseph and Harriet Blackstone, and Joseph's mother Lilian, are immigrants from England on the SS Albert into the South Island of New Zealand in 1860s. After settling the two women into accommodation in Christchurch, Joseph travels to the foothills near the Okuku river to build their Cob House. Joseph returns to Christchurch once the house has been built and the three of them set off to start their new lives on their farm. The harsh first winter brings with it problems which threaten the viability of their farm, but Joseph's chance finding of gold in the nearby creek changes the situation. Not telling Harriet about the find, Joseph abandons the farm and travels by boat to Hokitika on the West Coast of the South Island where major gold strikes have occurred. After Lilian's death, Harriet also travels to Hokitika and delivers that news to Joseph. The search for gold, the 'colour', goes on in difficult conditions. Joseph's encounters with Will Sefton, a young man whom he met on the boat bringing them to the West Coast, and Pao Yi, a Chinese gardener befriended by Harriet, add flavour to the dynamics of the searching couple's relationship which has become distant and strained. Joseph's guilt surrounding events in England prior to their emigration impact on this separation.

As the novel opens, Blacky is worried about the imminent grand final and the responsibility he carries as the team’s new first ruck. His opponent will be the unstoppable ‘Thumper’. To protect himself, Blacky has devised the ‘Thumper tackle’ which is the ultimate defence of the coward: it looks like he is trying to tackle his opponent but is really an elaborate dodge. During the teams after-party however, the coaches son is given the honour of the Best On Ground award, which he believes should have been bestowed upon Dumby Red, the star player of the team. Soon after the news reports that Dumby and his two brothers have been shot dead while robbing a Public Bar, resulting in the breakdown of Blacky's emotional life. Blacky spends much of that winter dodging responsibility in a similar manner. By the end of the following summer, however, he understands the importance of making a stand and is able to do so. His brothers and sisters join him in his stand and the novel ends with Blacky at peace with himself, happy in his relationship with his siblings, and confident that he will be able to deal with the problems that will come with the morning.

Rather than spotlight widely celebrated global baroque dramatists like Pedro Calderón de la Barca or William Shakespeare, Benjamin chose to turn to the lesser-known German dramatists of the 16th and 17th centuries: Martin Opitz, Andreas Gryphius, Johann Christian Hallmann, Daniel Caspar von Lohenstein, and August Adolf von Haugwitz. He argues that these playwrights—deemed crude, dogmatic, and violent by earlier critics and thus sidelined as genuine artists—embody the distinctive cultural and historical spirit of their era more vividly than their famed peers. He emphasizes the recurring motif of “sovereign violence” as the central thread tying together the German mourning-play tradition (trauerspiel). By fixating on courtly plots and princely bloodshed, they depart from classical tragedy’s mythic heritage and forge a novel aesthetic shaped by the tense encounter between Christian eschatology and human history. Anticipating his later preoccupation with history, Benjamin contends that these works strip history of its guaranteed redemptive end, transforming it into a secular backdrop for the profane contest for power.

Keith Richards’s life story unfolds as a memoir, tracing his beginnings in Dartford, Kent, through his rise with the Rolling Stones and into his current life in Connecticut. His musical spark came from his mother, Doris, who spun records by Sarah Vaughan, Billy Eckstine, and Louis Armstrong, and from his maternal grandfather, Augustus Theodore Dupree, a former big‑band musician who urged him to pick up the guitar. In adolescence, he reconnected with Mick Jagger, whom he had known since primary school, and the pair discovered a shared passion for the blues. In the early 1960s, Richards moved into a London flat with Jagger and Brian Jones, and, alongside Bill Wyman, Ian Stewart, and Charlie Watts, helped form the Rolling Stones in 1962, performing at venues such as the Ealing Jazz Club and the Crawdaddy Club. The book tracks Richards’s career with the band from their modest club shows to massive stadium tours, alongside accounts of his drug use, arrests, and convictions. It also details his relationships with several women, including Anita Pallenberg, Marianne Faithfull, Ronnie Spector, and Patti Hansen, whom he wed in 1983. The often tumultuous dynamic between Richards and Jagger runs throughout, drawing substantial media attention. A consistent emphasis throughout the volume is Richards’s love of music, his distinctive playing style, and his approach to chord construction. The narrative also covers his ventures outside the Stones—such as the X‑Pensive Winos and his Jamaica sessions with the Wingless Angels—as well as collaborations with Chuck Berry, Gram Parsons, and others, explored in notable depth.

In recent years, the career of Detective Chief Inspector Alan Banks has been stalled-and, in fact, very nearly destroyed-by the petty animosities of his politically ambitious senior officer Chief Constable Riddle. But when nude pictures of Riddle’s runaway teenage daughter show up on a pornographic Web site, he turns to Banks for help. The trail leads Banks first to London’s Soho, an area of strip clubs and sex shops, then to the upmarket Little Venice, where Emily Riddle is living with a dangerous gangster with ties to world of rock music. At first she refuses to come home, but later Emily turns up at Banks’s hotel, bruised and frightened and asking for his help. Soon she is back with her family in Yorkshire, and Banks’s work appears to be done. Other concerns occupy Banks’s time. A major reorganization and expansion of Eastvale Regional Headquarters has brought Detective Sergeant Annie Cabbot back into his life, and she soon finds demons of her own to face. As they begin an investigation into the slaying of Charlie Courage, a low-level petty crook, a murder occurs at an Eastvale nightclub, filling the tabloids with headlines that scream of scandal, sex and high-level corruption. It is a cold and savage homicide that shakes Banks to his core, and it soon leads to shocking revelations that suggest it is somehow linked to the Charlie Courage affair. The grim discoveries of the unfolding investigation lead Banks in a direction he does not wish to go: the past and private world of his most powerful enemy, Chief Constable Riddle.

The novel centres around Timoleon Vieta, a little mongrel dog with black and white patches of fur and eyes as pretty as a girl's. Timoleon lives with Cockcroft, a retired, gay composer, who lives in a run-down farmhouse in Umbria financed by the occasional royalties he receives from the theme tunes he wrote. He reminisces on his failed career and former lovers, but is surprised when a man claiming to be a Bosnian shows up at his door with a business card he says Cockcroft gave him in a bar in Florence; Cockcroft often has such drunken weekends when he attempts to pick up men. In return for the occasional odd job and weekly fellatio Cockcroft puts him up, but Timoleon Vieta, who is a good judge of character, takes against the Bosnian, and the dislike is reciprocated. Cockcroft is forced to choose between them and agrees to abandon the dog in Rome. The remainder of the novel is about Timoleon Vieta's journey back home, and the people he briefly comes into contact with, as he tries to make his way back to his beloved Cockcroft.

The story opens with an experimental starship causing a catastrophic blast on an uninhabited world as it tests a lethal weapon. From there, the narrative centers on two principal figures who are recruited by the Sutherlin Alliance to topple the Alcon Empire. The younger of the pair begins as a pilot in the Empire’s renowned Devil Squadron, while the elder, who had once served in that same fighter group, left years earlier to become a mercenary and bounty hunter. Bolstered by these two seasoned ex-Imperial soldiers and a cadre of raw youth gathered from across the galaxy, the Alliance presses its campaign against the Empire. When the Empire detects the Alliance’s rapid ascent, it responds by unleashing the weaponized world-starship, wiping out a portion of the surface. A few days before this vessel’s deployment, the two recruits learn of its existence and its target, and they devise a plan to disrupt both the ship and its sizable escort. A recurring thread in the narrative examines the need to belong and the pull of attachment, showing how each lead grapples with it in distinct ways: the elder struggles to reconcile his desire for independence with the obligations others impose, while the younger fights to shield himself from the pain of war by staying distant.

The events of Homeboyz takes place four to five years after the events in Hip Hop High School. The book's main character is 17-year-old Dixon Theodore Anderson, nicknamed Teddy. He is a smart teenager who is both a hacker and a bodybuilder. Teddy's entire neighborhood is overrun by gangsters and his sister, Tina Anderson, is killed in a crossfire. While the Anderson family mourns her death, Teddy goes to his car to seek vengeance. He is unsuccessful in getting revenge and is arrested. He then spends time in a California juvenile prison waiting for a judge to hear his case. During this time, Teddy is treated as if he was a gangster. He is set free, but is put under house arrest and is enrolled in a probation program. Teddy is forced to spend five days each week mentoring a kid named Micah. Teddy has difficulty tutoring Micah because he is wants to be a gangster. But through Micah, teddy is taught how to love someone and see how people can change. Also this book talks about when Teddy meets the person that killed his sister,and he wasn't from 0-1-0. He was a member of another rival gang. Teddy fought hard and he won but the guy was sent to jail and died there.

Marianne Pinhoe's family tries to keep their magic a secret. They don't want the "Big Man", or Chrestomanci, interfering, as he tends to do when people misuse magic. And the Pinhoes certainly are guilty of that. Gammer, the head of the Pinhoe clan, has ostensibly gone mad, but Marianne doesn't believe that she's completely 'round the twist. She's sure that Gammer's the one sending plagues to the Farleighs, a related clan that also wishes to stay out of the sights of the "Big Man". Until recently, the Farleighs and the Pinhoes had been working together, but it seems that Gammer has started a war, and it'll be hard to keep their operations under wraps for long. Meanwhile, up at the Castle, Cat acquires a horse. He also meets the man who was bootboy at the Castle when the current Chrestomanci was a lad, Jason, and helps him and his new wife choose a house. They finally settle on Woods House, Gammer's old place, and Marianne, while showing Cat around, gives him an old egg from the attic, an egg with strong "Don't Notice" spells placed on it. An egg that is sure to arouse the interest of the "Big Man" up at the castle – something the rest of the Pinhoe clan, and Gammer in particular, doesn't want at all.

Solomon is a Scottish boy in the last year of primary school who is considered to be stupid and lazy, though he is actually dyslexic. He is bullied by his form teacher at school, and at home his father, who it is revealed is also dyslexic, drinks all the time and neglects him. Solomon often goes to the local graveyard for refuge. Overhearing a discussion between a council official and Professor Miller, he is upset to hear that his special place is to become a construction site. When the graveyard's protective rowan tree is uprooted by workmen, he has bad dreams and hears mysterious whispers. Driven by his father's behaviour to spend the night in the graveyard, he witnesses one of the workmen being swallowed up by the ground after unearthing a mysterious chest marked with the word "Malefice". He later discovers that the word means "witchcraft", and that a victim of the Scottish witch hunt is buried there. It seems she has awoken and is intent on vengeance. Amy Miller, the professor's young daughter, who has struck up a friendship with him, is drawn to the graveyard. Solomon follows to protect her from the evil presence which tries to possess her. With his father's help, he manages to rescue her and save himself. With the encouragement of Ms Talmur, one of the teachers from school who has helped him throughout the book but leaves to get a promotion at the end, he begins to change his life, although he knows it will be an uphill struggle. His father agrees to attend an Alcoholics Anonymous class to perhaps change his life also.

During the Christmas season, a stray lump of coal tumbles from a barbecue grill, wishing for a miracle. This coal desires to become an artist and sets off in pursuit of something that might help it realize that dream. Its first stop is an art gallery it believes features artwork crafted from coal; upon entering, it discovers the exhibits are created by humans using coal, not by coal itself, and feels disappointed. Continuing along the street, the coal then encounters a man dressed as Santa. After hearing the coal’s plight, Santa’s look-alike offers a plan: slip the lump of coal into the stocking of Jasper, his troublesome son. Jasper, who has longed to create art with coal, is thrilled to find it there and begins crafting coal portraits. The coal and Jasper flourish together, eventually achieving wealth. They relocate to Korea, where they establish a bona fide Korean restaurant accompanied by a gallery showcasing their art.

Carthoris is maddened by his love for Thuvia, a passion foreshadowed at the conclusion of the prior tale. Thuvia, however, is pledged to Kulan Tith, the Jeddak of Kaol, and Barsoom’s code allows no breach of betrothal except through death—though a new suitor may not precipitate that fate. Consequently Thuvia rejects Carthoris entirely, leaving him in a tight spot. As the heroine often does in Burroughs’ world, Thuvia is abducted and needs rescue, which nudges Carthoris toward action. He sets out determinedly to win back the woman he loves. Yet misfortune sabotages his path: he ends up far to the southern reaches of Barsoom, amid the ruins of the ancient city Aanthor. There, Thuvia’s captors—the Dusar—have driven her, and Carthoris arrives just as Thuvia and her guards are assaulted by a green-skinned foe from Torquas’s hordes. In a move echoing his father, he rushes to save her. The rescue threads Carthoris and Thuvia into the ancient metropolis of Lothar, birthplace of a pale-skinned race famed for conjuring lifelike phantasms from pure thought. These people commonly marshal vast regiments of phantom bowmen alongside real and spectral banths (Barsoom’s lions) to fend off Torquas’s forces. Thuvia’s kidnapping is orchestrated in such a way that Carthoris himself becomes the scapegoat, sparking war among Barsoom’s red nations. Now Carthoris must hurry back to Thuvia to prevent a broader conflict, hoping that fate will allow his affection to be returned by the woman promised to another man.

This book takes a 'warts and all' sensible yet humorous look at the many stages of pregnancy. It explores the changes, physical and emotional, that any man can expect to see in his partner and in their relationship over the coming months. Becoming pregnant involved two people. The rearing of a child will involve two people; there is every reason that your partner's pregnancy should also involve the two of you, together. For any man that has been put off reading pregnancy books because he doesn't feel he was the intended audience or that something about the tone of these books was alien to him, yet he still has questions that need answers; then The Blokes' Guide to: Pregnancy is the book he's been looking for. As a father himself, Jon Smith realized, when his partner Lisa became pregnant that there was nothing out there that he could relate to. The Bloke's Guide to Pregnancy is the result. Jon takes a comical yet informed look at the ups and downs of life as a father to be. Guaranteed to educate you while making you laugh out loud!

Set in the town of Bolton, South Dakota, Reacher begins his latest adventure on a wrecked senior citizen tour bus after a near-miss with another motorist leaves the bus spinning on the icy road and trapped in a snowy bank. Immersed in a snowy, frozen landscape, Reacher works with local law enforcement to help the fragile victims. Hours later, Reacher learns Bolton is not like most towns. Beside its freezing, snowy climate, the town plays host to one of the largest prisons in the U.S., making the town and its law enforcement subject to the needs and demands of the gigantic correctional facility. At the same time, a band of outlaw bikers, settled outside the town, are on edge after their leader is arrested on drug charges. As the biker awaits trial, protecting Janet Salter, the only witness to the biker's drug transaction, becomes a top priority, and Reacher agrees to aid local law enforcement to help protect the elderly Salter. Throughout the story, brutal enemies, both foreign and domestic, are encountered. The foreign criminal from Mexico is named Plato, and the bad cop in Bolton is Chief Holland, who murders his deputy chief, Andrew Peterson; a crooked lawyer; and the witness Salter. Reacher finds help from one of his successors, Susan Turner, the current leader of the elite 110th Special Investigations Unit (Reacher's old command), while interesting new details of his past come to light, such as how a dent appeared in his desk (from injuring a corrupt general), and of how Reacher caught the attention of military command because of his childhood behavior patterns. The ending leaves the reader guessing as to the conclusion. We do not learn how Reacher manages to escape an underground facility filled with fuel by Plato's henchmen before it ignites. A brief description of how he survives the conflagration appears in the next Reacher novel, Worth Dying For.

The year is 12,090 A.D. Civilization lies in ruins after a cataclysm of wars and insanity. Yet a handful of humans endure, and with them something else lingers in the shadows. Doris Lang understood her fate the moment Count Magnus Lee, a vampire lord, sank his fangs into her. She faced a brutal metamorphosis into the undead, with villagers pursuing her or condemning her to wed the unholy nobleman and endure eternal torment fueled by bloodlust. There remained one glimmer of hope: as Magnus rode into view from afar, she sensed salvation might be possible. The answer lay with a vampire hunter known simply as D. Magnus himself. Meanwhile Magnus confronts his own troubles. His daughter, Larmica, resists accepting any human into her clan and is quick to murder the would‑be bride on the eve of the ceremony. To eliminate Doris, she enlists Garo, a loyal werewolf attendant, only to collide with D. Magnus standing in their path. The chief’s son, Greco Rohman, also covets Doris for himself. So too do the skilled fighter Rei-Ginsei and his Fiend Corps, who view D as a dangerous rival because of his prowess and Doris’s favor. Doris understands she faces danger on multiple fronts, and her younger brother is seen as a vulnerability others might exploit to wound her.”

Aboard an Emergency Dispatch Ship bound for the frontier world Woden, laden with crucial medical supplies, the tale unfolds entirely within the vessel. The pilot, Barton, uncovers a stowaway—a young woman of eighteen named Marilyn. According to regulations, EDS stowaways must be jettisoned, since these ships carry only the fuel strictly needed to reach their destination. Marilyn’s motive is simple: she wants to meet her brother Gerry, and she is unaware of the law. When she boards, she notices the ominous sign reading “UNAUTHORIZED PERSONNEL KEEP OUT!” but assumes she can simply pay any resulting fine if discovered. Barton explains that her presence would push the ship beyond its weight limit, directly threatening the colonists’ survival. With no cargo to discard and the captain’s essential role aboard, Barton cannot sacrifice himself. After a call to Gerry, Marilyn chooses to step out of the airlock and into space, accepting her fate. The narrative, first serialized in the August 1954 issue of Astounding, has since appeared in many anthologies and has even been adapted for dramatization.

Kin-Fo, a man of immense wealth with ample possessions, finds life dreadfully dull. When he learns that a major overseas investment—an American bank—is bankrupt, he resolves to end his life. He secures a $200,000 life insurance policy that covers accidents, death in war, and suicide alike. Preferring not to die by seppuku or hanging, he contemplates poisoning himself with opium but craves a true thrill first. In a bid to trigger a death-defying event, he hires his former mentor, the philosopher Wang, to kill him before the policy lapses. News soon arrives that the American bank was never ruined; instead, it orchestrated a stock-market ruse and is now richer than before. Yet Wang has vanished. In anticipation of Wang’s act and backed by two insurance-provided bodyguards, Kin-Fo, together with his loyal but indolent servant Soun, roams the country trying to dodge Wang and the humiliation of the fiasco. Then Wang contacts Kin-Fo with a confession: the pain of killing a friend is intolerable, and he will instead end his own life. He tasks a bandit he once knew with killing Kin-Fo, to carry out if possible. Desperate to save his life, Kin-Fo, Soun, and the two guards set out to locate the bandit and offer money for his lifeblood. A voyage turns disastrous when the ship is hijacked, forcing everyone to deploy life jackets equipped with sails to reach land. After being abducted by the very bandit they sought, they are blindfolded and brought back to Kin-Fo’s home, where old acquaintances—among them Wang, revealed to have staged the entire sequence to impart a lesson about cherishing life—await him. In the end, Kin-Fo marries a young, beautiful woman, and they live out their days in happiness together.

In Santa Barbara, California, the tale unfolds as Travis Cornell—an ex-Delta Force operative—questions the point of his life while wandering a nearby canyon. There he meets two escaped specimens from a secret government lab: a golden retriever endowed with extraordinary intellect that quickly befriends him, and a menacing creature called the Outsider that seems bent on hurting the dog. After escaping the pursuing Outsider, Travis brings the dog home and christens him Einstein. Parallel to this, Nora Devon, a shy young woman who has recently lost an abusive aunt, is assaulted in her residence by a man attempting a rape. Travis and Einstein intervene, and a strong bond soon forms among the trio. Before long, Travis, Nora, and Einstein are forced to flee—not only from the menacing Outsider but also from federal agents intent on recapturing the lab fugitives, and from Vince Nasco, a remorseless assassin hired to eliminate the creatures and silence any witnesses who cross his path.

The novel takes place at Rubicon, a fictional science fiction convention taking place in the Virginia suburbs of Washington, DC, and at which the guests of honor are Appin Dungannon, a fantasy author noted for his books about hero Tratyn Runewind, and Dr. James O. Mega, an electrical engineering professor at Virginia Tech, who, under the pen name Jay Omega, has written one novel. That novel, a hard science fiction book about a space station crew whose female members are affected by radiation from a star (their intellect is diminished), was retitled "Bimbos of the Death Sun" and given an R-rated cover by the publisher. Mega is somewhat lost in the world of hardcore SF and fantasy fans at the con, but his companion Marion, a professor of English literature, is more familiar with things, and she guides him through it. They have troubles, such as being asked to judge a fiction contest. All seems to be going somewhat well for Mega, but his co-Guest of Honor, Dungannon, is making it a point to offend everyone at the con. It is hardly surprising when he is killed, a bullet through his heart. The fans react by buying up everything with his signature in the huckster room. The police are equally at sea. Everyone had a motive to kill Dungannon, but no one had the opportunity, so it seems. Mega corrals the suspects into a role-playing game and works out a confession ala Hamlet. Also, a lot of science fiction fans sing folk tunes, such as "The Skye Boat song."

Kristien, a white academic narrator, returns to South Africa to visit her grandmother after an assault by black youths leaves the old woman bedridden. Before she dies, the grandmother hopes to share the story of their Afrikaner lineage, a mission both women deem crucial. Kristien’s memories of life in London reveal a period of aimlessness and passivity, during which she sought distance from South Africa and from parents who, in life, supported apartheid. Initially, relinquishing her self-imposed exile feels like mere resignation, but gradually she recognizes that her homeland is evolving for the better. With the first democratic elections approaching, Kristien meets both black and white people, and the grandmother’s tales—framing largely the female line and tracing back to a black matriarch—teach Kristien to claim South Africa as her homeland. On the eve of the vote, Kristien’s sister murders her own children and her violent, racist husband, then takes her own life to escape an unbearable existence. That same night, the grandmother dies from injuries sustained in the assault. Yet Kristien remains hopeful about her future in South Africa. The family farm is bequeathed to the household of the black domestic worker.

This book is about a man named Thomas Hunter in Denver, Colorado, 2010, who, after being knocked unconscious from a bullet wound to the head, wakes up to find himself in a strange world full of black, twisted trees. After being attacked by strange, bat-like beings called Shataiki and led out of the Black Forest by a white bat, he is rendered unconscious again due to blood loss. He wakes up to find himself back in Denver. Startled at the sudden change, he can’t figure out which world is real. He soon discovers that every time he falls asleep, he wakes up in the other world, until he falls asleep there. Outside of the Black Forest is the Colored Forest, a paradise inhabited by a civilization of immortal-yet innocent-humans beings who are watched over by Elyon, a God-like being, along with white, bat-like Roush, who are opposites of the Shataiki and act as servants of Elyon. Thomas eventually finds out that this other world is our own thousands of years in the future, and that a virus, mutated from a vaccine, would wipe out his present-day Earth later that year. Thomas is forced to fight evil in both worlds, a difficult prospect, for while evil is portrayed differently in each reality, it is equally as potent, and Thomas quickly finds that putting a stop to an event of apocalyptic proportions is no easy task.

Set in contemporary West Virginia, the story follows Summer, an orphaned girl passed from one indifferent relative to the next. At six, she meets Aunt May and Uncle Ob, a kindly elderly pair who notice that Summer is not abused but largely overlooked. They bring her into their creaky hillside trailer, and for the first time she senses a real, stable home. Six years later, Aunt May dies suddenly in the garden, leaving Summer to wrestle with grief while witnessing Uncle Ob’s struggle with living after her loss. In his despair, he turns to spirit contact, spurred by a sensation that May is trying to reach him. He is aided by Cletus Underwood, a classmate of Summer who knows of a famed medium. Although skeptical, Summer is willing to explore any path that might ease her uncle’s sorrow. The trio embarks on a road trip to consult the medium, only to learn she has recently passed away. Uncle Ob’s initial heartbreak threatens to extinguish his will to live, but a turn of hope comes on the return journey as he chooses to keep carrying on for Summer’s sake.

It's a winter day in Dalton (a New England town near Boston) and Leonidas Witherall, "the man who looks like Shakespeare", is returning to his new house, which he's never seen. He's inherited money from an uncle and toured the world, and left plans for his home to be built while on his travels, but now he must return home and produce the next volume of the adventures of Lieutenant Haseltine. On the train to Dalton, he meets a mousy woman named Miss Chard (known to all as Swiss Chard) and a beautiful young woman with a brown paper package and a secret. His new home proves a delight, and it includes a kitchen filled with red appliances, a library with ladders, and a garage complete with the pickaxed corpse of Medora, the crabby next-door neighbor. Leonidas assembles a gang of assistants, including dotty housewife Cassie Price and former car thief Cuff (who has reformed and joined the police force). Together, they defend Witherall's new red refrigerator against thieves, track down the missing envelope of money and bring the murderer to justice.

In 1857, after their attempts to smuggle contraband goods land them with a heavy fine from the British Customs, Captain Illiam Quillian Kewley and his crew of Manx sailors are forced to offer their ship for charter. The vessel is quickly hired by a party of Englishmen headed by an eccentric Vicar, the Reverend Geoffrey Wilson, who believes that the Garden of Eden is located in Tasmania and wants to mount an expedition there to find it. However, unbeknownst to the clergyman, one of his fellow travellers has an entirely different reason for journeying to the island. Dr Thomas Potter is a renowned surgeon who is developing a thesis on the races of man and hopes to find some interesting specimens there. Running parallel with this story, but starting some 30 or so years earlier, are the recollections of Peevay, one of Tasmania's natives, who describes the devastating impact the white settlers had on his people, and the aborigines' struggle to adapt to the cultural changes which were forced on them. Many of the chapters alternate between the two different time periods, but when the Manx ship eventually docks in Tasmania, both strands of the story are brought together for the book's conclusion.

A century later, Lyman Ward narrates the tale and sometimes offers his own interpretation, occasionally noting gaps he leaves unresolved. His life’s disappointments, including a divorce, tint how he presents his grandparents’ story. Near the novel’s end, he abandons the initial goal of producing a complete biography of his grandmother. The inclusion of Mary Hallock Foote’s historical letters, used by Stegner, grounds the places—Leadville, New Almaden, Idaho, and Mexico—with an authentic atmosphere; the letters also illuminate the Wards’ battles against the environment, corrupt businessmen, and political players. Placed within the late-sixties cultural milieu, Lyman’s standpoint adds another historical layer to the narrative. Counterpoints to this thread include his adult son, a sociologist trained in Berkeley who dismisses much of history, and a neighbor’s daughter who assists with transcribing Lyman’s taped notes during a summer break from UC Berkeley, where she has been involved in the hippie counterculture.

Twelve-year-old Heidi lives in the town of Reno, Nevada with her mentally-disabled mother and their neighbor, Bernadette. Her mother only knows twenty-three words, including one mysterious one, "soof," that no one can define. Meanwhile, Bernadette has a serious condition called agoraphobia, which causes her to be too afraid to go outside her house. Heidi must take on responsibilities beyond her years to provide for their households. When Heidi finds some photos of her mother at a Christmas party in New York, Heidi decides to go to that state, anxious to uncover more about her family history and to seek what the word "soof" meant, after hearing her mother mutter it all the time. Although Bernadette is anxious about Heidi leaving, she reluctantly allows her to go as long as she calls every night. During her road trip to Liberty, New York, Heidi meets Georgia Sweet, a kind and curious lady on the bus. When she arrived at Hilltop Home, she felt unwelcomed by Thurman Hill. Feeling sorrowful, Ruby takes Heidi into her own home where she and her husband, Roy, investigate. She discovers that Thurman Hill, is her grandfather, Elliot is her father, and that her grandmother was named Diana. She finally finds out what her mothers word, soof, meant, which was her nickname for Sophia Demuth. By the end her mom dies.

Albert, a 42-year-old still living in his father’s apartment in Harstad, faces his father’s sudden death as a chance to finally craft the life he’s longed for during years of caregiving. Much of the narrative unfolds through a flashback to 1985–86, detailing his European travels with a friend named Viktor, a stop in Hong Kong by sheer happenstance, and a later sojourn in Paris where he meets a girl and nearly chooses to stay, only to return to Hässelby to be with his father. What begins as a conventional exploration of father–son dynamics, suburban upbringing, friendship, and political currents gradually darkens as increasingly surreal imagery intrudes. The ending shifts into a nightmare: Albert learns that someone has been shadowing him for more than two decades across continents, and that the world itself is on the brink of collapse.

Tommy Segovia, Calder’s old friend who had left town a year earlier, has returned to Hyde Park in Chicago—and immediately feels envious of Calder and Petra, who earned the figurative “glory” of saving a Vermeer in the previous book, Chasing Vermeer. He believes he deserves a share of that recognition. On the first day of the new term, Ms. Hussey reveals that the world-famous Robie House is slated for demolition, calling it an act of murder. The class then tours the house, where Calder and Petra uncover a web of concealed truths about the building. After Tommy learns to tolerate Petra, the trio—calling themselves The Wright 3—band together to protect the house, even breaking in near the end. During their adventures, Tommy discovers a fish talisman in the Robie House garden and realizes its high value. In the end, after fending off burglars inside the Robie House, they succeed in preserving both themselves and the landmark. Throughout the drawings, a fish motif—referencing Frank Lloyd Wright’s lucky talisman—appears in nearly every illustration, often hidden by nature and aligned with the Fibonacci sequence in each chapter. One of the final illustrations even hides a dragon, signaling a shift from carp to dragon in the narrative. Near the bottom of the last image, footprints suggest the presence of the invisible man, and several pictures reveal a face if you look closely.

Four central figures drive the narrative: misfit ecologists who share a belief in protecting the land. Seldom Seen Smith, a river guide steeped in Jack Mormonism; Doc Sarvis, an unconventional yet wealthy and perceptive surgeon; Bonnie Abbzug, his young, sexually charged assistant; and George Hayduke, an eccentric Green Beret Vietnam veteran. They form, not always in perfect unity, the eponymous Gang—a collective dedicated to undermining what they view as a system that poisons and plunders the American West. As their campaigns against deserted bulldozers and abandoned trains persist, the law begins to close in. The work earned praise for its erudition, exuberant flair, and vivid, rustic depictions of life far from modern civilization. Abbey himself settled in the West and possessed rugged outdoor skill. viewed from a contemporary angle, the Gang diverges in several respects from how today’s media portrays environmentalists: the characters consume a lot of red meat, keep firearms, litter roadsides with beer cans, and drive large cars (habits reportedly echoed by Abbey). Although Abbey’s own politics are not typically “bleeding-heart,” many protagonists reject liberalism, attacking both Native Americans and whites for consumer habits, and showing little respect for the Sierra Club. (Despite some contradictory evidence, Edward Abbey described himself as liberal—“I’m a liberal, and proud of it,” he wrote in Abbey’s Road.) For the Gang, the true adversaries are those who would industrialize the American Southwest, fouling air and land and stripping away Nature and Abbey’s desert-tinged sense of sacred purity. Their deepest loathing targets the Glen Canyon Dam, a colossal concrete barrier that cages a wild river, which the saboteurs aim to topple. One of the book’s most enduring moments envisions Seldom Seen Smith kneeling on top of the dam, praying for a “precision earthquake” to remove the dam’s temporary Colorado River plug. The work arguably inspired the creation of Earth First! by Dave Foreman and Mike Roselle, a direct-action environmental group known for advocating acts resembling the book’s minor vandalism. Numerous scenes of ecological mayhem—such as an opening billboard arson and the deployment of caltrops to elude pursuers—are laid out with enough specificity to serve as a rough blueprint for would-be saboteurs, a narrative thread that helped spur the Earth Liberation Front.

Set against Saint-Domingue’s late-18th century backdrop, the tale follows Tete, born to an African mother she never knew and a white sailor who enslaved her. As a child she is purchased by Violette, a mixed-race courtesan, for Toulouse Valmorain, a Frenchman who has inherited a sugar plantation and dreams of wealth. Valmorain regards slavery as a tool to achieve his goals, not as a moral stance. After his marriage, Tete becomes the personal slave of his wife, a delicate beauty who slowly slips into madness. In her escalating instability, Valmorain compels the now-teenage Tete into sexual service, resulting in several children born outside wedlock. Over four decades, the story shifts among the era’s upheavals—beginning with the distant tremors of the French Revolution, moving through the brutal chaos of the Haitian slave rebellion, and ending in a New Orleans that is pulsing with cultural transformation.

Adela Gereth, a widow, confides to the tactful Fleda Vetch her fear that her son Owen will wed Mona Brigstock, a coarse-minded woman. Before long, Owen becomes engaged to Mona and plots to seize Poynton, the family home filled with Mrs. Gereth’s prized furniture and other works of art. He hopes Fleda will assist in coaxing his mother to depart with as little fuss as possible. Mrs. Gereth relocates to Dicks, the smaller house in the family’s estate. During a visit, Fleda is dismayed to see that the more valuable pieces from Poynton have been brought to Dicks, as Mrs. Gereth furnishes the place with them. Owen explains that Mona suspects the “theft” of the heirlooms. Simultaneously, Owen’s attention shifts toward Fleda, growing more drawn to her than to Mona, and he ultimately confesses his love. Fleda presses him to honor his engagement to Mona unless she herself ends it. At last, Mrs. Gereth returns the fine furniture to Poynton. Soon afterward, news arrives that Owen and Mona have been married and have gone abroad. A letter from Owen reaches Fleda, requesting that she choose one piece from Poynton to keep as her own. When Fleda visits Poynton to comply, she finds the house utterly consumed by fire.

The narrative opens by detailing Berkman’s imprisonment, tracing it to his act as an anarchist agitator who attempted to kill Henry Clay Frick, the Carnegie steelworks manager in Pennsylvania, a man who had crushed the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers during the Homestead strike that left about ten dead. Though Berkman fired three shots at Frick and repeatedly stabbed him in the leg with a poisoned blade, Frick survived and Berkman received a 22-year sentence. Berkman hoped his assault would wake up the oppressed American populace; however, the book explains that the nation lacked the political sensibility to interpret his deed, and even his fellow prisoners—people he claimed to defend—failed to grasp his political aim. Most of the work unfolds within Berkman’s years behind bars, written in the first person and present tense, English being his second language. It reads like a diary, though its composition followed his release. The memoir traces a coming-of-age arc as Berkman confronts prison life’s physical and psychological demands, at times nearing suicide and gradually losing his youthful, idealistic sentimentality. Initially he regards the other inmates with contempt, seeing them as unworthy peers while insisting he is duty-bound to aid the victims of social injustice and to resist social wrongs. Yet distance and moral superiority slowly erode as he recognizes the flawed humanity in everyone, including himself. The Prison Memoirs also serves, in part, as a tribute to his friendship with Emma Goldman, the activist he repeatedly mentions—though never by name—calling her “the Girl” throughout much of the book. She alone maintains correspondence with him during incarceration and later defends him from outside criticism, assisting him after release. The work follows Berkman’s evolving thoughts on political violence, with his reflections often forming a dialogue with Goldman, a figure with whom he shares an intimate understanding.

Guy Openshaw is 44 years old and on his death bed. Cancer is coming down hard on Guy, and he cannot stand the stream of visitors to his London flat. His wife Gertrude entertains the drop-ins, who were once part of a lively set that came by after work hours for a drink and chat. The visitors all relied on Guy for advice and money, and as he dies the varied people in the novel begin to fray. One of the visitors to the Openshaw flat is the youngish Tim Reede, an artist who cannot sell his work and who is lost without Guy’s support. He has a girlfriend named Daisy who dresses like a punk and talks and drinks like a sailor; they’re a perfect pair of starving misfits. Daisy makes Tim visit Gertrude once Guy has passed and ask her for money, but Gertrude begins questioning Tim about his craft and winds up wanting to support him in other ways, namely giving him run of her home in the French countryside. The Tim-Gertrude affair and subsequent marriage is the heart of the book, and it is a good study of class relations and the younger man-older woman romance. Tim is both a hero and a colossal screw-up, but he is also kind and lets Gertrude’s friends run him down because it doesn’t bother her and he still gets to be with her at the end of the day. Some of Gertrude’s circle are genuinely concerned, but most are either in love with her or what she could do for them with Guy’s inheritance.
