Other characters include the fathers of the children, who are all fishermen; Lina's aunt, who lives in Nes; Evert, the man living across from Lina's aunt; Lina and Auka's younger siblings, Linda and Jan; Jana, Janus's wife; and the mothers of the children. The dedication reads: "To my nieces, Shirley and Beverly, and their flying fingers".

In the present-day echo of global conflict, The Palace of Illusions reimagines the Mahabharata—an era that blends history and myth while shimmering with magic. Narrated through Panchaali, the wife of the five Pandavas, Divakaruni offers a distinctive feminist reading of a legendary saga. The narrative charts Panchaali’s life from her miraculous birth, born of fire as a king’s daughter, to her bold navigation of a household where she shares power with five husbands who themselves have been deprived of their ancestral throne. Drawn into their mission to recover what is rightfully theirs, she remains by the brothers’ side through years of exile and the devastating great war. Alongside this arc, we follow her schemes to assert command over her in-laws’ domain, her intricate bond with the enigmatic Krishna, and the secret pull toward the man who stands as her husband’s deadliest foe. Panchaali speaks with a fierce, feminine voice amid a world of warriors, divine beings, and fate’s ever-shifting hands. Love, the story implies, can arrive unannounced, piercing the human heart. Draupadi herself—tangible and mortal, with a heart capable of feeling for Arjuna—becomes more than a mere prize in the cruel machinery of fate. She accepts four husbands and fulfills her duties with fidelity. The work unfolds as a vision of enduring concepts—submission, patience, sacrifice, joy, sorrow, and punishment—tracing a woman’s journey that resonates with the experiences of many modern women. It presents feminine beauty, strength, and glory as inseparable from inner resolve.

Told through a first‑person lens, the narrative unfolds the people and events of iDEATH. Central tension stems from Margaret, once the narrator’s lover, and inBOIL, a defiant figure who absented himself from iDEATH to dwell near a forbidden zone known as the Forgotten Works. This vast rubbish dump houses the discarded remains of a bygone civilization, left in towering heaps. Margaret, who collects such “forgotten things,” maintains a cordial relationship with inBOIL and his followers, who probe the area and distill whiskey there. InBOIL’s departure from the group may be tied to the massacre of “The Tigers”—a slaughter that befell many years earlier at the hands of the people. The text never makes clear whether the Tigers were actual tigers, humans, or something more ambiguous: while they killed and consumed people (even the narrator’s parents), they could also converse, sing, play instruments, and showed arithmetic aptitude. On a bridge—later called “the abandoned bridge”—two Tigers were slain, and the final Tiger met death at a site that would later become a trout farm. The novel’s violent climax finds inBOIL returning with a small following, claiming to reveal what iDEATH truly is. The townsfolk sense only that something ominous is imminent; they fear a massacre, though the exact plan remains unknown. Margaret seems oblivious to the danger and unconcerned for the safety of her relatives and friends. Many suspect she was aware of inBOIL’s true objectives but kept them hidden, effectively collaborating with the malevolent men. Semi‑ostracized from iDEATH, she becomes entangled in the fabric of suspicion, and the narrator reveals at the outset that he ended their relationship because of these events.

Joe Leland, a private detective, begins investigating a case for the recently widowed Norma MacIver. Norma requests that Leland find out everything he can about her deceased husband. Norma requests Leland personally because her husband had mentioned knowing him in the past. It turns out that Leland and Colin MacIver served in the same military unit during World War II, but at different times. Leland interviews Colin's first wife, his mother and the security guards at the track where Colin supposedly killed himself. Norma introduces Leland to her neighbor and former therapist, Dr. Wendell Roberts. During their conversation Wendell reveals that he knew Leland's wife. It turns out Wendell was friends with the man with whom Karen Leland had had an affair. As Leland's investigation deepens he uncovers evidence of corruption and murder. Eventually, Leland discovers that Colin was connected to a homicide during Leland's earlier life with the police department as a detective. During the investigation of Teddy Leikman's death a confession was obtained from Felix Tesla, Leikman's roommate. Tesla was subsequently executed by electric chair. It turned out that Colin MacIver was the true murderer. Joe's partner, Mike Petrakis, managed to decipher Colin's coded notes and reveal a paper trail of corruption.

The Deed of Paksenarrion was written as one long story, but published as three separate books. A number of people have pointed out resemblances between the story setting and Dungeons & Dragons, in particular alleged similarities between Moon's town of Brewersbridge and Hommlet (a village in The Temple of Elemental Evil module for AD&D) and between Moon's religion of Gird and the faith of Saint Cuthbert of the Cudgel in Greyhawk. However, such themes may often be similarly found in many brands of high fantasy, and are not unique to any one fictional world. The Deed of Paksenarrion revolves around the adult life of Paksenarrion Dorthansdotter, known as Paks, of Three Firs. It takes place in a fictional medieval world of kingdoms of humans, dwarves, gnomes and elves. The story begins by introducing Paks as a headstrong girl of 18, who leaves her home in Three Firs (fleeing a marriage arranged by her father) to join a mercenary company and through her journeys and hardships comes to realize that she has been gifted as a paladin, if in a rather non-traditional way.

Presented as a fabricated document, the narrative unfolds starting with a foreword by Meyer. He explains that a woman, linked to Horace Vernet by family ties and also an ancestor of Holmes, brought the manuscript to his attention after reading The Seven-Per-Cent Solution. Although water-damaged, the manuscript is authenticated. In his own preface, Dr. Watson explains why he initially withheld publication: the tale would implicate a number of famous individuals whose identities could not be concealed. Holmes had long resisted giving Watson permission to tell the story on those grounds, but Watson wins him over by vowing to place the complete manuscript in Holmes’s custody, provided that Holmes does not destroy it. The plot features a host of notable figures, among them George Bernard Shaw, who commissions Holmes to investigate the death of a disliked theatre critic; Sir Arthur Sullivan, whose troupe at the D’Oyly Carte Opera Company lost one singer to the same killer; and others such as W. S. Gilbert, Oscar Wilde, Bram Stoker, Henry Irving, Ellen Terry, and Frank Harris. Within the fiction, Holmes exonerates a timid Parsee Indian who has been wrongly accused of murder. In real life, Conan Doyle played a meaningful role in aiding George Edalji, a Parsee man wronged by the English judiciary.

It is now 1985 and much of the action is set in the Russian River area north of San Francisco. Here, successful businessmen from around the globe gather at Bohemian Grove for a three-week encampment of male bonding, while downriver from them events at Wimminwood, a lesbian music and arts festival, threaten the relationship of DeDe Halcyon-Day and D'orothea Wilson. Returning characters include Mary Ann Singleton, who is having difficulty balancing her commitment to her career as a local talk show hostess with her obligations as a wife to Brian and mother to Shawna, the child of her friend Connie, who entrusted the girl's care to Mary Ann on her deathbed; Michael Tolliver, the romantic gay man who has tested HIV-positive and is taking AZT to combat the threat to his immune system; and Anna Madrigal, the transgendered landlady who mothers her tenants at 28 Barbary Lane on Russian Hill and is fighting to preserve the historic wooden steps of the lane. New characters include Thack Sweeney, who meets Michael during a tour of Alcatraz and Wren Douglas, a plus-size model whose best-selling self-help book offers hope to overweight women. There is also a focus on a previously minor character, Roger "Booter" Manigault, DeDe's stepfather and a member of the Bohemian Club, who accidentally stumbles into Wimminwood and is held captive by one of its more militant organizers. Brian's college-aged nephew Jed also makes an appearance as a young Reaganite more interested in getting into Harvard Law and making money than having fun.

Wedge Antilles persists in defending Borleias from the Yuuzhan Vong, continuing the arc begun in Rebel Dream. After tracking down and eliminating a spy within the Vong-ruled Tam Elgrin, he sets about building a superlaser—identical to the Death Star in design, but it is defective by intent. Antilles engineers a ruse: using both the feverish fixation of Commander Czulkang Lah on capturing Jaina Solo and the laser’s dubious functionality, he lures Lah’s fleet away from the Lusankya, Lah’s flagship. While the Yuuzhan Vong force is diverted, the Super Star Destroyer Lusankya is equipped with a spear and steered straight into the worldship, bringing it down and sealing Lah’s fate. On Coruscant, Luke Skywalker, Mara Jade Skywalker, Tahiri Veila, and Wraith Squadron press on with their reconnaissance, encountering a Dark Jedi who resembles the mythic Nyax but is, in truth, the engineered Dark Jedi Irek Ismaren. Though Nyax proves to be stronger than Luke, the combined Jedi-Yuuzhan Vong effort overpowers him and defeats Nyax. Simultaneously, Viqi Shesh’s plan to flee Coruscant is thwarted by Wraith Squadron, driving her to suicide. In parallel, Han and Leia Organa Solo, accompanied by C-3PO and R2-D2, undertake missions to unseat any planetary government willing to bend to Yuuzhan Vong rule. Their perilous assignment on Aphran IV tests their nerve, but they emerge victorious with the mission accomplished.

In the book, Nick meets Uncle Giles for tea at the Ufford Hotel and is introduced to the clairvoyant Mrs. Erdleigh who proceeds to tell their fortunes. Jenkins arranges to meet Members at the Ritz, but the appointment is kept by Quiggin who has replaced Members as secretary to novelist St John Clarke; Nick eventually dines with Peter & Mona Templer and Jean Duport and is invited for a weekend at the Templers' in Maidenhead. This house party sees the start of an affair with Jean. Quiggin is invited for Sunday, but has to leave due to concerns over his master. Mrs. Erdleigh is also there with Jimmy Stripling in tow, and presides over a seance. Later in spring 1933 Nick spends a day in encounters with Quiggin and Members including a demonstration led by St John Clarke, wheeled in his chair by Quiggin and Mona. There follow various further encounters with Jean and a visit to Foppa's restaurant. Summer 1933 sees Jenkins, Templer, Stringham and Widmerpool at the Le Bas dinner for Old Boys at the Ritz. Stringham arrives the worse for drink and Widmerpool makes an uninvited, boring and pompous speech, silenced only by Le Bas collapsing with a stroke. Widmerpool and Jenkins take the drunken Stringham home to bed. The book ends with intimations of an end to Nick's affair with Jean.

The novel has two narratives in alternate chapters. The first follows two citizens of the Amalgam, a Milky Way-spanning civilisation, investigating the origin of DNA found on a meteor by the Aloof. The Aloof control the galactic core and until the novel begins, have rejected all attempts at contact by the Amalgam. The second narrative is set on a small world known as the Splinter, and covers the attempts by its inhabitants to understand the environment within which their home exists. As the story progresses, it becomes clear that the Splinter orbits a collapsed star within its accretion disk and is subject to various dangers. The two stories come together in a complex twist which involves a kind of past/future first contact role reversal. Much of the narrative explores the effects of orbital dynamics around a high mass object and requires an understanding of Newtonian gravitation and at least a basic familiarity with general relativity and its application to black holes and neutron stars to be compelling. Understanding the story's wider frame of reference and the Splinter's encounter with the Wanderer are tied in with this. The Amalgam is explored in two other short stories, "Glory" and "Riding the Crocodile".

Kin-Fo is a very wealthy man, who certainly does not lack material possessions. However, he is terribly bored and when news reaches him about his major investment abroad, a bank in the United States, going bankrupt, Kin-Fo decides to die. He signs up for a $200,000 life insurance covering all kinds of accidents, death in war, and even suicide. He rejects seppuku and hanging as means of dying, and is about to take opium laced with poison when he decides that he doesn't want to die without having ever felt a thrill in his life. Kin-Fo hires his old mentor, the philosopher Wang, to murder him before the life insurance expires. After a while news reaches Kin-Fo that the American bank he had invested in was not bankrupt, but instead had pulled off a stock market trick and is now wealthier than ever. Unfortunately, Wang has already disappeared. Together with two body guards assigned by the insurance company, and his loyal but lazy and incompetent servant Soun, Kin-Fo travels around the country in an effort to run away from Wang and the humiliation from the affair. One day he receives a message from Wang, stating that he can't stand the pain of having to kill one of his friends, and instead decided to take his own life while giving the task of killing Kin-Fo to a bandit he once knew. Kin-Fo, Soun and the two bodyguards now try to get to the bandit, planning to offer money in return for his life. The ship they travel with is hijacked, and they are forced to use their life vests with built-in sails to return to land. After being kidnapped by the bandit they were looking for, they are blindfolded and returned to Kin-Fo's home, where his old friends (including Wang, who we now find out staged this entire history to teach him a lesson about how valuable life is) are waiting for him. He marries a young, beautiful woman and they live happily forever after.

Middle-aged actor Toby Flood is touring the South of England with a recently discovered play by Joe Orton called Lodger in the Throat. When the company arrive in Brighton for a one-week run at the Theatre Royal, Flood is confident that he will be able to use his stay to get in touch with his estranged wife Jenny, who has filed for divorce and is now living with Roger Colborn, a local businessman, on the outskirts of the city. Flood is surprised to find that it is Jenny who contacts him first: She tells him she is being stalked and, as she believes that her husband is to blame for it, asks him to do something about it. This is how Flood meets Derek Oswin, the alleged stalker, an eccentric man his own age who, just like his deceased father and grandfather before him, worked for the Colborns' family business until its liquidation in 1989. It turns out Oswin has written a history of the company but so far has not found a publisher. Talking to Oswin and to other people he meets, either by chance or by design, Flood more and more gets the impression that Roger Colborn is a dangerous man who has something to hide, and that Jenny must be saved from the clutches of the Colborn family before it is too late. Thus, Flood's interest in the affairs of a now defunct company is fuelled by his desire to win back Jenny, so much so that his professional life is affected. Trying to dig up dirt on the Colborns, he is drawn into a quagmire of events he cannot make head or tail of and eventually misses an evening's performance without giving any notice. When, however, on the following day he finds his understudy—the man who saved his neck the previous night—dead in the streets of Brighton he realizes the seriousness of the situation. In the course of one week homes are broken into, evidence is stolen, several people die, family secrets are uncovered, and an inheritance is reclaimed. Justice triumphs in the end.

Legacy serves as the immediate follow-up to Beguilement within the Sharing Knife saga, tracking the married life of farmer Fawn and lakewalker Dag after their union at Fawn’s homestead in the prior volume. Their wedding occurred with little resistance, harmonizing the customs of both communities. The duo then travels to Hickory Lake, the camp of Dag’s clan, where they confront the conventional prejudices against interbreeding between Farmers and Lakewalkers. When Dag leads a patrol to confront a rising, insidious threat, he chooses to tackle the malice head-on rather than attempt to rescue several Lakewalkers who have fallen under the enchantment that the malice uses to forge its slaves. Following the eradication of the malice by Dag’s force, Dag himself also becomes entranced. Fawn maintains her heroine’s agency by devising a plan to revive him and, through him, the rest of the Lakewalkers. Yet neither of these feats sways Dag’s brother and mother, who continue to oppose the pairing. The two relatives function as antagonists, though their peculiarities are given clear, understandable motives. Although some Lakewalkers accept the marriage and even recognize Fawn’s potential value within the camp, Dag and Fawn’s union nonetheless creates uneasy precedents that threaten exile. Dag disrupts the proceedings by declaring his intention to leave his homeland regardless. He and Fawn then seize as many movable possessions as they can and depart toward chosen exile in the southeast. There, Dag believes he may test his theory about a close kinship between Farmers and Lakewalkers and explore ways to unite their efforts against the malices. These ideas are carried forward in the following two books.

Up to this time Cornwell had been going back through the period of the Napoleonic Wars to find new incidents into which to place his hero. Rather than do this, he adopts a "prequel" approach and uses an earlier campaign period in the history of the British Army, that of colonial India. The novel opens with Richard Sharpe serving as a private with the British army, then invading Mysore and advancing on the Tippoo Sultan's capital city of Seringapatam. Sharpe is contemplating desertion with his paramour, widow Mary Bickerstaff. His sadistic company sergeant, Obadiah Hakeswill, deliberately provokes Sharpe into attacking him, and engineers the virtual death sentence of 2,000 lashes for the private. But Sharpe is rescued by Lieutenant William Lawford after 200 lashes are inflicted, in order to effect a rescue mission behind the Tippoo's lines. Lawford and Sharpe are ordered to pose as deserters to rescue Colonel Hector McCandless, chief of the British East India Company's intelligence service. Although Lawford is nominally in command, Sharpe quickly dominates the lieutenant by force of personality and, without authorization, brings Mary on the mission. Joining the Tippoo's army, they discover that the Tippoo has set a trap for the invading British by mining the weakest (and thus most inviting) portion of Seringapatam's walls. Before Sharpe and Lawford can discover a way to transmit a warning to the British, they are betrayed by Sergeant Hakeswill. Hakeswill has been captured in battle and the Tippoo orders him made a human sacrifice for victory, but Hakeswill secures the Sultan's mercy in exchange for revealing Sharpe's and Lawford's identity as spies. Sharpe and Lawford are imprisoned as the British army prepares to assault the booby-trapped wall of the city. Mary helps Sharpe to escape, and Sharpe blows up the mine before the main British army can enter the trap. As the Tippoo tries to flee the city, Sharpe finds him in a dark tunnel, kills him, and steals his rich jewels. Sharpe throws Hakeswill to the Tippoo's tigers, but the recently fed animals ignore Hakeswill, and Sharpe's enemy survives to plague him in later adventures.

In the dead of night, a fishing vessel sinks in the English Channel, and the circumstances strongly suggest murder. Ex-Special Branch operative Dominic Elder resurfaces from retirement to spearhead the probe into the boat’s blast, convinced that his longtime fixation—the female assassin known as Witch—may be behind it. Witch used the voyage from France to reach England as a conduit, leaving a discreet breadcrumb trail to signal her arrival and to warn Elder off. Yet that warning is only a fraction of Special Branch’s concerns, for Elder’s finely tuned intuition suspects a far more perilous game. He recalls Witch’s resourcefulness and her habit of staying one step ahead of the authorities, making her a formidable adversary. With a looming world-leaders’ summit in London, Witch’s target appears increasingly clear. Michael Barclay, thorough and persistent, follows Witch’s trail and enlists the help of Dominique, a French police liaison who also guides him in Paris. Beyond language support and local insight, Michael finds himself drawn to Dominique. As detectives, MI5 officers, and Witch herself engage in a tense cat-and-mouse pursuit, the chase spans Scotland, England, and France, briefly tracking Witch to a former associate’s prison in Germany as well.

Rosemary Woodhouse, a young woman newly settled in Bramford, a Gothic Revival apartment building in New York City, shares the space with her husband, Guy, an aspiring actor facing career hurdles. Despite warnings about Bramford’s lurid past—linked to witchcraft and murder—the couple chooses to ignore the rumors. Rosemary longs for children, while Guy postpones the idea until he feels securely established. The elderly, quirky Minnie and Roman Castevet quickly befriend the pair, and Rosemary finds their meddlesome, farcical nature off-putting, even as Guy grows to visit them often. After a theatre rival suddenly loses his sight, Guy lands a lead in a new play, and soon he insists that Rosemary begin trying for a baby. His ascent continues: more prominent stage roles followed by talk of a future in Hollywood. A friend’s warning—and that friend’s subsequent mysterious illness—sparks Rosemary’s investigation. She uncovers that their neighbors run a Satanic coven, and she becomes convinced they covet her unborn child to serve as a devilish sacrifice. Yet she cannot persuade anyone else to believe her—or to help. It seems no ally remains, not even Guy. In the climactic twist, Rosemary realizes her worst fears about the coven’s motive are not quite right, but the real horror is far beyond anything she imagined: they intend to render Rosemary a vessel for a child sired by Satan himself.

Misha’s father murders a major Oklahoma businessman, triggering the INS to freeze entry for the entire Vainberg family and leaving Misha stranded in his homeland of Saint Petersburg, which he wistfully calls “St. Leninsburg.” Known also as “Snack Daddy” from his days at Accidental College in the Midwest—an institution echoing Oberlin (Shteyngart’s nod) with a nod to Occidental College—Misha longs to reunite with his true love, Rouenna. Rouenna, whom he met while she worked at a strip club, currently studies at Hunter College and is financially supported by him. When his father is killed by another oligarch, Misha’s chance appears: a crooked diplomat in the fictional Absurdsvanϊ, a former Soviet republic also called Absurdistan, offers to sell him a Belgian passport. Absurdistan’s oil wealth earns it the nickname “Norway of the Caspian.” The country is split between the Sevo and Svanϊ peoples, whose deep-seated enmity centers on a dispute over the tilt of the footrest on an Orthodox cross. As civil war erupts, Misha must align with a new beloved while taking on the role of “Minister of Multiculturalism.” His task is to seek financial aid from Israel, yet it soon becomes clear that the Sevo leader has manipulated him, secretly colluding with the rival Svanϊ chief.

This novel deals with the attempts of the son of (fictional) Chola king Parthiban, Vikraman, to attain independence from the Pallava ruler, Narasimhavarman. The Cholas remain vassals of the Pallavas. Parthiban conveys his dream of the Chola dynasty regaining its glory - which he believes is lost since they are no longer the independent rulers of their land - to his young son Vikraman. Parthiban refuses to pay the taxes to the Pallavas and this triggers the Pallavas to wage war against the Cholas. In the resulting war Parthiban is killed and in the battlefield an enigmatic monk promises to Parthiban that he will make sure that Vikraman fulfills Parthiban's dream. Vikraman grows up and plans his retaliation against Narasimhavarman. But his uncle, Marappa Bhupathi, betrays him and Vikraman is arrested and banished from India by Narasimhavarman. The narrative moves on to describe how Vikraman comes back longing to meet his mother and the mysterious beauty whom he saw before being deported. To his woe he later discovers that his mother has disappeared and has in fact been kidnapped by the savage Kapalikas - a tribe which believes in human sacrifice. He also comes to know that the beauty he has fallen for, Kundhavi, is none other than the daughter of his sworn enemy, Narasimhavarman. The novel climaxes with the identity of the monk being finally being revealed as pallava king, Narasimhavarman and establishment of the independent Chola kingdom under Vikraman in Uraiyur. Vikraman also marries kundhavi in the final chapter.

Second Glance follows several characters throughout the book, in Jodi Picoult's typical fashion, flashing back and forth many decades to piece together the story. It is set in Comtosook, VT. The main plot is that an Abenaki land space is planned to be turned into a shopping mall. However, if the Abenaki can prove that an ancestor was buried on the land, it cannot be built on. Ross Wakeman comes to town to stay with his sister. He is the survivor of many varied suicide attempts, which began after his fiancee Aimee was killed in a car accident years ago. He became a ghost hunter hoping to someday encounter her spirit. Comtosook begins to experience many strange phenomena as the result of the threat of development on the sacred land, including water that refuses to boil. With the help of a local detective, Ross uncovers a decades-old murder mystery that helps to prove that the land in question truly is a Native American-burial ground, and in turn is able to save the land from development. But the Native American that was buried there surprises everyone and makes Ross think with parts of his brain that he has not paid attention to in years.

It is the surreal story of two boys, Hashi and Kiku, who were both abandoned by their mothers during infancy and locked in coin lockers at a Tokyo train station in the summer of 1972. Both boys become wards of the Cherryfield Orphanage in Yokohama, where the tough and athletic Kiku comes to the defense of the slight, and often picked on, Hashi. They are adopted by foster parents, the Kuwayamas (the wife is Zainichi Korean) who live on an island off Kyushu. At the age of 16 both find themselves in a diseased urban wasteland in Tokyo named Toxitown. Hashi, whose voice has deep effects on those who hear it, becomes a bisexual rock star, employed by an eccentric producer named D. Kiku becomes a pole vaulter and with his girlfriend Anemone, a model who has converted her condo into a swamp for her crocodile, searches for a substance named DATURA in order to take his revenge upon the city of Tokyo and destroy it. Along the way, however, in a search for Hashi's real mother, Hashi and D come upon a woman who turns out to be Kiku's... with grave consequences for them all.

A stubborn sticker reading “I’m up, what more do you want from me?” clings to the back of Ayden Kosacov’s bedroom door. Once a joke, that label now edges toward becoming his own oddly exalted creed, a mantra he half-admires and half-defies. Ayden is very much alive, and that seems to be the bluntest truth about him. Trapped in a routine so dull it hurts to remember, he begins to question whether, if life is merely a stage, it would matter at all to him whether he steps into the final scenes or stays offstage. After a near-fatal, almost accidental attempt at suicide and the subsequent road to recovery, he discovers that living entails more than merely existing. As he encounters a spectrum of people and experiences, Ayden reconciles with questions about God, with the pressure and support of his family, and with the person he is becoming. The Orphaned Anything’s voice nods to writers like Denis Johnson (Jesus’ Son) and Dave Eggers (A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius) while aiming to impart practical lessons, encouragement, and hope in the spirit of Paulo Coelho (The Alchemist) and Donald Miller (Blue Like Jazz).

Near to the Wild Heart defies a conventional storyline, instead collectionizing brief glimpses from Joana’s life that oscillate between her current adulthood and childhood. As with many of Lispector’s works, the emphasis rests on internal, emotional landscapes. The narrative opens with Joana as a girl at play in the garden, composing poems for her father. Her unruly spirit, almost palpable violence, and inventive use of language stand out as defining traits. Throughout the tale she is likened to various animals—described as a bird, a snake, a wildcat, a horse, and a dog. Her actions border on transgression: as a child she hurls a book at an elderly man’s head; later, as a grown woman, she abandons her husband Otávio and reacts with flat apathy to news of his affair—his liaison with another woman, his old acquaintance Lídia, whom he has made pregnant. Rather than a straightforward moral judgment, Joana appears amoral rather than immoral, encapsulated in the line, “Evil is not living, and that’s it. Dying is already something else. Dying is different from good and evil.” The text also quotes lengthy passages from Spinoza—arguably the most substantial direct excerpts in Lispector’s entire body of fiction—suggesting a deep kinship with the Dutch thinker’s amoral worldview.

Returning to the small coastal town of Dunnet, Maine, after a brief summer visit years earlier, the narrator comes back to finish her book. She makes her home with Mrs. Todd, an elderly local apothecary and herbalist. While Mrs. Todd steps out, the narrator begins some work, yet this interruption disrupts her writing flow. To focus, she rents an empty schoolhouse nearby. After a funeral, Captain Littlepage, an eighty-year-old retired sailor who knows Mrs. Todd, visits the schoolhouse to chat with the narrator and recount his sea memories. Her bored reception signals that she’s offended him, prompting her to salvage the moment by inviting him to share more of his tale. Yet the Captain’s reminiscences pale in comparison to the livelier stories told by Mrs. Todd, her brother and mother, and other residents of Dunnet. Over the course of the summer, the narrator’s bond with Mrs. Todd deepens, and her admiration for the Maine coast and its people grows with each passing day.

In town, Willy and his dog Searchlight discover his grandfather is bedridden and despondent about living. The sole physician, Doc Smith, informs Willy that his grandfather wishes to die. Later, tax collector Clifford Snyder infiltrates Willy’s home, pistol in hand, pressing for the grandpa’s debt to the state and, after glancing at papers, declares a Wyoming tab of 500 dollars. The following day, Willy enters a dog-sled race carrying a prize of 500 dollars. He notices a sled drawn by five fast Samoyeds; the entrant turns out to be Stone Fox—the enigmatic Native American who speaks to whites rarely and has never lost a race. As the competition unfolds, Willy’s lightweight, single-dog sled proves unusually adept at navigating sharp bends and even enables a dangerous shortcut across a frozen lake. Tragically, Searchlight collapses from exhaustion just ten feet from the finish line, her heart bursting on impact. Stone Fox marks the path with a booted line, draws a rifle, and warns that any other racer who crosses first will be shot. Yet in a stunning turn, he relinquishes the victory to Willy, allowing Searchlight to be carried over the finish line to the astonishment of everyone watching.

Arthur Zouch, portrait painter and self-declared "superman," comes to stay at Passenger Court, ostensibly to paint the portrait of the younger Passenger daughter, Mary, but in no small part on the lookout for any opportunity he can find to improve either his social, financial, or sexual satisfaction. At Passenger court, he finds opportunity for all three, but he also finds unanticipated conflict in the person of Vernon Passenger, also a self-proclaimed "superman." Meanwhile, the neighboring Fosdick family – the Major, his sons Torquil and Jasper – carry on a seemingly perpetual feud with the Passengers that is as often characterized by displays of better manners and more proper etiquette as it is by bad temper and argument. Joanna Brandon, a local young woman, further complicates the lives of several of the principals; she may be Powell’s most sensitively rendered female character. The novel moves through ten chapters toward an inescapable denouement, though never tipping its hand as to precisely how the foreshadowing of the title shall be brought to fruition. The parallel plots (at times almost Lear-like in the development of the neighbouring families) reach a double climax from which only one ‘superman’ can emerge.

The story itself is loosely based around Billy, a young boy who has always dreamed of owning a sweet shop, especially since there is an abandoned one named The Grubber (an old [[English word for sweet shop) near where he lives. One day, he finds that the old building has been renovated and has become the head office for the Ladderless Window-Cleaning Company. Billy then meets its workers, a Giraffe with an extendable neck, a Pelican (or "Pelly" as he is called by the others) who can retract his upper beak, and a Monkey, whom he then befriends. They all band together when they receive a letter from the Duke of Hampshire asking them to clean the windows of Hampshire House. When they get there, things go smoothly until the Giraffe and the Monkey, while cleaning the windows of the Duchess's bedroom, spot a burglar who attempts to steal the Duchess's diamond jewellery. The Pelican then flies in and catches the burglar in his beak, holding him there while the others panic. Eventually, the police arrive to arrest the burglar, whom the Chief of Police identifies as "The Cobra", one of the world's most dangerous cat burglars. As a reward for retrieving the Duchess's diamonds, the Duke invites the L.W.C.C. to live on his estate as his personal helper. Billy's dreams come true because the Giraffe, Pelican and Monkey will no longer be needing the Grubber building; with a little help from the Duke, the Grubber is reopened into the most fantastic sweet shop in the whole town (even selling sweets from the Willy Wonka company). And they live happily ever after.

Maerth argued that consuming brain produced an aphrodisiac effect—likely due to the large hormone content—and that this initially led apes to crave it, prompting brain-hunt episodes where males from rival bands were killed and females subjected to rape in a frenzy linked to brain-induced sexuality and violence. The diet, however, inadvertently increased brain size and intelligence while causing hair loss and a decline in our innate psychic abilities. Over time, humans emerged, remaining cannibalistic until about 50,000 years ago. Modern humans, now estranged from their surroundings after losing telepathic contact with nature and with other animals, suffer from distorted sexuality caused by hormonal imbalances and are driven toward madness by the constant pressure of oversized brains pressing inside the skull. Maerth (1974), p. 53, predicts that humanity is inevitably destroying itself through pollution, overpopulation, racial mixing, and eventually nuclear war. He also forecasts a near-future return to cannibalism (Maerth, p. 199) and urges readers to withdraw from society, adopt a vegetarian diet, study Eastern wisdom, and perhaps use wooden frames and wire devices to alter the skull’s shape as some ancient cultures did, thereby relieving brain pressure and partially restoring psychic powers.

In the not-too-distant future, a cold war threatens to turn hot. Colonization of Mars seems to be mankind's only hope of surviving certain Armageddon. To facilitate this, the American government begins a cyborg program to create a being capable of surviving the harsh Martian environment: Man Plus. After the death of the first candidate, due to the project supervisors forgetting to enhance his brain's ability to process sensory input to cope with the new stimuli he is receiving, Roger Torraway becomes the heart of the program. In order to survive in the thin Martian atmosphere, Roger Torraway's body must be replaced with an artificial one. At every step he becomes more and more disconnected from humanity, unable to feel things in his new body. It is only after arriving on Mars that his new body begins to make sense to him. It is perfectly adapted to this new world, and thus he becomes perfectly separated from his old world, and from humanity. The success of the Martian mission spurs similar cyborg programs in other spacefaring nations. It is revealed that the computer networks of Earth have become sentient, and that ensuring humanity's survival will guarantee theirs as well. In the end, the network is puzzled...it appears that something else was behind the push to space, a mystery even to the machines.

In Adventure in Australia, the Count of Champignac, joined by a young professor, Walker Donahue, believes he has made an extraordinary find: a colossal indigenous monolith near a mining village in Australia. He invites Spirou and Fantasio to come along, and they travel there with Seccotine, whose presence proves indispensable. Upon their arrival, Donahue reveals that the Count was killed by some miners. Following their investigation, they learn that the Count is not dead; instead, they encounter him severely battered, confronting Sam—a gangster who makes his fortune by extorting prospectors. Sam ultimately dies when a truck explodes due to a nitroglycerin bottle. Benefiting from the aid of the local aboriginals, Spirou, Donahue, and the Count drive Sam’s henchmen from the field, those who had been targeting Fantasio and Seccotine. In the end, the monolith is unearthed, and an agreement is reached whereby the indigenous community shares resources with the prospectors, who are grateful to them for removing Sam from the equation.

It is 1934 and Nick is working, without great success, as a script writer at a film company. He gets invited by a colleague, Chips Lovell, to a party at the home of Lady Molly Jeavons. There he learns that Widmerpool is to marry the twice widowed, somewhat notorious (somewhat insane according to Nick) Mrs. Mildred Haycock. Nick subsequently has to endure having to lunch with Widmerpool and fending-off questions from Widmerpool's prospective in-laws becomes, for Nick, a motif throughout the novel. Also re-encountered at Lady Molly's gathering is old Alfred Tolland. A chance meeting by Nick with Quiggin (at a cinema where Man of Aran is showing) leads to a surprising and rather mysterious invitation of a weekend visit to the country. Quiggin and Mona Templer are staying, it transpires, in a cottage loaned to them by Erridge (Lord Warminster, eccentric head of the Tolland family). While there they all visit the Tolland ancestral home, Thrubworth Park, for a frugal but eventful dinner. Just as the meal is finishing two Tolland sisters, Susan and Isobel, arrive. Some while later Nick meets Lady Molly's husband, Ted Jeavons, in a Soho pub and they visit Umfraville's nightclub. They encounter Widmerpool (suffering another bout with jaundice), Mrs Haycock and Templer. In Autumn 1934 Jenkins becomes engaged to Isobel. Erridge, wanting to study conditions for himself, goes to China at a time when the Japanese army are undertaking offensive operations. Mona goes with him, ditching Quiggin. Widmerpool's engagement to Mildred Haycock is broken off in farcical and, to most men, crushing circumstances. However, Widmerpool remains undaunted. *Adapted in part from material published by the Anthony Powell Society with consent

In a race against a merciless foe, Mary Russell and Sherlock Holmes pursue the villain and safeguard Holmes’s artist son, Damian Adler, and his daughter Estelle—Adler’s half-Chinese three-year-old. Their hunt leads them into the orbit of The Children of Lights, a Shanghai-rooted religious sect operating within Britain. Set in the summer of 1924, the narrative begins beside an ancient stone circle on Orkney Island not long after the fanatic Thomas Brothers—a man intent on releasing psychic forces through ritual murder—shoots Damian. To obtain medical aid for his son, Holmes travels to the Netherlands, while Mary traverses the country to shield Estelle from Brothers and his associates. Brothers’ tenuous network reaches into the highest levels of government, creating a conspiracy that Scotland Yard ardently pursues. Amid this tension, the Holmes family finds themselves under intense scrutiny and pressure from law enforcement. Amidst the peril, a contemporary, elusive figure reminiscent of Robin Goodfellow surfaces to aid Mary and her family.

The story concerns four people - Dr. Lionel Barrett, a physicist with an interest in parapsychology, his wife Edith, and two mediums (Florence Tanner, a Spiritualist and mental medium, and Benjamin Franklin Fischer, a physical medium) - who are hired by dying millionaire William Reinhardt Deutsch to investigate the possibility of life after death. To do so, they must enter the infamous Belasco House in Maine, regarded as the most haunted house in the world. The house is called "Hell House" due to the horrible acts of blasphemy and perversion that occurred there under the silent influence and supervision of Emeric Belasco. Fischer is the only survivor of a failed investigation attempt thirty years earlier. The novel combines supernatural horror with mystery as the researchers attempt to investigate the haunting of the house while their sanity is subtly undermined by its sinister supernatural influence. During the investigation, various influences begin to affect each character's personal weaknesses: Florence through her belief in Spiritualism and her over-eagerness to rid the house of its evil; Dr. Barrett through his almost-arrogant disbelief in/disregard for Spiritualism, his belief in science, and his debilitated physical condition (having suffered from polio when young); Edith through her personal fears, insecurities and pent-up desires; and Fischer through his deliberate inaction (which he calls "caution"). Hell House's potency comes from its apparent ability to corrupt those who enter its walls, before bringing about their destruction, both mental and physical.

18-year-old April Lancaster, the child of Janice and Hugh Lancaster, enters the hospital for testing as she has been suffering from headaches, blackouts, and eventually passed out in English class. During this time, April becomes acquainted with Mark Gianni, who suffers from cystic fibrosis, and has been in and out of the hospital since he was born. Mark is very interested in April, and even tells her that he intends to marry her, but she declines his offer to go out, as she already has a boyfriend, Chris. April is told by her doctor that she has an inoperable brain tumor, a recurrence of the case she had as a five-year-old, and needs to start radiation treatments. Soon after breaking the news to Chris, he ends their relationship, and April begins to date Mark. Over time, the two fall in love, and Mark proposes to April. She accepts, although her parents aren't thrilled about the match. Eventually, they do reconcile to the idea. Shortly afterward, the car that Mark is driving in during a race (he is an avid racing fan) flips over and ignites. Mark survives the crash, but he develops pneumonia and dies. The book ends with April and her parents in St. Croix for a vacation. April releases a red balloon for Mark, as he had once done for her. The sequel, For Better, For Worse, Forever begins with April in St. Croix.

Written in 1914, the novel unfolds across three sections set a few years earlier. In the opening segment, the narrator—a straightforward university student—befriends Sensei, an older, unnamed man who lives as a recluse. Sensei remains largely distant, conversing only with his wife, the narrator, and the occasional unseen visitors, while keeping others at arm’s length. He is seen visiting a friend’s grave, yet he withholds details of his own past. The middle portion follows the narrator’s graduation and return to the countryside, where he awaits his father’s impending death. As the father nears death, Sensei’s letter arrives, and the third part—Sensei and His Testament— recounts its contents. Sensei discloses that during his university years he was swindled by an uncle, prompting a move to Tokyo and a life with a widow and her daughter, with whom he falls in love. He then convinces his childhood friend, simply known as K, who is in precarious circumstances, to move in. Over time, K recovers but also falls for the landlady’s daughter. When K confesses this love to Sensei, Sensei is shocked and increasingly jealous. He proposes marriage; soon after, K commits suicide. Having been betrayed by his uncle, Sensei’s faith in humanity is shattered. He discovers the same dark tendencies within himself and is overwhelmed by guilt over his friend’s death. In the closing frame, set in 1912, Sensei, moved by General Nogi Maresuke’s suicide following the Meiji Emperor’s death, resolves to end his own life and pens a letter to his sole friend explaining his choice.

The Shepherd's Paradise deals with a mythical pastoral community dedicated to Platonic love, a refuge for unrequited lovers of both genders — "a peaceful receptacle of distressed minds." The Shepherd's Paradise is ruled by Bellesa, "beauty," who was certainly played by Henrietta Maria. The heroine of the piece is Fidamira. Much of Montagu's plot, such as it is, centers upon a prince named Basilino and his bosom friend Agenor, who have a shared tendency to fall in love with the same women. (The work is complicated by the fact that characters take on pseudonyms when entering the Paradise: Basilino becomes Moramente, while Agenor calls himself Genorio.) By the close of the play, Agenor/Genorio is revealed to be Prince Palante, long-lost son of the king of Navarre. The masque also features an extended debate on the nature of love, between Martiro, who speaks for the Platonic ideal, and Moramente and Melidoro, who argue for marriage. Since the play ends in the marriages typical of comedy — Basilino/Moramente marries Bellesa who is actually Sapphira, Princess of Navarre, his original betrothed, while Agenor/Genorio/Palante marries Basilino's sister — the text can be interpreted as suggesting a triumph of marital union over Platonic love. Fidamira is revealed as sister to both Bellesa/Sapphira and Agenor/Genorio/Palante, the lost princess Miranda; she remains chaste, but she gets to be queen of the Shepherd's Paradise at the end.

Ryan Bingham, a 35-year-old career-transition counselor, works for Integrated Strategic Management, a Denver-based management consulting outfit. His job sends him across the country to fire recently laid-off workers, then coach them on reentering the job market. He aims to accumulate one million Frequent Flyer miles, a threshold only nine others in the same mileage club—run by the fictional Great West airline—have reached. All of this unfolds before his boss returns from vacation, discovers his resignation letter, and cancels the company credit card. Meanwhile, Bingham is courting a potential employer: MythTech, a shadowy Omaha-based firm. He is divorced, and his volatile younger sister is about to dive into another doomed relationship. His world is built around Palm Pilots, rental cars, salted almonds, Kevlar luggage, and nameless suite hotels where email and voicemail are the primary modes of communication. He relies on a heavy daily medication regimen and spends time with women in Las Vegas. A looming fear haunts him: someone might be quietly siphoning off his precious miles, a theft he equates with stealing his very soul.

Set in three distinct parts, An Open Swimmer is a 'coming of age' novel; it details the late-teen life of a young man named Jerra Nilsam. A considerable part of the novel describes the camping trip taken by Jerra and his childhood friend, Sean. On this camping trip, Jerra and Sean meet an old man living in a shack on the beach near their camp site. As the story progresses, it becomes apparent that the old man had murdered his wife in a similar shack on a nearby beach by burning it down with her inside. Many sub-plots are scattered throughout this book in the form of spontaneous paragraphs and dialogues between unnamed characters (but presumably one of them is Jerra). In the end, after having returned home and parted ways with Sean, Jerra returns to the camping site alone. While Jerra is sleeping in his van, there is a violent storm which results in a large tree falling on the Kombi. Jerra awakes in the old mans hut, the storm having passed and having been saved by the old man. In the final paragraph, Jerra returns to his Kombi, opens the fuel tank and drops a match into it before running.

Next to a church in a prosperous Scottish industrial town is the "Garden of Eden", a dance hall of dubious reputation. The "Garden of Eden" is a thorn in the side of the innocent and unworldly Catholic priest Father Malachy, who is praying to God that He will close the dance hall. During an argument with a Protestant minister, Father Malachy claims that God could miraculously remove the "Garden of Eden". The skeptical Protestant scoffs and Father Malachy inadvertently predicts that God will indeed remove the "Garden of Eden" on a specific date. The date comes and the building and all the people inside vanish and reappear on Bass Rock, a small island in the Firth of Forth. This apparent miracle draws the attention of the media, politicians and scientists, all trying to find rational explanations. The Catholic Church is reluctant to officially recognize this occurrence as a miracle, fearing either a loss of control in matters of faith, or a loss of face if the disappearance of the "Garden of Eden" should turn out to be a hoax or fabrication. Meanwhile, believers from all over the world come on pilgrimage to the former location of the dance hall. Soon the site becomes a fairground, with the town’s people, entrepreneurs and journalists trying to make a profit from the miracle and the resulting sudden influx of pilgrims. This includes the sale of holy water and miniature models of the "Garden of Eden". A young woman, who was in the dance hall during the night it vanished, becomes a media star. Financial investors are buying the island where the "Garden of Eden" reappeared, and construct a casino that soon attracts crowds of people. Father Malachy is confronted with interview requests from journalists, and pilgrims beleaguer the church, hoping to meet the miracle-working priest. As he has spent most of his life in the monastery, he feels helpless in the face of the excesses of modern society. He soon regrets that he asked God for the miracle. He travels to the island and prays for a second miracle that will end the frenzy, and is heard by God, who returns the "Garden of Eden" to its original location.

Faia Rissedote’s tale, Fire in the Mist, opens with her as a village shepherd. After returning from the fields, she discovers her community murdered by plague, and in her grief she loses control of her magic, unleashing devastation that wipes out the entire village. The catastrophe resounds as far away as the town of Ariss, where university staff dedicated to training mages journey to investigate. They locate Faia and escort her back to their institution. There, however, she cannot fit in: her power is immense, yet her self-control is lacking, and her peers—fellow mages—either doubt her abilities or resent her humble origins. She forms a bond with a young mage, engaging in a forbidden sexual encounter that is believed to sap magical talent. A string of murders then erupts, chiefly aimed at promising young mages. The female faculty members suspect the male students, arguing the killings echo an older legend that cast men as the killers. Soon Faia’s body is possessed by the killer’s spirit—the figure from the legend—and the murders resume within the university. The truth is revealed: the murderer is a woman, the same figure connected to the legend, now inhabiting Faia’s body. Faia defeats her by exposing the killer’s pregnancy, reclaiming her own body, and fleeing the institution. Despite explanations, the university staff retain their resentment, and she sets out on a journey.”

In a town highly suspicious of the government and of outsiders in general, the arrival of a charismatic figure from the desert—Oyster—occasions an intensification of the town's insularity and repression of dissident voices. The conjunction of conservative forms of Christianity and anti-government landowners is ripe for the messianic presence of Oyster and the cult community he establishes, a community closely integrated into the shadowy capitalism of the area's illegal opal trafficking. The fragmented structure of the novel, in which various moments in the past are interspersed with events in the present, generates heightened suspense and tension as its several sub-plots come together in the apocalyptic destruction of the town and the cult. The paranoia and violence with which the town polices its "lost" status are repeatedly delineated, until events come to a head and the vicious forms of control begin to unravel. Women are crucial to the destabilisation and destruction of the menace represented above all by powerful men. The discourse of proud outsiderness on the part of these men is highlighted as being hypocritical and self-serving, while the real outsiders are revealed to be mostly women, and men who do not wield social power.

Guadalupe “Lupe” Guardado, a middle-aged Salvadoran woman, lives near Chalatenango, El Salvador. To support her family during the day, she does what she can while her husband works for a wealthy landowner. José, her husband, has joined the rebellion against the prevailing economic conditions and leads a Christian farmers’ organization. Fearing retaliation for his activism, José frequently retreats to the hills after work and scarcely sees his family. Their son Justino was killed by the authorities before the events of the novel, and their son-in-law Helio has vanished. Adolfina, Guadalupe’s granddaughter, recounts a protest at a cathedral and a massacre of students on a bus. Toward the novel’s end, authorities present Guadalupe and Adolfina with a beaten man who uttered the name “Adolfina” under torture. Although Adolfina does not recognize the man, Guadalupe recognizes her husband José. Following his prior advice, she denies knowing him, and he is taken away.”

After rejecting the shadowed trade, Kylar Stern begins anew following a brutal coup by the Godking. With his master slain and his closest ally dead—Logan Gyre, Cenaria’s heir—the ruling class is decimated, leaving little to mourn. He relocates to start over: a fresh city, new companions, and a different path. Yet the possibility that Logan survives, hidden and imprisoned, forces Kylar to confront an unwinnable choice: renounce the way of shadows forever and seek peace with a young family, or lean into his destructive talents—the training he poured years into—in order to rescue his friend and his homeland, thereby sacrificing what he holds most dear. Cenaria’s new ruler, Godking Garoth Ursuul, now wields power and steers the fates of all who inhabit the realm. In the chaos, many nobles—led by self-styled Queen Terah Graesin—have abandoned the city to the Khalidorans, leaving ruin in their wake. In an effort to escape the life of shadows that ruined his mentor, Kylar flees to Caernarvon, seeking an idealized life with Elene. But darkness pursues him on the road toward light as old allies return for one final mission, and Kylar learns more about the identities of Durzo and, ultimately, himself. The twilight-tinged hero stands poised between light and shadow, a formidable force, yet the question remains: which fate will he choose?

Wings Shenah Peshah is a young janitress whose life is painfully isolating and impoverished. Her hope flickers when a sociologist moves into her building to study the residents he writes about, and she unexpectedly falls in love with him. Hunger: a follow-up to Wings, Peshah takes a job at a shirtwaist factory where one of her coworkers falls for her. The Lost “Beautifulness” follows a mother who teeters on self-destruction as she whitewashes her kitchen for her son’s homecoming from the military, only to have the rent increased by a cruel landlord in retaliation. The Free Vacation House centers on a woman overwhelmed by motherhood who is offered a stay at a complimentary vacation residence, yet the stern, humiliating living conditions prove harsher than her life in poverty. The Miracle recounts a Jewish girl’s voyage to America in search of love, only to encounter hardship and loneliness. Where Lovers Dream depicts poverty driving a wedge between a once-happy pair, forever partitioning their lives into incompatible paths. Soap and Water follows a student who is denied her diploma due to her unkempt appearance from a grueling life spent balancing school and grinding poverty, sparking rebellion against class divisions. The Fat of the Land traces a mother who ascends from poverty to wealth, chasing happiness only to confront a cruel Catch-22. My Own People introduces a young writer who discovers purpose and meaning through the suffering of her fellow kin. How I Found America brings the collection to a close with a meditation on the quest for belonging.

Timoleon Vieta, a small mongrel with black-and-white fur and eyes that rival a girl’s for beauty, is the central figure. He shares a dwelling with Cockcroft, a retired, openly gay composer living in a shabby Umbrian farmhouse funded by occasional royalties from his past theme tunes. As Cockcroft ruminates on a stalled career and old flames, a Bosnian man arrives at their door bearing a business card Cockcroft supposedly handed him in a Florence bar—a scene that stems from the composer’s notorious, alcohol-fueled weekend seductions. In return for occasional odd jobs and weekly sexual favors, Cockcroft offers Timoleon shelter, yet the dog, discerning and perceptive, distrusts the Bosnian, a sentiment the visitor mirrors. Faced with a terrible choice, Cockcroft decides to sever ties with the dog and leaves him behind in Rome. The rest of the book traces Timoleon’s arduous trek back to his beloved master, following a string of brief encounters with various people as he navigates the long road home.

Koestler starts off the book by looking back into his childhood about his philosophy of the world. He states that when he looks at the world, he looks at it as how the Babylonians did. He goes on to talk about where the Babylonians and Egyptians left off and the Greeks took over philosophy. "Homer's world is another, more colourful oyster, a floating disc surrounded by Okeanus." A central theme of The Sleepwalkers is the changing relationship between faith and reason. Koestler explores how these seemingly contradictory threads existed harmoniously in many of the greatest intellectuals of the West. He illustrates that while the two are estranged today, in the past the most ground-breaking thinkers were often very spiritual. Another recurrent theme of this book is the breaking of paradigms in order to create new ones. People - scientists included - hold onto cherished old beliefs with such love and attachment that they refuse to see the wrong in their ideas and the truth in the ideas that are to replace them. "The conclusion he puts forward at the end of the book is that modern science is trying too hard to be rational. Scientists have been at their best when they allowed themselves to behave as "sleepwalkers," instead of trying too earnestly to ratiocinate."

The tale centers on Lord Montfallcon and his bid to shape courtly power in opposition to Captain Quire. Both men manipulate Albion’s secretive web of espionage and deception to serve their aims, with Gloriana ensnared in the midst. For years Montfallcon has kept the realm peaceful during Gloriana’s thirteen-year rule through fear, coercion, and a vast network of informants. He stands as the real force behind Gloriana’s throne, one of the few survivors from King Hern’s court, a regime under which much of his family perished to entertain the brutal ruler. Montfallcon’s sole mission is to preserve a tyrant-free Albion under Gloriana; yet in pursuing that goal he mirrors the worst tactics once employed by Hern’s henchmen. Quire, regarded as Montfallcon’s most capable ally, grows resentful when he believes he has been affronted, and he plots vengeance by wooing the discontented Gloriana. He retreats into the walls to spy on the court, rallies the palace rabble into a private force, and conducts incursions into the court to kill and leave clues that implicate other courtiers. Eventually Quire emerges, presenting himself as Gloriana’s champion at court, later ascending to lord chancellor and, eventually, becoming her lover—an arrangement that endangers her sovereignty and risks undermining the symbol of Albion itself.

The Hardy Boys travel to France for a holiday, where a chance sighting of The Gray Man in Manhattan reveals a probe into a terrorist network operating in France. Although the Gray Man warns that involvement would be too risky for youths, the brothers secretly insert themselves into the investigation, eventually slipping undercover in France as a pair of gun dealers immersed in the punk scene—dyed hair and ragged attire included. Their path drifts into the operations of Renyard and Company, a front that secretly traffics firearms and other illicit goods to hidden buyers. Denise lends a hand when a deadly trap nearlyclaims them inside a machine, enabling their escape. The narrative unfolds with a web of betrayals: Renyard and Company, Denise, and numerous others all double-cross one another. At one point, the Hardy Boys are seized by the French police force known as the Sûreté, yet they manage a breakout through a a physical confrontation. As the climax approaches, the mastermind behind Renyard & Company and his partners close in, intent on eliminating them. Denise intervenes at the last moment to rescue the siblings. With the danger averted, the Hardy Boys crack the case and return home to the United States.

This book offers a candid, humorous, and practical tour through the many phases of pregnancy. It details the physical and emotional changes you can expect to see in your partner—and how those shifts affect your relationship over the months ahead. Pregnancy is a shared journey for two people, and parenting will be too; therefore, your partner’s pregnancy should involve both of you, together. If you’re male and have previously avoided pregnancy books because you felt out of place or the tone didn’t connect with you, yet you still have questions, The Blokes’ Guide to: Pregnancy is the resource you’ve been seeking. As a father myself, I recognized—when my partner Lisa became pregnant—that there was nothing out there that spoke to my perspective. The Blokes’ Guide to Pregnancy responds to that gap. Jon offers a witty yet informed glimpse into the realities of becoming a father, delivering both education and laughter in equal measure.

Martin Springfield and Rachel Mansour return to Earth to recuperate following the events of Singularity Sky, however Rachel is quickly called upon to explain the administrative expenses she incurred during her previous assignment. Shortly thereafter she finds herself negotiating with a lunatic believing himself to be a reincarnation of Idi Amin and in possession of an armed nuclear device which, in the black humor typical of the series, he has threatened to detonate after receiving an eviction notice from his apartment. Meanwhile, a young and hopeful planetary civilization is murdered by the apparent use of a causality violation device which causes their sun to explode without warning (the "iron sunrise" of the title), and their defense systems to deploy automatically against the homeworld of the suspected perpetrators of the atrocity. Rachel and Martin set off to investigate these events and prevent the assassination of the remaining members of the murdered civilization's leaders, who can abort the retaliation strike. In the background the Eschaton continues to play its own game.

Treading Air follows the life of Ullo Paerand, narrated through a blend of perspectives: the protagonist’s own memories and the alternating voice of Jaak Sirkel, Paerand’s schoolmate who recurs in several of Kross’s recent works. The narrative begins with Ullo recalling a childhood journey to Germany in the 1920s and closes as he envisions a meeting with his aged father, who had fled west with his lover. Paerand clings to the vivid happiness of his early years, even as hardship grows after his father’s departure. With his mother’s support, he pursues a better future and, despite some humiliations, completes a solid secondary education at one of Tallinn’s premier grammar schools. His sharp memory and entrepreneurial drive propel him toward professional achievement: a position within the Prime Minister’s Office beckons. Yet fortune betrays him. The occupations of Soviet and German forces bars him from a respectable career path. Aligning with nationalist circles, he dedicates himself to Estonia’s restoration, and he even declines a chance to flee west offered by a Vatican emissary. The remainder of his life, about four decades, is spent in modest labor and in making suitcases in a factory. Among Kross’s most acclaimed works, Treading Air stands with Keisri hull (The Czar’s Madman) as a landmark, often cited as the author’s finest novel by many readers. de:Paigallend et:Paigallend

The book's eponymous protagonist, Timofey Pavlovich Pnin, is a Russian-born professor living in the United States. Pnin, a refugee in his 50s from both Communist Russia and what he calls the "Hitler war", is an assistant professor of Russian at fictional Waindell College, possibly modeled on Wellesley College or Cornell University, at both of which Nabokov himself taught. At Waindell, Pnin has settled down to an uncertain, untenured, but semi-respectable academic life, full of various tragicomic mishaps, misfortunes, and difficulties adjusting to American life and language. Characters in the book include his departmental supervisor, various professors and university staff, his landlord, his ex-wife, and her son. The book's seemingly unreliable narrator identifies himself as one 'Vladimir Vladimirovich N---' and bears similarities to Nabokov himself, such as his interest in lepidoptery and his landed-gentry Russian émigré past. Pnin is last glimpsed fleeing Waindell College, jobless, for an unknown destination.

Gemma and Alice have shared a life-long bond, yet a sleepover revelation—Gemma reading Alice’s diary—foreshadows an impending move for Alice. The growing distance strains their friendship, and the prospect of new companions looms large. Throughout the tale, the central message remains that true friends endure to the end. From birth, Gemma and Alice have been inseparable best friends: born on the same day in the same hospital, their connection has endured unbroken. They are complete opposites—Gemma’s energy and messiness contrast with Alice’s grace and tidiness—but their trust remains unshakable, and each birthday they silently wish to stay friends forever. Everything shifts when Alice’s father accepts a distant job, forcing the family to relocate hundreds of miles away. Suddenly, both girls must learn to navigate life apart and the challenges of sustaining their friendship. In Alice’s social circle, Flora appears as another friend, a decidedly posh presence that Gemma resents. A clash erupts when Gemma visits Alice at the same time Flora is there; Gemma storms in with a cake and, in a moment of anger, flings it at Flora. The narrative concludes with Alice sending a birthday card, bringing the story to a close.

Mark Mathabane was born into a poverty-stricken family during the apartheid years in the township of Alexandra. Throughout childhood, he witnesses and suffers from hunger, violence, and racial stereotypes, learning to hate and fear whites. At his mother’s insistence, Mathabane starts school and learns to love it, rising to the top of his class in spite of frequent punishments due to his family’s late payments for school fees and inability to afford school supplies . He graduates from primary school with a scholarship that will pay for his secondary education. Mathabane’s grandmother becomes a gardener for a kind family, the Smiths, who introduce Mathabane to books and tennis by sending books and even a tennis racket home with his grandmother for him. He learns English from these books, and begins to play tennis frequently, eventually befriending a black tennis player who trains him. Mathabane joins the high school tennis team and begins to play in tournaments, unofficially sponsored by Wilfred Horn, owner of the Tennis Ranch. It is technically illegal for Mark to play there, but the law is ignored and he becomes comfortable with whites. Eventually renowned tennis player Stan Smith takes Mathabane under his wing when the two meet at a tournament. Stan pays for Mathabane to compete in tournaments and talks to his coach at the University of Southern California about Mathabane attending college in the states. The coach writes to colleges on his behalf and Mathabane earns a tennis scholarship to Limestone College and leaves for the U.S. in 1978.

Maigret probes the events surrounding a homeless man found battered and rescued from the Seine after an assault. The discarded doctor, nicknamed by other transients as “The Doc,” had left his family two decades earlier to practice in Gabon, then came back to Paris to live rough, mostly under bridges. Through Madame Maigret’s sister in Mulhouse, he pieces together more about the doctor’s family history. His wife, though separated and not formally divorced, agrees to visit him in the hospital but shows little warmth or desire for reconciliation. The rescued tramp is identified as François Keller, saved by Jef van Houtte, a Belgian barge owner. While hospitalized, Keller remains silent, refusing to speak. Yet Maigret suspects Keller holds knowledge about his assailant and is concealing a crucial reason. He also doubts van Houtte is telling the full story. Under strenuous questioning, van Houtte finally admits that years earlier he caused his father-in-law’s death by drowning, and Keller witnessed it. Nevertheless, Keller still refuses to talk, leaving Maigret with insufficient evidence to press charges. Keller goes back to life on the streets.

The volume features a well-known appendix that circulated separately as the Pseudomonarchia daemonum—a catalog of infernal spirits, with the names, titles, and supposed powers attributed to each. Weyer says his informant for this material was a work titled Liber officiorum spirituum, seu liber dictus Empto Salomonis, de principibus et regibus demoniorum (The Book of the Offices of Spirits, or the Book Called Empto, by Solomon, on the princes and kings of demons). Rather than aiming to teach occult practices, Weyer's purpose was to reveal the pretensions of self-styled magicians to all readers, exposing their boastfulness, oddities, deceptions, vanity, folly, fakery, madness, and misjudgments by bringing their visions into daylight. According to Weyer's source, the demon population was estimated at 7,451,926, organized into 1,111 legions and governed by 72 infernal princes. The source further claimed that Hell itself is structured as an infernal court, with a hierarchy comprising princes, ministries, and ambassadors.

In a vastly overpopulated world, businesses have taken the place of governments and now hold all political power. States exist merely to ensure the survival of huge trans-national corporations. Advertising has become hugely aggressive and by far the best-paid profession. Through advertising, the public is constantly deluded into thinking that the quality of life is improved by all the products placed on the market. However, the most basic elements are incredibly scarce, including water and fuel. The planet Venus has just been visited and judged fit for human settlement, despite its inhospitable surface and climate; the colonists would have to endure a harsh climate for many generations until the planet could be terraformed. The protagonist, Mitch Courtenay, is a star-class copywriter in the Fowler Schocken advertising agency who has been assigned the ad campaign which would attract colonists to Venus. But a lot more is happening than he knows about. It soon becomes a tale of mystery and intrigue, in which many of the characters are not what they seem, and Mitch's loyalties and opinions change drastically over the course of the narrative.

Cugel yields to Fianosther the merchant's coaxing and agrees to attempt the burglary of Iucounu the Laughing Magician’s manor. Caught and cornered, he bargains for his freedom with a task: recover a tiny violet-glass hemisphere, an Eye of the Overworld, to match one already in the wizard’s possession. An attached, calculating alien on his liver—Firx, a spiny, hooked appendage—keeps him in line with promises of loyalty, zeal, and single-minded purpose, while Iucounu uses magic to ferry Cugel by flying demon to the distant Land of Cutz. There, two villages stand: one inhabited by those who wear violet lenses, the other by peasants serving the lens-wearers in hopes of advancement. The lenses distort perception, letting their bearers glimpse the Overworld instead of their squalor—where a hut can be a palace and meager gruel a grand feast, a metaphorical “rose-colored glasses” vision on a cosmic scale. Through guile, Cugel secures an Eye and escapes from Cutz, then endures a grueling journey back to Iucounu, cursing the magician every step of the way; this ordeal constitutes the novel’s core. After countless trials, including Firx’s removal from his system, Cugel returns to the manse only to discover the wizard’s will has been seized by a Firx twin. He proceeds to purge the alien and subdue the sorcerer, savoring an easy life within the mansion—until he attempts to banish Iucounu and Fianosther (the latter having come to steal from him) with the same spell that had been used on him. A misstep of language during the incantation, however, causes the flying demon to seize him once more, delivering him to the very same location as before. Michael Shea later penned an authorized sequel, A Quest for Simbilis (DAW Books, 1974). The author’s own Cugel continuation, Cugel’s Saga, appeared in 1983.

Captain Jonathan Archer and the Enterprise crew find their path blocked by a mysterious alien vessel manned by a race they will come to know as the Antianna. Refusing to risk a confrontation, they abandon their planned course rather than attempt to engage. Soon they slip into a region of space dominated by the Thelasian Trading Confederacy, which has its own dealings with the Antianna. In the Thelasian capital, Governor Maxim Sen is secretly plotting a war to eradicate the Antianna and safeguard the Confederacy’s trade routes. Archer suspects Sen’s motives reach further than simple restraint of a rival; he senses a hidden purpose behind the Antianna’s apparent hostility as well. Yet with an entire sector arrayed against him, he cannot rely on hunches alone. He requires solid evidence. The only source that might provide it is Ensign Hoshi Sato. If she can crack the Antianna language, a chance for peace may emerge; without her translation, a devastating sector-wide war seems unavoidable."

It is the year 12,090 A.D. The world has ended, ravaged in a firestorm of man's wars and madness. But from the wreckage a few humans manage to survive. A few humans... and something else. Doris Lang knew what her fate was when the vampire lord Count Magnus Lee bit her. An agonizing transformation into one of the undead, to be stalked by her fellow villagers or cursed to become the bride of the unholy creature and face an eternity of torment, driven by the thirst for human blood. There was only one chance, and as she watched him ride in from the distance she knew there was hope. Salvation... from a vampire hunter named D. Magnus has his own problems; his beautiful daughter Larmica refuses to let a human into her family, and is all too willing to kill the bride before the wedding can take place. Enlisting the help of Garo, a werewolf retainer, she attempts to kill Doris, only to find D in her way. Greco Rohman, son of the chief, also wants Doris for himself. The same goes for the skilled figher Rei-Ginsei and his Fiend Corps. Both men are eager to eliminate D, as his skills and Doris' favor makes them see him as a threat. Doris knows she isn't the only one in trouble, her younger brother is perceived as her weakness, and there are more than one person out there willing to use him as leverage against her.

Djinn twins, John and Philippa Gaunt, are off on another trip around the world in book four of the bestselling Children of the Lamp series. It's a race against time as the twins attempt to save their mother, Layla Gaunt from her destiny of being Blue Djinn of Babylon, save their father, Edward Gaunt, from an aging curse brought from a binding their mother Layla put on their father to make sure the twins were home with him, and museums worldwide from unexplained robberies and bizarre hauntings. As John and Philippa and their friends travel across the globe on their rescue mission, they notice that something very strange is happening: An evil force has woken the terracotta warriors created by an ancient Chinese emperor, and a spell has been cast possessing the soldiers with wicked spirits. Now, the very fate of the world hangs in the balance. It's up to the twins to solve the mysterious robberies, stop the terracotta warriors, rescue their parents, and save the world before it's too late.

The main character is Steven Masters. A spoiled 23-year-old who happens to be the only son of the world's richest man. At a party he (while drunk) states that he wishes to go on a proposed space flight to a distant life bearing planet called Mittend.
