The Rat God, however, has an evil plan to unleash the Black Death on the world once more, ridding it of humans and enabling him to conquer it. After a tense-confrontation with Jupiter in this throne-room during which the malevolent deity is revealed to be a monstrous cat, Audrey defeats the Dark Lord by flinging her mousebrass at him. The talisman explodes and Jupiter falls into the water that is rapidly flooding his chamber. The spirits of the many mice and rats he has tortured and devoured then rise up and drag the dark god down to a watery grave. Audrey glimpses her father among the legion of spirits as they depart and despairs, realising that he is truly dead. The sewer floods and the Black Death is destroyed. Thankful that they are alive and resolving to celebrate Jupiter's downfall once they return home, the mice begin the journey back to the surface but as they leave, Orfeo the bat foretells doom.

The novel is the story of Jamie Towfeek, a teenager living in Sydney's western suburbs. Jamie wants to be the real thing. From the roots of her dyed blonde hair... There are a lot of things Jamie hates about her life: her dark hair, her dad's Stone Age Charter of Curfew Rights, her real name - Jamilah Towfeek. For the past three years, Jamie has hidden her Lebanese/Muslim background from everyone at school. It's only with her email friend John that she can really be herself. But now life is getting more complicated. The most popular boy in school is interested in her, but there's no way he would be if he knew the truth. Then there's Timothy the school loner, who for some reason Jamie just can't stop thinking about. As for John, he seems to have a pretty big secret of his own. To top it all off, Jamie's school formal is coming up. And her band at her Muslim school is performing at the formal. The only way she'll be allowed to attend is by revealing her true identity. But who is she ... Jamie or Jamilah? Various other stories also happen in this book. Her older sister Shereen is a human rights and anti-war protester, and their father wants her to settle down. She gets closer to her friend Amy, and tries to find the reason why she has suddenly become more secretive to her. She is the first person she tells that she is a Muslim and at the end, the two become best friends, and leave their other friend, Liz behind with the other discriminatory students at school.

Nita and Kit are drawn into a swap of duties when Dairine’s unauthorized sign-up for an intergalactic exchange triggers their local advisors to reassign the mission to the two friends. What begins as a vacation hope—an apparently perfect planet as their destination—soon collides with an unsettling reality. The visitors who arrive at Dairine’s home look unmistakably alien, yet Nita’s dreamlike expectations are overturned as Alaalu reveals a hidden horror: an avatar of the Lone Power has been imprisoned there, a consequence of the Alaalu people’ s rejection of Its entropy. While that refusal averted downfalls like war, crime, and natural disasters, it also halted inevitable change, stalling evolution and leaving the Alaalu mired in a static fate despite their true potential. The young wizards must persuade the Alaalu’s resident wizard and her people to embrace this transformative moment, which would release the Lone Power. Back on Earth, the youthful wizards observing Dairine’s world learn that their own Sun may flare into a catastrophe. Yet hope arrives when a visitor from another planet—one who acts as a guardian against a repeat of such disaster—recognizes the danger in time and helps to avert a planetary catastrophe.

Set at the dawn of the twentieth century, the story centers on Álfgrímur, an orphan, and the grandparents who raise him, within the small, tolerant circle of misfits and eccentrics that gathers around Brekkukot—the cottage on Reykjavík’s outskirts. As Álfgrímur begins to meet Reykjavík’s emerging cadre of minor politicians, merchants, and social climbers, he starts doubting his prospects as a fisherman’s grandson and becomes increasingly drawn to Garðar Hólm, Iceland’s famed “world singer.” Garðar’s intermittent returns to Iceland spark Álfgrímur’s longing to express himself personally. Only when he steps onto a road that will separate him from his past does he truly recognize the value of his boyhood experiences. The given name Álfgrímur is interpreted in the novel as a fusion of Álf (elf) and grímur (a poetic term for night), meaning “the one who spends the night with the elves.” The book’s Icelandic title is Brekkukotsannáll, or Annals of Brekkukot. (Note: German title reference “Das Fischkonzert” corresponds to Brekkukotsannáll.)

The book is about a story that a kindly and elderly grandfather tells to his grandchildren about the town of Chewandswallow, where the weather comes three times a day, at breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and is always food and beverages. The rain is juice and soup, the snow is ice cream, and the wind brings hamburgers. Because of this phenomenon, there are no grocery stores. However, the weather soon takes a turn for the worse, at first simply just giving the people disgusting things, like pea soup fog, soggy green beans and Brussels sprout cakes. However, it quickly becomes catastrophic, and the portion sizes of the food grow to massive sizes, and the entire island is bombarded with a severe amount of food that completely buries buildings, crushes homes and blocks traffic. The people decide to use stale bread and pizza to build boats to escape from Chewandswallow, while they still have a chance before the weather completely destroys the island. Soon, the population of Chewandswallow arrive in a new town, where they struggle to adapt to their new lives in the world where the sky doesn't bring food.

The Emersons are at home in England, aching to return to Egypt, but finding no excuse to return until Lady Baskerville asks them to finish the excavation started by her husband, who died mysteriously just before opening a tomb in Luxor. No one else will continue as rumors of a curse on those who desecrate the tomb fly through the region. Leaving their son Ramses at home, the Emersons arrive at the Baskerville compound near the Valley of the Kings to find sick employees, over-eager reporters, and an assortment of other characters trying to either get into the tomb, or keep the Emersons out. Three recurring characters are introduced; Cyrus Vandergelt, Karl von Bork and Kevin O'Connell. Vandergelt is a wealthy amateur American Egyptologist, and over the years becomes Professor Emerson's closest friend. Bork is an expert in hieroglyphs who appears in a number of stories, usually assisting other Egyptologists. O'Connell is a reporter who eventually becomes a valuable outlet for the Emersons and their adventures.

Irith Hardey watches her life spiral beyond control as global chaos erupts around her. The climate spirals into crisis, seas rise and have displaced hundreds of millions, while refugees flood into the West. The world economy teeters on collapse and democracies buckle under the pressure from the anti-refugee Yellow Armbands. Yet an even darker horizon awaits: the great powers gamble everything on a plan titled 100 Days to Save the World, attempting to avert an ice-age that could annihilate civilization. Irith, a climate scientist, distrusts the strategy, convinced it will wreck more than it mends. As she digs into the grim truth behind the project, she faces the harassment of the Yellow Armbands and is chased from a blizzard-haunted London to the Scottish Highlands and across the tempestuous North Sea. In a United States where militias with guns threaten the President, Irith must confront a nightmare befitting a 21st‑century woman: uncovering the Life Lottery’s horrifying secret before the 100 days expire.

From the hardcover jacket: "It looks as though Australia will be overrun by rabbits. Millions of them, immune now to the myxomatosis that decimated them in the nineteen hundred fifties and sixties, are teeming over the land. With an election imminent, Prime Minister Kevin Fitzgerald, known to his cronies as Ella, is forced to act. It is obviously an emergency. The rabbits must be wiped out. Scientists assemble; experiments begin. "The results are shattering. Australia suddenly becomes the most feared nation on earth: America and Russia hurriedly surrender to her their nuclear devices, as do the other powers; Fitzgerald becomes virtual dictator of the rest of the world. "The Commonwealth Government establishes peace on earth except for limited wars which are fought under strict supervision, according to rules laid down in Canberra. Only two nations are allowed to fight at one time, for example. "On the crest of this incredible wave of prosperity a tiny news flash is overlooked. It says: RABBIT AS BIG AS ALSATIAN SHOT BY SUNDAY-SCHOOL TEACHER THREE MILES NORTH OF MUDGEE...."

When two boys find a mysterious ad in a newspaper asking for two young boys to build a spaceship, they quickly construct one out of old tin and scrap wood, and bring it to the advertiser. This man is the mysterious Mr. Bass, a scientist living in an observatory who goes unnoticed by most of the townspeople for some reason. He shows the boys a previously undetected satellite of the earth, the eponymous planet, that can only be seen with a special filter he has concocted. He gives them some special fuel he invented to power their spaceship, and tells them to fly to the mushroom planet (after getting their parents' permission). He warns them that their trip will only be successful if they bring a mascot. When it is time for launch, they grab a hen at the last moment for a mascot, and rocket into space. They wake up on the mushroom planet, a small, verdant world covered in soft moss and tree size mushrooms. They quickly meet some residents of the mushroom planet, small men with large heads and slightly green skin, the cousins of the mysterious Mr. Bass. They tell the boys that their planet has had a crisis and everyone is slowly dying. The boys meet up with the king of the planet, the Great Ta, and end up solving the natives' problem, before returning to Earth. The mushroom people's crisis was a lack of sulfur. They resolved this with their mascot hen, as chicken eggs have a high sulfur content.

A writer by trade, the story’s narrator works as a fact-checker for a prestigious magazine—one that resembles Harpers or The New Yorker, the very outlet where McInerney once held a similar post and had hoped to write himself. After dark, he becomes a cocaine-fueled partygoer, chasing the mindless revelry of 1980s yuppie nightlife and frequently slipping into Heartbreak, a nightclub he visits. His wife Amanda has recently left him, and he masks the absence by acting as if nothing has changed and keeping her departure to himself. At first, he clings to the hope that she might return, but that belief fades as he begins stalking her presence at a fashion event. He fixates on every possession of hers in his apartment, scrutinizes every modeling photo, and follows her to clubs again and again, even visiting a mannequin modeled after her. Meanwhile, his indulgent lifestyle bleeds into his professional life, and his volatile boss threatens to fire him. The novel later provided the basis for the 1988 film Bright Lights, Big City, which McInerney also wrote. In 1999, New York Theater Workshop produced an off-Broadway musical adaptation written by Paul Scott Goodman and directed by Michael Grief, with orchestrations and musical direction by Richard Barone.

Solomon, a Scottish pupil in his final primary-year, is unfairly labeled as dull and lazy, yet the truth is that he struggles with dyslexia. He endures bullying from his form teacher and, at home, a father who drinks heavily and neglects him, a situation partly explained by the father’s own dyslexia. Solomon often seeks solace in the nearby graveyard. After overhearing a council official speaking with Professor Miller, he learns that the place he cherishes is slated to become a construction site, which deeply unsettles him. When workmen uproot the protective rowan tree, his dreams grow troubled and eerie whispers haunt him. Circumstances at home push him to spend a night in the graveyard, where he witnesses one of the workers vanish into the earth after uncovering a mysterious chest marked with the word Malefice. He later learns that Malefice denotes witchcraft and that a victim of the old Scottish witch hunts lies buried there, apparently awakening with a desire for vengeance. Amy Miller, the professor’s young daughter who has befriended Solomon, is also drawn to the graveyard. Solomon follows to shield her from the malevolent force attempting to possess her. With his father’s aid, he succeeds in rescuing Amy and saving himself. Encouraged by Ms. Talmur, a school teacher who has supported him yet leaves to pursue a promotion, Solomon begins to change his life, though he anticipates a difficult journey ahead. His father agrees to attend an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting in the hope of reform.

Jung regarded the Book of Job as a pivotal shift in the divine drama, presenting for the first time a contemplation of questioning God (Gotteskritik). He even described the work as "pure poison" due to its provocative nature, though he felt compelled to undertake writing it. Central to his argument is the claim that God possesses not only a benevolent aspect but also a fourth, evil facet. This stance is inherently controversial, yet Jung argued that biblical references support it. The text has drawn criticism, for instance, over its assumption that the John who authored the Gospel of John is the same figure who wrote Revelation—an identification that most contemporary Bible scholars contest. Jung proposed that this malevolent aspect constitutes the missing fourth element of the Trinity, which he believed should be replaced by a Quaternity. At the same time, he investigates whether the authentic missing fourth element might instead be the feminine aspect of God. He even highlighted the 1950 papal definition of the Assumption of Mary by Pope Pius XII as the most important religious event since the Reformation.

Stormblade follows Stanach, a dwarf orp han, as he tracks the legendary stormblade—a kingly sword meant to break the council’s deadlock among the Thorbardin thanes and usher in a new king. When the blade is stolen and later recovered, only Stanach dares to pursue it. Though he was an orphan who grew up like other dwarves, he learned basic smithing, a craft that becomes pivotal. With the blade absent, his teacher descends into despair, eventually losing his sanity. Driven by loyalty to his mentor and a desire to restore balance, Stanach embarks on the perilous quest. His journey begins with Lavim, a caricatured kender, and, as they travel, they are joined by the human Kelida and the elf ranger Tyrol. Their party eventually encounters a member of the Irda, who reveals crucial information about their mission. After a string of missteps, battles, and misfortunes, they return to Thorbardin. There, the Theiwar thane plots to kill Hornfel, the Hylar thane, hoping to seize control of the thanes and rule. A lengthy confrontation ends with the Theiwar thane dead and the stormblade restored to its rightful place. In the aftermath, Tyrol is mortally wounded and dies. In tribute, the dwarves grant him the honor of burial in the garden of thanes—an exceedingly prestigious rite for a dwarf, and even more meaningful for an elf.

While traveling to Tunis on honeymoon with his new bride, the Parisian scholar Michel is overcome by tuberculosis. As he recovers, he re-discovers the physical pleasures of living and resolves to forgo his studies of the past in order to experience the present—to let "the layers of acquired knowledge peel away from the mind like a cosmetic and reveal, in patches, the naked flesh beneath, the authentic being hidden there." This is not, however, the Michel his colleagues knew—not a Michel that will be readily accepted by traditional society—and he must hide his new values under the patina of what he now reviles. Bored by Parisian society, he moves to a family farm in Normandy. He is happy there, especially in the company of young Charles, but he must soon return to the city and academe. Michel remains restless until he gives his first lecture and runs into Ménalque, who has long outraged society, and recognizes in him a reflection of his torment. Michel returns south, deeper into the desert, until, as he confides to his friends, he is lost in the sea of sand. Gide's story is filled by his descriptive prose, which evokes the exotic nature of Michel's inner and outer journey: "I did not understand the forbearance of this African earth, submerged for days at a time and now awakening from winter, drunk with water, bursting with new juices; it laughed in this springtime frenzy whose echo, whose image I perceived within myself." de:Der Immoralist es:El inmoralista fr:L'Immoraliste pt:L'Immoraliste ro:Imoralistul

The novel unfolds through two intertwined threads, shifting between them in alternating chapters. In the odd sections, we follow the 15-year-old Kafka as he flees his father’s house to break free from a looming Oedipal fate and to search for his mother and sister. After various escapades, he secures refuge in a secluded private library in Takamatsu, overseen by the distant, aloof Miss Saeki and the perceptive, more welcoming Oshima. There, his days are spent immersed in the unabridged Richard Francis Burton translation of One Thousand and One Nights and in the collected writings of Natsume Sōseki, until police inquiries about a brutal murder begin to circulate. The even-numbered chapters shift focus to Nakata, whose peculiar powers have allowed him, in old age, to work part-time as a finder of lost cats—a nod to The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. One particular missing-cat case sends him away from home and onto the road for the first time in his life. He befriends a truck driver named Hoshino, who hires him as a passenger and soon grows deeply fond of the elderly man. Throughout the novel, a collision looms between Kafka and Nakata, a confrontation that manifests as much in the metaphysical realm as in the waking world, reflecting the book’s own nature. Oedipal themes permeate the narrative, prompting many to style Kafka on the Shore as a contemporary Greek tragedy.

Raised in the tranquil beauty of the Summer Country, Princess Guenevere has had a charmed and contented life until the sudden, violent death of her mother, Queen Maire, leaves the Summer Country teetering on the brink of anarchy. Only the miraculous arrival of Arthur, heir to the Pendragon dynasty, allows Guenevere to claim her mother's throne. Smitten by the bold, sensuous princess, Arthur offers to marry her and unite their territories, while still allowing her to rule in her own right. Their love match creates the largest and most powerful kingdom in the isles. Arthur's glorious rule begins to crumble, however, when he is reunited with his mother and his long-lost half-sisters, Morgause and Morgan. Before Arthur's birth, his father - the savage and unscrupulous King Uther - banished his wife's young daughters, selling Morgause into a cruel marriage and imprisoning Morgan in a far-off convent. Both daughters have reason to avenge their suffering, but only one will strike the deadliest blows against the King and Queen, using her evil enchantments to destroy all Guenevere holds dear. When the Queen flees to Avalon, even her marriage with Arthur comes under threat. In the chaos that follows, a new young knight comes to Arthur's court to offer his services to the Queen. Her loyalty to Arthur betrayed, Guenevere falls in love with Lancelot, a love that may spell ruin for Camelot.

The book starts three months after the end of Peter and the Starcatchers. Slank returns to the island with more of the Others, including a certain Lord Ombra, to reclaim the trunk of starstuff lost in the previous book. When they learn that the Starcatchers have taken the trunk back to England, they set sail for London. Peter follows, fearing for Molly's safety, and with Tinker Bell's help conceals himself on their ship. Once in London, Peter does not know where to find Molly. After unpleasant encounters with beggars, traders and the police, Peter finally gets directions from J. M. Barrie to Lord Aster's house, and rescues Molly from Lord Ombra in the nick of time. However, Louise Aster- Molly's mother -has been kidnapped by the Others, and the children must find Lord Aster who is guarding the starstuff. Meanwhile, back on the island, the pirates are hunting the Lost Boys. They capture the boys to use as bait for Peter, not knowing he is not on the island. In the end, Molly is saved by Peter, and she takes Peter to her old best friend's house. Where she introduces Peter to George and they become best friends.

A London-based artist by the name of Griffin Moss makes his living producing postcards, yet he struggles with unhappiness and isolation, largely unaware of these inner tensions. His life takes a dramatic turn after receiving a mysterious postcard from Sabine Strohem, a woman he has never met. Sabine, like Griffin, is an artist (she designs postage-stamp imagery) and hails from a mythical cluster of small South Pacific islands—the Sicmon Islands, consisting of Arbah, Katie, Katin, Ta Fin, Quepol, and Typ. The correspondence between them deepens into a steady exchange, and Griffin gradually realizes that he is in love with Sabine, who returns his affection, leading him to believe they are soulmates. Yet as Sabine’s true nature and the impact of her influence on his life become more uncertain, fear takes hold, culminating in his decision to reject her invitation to meet in person. He concludes that Sabine is nothing more than a projection of his loneliness. The theory seems confirmed until another postcard arrives from Sabine, bearing a chilling warning: if he refuses to travel to her, she will come to him instead.

A British Intelligence officer, Colonel R., recruits a playwright named Ashenden. He is dispatched to Switzerland, where a string of escapades unfolds: at one point he escorts a man known as the Hairless Mexican to Italy, where a Greek German agent is slated for assassination; in another, he must persuade an Italian dancer to coax her Indian lover—also a German agent—across the border into Switzerland so that Ashenden can seize him. The collection of chapters later appears in various volumes under alternate titles, and it is unclear whether minor rewrites were made after initial publication. The paired or grouped sections include: - “A Domiciliary Visit” and “Miss King,” treated as Miss King; - “The Hairless Mexican,” “The Dark Woman,” and “The Greek,” treated as The Hairless Mexican; - “A Trip to Paris” and “Giulia Lazzari,” treated as Giulia Lazzari; - “Gustav” and “The Traitor,” treated as The Traitor; - “Behind the Scenes” and “His Excellency,” treated as His Excellency; - “A Chance Acquaintance,” “Love and Russian Literature,” and “Mr. Harrington’s Washing,” treated as Mr. Harrington’s Washing.

Marlowe’s verse retells the Greek tale of Hero and Leander, two youths who dwell in cities separated by the Hellespont, a narrow strait in today’s northwestern Turkey. In Sestos, Hero serves as a priestess or devotee of Venus, living in chastity though wholly devoted to the goddess of love. During a festival honoring Venus and Adonis, Leander, a young man from Abydos on the opposite shore, notices her and falls in love; she responds in kind but with caution, having vowed chastity to Venus. Persuaded by Leander, Hero overcomes her fears. From a lofty tower above the water, Hero lights a lamp for him and he vows to swim the Hellespont each night to be with her. She complies. On his first nocturnal voyage, Neptune, the Roman sea-god, mistakes him for Ganymede and drags him to the ocean floor. Realizing the error, Neptune returns him to shore bearing a bracelet believed to safeguard him from drowning. Leander reaches Hero’s tower, knocks on the door, and Hero opens to him, finding him entirely naked. She surrenders to him after allowing him to murmur, flatter, beg, promise, protest, and swear in her ear. Following a sequence of coy, halfhearted defenses of their affair, she yields to shared joy. The poem ends abruptly with the break of dawn. Scholars are divided on how Marlowe would have concluded the work—if he would have finished it at all, were he to have lived.

Joe Stoshack goes back in time to find out whether Babe Ruth called his shot in the 1932 world series. His dad tags along to keep him safe, per his mom's request, and to try to make some money, because he has just gotten laid off. Joe Stoshack ends up meeting Babe Ruth right after almost getting killed by a guy with a knife. Babe Ruth assumes that Joe has just saved him from an assassination attempt, so he invites Joe and his dad to come along with him. Joe's dad gets Babe Ruth to sign a bunch of baseballs, fulfilling what he wanted to do, and then they go to the baseball game, fulfilling what Joe wanted to do. However, Joe's dad sees presidentential hopeful Franklin Roosevelt (Who was elected president a month later) in the stands, and tries to warn him about the Holocaust. But security guards see him as a potential assassin, and take him away. Joe ends up watching the game and discovers that Babe Ruth really did call his shot and then gets re-united with his dad. His dad's sack of baseballs that got signed by Babe Ruth were confiscated, but he doesn't care because he got to spend some quality time with his son, something that almost never happens. Then they return to the present and Joe Stoshack hits a Walk-Off home run in his next Little League game, somewhat mirroring Babe Ruth's home run.

The novel follows Joseph Süß Oppenheimer, a Jewish businessman whose exceptional skill in finance and politics elevates him to the position of the Duke of Württemberg’s chief advisor. Envy and animosity from fierce enemies circle him as he helps the Duke cultivate a corrupt regime that enriches both men. Amid these power games, Süß learns he is the illegitimate son of a respected nobleman, yet chooses to continue living as a Jew, taking pride in having reached such a stature despite that lineage. Meanwhile, the Duke discovers Süß’s concealed daughter; in an attempted rape, he inadvertently murders her, leaving Süß grief-stricken. He then schemes and enacts vengeance. By first fomenting and then revealing the Duke’s bid to seize the Parliament, Süß provokes the Duke’s furious demise; yet he realizes that nothing can restore his daughter. He voluntarily surrenders. Although declared innocent, public pressure drives a death sentence by hanging. Even at the last moment, he does not disclose his noble origins or convert to Christianity, dying while reciting the Shema Yisrael, Judaism’s central prayer.

The novel tells the story of a Jewish businessman, Joseph Süß Oppenheimer, who, because of his exceptional talent for finance and politics, becomes the top advisor for the Duke of Württemberg. Surrounded by jealous and hateful enemies, Süß helps the Duke create a corrupt state that involves them both in immense wealth and power. In the meantime, Süß discovers he is the illegitimate son of a respected nobleman, but decides to continue living as a Jew, as he is proud of having achieved such a position despite this. In the meantime, the Duke finds out about Süß’s hidden daughter and when trying to rape her accidentally kills her. Süß is devastated. He plans and executes his revenge. After he encourages and then exposes the Duke's plan to overthrow the Parliament, thus infuriating the Duke to death, Süß realizes nothing will bring back his daughter, and apathetically turns himself over. He is found innocent, but under the pressure of the public he is finally sentenced to death by hanging. Despite it being his last chance for reprieve, he never reveals his noble origins nor converts to Christianity, and dies reciting the Shema Yisrael, the most important prayer in Judaism.

Chelsea's parents don't want their daughter to have a birthday party, because it will be too expensive. Chelsea becomes jealous of her siblings Geneva and Warwick, who receive more money from their parents. Chelsea befriends Bex in the Stomping Ground nightclub. A few weeks later, their friendship is cemented after Fee's friend Eddie tries to assault Chelsea, and Bex comes to her aid. Barry Gee buys his own restaurant, which will be called Gee Zone. Jemma wants to be an actress, but her parents aren't happy when she neglects her schoolwork to attend acting and dancing lessons. Jemma ignores them, and trusts Ms. Olivia Ockley, the owner of the acting school, who praises her talent. However, Jemma is annoyed when Alexa Browning receives a lead role instead of her. Jemma also dates Rob, which causes friction between her and Chelsea, although they reconcile after Chelsea's encounter with Eddie. Jon wants to date Sumitha, but she is no longer interested. Jon is annoyed by his parents, who have little time for him. However, after Laura is injured in front of him at one of his mother's animal rights demonstrations, he realises that he likes her and asks her out. Laura's mother is pregnant, and her boyfriend Melvyn objects to Laura spending time at demos with her neighbour Daniel. Laura's brother is born prematurely, and at Laura's suggestion is named Charlie. Sumitha becomes a swot when she develops a crush on her new science teacher, Paul Sharpe. At the end of the term she tells him about her feelings, but learns that Paul is engaged to Mrs. McConnell. Sumitha is dismissive when Sandeep asks her to come back home with him, and feels bad after learning that he is being bullied by Kevin and Matthew.

Martin, the main character, is supposed to be writing a book. He finds himself invited to dinner at the house of a repellent and warring couple, on whom the land and property they own seems entirely wasted. Martin happens on a painting which he takes to be by Brueghel. Painstaking research leads him (via a full scale reassessment of the interpretation of the five surviving pictures in Brueghel's The Months) to identify the picture as the missing sixth picture of Brueghel's famous book of hours. Meantime his wife, (an actual art historian whereas he is only peripherally connected with the scholarly art world), and their baby live in a cottage and he fears his wife eyes him with increasing disdain as, instead of working on his book, he pursues the Breughel data. Martin has to fake the promise of an affair with the woman of the house to get hold of the picture, and indulge in a series of implausible transactions in other pictures to keep his access to the Brueghel open. Once he gets it, his troubles have only begun. Finally, as he is about to succeed in taking it to a safe place and secure his fortune, he crashes the old Landrover and the picture goes up in smoke. You never do find out whether it was actually a Breughel or not.

Camilla confronts a host of crises at home. Her mother Rose has begun an affair with a man named Jacques and asks Camilla to keep the affair secret, while her father Rafferty urges honesty and truthfulness. Caught between loyalty to both parents, Camilla gradually recognizes their deep flaws. In her effort to cope, she befriends Frank, the older brother of her best friend. He listens with empathy, helping her accept her parents’ shortcomings and urging her to define herself by more than family ties, discovering a sense of self for the first time. Their conversations about life, faith, and philosophy deepen into a budding romance. But the couple’s happiness is disrupted as the family problems intensify. Frank’s parents separate, and he must relocate with his father. Meanwhile, Camilla’s parents decide to salvage their marriage and embark on a European vacation together. While they travel, Camilla learns she will be sent to a Swiss boarding school. Although she is devastated by losing Frank, she leans on the inner strength she has built up in recent weeks to navigate the upheaval ahead.

In Brittany’s Saint-François-Xavier, a Jesuit priest—also a pedagogue at the private boys’ school—narrates a harrowing account: the murder of a child’s soul. Mirbeau, who attended there for four grueling years, was expelled at fifteen under clouded circumstances. At eleven, Sébastien is sent to boarding school by his father, a harsh ironmonger with a flamboyant pride. The newcomer, from the outset, fails to belong among the school’s aristocratic, affluent circle, and is largely ignored. His isolation deepens when a pedophile priest begins to show him attention. Seized by inappropriate affection, the 13-year-old boy becomes a victim of Father de Kern’s sexual abuse. Soon after, Sébastien and his sole companion Bolorec are expelled, accused of engaging in improper acts. The accusations, orchestrated by Father de Kern, are false, leaving Sébastien ruined: he cannot hold a job, cannot forge friendships, nor sustain a romance with Marguerite, his childhood love. Years pass, and, at twenty-one, Sébastien dies on the battlefield during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, his corpse borne off by Bolorec after the fighting."

In ancient China, a family of five brothers bore strikingly similar appearances, each endowed with a unique talent. One could swallow the sea; another possessed an iron neck; a third could stretch his legs; a fourth could endure fire; the fifth could hold his breath indefinitely. A successful fisherman among them invites a young boy to join his next fishing expedition, but trouble soon arises. The sea is literally kept in the fisherman’s mouth, enabling the boy to fish and to uncover hidden treasure. When the fisherman can no longer keep the sea contained, he signals for help, yet the boy ignores him, and, as water pours forth, the boy drowns. The fisherman faces murder charges and is condemned to death. One after another, the other four brothers step up to take his place at the executioner’s block, each relying on his extraordinary power to evade death: one cannot be beheaded, another cannot be drowned, a third cannot be burned, and the fourth cannot be smothered. In the end, a judge concludes that the initially accused brother must have been innocent, since he could not be executed, and the five brothers return to their home a single family once more.

After Singularity Sky, Martin Springfield and Rachel Mansour return to Earth to recuperate, but Rachel is soon pressed to account for the administrative costs of her prior mission. Not long after, she finds herself negotiating with an unstable man who believes himself to be Idi Amin’s reincarnation and who wields a nuclear device. In a darkly comic twist common to the series, he threatens to detonate it after receiving an eviction notice. Meanwhile, a nascent planetary civilization is cruelly struck down when a causality-violation device appears to trigger their sun’s sudden explosion, prompting their defense systems to retaliate automatically against the homeworld of those suspected of the atrocity—the event dubbed the “iron sunrise.” Rachel and Martin embark on an investigation to thwart the perceived murderers and prevent the mass retaliation by the remaining leaders of the victim society, who alone can halt the proposed strike. Throughout all this, the Eschaton continues to pull its own strings, shaping events from behind the scenes.

Fifteen-year-old Kira Landon’s world, once ordinary, spirals when her friends urge her into hypnosis. In a trance-like state she uncovers memories she never knew—her mother carrying her through war-ravaged streets and speaking a language across which she once forgot to translate. Encouraged by her best friend Lynne to dig deeper, Kira’s investigation is abruptly derailed when Mrs. Landon vanishes. That very night, a mysterious woman arrives at Kira’s home, claiming to be her “Aunt Memory.” This figure escorts Kira to Crythe, a realm where people are molded from childhood to retain every detail of every event. There, Kira learns startling truths: her mother is a captive in Crythe, and many inhabitants are not who they appear to be. It unfolds that Mrs. Landon is truly Kira’s real Aunt Memory, while the woman posing as “Aunt Memory” is Rona Cummins—an ancient foe of Kira’s parents who seeks access to their secrets. As Rona intensifies her schemes, Kira must act to rescue Lynne, Mrs. Landon, and herself, as well as preserve the memories that belong to her parents.”

Spock travels back to the time and place of Here Come the Brides, a television program loosely based upon Asa Mercer's efforts to bring civilization to 1860s Seattle by importing the marriageable Mercer Girls from the war-ravaged East Coast of the United States. The show's premise was that eldest brother, Jason Bolt, bet his entire logging operation that he could persuade one hundred marriageable ladies to come to Seattle, and that all of them would be married or engaged within one year. Much of the dramatic and comic tension revolved around the efforts of their benefactor Aaron Stemple to thwart the deal and take control of the Bolts' holdings. Spock discovers a Klingon plot to destroy the Federation by killing Aaron Stemple before Stemple could thwart an attempted 19th-century alien invasion of Earth. During most of the story, Spock has lost his memory and is cared for by Stemple, who passes him off as his nephew "Ishmael" and helps him hide his alien origins. Spock identifies one of the women in the story as likely to be an ancestress of his.

Ten years ago, 21-year-old Charles MacKenzie, Jr. ("Mack") walked out of his apartment without a word and has never been seen again. He does, however, call his mother annually on Mother's Day to assure her of his health and safety, then hangs up, leaving her frantic questions unanswered. Even his father's death in the 9/11 attacks didn't bring him home or break the pattern of his calls. Now, Carolyn MacKenzie has decided the only way to move on with her own life is to find closure and bring an end to the mystery of her brother's disappearance. This year when Mack makes his regular Mother's Day call, she declares her intention to track him down, no matter what. The following day, Monsignor Devon Mackenzie receives a scrap note reading: Uncle Devon, tell Carolyn she must not look for me. Despite the disapproval and angry reactions of loved ones, Carolyn persists in a search that plunges her into a world of unexpected danger and winding questions. What secret does the superintendents of Mack's former apartment have to hide? What do his old roommates know about his disappearance? Is he somehow connected to the girls who have themselves gone missing in the past ten years? Could he possibly be responsible for the brutal murder of his drama teacher and for what purpose? Carolyn's persistence for the truth leads her into a deadly confrontation with someone close to her whose secret they cannot allow her to reveal.

Dwight Stanhope, a wealthy art collector, hosts a mansion-filled gathering at Waldemere with his stylish wife Christabel and their two sensible daughters, Betty and Eleanor, who is described as neurotic. They invite two guests: Vincent James, a charming but somewhat scatterbrained “weekend perennial,” and Nick Wood, a strikingly attractive young man about whom little is known. Curiously, Stanhope’s prized works—including a Rembrandt—have been relocated from a burglarproof gallery to the main floor, and the mansion’s insurance on the paintings has just been cancelled. A sense of unease pervades every corner of the house, which Flavia Jenner—an actress of the Victorian era noted for her lax morals—built and also contains her own private theater. In the middle of the night, a loud disturbance shatters the quiet, and a masked intruder is discovered stabbed beside the paintings. Yet the real shock comes with the revelation that the slain burglar is Dwight Stanhope himself. Enter Sir Henry Merrivale, whose arrival marks a cascade of suspicious happenings. He deftly blends sleuthing with a humorous magician’s act at a children’s show, ultimately cracking the case.

Near to the Wild Heart does not have a conventional narrative plot. It instead recounts flashes from the life of Joana, between her present, as a young woman, and her early childhood. These focus, like most of Lispector's works, on interior, emotional states. The book opens with a scene of the child Joana playing in the garden, making up poems for her father. Joana's wildness and barely suppressed violence, along with her linguistic creativity, are her most notable features. She is frequently compared to animals: over the course of the book Lispector describes her to a bird, a snake, a wildcat, a horse, and a dog. She commits transgressive acts—as a child she throws a book at an old man's head, for example, and as a married woman she leaves her husband, Otávio, and greets the news of his adultery—he has made another woman, his old friend Lídia, pregnant—with utter indifference. She is not so much immoral as she is amoral: “Evil is not living, and that’s it. Dying is already something else. Dying is different from good and evil.” In the book, she cites long passages from Spinoza, the longest quotes that appear anywhere in her novels; it seems that she felt an affinity with the Dutch philosopher's amoral conception of the world.

The story takes place in the year 2363. The protagonist is Cadet Larry Stark, a 20-year-old, fresh graduate of the Space Patrol Academy who comes from a long line of Space Patrol commanders. As the story begins, he is embarking on the customary final training cruise on the interstellar ship Carden. At the end of this cruise, he will be awarded a commission as officer of the Space Patrol. The ship makes the four and a half light-year journey to the star Alpha Centauri in a span of 15 days using the faster-than-light overdrive. The fourth planet orbiting Alpha C, an earth-like planet inhabited by dinosaurs, has been colonized 125 years earlier. Cadet Stark, who has been taught to obey orders and to trust the infallibility of Earth and the Space Patrol, arrives at planet IV of Alpha C just as the colonists are voting to declare, and possibly fight for, their independence from Earth. The arrival of the Carden and its crew can potentially affect the course of events in this revolution. The young cadet, for the first time in his life, must choose the proper and honorable course of action in a situation where there is no clear right and wrong. The consequences of his actions may place in jeopardy his career with the Space Patrol and the love of his father. The story is apparently a metaphor for the American Revolution, with Earth representing England and Alpha Centauri representing the US. Ultimately Cadet Stark sides with the Alpha C colonists, but he feels confident that his father would be proud that he had been true to himself. Distinctive things to note about the 1955 novel include: 1) The overdrive is based on the principle of warping space; 2) The phrase "electronic guitar" is used for electric guitar and "wristchron" is used for wrist watch; and 3) the ship radio uses vacuum tube technology. Also the character named Harl Ellison was named after science fiction writer Harlan Ellison, who was a neighbor of Silverberg in New York at the time he was writing the book. This was confirmed in a special edition on the occasion of Silverberg's 35th year in the business.

Harold Barnaby, a gifted Egyptologist, uncovers a concealed inscription while translating hieroglyphs, revealing a tomb belonging to an unnamed Pharaoh yet to be unearthed. The find thrills him, promising fame and fortune that would accompany such a discovery. The snag is clear: Barnaby lacks the means, influence, and resources to execute the plan without drawing the attention of Egyptian authorities who would certainly intervene. Fate intervenes when he encounters Robert Pierce, a wandering freelance writer between gigs, craving a dash of excitement. In a moment of drunken impulse, Barnaby reveals both his groundbreaking discovery and the logistical hurdle he faces. Pierce, whose line of work has earned him a wide network of connections across high and low circles, volunteers to orchestrate the “extraction” for a share of the spoils. He enlists Lord Grover, the fifth Earl of Wheatston, to fund the operation; smuggler Alan Conway; and the internationally renowned thief Nikos Karagannis. This eclectic ensemble camps out in the inhospitable Egyptian desert, preparing for a protracted venture. Their plan is thrown into sharper relief when a vigilant Egyptian official begins to suspect their activities. tr:Easy Go

In a world overwhelmed by population, corporate power has supplanted government, with business interests wielding the political authority. States exist merely to safeguard the interests of vast multinational corporations. Advertising has evolved into the most aggressively marketed and best-compensated field, shaping public perception by convincing people that consumer goods enhance quality of life, even as essential resources like water and fuel grow scarce. Venus has just been deemed suitable for human settlement, despite its harsh surface and climate, requiring generations of tolerance before terraforming could even begin. Mitch Courtenay, a top-tier copywriter at the Fowler Schocken agency, is tasked with creating a campaign to entice settlers to Venus. Yet far more is unfolding beneath the surface. The story soon spirals into mystery and intrigue, with many characters concealing their true selves, and Mitch undergoing drastic shifts in loyalties and outlook as events unfold.

Spanning 32 pages, this volume opens with a two-page overview. The adventure centers on a fortress that vanished underground long ago and came to be known as the Sunless Citadel. Within its depths, the Gulthias Tree—tended by the sinister druid Belak the Outcast—blooms, offering life-giving magic as well as life-draining danger. The tree also gives rise to malevolent beings called twig blights. The journey begins as rumors about the citadel reach a group of adventurers while they rest in the nearby town of Oakhurst. From there, most of the campaign involves navigating the citadel’s halls, contending with the evil denizens such as kobolds and goblins. Eventually, the party reaches the Twilight Grove, its corrupted foliage signaling the presence of the Gulthias Tree and Belak himself. Belak reveals that the tree originated from a green, wooden stake used to slay a vampire at that exact site; the tree compels those bound to its trunk to become willing subordinates, rendering them utterly obedient. A three-page appendix at the end provides statistics for every creature the adventurers meet, along with three new magical items and an entry on twig blights.

Told in the third person, the novel unravels the intertwined fates of John Johnson and Susan Colgate. It opens with a reunion after a year of withdrawal from the world, then moves into their disappearances through a mosaic of flashbacks that lack a fixed chronology. Each chapter presents a distinct memory, interspersed with sections that advance the present-day narrative. Susan Colgate is sketched as a former child-pageant star, a daughter from an 1980s television family, a wife to a closeted rock star, and a B-movie actress. She survives a cross-country plane crash unscathed and decides, in the aftermath, to vanish, shedding her former identity. John Johnson, by contrast, is a decadent film producer whose existence centers on drugs and women. His life ends with the flu, yet that death is only temporary: during the dying moment he envisions Susan Colgate, and upon revival he abandons excess and takes to the road, channeling the wanderer’s freedom of Jack Kerouac. As the tale unfolds, we follow not only their own arcs but also the people they meet and the chapters of their lives that unfold after they finally intersect. The narrative maintains a third-person perspective throughout.

Jamie Reardon, an eleven-year-old, endures a sequence of traumas: the death of his cat, his father leaving home, and his Aunt Sapphy suffering a memory-impairing accident at work. At school he faces relentless teasing, while at the same time he clings to memories he would trade anything to forget. His academic performance falters, and Miss Miller, a teacher lacking sympathy, presides over his difficulties. A visiting author—heard by Jamie as “Arthur”—perceives that the boy is troubled, yet the two never manage any real connection. Ultimately, Jamie must confront his troubles alone. He searches for a magical trigger to unfreeze Sapphy’s memory, hoping for a scratch-like jump in recall, much as a needle on a record can restart a song. The breakthrough comes when Audrey Krouch, a girl from the neighborhood, hypnotizes him. During the hypnosis, as Jamie longs to forget, he is forced to confront the recent sexual abuse he endured at Old Gray’s hands, a paedophile caretaker at the Traverse City trailer park where he lives. The emotional fallout from the suppressed incident resurfaces for Sapphy as well, enabling Jamie to reveal everything to her. The book does not depict the abuse in explicit detail. As author Sarah Weeks explains, she aimed to protect Jamie’s privacy because the boy did not want others to know what happened in Old Gray’s office on Christmas Eve, and she chose not to disclose the specifics either.

A walk in the Black Forest for twins Jacob and Erin turns into an adventure through time when they meet Shadow, a red fox with an unusual set of talents. They are welcomed to his underground laboratory, Hora Cella, and witness the power of Nikola Tesla's time travel device, the Wall of Light. On their first journey through the Wall of Light, they travel to Boston in 1775, to help Paul Revere and the Sons of Liberty spread the word that British Redcoats are on the march. Shadow has discovered seven gaps in the story of Paul Revere's midnight ride. If those gaps are not filled, the American Revolution may never be fought, and liberty as we know it will cease to exist. Travel through time with them and follow Paul Revere, William Dawes, and Samuel Prescott, ordinary men who choose to act for the cause of liberty. Meet Dr. Joseph Warren, one of the leaders of the Sons of Liberty, as he sets the famous ride in motion. Watch Robert Newman and John Pulling as they attempt to place signal lanterns in the steeple of the Old North Church. But, look out for Pratt! If he has his way, you could become trapped in a time when King George III rules, and there is no liberty and justice for all.

In Jodi Picoult’s signature style, Second Glance weaves together multiple characters through a narrative that hops across decades to reveal the truth. Set in Comtosook, Vermont, the central conflict centers on plans to convert an Abenaki burial site into a shopping mall. The key twist is that development cannot proceed if an ancestor is proven buried on the land. Enter Ross Wakeman, who travels to stay with his sister. His life has been scarred by repeated suicide attempts following the death of his fiancée, Aimee, in a car crash years earlier; he has since become a ghost hunter hoping for a chance to encounter her spirit. As the threat to the sacred land grows, the town experiences eerie disturbances—phenomena such as water that will not boil, among others. A local detective teams up with Ross, and together they uncover a murder mystery dating back decades. This discovery helps establish that the land is indeed a Native American burial ground, thereby blocking the development. The revelation about the buried Native American surprises everyone and prompts Ross to engage parts of his psyche he had long neglected."

The story concerns a small town Michigan cafe owner, Tom McKenna, who becomes a local hero after defending his store from an attempted robbery. When his story receives national attention, several members of the New York City Mafia arrive in town, believing him to be someone named Joey, who crossed them 20 years earlier. Tom protests his innocence to everyone, but eventually his façade is dropped and he is forced to confess his history of violence to his wife and son and eventually the police. Namely, he and his friend performed a well planned and spectacular assassination and robbery of mobsters in their youth in retaliation for the murder of a relative. Unfortunately, Tom's friend foolishly decided to flaunt his take, which allowed the mob to identify him as one of the assailants and abduct him for revenge. Meanwhile, Tom barely escaped the same fate and fled the city with the intent of starting over with a new identity. Fortunately for McKenna and his family, their lawyer arrives and learns that the police failed to Mirandize him, which makes his confession inadmissible in court. However, as the McKenna family is transported to the father's original city to deal with related legal matters, the mobsters learn of McKenna's detention and plan their revenge with a horrific surprise.

Tally Hamilton, beloved daughter of the town’s esteemed doctor, enjoys a full, sociable life—popular and well-liked by all. Her happiness is shaken, however, when war compels her to depart for a boarding school in England, a move she makes for her father’s sake. At Delderton Hall, she quickly discovers this institution is unlike any other: the dancing instructor urges them to become seeds that burst into light, while the mysterious biology tutor Matteo leads them on dawn study walks at four o'clock. Gradually, Tally finds her place, befriending many and even arranging a trip for Deldertonians to a dancing festival in Bergania. Across the sea, Prince Karil of Bergania longs for normalcy and genuine companionship, disliking the stiffness of formal attire and endless obligations. A chance meeting at the Dragonfly Pool, his sanctuary, forges an immediate friendship with Tally. Yet tragedy strikes when Karil’s father, the King, is assassinated, forcing Karil to flee to England with Tally and the Delderton pupils. The German forces then seize Bergania as part of their broader plan, having orchestrated the King’s murder.

Sophie begins the novel freshly dumped by Lou, her current boyfriend, only to plunge into a new romance with Dylan—whom her friends deem the epitome of masculine charm. As their relationship unfolds, she gradually realises she neither loves nor even likes Dylan, and she ends things to escape his personality. Subsequently, she embarks on a clandestine affair with an online chat-room boy named Chaz, but after meeting him in person she quickly discovers he is a pervert and terminates the liaison. Left to herself in the real world, she encounters Robin Murphy, an awkward classmate, at the local art museum. To her surprise, despite his lack of conventional attractiveness and her friends’ disapproval, she finds herself falling for him. The narrative reaches its close as Sophie chooses to sit with Robin in the cafeteria, deciding that sharing the truth about her secret relationship with friends and peers would be acceptable. A companion volume, What My Girlfriend Doesn’t Know, retelling events from Robin’s (Murphy’s) viewpoint, appeared in 2007.

Inspired by Edwin Abbott Abbott’s Flatland, a group of Dewdney and his computer-science students crafted a vertical 2D world—east-west and up-down, with no north-south dimension—and explored how biology and society would play out within its inhabitants. Unexpectedly, their synthetic 2D realm becomes a conduit for communication with a real 2D world—Arde. Through a kind of telepathic exchange with a resident named Yendred (the students nickname him YNDRD, or Yendred), the narrative follows his journey across the continent of Ajem Kollosh as he seeks to learn about a mysterious philosophy held by the people he is approaching. The students and narrator type questions on a keyboard, and Yendred describes how he senses their thoughts in his mind. For his replies, he thinks an answer and it appears on the printer. Yendred’s name is actually Dewdney reversed, or “Yendwed,” as one student with a stammer pronounces it. Framed as a travelogue, Yendred wanders the world to unveil its features, while he explains to the students a range of topics: politics, geography, and architecture (all dwellings are underground so as not to impede movement), tools (nails prove useless for joining two objects; tape and glue take their place), biology (most Ardean beings lack a digestive tract due to the peril of splitting into two; evolution, however, offered a workaround), astronomy, and even games like one-dimensional Alak—each crafted to fit within a 2D reality. An appendix rounds out the work with essential notes on Ardean two-dimensional physics and chemistry.

Set in 1968 New York in an alternate universe to the Dryco universe of the previous five iterations of the series, Going, Going, Gone nevertheless disposes of several of the series' characters in its closing chapters. Its protagonist is Walter Bullitt, an egocentric expert in psychoactive substances who freelances for various branches of the United States government spy apparatus. Though he passes for white, Bullitt is in fact of African-American descent in a world where almost all full-blooded members of that race died sometime in the early twentieth century in an apparently engineered plague and all black music is banned. Walter becomes subject to increasingly strange experiences, hearing voices and seeing ghosts from a parallel New York which is blending into his one. Walter is taken to this alternative New York which has been flooded and moved north, populated by black people and an analogue of television absent from his world. The novel ends with the two epistemic worlds converging into a New York which is, in the words of critic Paul Dukes a "morally better place than either of the two which composed it".

Titus Brothers Contractors secure a government project in Peru to bore a tunnel through a mountain, linking two isolated rail lines. As the deadline nears, they confront a literal obstacle: rock of extraordinary hardness that resists standard blasting methods. With the clock ticking and the risk of default looming, the firm faces losing the contract to Blakeson & Grinder. In hopes of overcoming the impasse, Mr. Job Titus learns of Tom Swift and his renowned giant cannon, famed for Panama Canal protection, and contemplates hiring Tom to devise a specialized blasting powder for the excavating task. Meanwhile, Tom’s close ally, Mr. Damon, arrives during this discussion, unaware of the current crisis. Coincidentally, Damon is invested in a Peruvian cinchona bark venture that has nearly halted production; this prompts him to invite Tom to Peru to uncover the root cause. Tom, Damon, Titus, and Tom’s immense assistant, Koku, set off for Peru. En route, they meet Professor Swyington Bumper, who has spent years pursuing the fabled lost city of Pelone. Although Professor Bumper has repeatedly returned to Peru each season without success, he learns that Tom is bound for the same region, Rimac, and chooses to join the expedition.

Fantasio accepts a commission from Le Moustique to craft a feature on Incognito City, a gleaming metropolis where the rich and famous reside under stringent security and a blanket ban on photography. To bypass this prohibition, Fantasio conceals miniature cameras inside ordinary objects, like his pipe. Before he and Spirou can depart, the Marsupilami unexpectedly arrives at their home, having somehow journeyed solo from the Count’s Champignac manor. With the Count unreachable by phone, they drive toward Incognito City, where a tense traffic clash with Juan Corto Dos Orejas leaves them with a sour impression and a curious object found in the street. As they encounter more thugs and puzzling incidents, a sinister scheme gradually comes to light: the Count of Champignac has been kidnapped. In The Quick Super, Fantasio tests a Genial Motors-made automobile called a “Quick” for a weekend assignment, intending to review it for Spirou Méchanique. Yet ominous patterns emerge: every prior test-Quicks has vanished, and this one vanishes too. As the tale develops, familiar faces from Circus Zabaglione, first seen in Les voleurs du Marsupilami, reappear.

Beth is a successful pop music singer and a devout Protestant Christian from Texas, USA. She and her boyfriend Steve both belong to a group known as the "Cowboys for Christ", who travel to "heathen areas" of the world to preach Christianity. They travel to Glasgow, Scotland, hoping to save some souls once there. However, they are shocked when they receive a very negative reception, Beth even being set upon by a large dog. After performing a concert at a local cathedral, the duo are approached by Lord Lachlan and his wife Delia, aristocrats from the small village of Tressock in the Scottish lowlands. They invite Beth and Steve to come back with them to Tressock in order to preach. Meanwhile, detective Orlando is sent to Tressock, posing as the local police officer, in order to secretly investigate reports of a pagan cult. Beth and Steve decide that they shall begin their preaching at the May Day celebrations in the village. Meanwhile Orlando discovers that the people of the village worship the ancient Celt goddess Sulis. In an attempt to impress the locals, Steve and Beth agree to becoming the local Queen of the May and the Laddie for the festival. In this role, they must split up for the day, and it is during this that the Laddie is devoured by the locals on an island in the middle of the river Sulis. Beth discovers this, and tries to escape, but is captured and embalmed.

Augustine’s early life is depicted as sinful, followed by his eventual turn to Christianity. Regarded by many as the inaugural Western autobiography, it set a precedent for Christian authors across a millennium of the Middle Ages. Though not a complete autobiography—written when he was in his early forties and before his later years’ works—its account remains the most thorough single-person record from the fourth and fifth centuries, outlining the evolution of his thoughts in a continuous arc and constituting a major theological work. In this narrative, Augustine confesses deep remorse for his licentiousness and immoral conduct, including his prior Manichaean commitments and his belief in astrology. He credits Nebridius with helping to convince him that astrology is not only erroneous but pernicious, and he credits St. Ambrose with guiding him toward Christianity. Structurally, the first nine books are autobiographical, while the final four offer commentary. The author conveys acute sorrow over his sexual sins and stresses the importance of sexual morality. Written as prayers to God, the work bears a title rooted in the Psalms of David and opens with the line, “For Thou hast made us for thyself, and our hearts are restless till they rest in Thee.” Scholars often interpret the structure as a division into sections that symbolize different facets of the Trinity and trinitarian belief.

The narrative traces the intertwined paths of three senior students, with chapters alternating between their distinct viewpoints. Jason Carrillo, the star athlete, grapples with questions about his heterosexual identity and chooses to attend a support gathering for gay youth, not expecting to encounter Kyle Meeks and Nelson Glassman there. Afterward, Kyle—who has kept his sexuality mostly under wraps—offers to tutor Jason in math, and it emerges that Kyle has harbored a crush on Jason for three years. Their shared explorations of coming out and family dynamics bring them closer, developing into something beyond friendship. Meanwhile, Nelson, the outgoing class clown, wrestles with his feelings for Kyle and the nature of their relationship. He is very close to his mother, who claims she’s always sensed his sexuality, while his father remains largely absent. A quarrel with Kyle leads Nelson to seek solace with an online stranger named Brick, with whom he has sex for the first time and worries about HIV. Nelson then befriends Jeremy, who is HIV-positive, and the two begin a romantic connection.

An unidentified corpse discovered at the edge of the Jicarilla Apache natural gas field in the San Juan Basin involves Navajo Tribal Police Sergeant Jim Chee in a mystery involving diverted oil and gas revenues, abandoned pipelines, Washington D.C. insiders, and illegal drugs. Assigned to patrol the basin and range topography of the rugged Animas Mountains of Hidalgo County in the extreme southwestern corner of New Mexico, U.S. Border Patrol Officer Bernadette Manuelito photographs a suspicious construction crew on the Tuttle exotic game ranch. After a complaint about her activities by ranch personnel, Manuelito's supervisor advises her that the Border Patrol has a special arrangement with the ranch whereby ranch personnel monitor the border and provide tips to the Border Patrol. In return, the Border Patrol does not patrol the ranch. New to the Border Patrol service, Officer Manuelito accepts this explanation until she learns that a photograph of her, taken by her supervisor, has been distributed to the criminal element across the border in Mexico. Officer Manuelito shares her concerns with her former Navajo Tribal Police supervisor Jim Chee and retired Lieutenant Joe Leaphorn who are then able to make a connection between the unidentified corpse and the activities Manuelito has observed in Hidalgo County.

In a town where suspicion toward the government and toward outsiders runs deep, the arrival of a magnetic desert wanderer named Oyster sharpens the community’s isolation and its suppression of dissent. A landholding class rooted in anti-government sentiment and conservative Christianity creates a fertile ground for Oyster’s messianic aura and for a cult he forms, a group intricately linked to the shady underbelly of nearby illegal opal trafficking. The novel’s fractured timeline—juggling past moments with present events—amplifies suspense as its multitude of subplots converge in the town’s apocalyptic downfall and the cult’s collapse. Recurrent depictions of the town’s vigilant paranoia and violent policing of its own perceived “lostness” escalate until crisis erupts and the brutal mechanisms of control begin to fall apart. Women play a pivotal role in destabilizing and ultimately destroying the menace embodied by powerful men. The self-congratulatory rhetoric of male outsiders is exposed as hypocritical and self-serving, while the real outsiders prove to be predominantly women, along with men who lack social power.

Henry Coningsby’s life, the orphaned grandson of a wealthy marquess known as Lord Monmouth, unfolds as the central thread of the tale. Although Monmouth initially opposed the marriage of Coningsby’s parents, he relents after their deaths and sends the boy to receive his education at Eton. There, a friendship forms between Coningsby and Oswald Millbank, the offspring of a prosperous cotton magnate who despises Monmouth. The two patriarchs embody contrasting epochs of wealth—old lineage versus emerging capital. As Coningsby matures, he cultivates liberal political ideas and grows fond of Edith, Oswald’s sister. Monmouth’s anger at these developments leads him to disinherit his grandson in secret. After Monmouth’s passing, Coningsby finds himself ruined and must support himself, deciding to pursue a legal career and become a barrister. This display of resolve wins Edith’s father’s approval, who had previously opposed the match, and he finally consents to their nuptials. By the conclusion, Coningsby is elected to Parliament representing his father-in-law’s constituency, and his fortune is restored. The character mirrors the real George Smythe, and the novel’s themes and several figures reappear in Disraeli’s later works, Sybil and Tancred.”

Frostbite takes place in the remote wilderness of Alberta. The setting is similar to the real world, but where werewolves (and possibly other supernatural phenomena) are rare but known phenomena. The novel opens with Cheyenne "Chey" Clarke parachuting into the wilds of Alberta, provisioned with extensive hiking supplies, most of which are immediately lost. Chey is soon attacked by a werewolf (it is indicated to the reader that the creature is obviously not a normal wolf), but survives with only a scratch, which is enough to curse her with lycanthropy. In wandering the wilderness, she meets the enigmatic Dzo, who introduces her to Monty Powell, a werewolf (presumably the one who attacked Chey). After their meeting, it is revealed that Chey has secretly come looking for the werewolf, and is working with outside parties who want him removed. After a failed attempt to kill Powell, Chey is left in the care of her backers, and used as bait to lure Powell while her own future at their hands remains questionable.

Blankets chronicles Craig Thompson's adolescence and young adulthood, his childhood relationship with his younger brother, and the conflicts he experiences regarding his Christianity and his first love. Though written chronologically, Thompson uses flashbacks as a literary and artistic device in order to parallel young adult experience with past childhood experience. Major themes of the work include: first love, child and adult sexuality, spirituality, sibling relationships, and coming of age. Thompson begins by describing his relationship with his brother during their childhoods in Wisconsin. Though their relationship is marked by typical sibling conflict, they are also very close, and their rapport helps them deal with verbal and physical abuse from their overly religious parents, and sexual harassment and abuse from bullies at school. During his preteen years, Thompson finds himself a misfit because of his physical appearance and home life. Through his teen years, he continues to find it hard to fit in with his peers, but at a Bible camp one winter, he comes to associate with a group of teens he feels he will fit in with, which includes Raina, a beautiful and interesting girl who captivates him. The two become inseparable and arrange to spend two weeks together at Raina’s home in Michigan. He meets Raina’s family, consisting of her separated parents, her adopted siblings Ben and Laura, her biological sister, and her infant niece Sarah. Because Laura is mentally retarded and Sarah is often ignored by her own parents, Raina feels the responsibility to take care of the both of them. Although she is extremely close to Craig while he’s staying with her, she feels she can’t handle one more person dependent on her and breaks up with him soon after he leaves. He then destroys everything Raina had ever given to him, and every memento of their relationship, except for the quilt she had made for him. He stores it and other possessions in the attic in the house, and moves out to start his own life elsewhere. Thompson comes to terms with his religion and spiritual identity while away from his family. He returns to his childhood home after several years, seemingly a different person. He rekindles his old familial relationships, and the bonds between the family become stronger. The story ends with his finding peace with those he loves and himself.

Volpone, a Venetian gentleman, pretends to be on his deathbed after a long illness in order to dupe Voltore, Corbaccio and Corvino, who aspire to his fortune. They each arrive in turn, bearing luxurious gifts with the aim of being inscribed as Volpone's heir. Mosca, Volpone's "parasite", encourages them, making each of them believe that he has been named as the heir in the will, and getting Corbaccio to disinherit his son in favour of Volpone. Mosca mentions to Volpone that Corvino has a beautiful wife, Celia, and Volpone goes to see her in the disguise of Scoto the Mountebank. Corvino drives him away, but Volpone is now insistent that he must have Celia for his own. Mosca tells Corvino that Volpone requires to sleep with a young woman to help revive him. Corvino offers Celia in order to please Volpone. Just before Corvino and Celia are due to arrive for this to take place, Corbaccio's son Bonario arrives to catch his father in the act of disinheriting him. Mosca guides him into a sideroom. Volpone is left alone with Celia, and after failing to seduce her with promises of luxurious items and fantasies, attempts to rape her. Bonario comes forward to rescue Celia. However, in the ensuing courtroom sequence, the truth is well-buried by Mosca, Volpone and all three of the dupes. There are episodes involving the English travellers Sir and Lady Politick Would-Be and Peregrine. Sir Politic constantly talks of plots and his outlandish business plans, while Lady Would-Be annoys Volpone with her ceaseless talking. Mosca co-ordinates a mix-up between them which leaves Peregrine, a more sophisticated traveller, feeling offended. He humiliates Sir Politick by telling him he is to be arrested for sedition, and making him hide inside a giant tortoise shell. Volpone insists on disguising himself and having it announced that he has died and left all his wealth to Mosca. This enrages Voltore, Corbaccio and Corvino, and everyone returns to court. Volpone gets badly entangled in the circumstances devised by him and Mosca. Despite Volpone's pleas, Mosca refuses to give up his wealthy new role, and Volpone decides to reveal himself in order to take Mosca down with him. Finally they, Voltore, Corbaccio and Corvino are punished.

Dave Hirsh is a cynical Army veteran who winds up in his hometown of Parkman after being put on a bus in Chicago while intoxicated. Ginny Moorehead, a woman of seemingly loose morals and poor education, has taken the same bus. Hirsh had left Parkman 16 years before when his older brother Frank placed him in a charity boarding school, and is still embittered. Frank has since married well, inherited a jewelry business from the father of his wife Agnes, and made their social status his highest priority. Dave's return threatens this, so Frank makes a fruitless stab at arranging respectability, introducing him to his friend Professor French and his daughter Gwen, a schoolteacher. Dave moves in different circles, however. He befriends Bama Dillert, a gambler who has serendipitously settled in Parkman. Two factors seem to offer Dave hope and redemption: he takes a fatherly interest in his niece, Frank's daughter Dawn, and falls in love with Gwen. Despite his somewhat notorious reputation, Dave is basically a good, honest man, well aware of his own shortcomings. His cynicism is often a mask to hide the pain of rejection. Though Ginny is not his social or intellectual match, he eventually sees the basic good in her and responds to her unconditional love. In the end, Ginny, stalked by her former boyfriend (a Chicago hoodlum), proves unequivocally the depth of her love for Dave by taking a fatal bullet for him. In the novel, however, it is Dave who is the innocent victim.

At the opening of the book, the narrator, Rabo Karabekian, apologizes to the arriving guests: "I promised you an autobiography, but something went wrong in the kitchen..." He describes himself as a museum guard who answers questions from visitors coming to see his priceless collected art. He shares the lonely home with his live-in cook and her daughter, Celeste. One afternoon, Circe Berman wanders onto Karabekian's private beach. When he reaches out to greet her, she catches him by surprise with the forward statement "Tell me how your parents died." He tells her the story and proceeds to invite her back to his home for a drink. After a drink and supper, Karabekian invites her to stay with him, as Paul Slazinger does. After a time, he begins to find her charm "manipulative", as she typically gets her way. Mrs. Berman does not respect his abstract art collection, including works by Jackson Pollock. She explores every inch of Karabekian's home, constantly asking him questions. The only place that is off-limits to her is the potato barn. The potato barn is the home of Karabekian's studio and holds his "secret". The barn has no windows, and Karabekian has gone through the trouble of nailing one end shut and immobilizing the other with six padlocks. The secret of the potato barn has enticed collectors to make outrageous offers and to raise suspicions of stolen masterpieces. It is to remain locked until after Karabekian passes away.

Sam, Anastasia Krupnik’s younger brother, longs for fangs more than anything. Yet one obstacle stands in his way: Mrs. Krupnik, Sam’s mother, suffers from fangphobia and forbids him from even touching plastic vampire fangs at home. Why can’t she recognize how cool they are? They make eating hot dogs awkward, but Sam loves looking gross, and he’s eager to embrace that image. Determined, he hatches a plan to flee to Alaska, a land where fanged walruses supposedly roam and sharp teeth are commonplace. He stuffs his mittens and a bear into his father’s Harvard gym bag and heads out, only to be halted by the mailman, Lowell Watson, who reminds him he’ll need food for the journey. Neighbor Gertrude Stein’s homemade chocolate chip cookies seem perfect for the trip. Before leaving, he wants to say goodbye to the Sheehans’ baby, Kelly, and he also craves a glass of water, discovering that there isn’t any real rush toward Alaska after all. In See You Around, Sam!, Lois Lowry again gives Sam a voice distinct from his sister’s, as the neighborhood’s odd assortment of residents open their doors to him. Through their warm welcome, he learns what community truly means.

On a school field trip Jonk Winters, an independent-minded teenage girl, is attacked by a large black dog whilst exploring the nearby woods where she has found a mysterious and rather old buckle. She is rescued from the dog by a woman named Elizabeth Goodenough, who possesses magical powers. After she goes home, Jonk is stalked by the dog and its curious stone-faced master. Jonk's friend, Bill has read of a local legend that describes how a Green Man once strode across the countryside from Wiltshire to East Anglia. Believing the legend is the key to understanding Jonk's experience in the woods, Jonk, Bill and their rather sceptical friend Arf set out to solve the riddle of the Green Man. It soon becomes apparent that the stone-faced man is an ancient warlord who needs the golden buckle to regain his malevolent power. The buckle is the key to victory and the trio soon find themselves under attack from the minions of the warlord, the terrifying 'leather men', and are relentlessly followed by the black dog. However, cleverly guided by Elizabeth and aided by the gift of flight, Jonk and her friends determine to defeat the warlord and his sinister allies at any cost.

As the story opens, Lia, 15, is at her great-grandmother Sarah's bedside. Delirious, the old woman begins to speak of Graymoss Plantation, the Louisiana family estate left unoccupied for decades because of a "terrible, fearful evil." After the woman's death, Lia discovers that the house has been willed to her mother, who plans to move the family in and adopt a group of hard-to-place children. Lia is against this idea and vows to prove to her mother that the house is truly haunted.
