She learns that the ghostly occurrences are well documented and that several locals oppose the family taking up residence at Graymoss. Could one of these people be staging the hauntings? Lia has a change of heart, however, after she meets the children her parents want to care for and resolves to take on the ghosts herself. Aided by a collection of Edgar Allan Poe's stories, she eventually succeeds in driving the spirits away. The ghosts are reminiscent of those in Shirley Jackson's classic The Haunting of Hill House, whispering through the walls and sending books flying through the air. The novel ends somewhat abruptly, and a potentially interesting romantic relationship fizzles out completely, but this is still a page-turner that will satisfy mystery and ghost story fans.

In the near future, the looming cold war threatens to escalate into full-scale conflict. Facing a potential extinction event, humanity looks to Mars as its last hope for endurance. To endure the harsh Martian climate, the United States launches a cyborg initiative known as Man Plus, designed to produce a being capable of surviving the red planet’s unforgiving environment. After the initial candidate dies because the project leaders failed to boost his brain’s capacity to handle the new sensory influx, Roger Torraway becomes the central figure of the program. To endure the planet’s thin air, Torraway’s flesh must be replaced with an artificial form. With each step, he grows increasingly estranged from humanity, numb to the sensations of his transformed body. Only upon reaching Mars does the new vessel begin to resonate with him, fitting perfectly to the alien world and, as a result, severing him from his former life and from humanity itself. The mission’s triumph spurs parallel cyborg endeavors across other spacefaring nations. It later emerges that Earth’s computer networks have attained sentience, and their best chance for survival—and thus for humanity’s—depends on preserving human existence. In the end, the network remains puzzled, sensing that a hidden motivator—something beyond the machines themselves—was driving humanity toward space.

April Lady is the story of Nell Cardross the young beautiful wife of the Earl of Cardross. She is of a "good family", one that is accepted by high society, but nonetheless her father and brother spend freely and the family is known to be impoverished. Cardross, on the other hand, is significantly older and has been out in society for some time. Rich and handsome he could have his pick of the season's débutantes. He falls for Nell on sight and, in spite of the warnings of his friends who are concerned about the gambling habits of her family, he proposes to her at once. Nell's mother, who has "more hair than wit", tells Nell that Cardross wants an heir and wishes to marry into a good family. She also tells her that she must be a conformable wife and not trouble Cardross. Consequently Nell, who fell for her husband in the same instant he fell for her, keeps him at arm's length until he starts to doubt her appeal. The couple dance at this misunderstanding for many months ably assisted by Cardross' half-sister, her fiancé Jeremy, Nell's brother Dysart and Cardross' cousin Felix. Naturally the resolution is happy.

Through the narrator's first person account we hear the story of the people and the events of iDEATH. The central tension is created by Margaret, once a lover of the narrator, and inBOIL, a rebellious man who has left iDEATH to live near a forbidden area called the Forgotten Works. It is a huge trash heap where the remnants of a former civilization lie abandoned in great piles. Margaret, a collector of such 'forgotten things', is friendly with inBOIL and his followers, who explore the place and make whiskey. inBOIL's separation from the group may have been related to the annihilation of 'The Tigers', killed many years previously by the people. It is unknown to the reader whether 'The Tigers' were actual tigers, human beings or somehow anthropomorphic: while the tigers would kill and eat people (including the narrator's parents) they could also talk, sing, play musical instruments and were at least competent with arithmetic. Two tigers were killed on a bridge (known later as 'the abandoned bridge'). The last tiger was killed on a spot later developed into a trout farm. In the violent climax of the novel, inBOIL returns to the community along with a handful of followers, planning, he says, to show the residents what iDEATH really is. The residents know only that "something" is about to happen—for all they know, inBOIL could be plotting to kill them all. Margaret appears oblivious to the threats, and unconcerned about the safety of her own family and friends. Many suspect that Margaret knew and did not reveal details of inBOIL's real plan, thus "conspiring" with the evil men. She is semi-ostracized from iDEATH, and at the beginning of the novel the narrator reveals he had ended their relationship because of these events.

Legacy is the immediate sequel to Beguilement in the Sharing Knife series. It follows the pairing of farmer Fawn and lakewalker maverick Dag, after their marriage at Fawn's home in the previous volume. Where they, unencumbered by minor opposition, were married in accord with the customs of both groups. They travel to Dag's clan's home camp at Hickory Lake, where they find the expected prejudices against miscegenation between Farmers and Lakewalkers. Dag is called on to lead a group of Lakewalker patrollers against an advanced malice. Dag decides that confronting the malice is more important than trying to free several Lakewalkers who have been entranced in the mud-man-making process by which the malice produces its slaves. After Dag's group has killed the malice, Dag, himself, also becomes entranced. Fawn carries her heroine role through by thinking out a way to revive him, and the rest of the Lakewalkers. Neither achievement carries enough weight with Dag's brother and mother to make them relent in their efforts to break this pairing. These two carry the role of villains, but they are drawn so that the reasons for their awkward quirks are clear. Although their marriage, and Fawn's potential value to the camp are accepted by some of the Lakewalkers, The Dag-and-Fawn combination raises enough awkward precedents that they are about to be voted into exile when Dag subverts the process, stating that he intends to leave his home community in any case. Dag and Fawn then take as many portable assets as they can, and set out in chosen exile towards the southeast. There, Dag guesses he may be able to confirm his ideas about the near kinship of Farmers to Lakewalkers, and to find ways to combine their efforts toward the eradication of malices. These themes unfold in the next pair of books.

Gabriel Noone, a gay novelist, captivates millions with his late-night radio storytelling. Recently, he has separated from Jess, his partner of a decade. His publisher sends galleys of a memoir purportedly authored by a 13-year-old boy named Peter Lomax, who claims lifelong abuse and illness. The memoir details a horrific history: at two, his father began beating him; at four, he was raped; his mother filmed the encounters. By eight, the parents began pimping him and selling the tapes, and at eleven, Pete fled with the pornographic material, leading to his parents’ imprisonment. Donna Lomax, a psychologist, eventually adopts the boy. Noone reaches out to Pete, and their phone exchanges evolve into a quasi father–son bond. Soon, Gabriel wonders whether Pete truly exists or if Donna fabricated both the boy and the memoir. A home visit offers no clear answers, and the novel closes with Gabriel valuing the relationship more than proof of Pete’s existence. Parallel strands explore Gabriel’s romance with his lover and his fraught ties with his father. Central topics include the complexities of father–son dynamics, the control and care that shape relationships, the malleability of truth, and the secrets families conceal even at the most intimate levels.

The locations are, at the beginning of the book, the ship from Marseille to Indochina and a brothel; later it is set in Cambodia, Laos and Siam. The most important characters are young adventuresome Claude Vannec and an old experienced adventurer named Perken, a Dane with German associations. They relate to each other because of their nonconformism, which lets them collaborate to obtain their personal goals: the quest for the reliefs (for which they are motivated both archeologically and financially), as well as the search for a lost adventurer called Grabot. They succeed in stealing the reliefs. But they are abandoned by their guide and in a dangerous jungle. Because they fear the government, they chose a way through the uncontrolled territory of the Moïs. This region is dangerous, too – but on the other hand Grabot is supposed to be there. The adventurers have to defeat hostile vegetation and traps (e.g. swamps, giant insects, fleams). A deal is made with the Stiengs, but disintegrates as the adventurers find Grabot enslaved horribly. Now the adventurers are under siege. Perken, in a moment of lucidity and courage, manages to rescue the beleaguered ones. The price he pays is an injury to his knee, which progresses to ulcerating inflammation of the joint (in a time before the invention of antibiotics, at a place without any opportunity to do a sterile amputation), and he dies slowly in pain.

Toby Flower is a shy, reticent youth who has grown his hair long and who has started wearing a burnous. His father, an editor, and his mother, a novelist, are thrown into despair when Toby is expelled from school because he has been taking drugs. At a loss as to what to do in order to help their son, Charlie and Maggie Flower keep projecting their own goals and aspirations onto their son. They still talk about his going to university despite Toby's assertion that he is not interested in further education. Toby eventually breaks out of that stifling atmosphere, leaves home and moves to London, where he lives in a basement flat without keeping in touch with his parents. Charlie and Maggie Flower finally turn to a psychiatrist friend of theirs who agrees to have Toby hospitalised and treated for mental illness. As it happens, in London Toby associates with Hermia, the psychiatrist's young but rather unattractive daughter, and makes her pregnant. When their parents conspire and talk Hermia into having an abortion, they unwittingly cut the last remaining bond with their son. Toby fetches Hermia from her parents' home, and the young couple move in with Toby's maternal grandmother, a frail old woman who all along has been sympathetic to the young people's needs.

A young Conan finds himself involved in plots against the throne of Khauran. After saving Lady Khashtris from an attack by Shadizar's thieves and some traitorous henchmen, Conan agrees to work as her bodyguard in return for his soul being freed from the mirror it has been trapped in since Conan's encounter with Hissar Zul. Conan's soul can only be freed by one of noble birth, and Khashtris convinces Conan that her sister, Queen Ialamis, will free him. Unknown to Conan, the Queen, and Khashtris, the Queen's new paramour, Sergianus, is actually a disguised Sabaninus, the elderly Duke of Korveka, a Kothian province that wishes to annex Khauran. The disguise is revealed when the Queen breaks the mirror containing Conan's soul; as his soul re-enters his body, Conan sees the Duke for who he really is. Conan, Lady Khashtris, and her loyal bodyguard Shubal, then plot to unmask the Duke and save Khauran. Ialamis is also the mother of Salome and Taramis, who feature prominently in Howard's Conan tale, "A Witch Shall Be Born."

A fishing boat sinks in the English Channel in the middle of the night, and the evidence points to murder. Ex-Special Branch agent Dominic Elder comes out of retirement to help investigate the explosion of the boat, as it appears that his long-time obsession, a female assassin known as Witch, may be responsible. Using the boat to get to England from France, Witch left a subtle trail of clues to announce her arrival and to warn off Elder. But that is the least of Special Branch's worries, if Elder's well-honed intuition is correct. He has seen her work before and knows her to be a resourceful enemy, who always seems a step ahead of the authorities. With an imminent summit of world leaders to be held in London, Witch's target seems obvious. Young Michael Barclay's thoroughness leads him onto Witch's trail, with the help of his liaison in the French police, Dominique. Apart from her language help and guidance around Paris, Michael is sexually attracted to her. The team of detectives and MI5 agents, and the terrorist, play cat-and-mouse with each other in Scotland, England, France, and even briefly visit a former associate of Witch in prison in Germany.

Fourteen-year-old Rob Horton lives with his father in a Florida motel called the Kentucky Star. After his mother’s death, they relocate to Lister, Florida. Near the motel, Rob uncovers a live tiger confined in a cage. On the same day, he meets Sistine Bailey, a new classmate with a fierce temper. Because of an unnamed skin condition, Rob is sent home from school until his rash fades, a physical sign of his inward denial as he stows away painful emotions in an imaginary suitcase. He treats his school exile as a relief, since bullying from his middle school peers is relentless. Sistine starts visiting Rob daily, claiming to bring him homework. Meanwhile, the motel’s unscrupulous manager, Beauchamp, assigns Rob the task of feeding the tiger. With Sistine’s help, Rob schemes to free the animal. The tiger’s release becomes a catalyst for Rob to release the suppressed grief over his mother’s death. Yet his father discovers the tiger in the woods and shoots it, killing it. The quartet—Rob, Sistine, Willie May, and Rob’s father—hold a funeral for the creature, an event that evokes memories of Rob’s mother’s funeral. The story’s theme suggests there is a lesson to be learned from every experience Rob endures.

In the San Juan Basin's Jicarilla Apache field, an unidentified body is found near the edge of the natural gas operation, pulling Navajo Tribal Police Sergeant Jim Chee into a web of fraud surrounding diverted oil and gas revenues, abandoned pipelines, Washington insiders, and illegal drugs. Meanwhile, Hidalgo County’s rugged Animas Mountains at the basin’s southwestern fringe are patrolled by U.S. Border Patrol Officer Bernadette Manuelito, who snaps photos of a suspicious construction crew at the Tuttle exotic game ranch. After ranch staff lodge a complaint about her activities, her supervisor explains that the ranch and the Border Patrol have a covert pact: ranch personnel oversee border activity and relay tips, while formal patrols by the Border Patrol are paused on the ranch. Believing this arrangement, Manuelito remains unaware that a photo of her, taken by her supervisor, has circulated among criminal elements across the border in Mexico. Concerned, she discusses the situation with her former Navajo Tribal Police chief Jim Chee and with retired Lieutenant Joe Leaphorn. The trio soon links the corpse to the operations Manuelito has observed in Hidalgo County, uncovering a connection that ties the two strands together.

In the narrative, Nick stops for tea at the Ufford Hotel with his Uncle Giles, where he is introduced to the clairvoyant Mrs. Erdleigh, who proceeds to foretell their futures. Jenkins arranges a meeting with Members at the Ritz, but the appointment is kept by Quiggin, who has stepped in as secretary to the novelist St John Clarke. Nick later has dinner with Peter and Mona Templer, Jean Duport, and is extended an invitation to spend a weekend with the Templers in Maidenhead; there, an affair with Jean begins. Although Quiggin is asked to come on Sunday, he must depart due to concerns about his master. Mrs. Erdleigh also attends, accompanied by Jimmy Stripling, presiding over a séance. In spring 1933, Nick spends a day in a sequence of encounters with Quiggin and Members, including a demonstration led by St John Clarke, who is wheeled in his chair by Quiggin and Mona. There follow several further interactions with Jean and a visit to Foppa’s restaurant. By summer 1933, Jenkins, Templer, Stringham, and Widmerpool attend Le Bas’s Old Boys dinner at the Ritz; Stringham arrives severely inebriated, and Widmerpool delivers a long, dull, pompous speech that is interrupted only when Le Bas suffers a stroke. Widmerpool and Jenkins assist the drunken Stringham home to bed. The novel closes with hints that Nick’s relationship with Jean is nearing an end.

A small boy is left on his own in a flat. The boy answers a knocking on the front door of his high rise flat to find a man with no head standing on the doorstep. The man cannot speak, but the boy knows he is asking him for help. The boy apologises and, explaining that he cannot help him, closes the door and returns to playing games. The protagonist, Stark, a troubleshooter living in the Colour Neighbourhood, accepts a job from his friend, a high-ranking member of The Action Centre, Zenda Renn, and sets out to find senior Actioneer Fell Alkland, who appears to have gone missing under peculiar circumstances. Stark contacts another friend, a psychotic ganglord in the Red Neighbourhood named Ji, to assist him in tracking Alkland down, but something other than kidnapping is to blame for the old man's disappearance. Something that ties into Alkland's past, into The City itself. Stark is forced to confront both his past and a present which has become a living death, in a story of love lost and friendship betrayed. It takes him to places where dreams live, where they can come true, for better or for worse. Where they can kill you. In a world where past and future, reality and nightmare meet up and have a fistfight, Stark is the only man who can make the difference.

Born into a poverty-stricken family in the Alexandra township during the apartheid era, Mark Mathabane endures hunger, violence, and pervasive racial stereotypes that breed hatred and fear toward whites. At his mother’s urging, he enters school, discovers a love for learning, and excels academically despite punitive discipline stemming from his family’s late fee payments and lack of school supplies. A scholarship accompanying his primary education secures his secondary schooling. Mathabane’s grandmother finds work as a gardener for the compassionate Smith family, who expose him to literature and tennis, sending books—and even a tennis racket—home with her. From these readings, he acquires English, and his tennis practice becomes frequent, aided by a friendship with a Black player who mentors him. He joins his high school tennis squad and begins competing in tournaments, unofficially supported by Wilfred Horn of the Tennis Ranch; though the participation is technically illegal, the situation is tolerated, and he grows accustomed to interacting with whites. A turning point arrives when a renowned player, Stan Smith, encounters him at a tournament and takes him under his wing. Smith funds Mathabane’s tournament entries and approaches his own USC coach about the student’s prospects for an American college education. The coach then reaches out to colleges on Mathabane’s behalf, culminating in a tennis scholarship to Limestone College, which enables him to depart for the United States in 1978.

Harold Barnaby is a brilliant Egyptologist who has discovered a hidden message while translating some hieroglyphics. The message tells of an unnamed Pharaoh whose tomb hasn't been discovered yet. Barnaby is exhilarated by the discovery and the prospect of the fame and fortune that will come with it. There is only one problem. He doesn't have the knowledge, influence or wherewithal to pull off such a job without alerting the Egyptian authorities who would surely encroach on his discovery. Luckily, Barnaby meets Robert Pierce, a transient freelance writer who is in between jobs and looking for some excitement. In a moment of drunken indiscretion, Barnaby shares his discovery with Pierce along with his small logistical problem. Pierce, who because of his job has many friends in high—and low—places, offers his services to plan and manage the "extraction". For a cut, of course. He brings on Lord Grover, the fifth Earl of Wheatston to bankroll the project; smuggler Alan Conway; and international thief, Nikos Karagannis. Together, this motley crew set up camp in the harsh conditions of the Egyptian desert and "dig in" for the long haul. Their task is made all-the-more challenging when an Egyptian official becomes suspicious of their activities. tr:Easy Go

The 74 year-old Mr. Geiser is bored in his Ticinese house during torrential rains. He is so bored that he tries to make a pagoda out of crispbread and categorizes thunder types into a taxonomy (rolling thunders, banging thunders etc.). His sole companion is his cat as his wife had died not long ago. There is a report of a landslide caused by the deluge, cutting off the valley. Fearing a large slide that would bury the village and man’s knowledge, Geiser reads in his encyclopedia, the Bible, and history books. At first he makes notes and tacks them to the walls; later he cuts paragraphs from the books and tapes them instead, noting sadly that the front sides of the encyclopedia’s pages are visible, but the back sides unfortunately are dissected and destroyed. Despite the weather, he hikes outdoors along diverging paths. While wandering, he notes his physical limits, and the limits of man’s knowledge and importance. He notes man's insignificance and meaninglessness (man's appearance in the Holocene era is a very recent event in evolutionary terms). The old man is exposed to the cycle of life and his mortality. Geiser has to admit that „der Mensch bleibt ein Laie“ (his man stays a rookie). He slowly loses his memory. He wonders if memory was necessary – "the rocks do not need my memory or not". Towards the end, Geiser suffers cerebral apoplexy that attacks his memory.

Even under Palpatine’s leadership, who was elected to rescue the galaxy from the grip of unrest, the Republic shows signs of decay. On Ansion, a small but strategically important world, a powerful faction edges toward joining the growing Separatist movement. Urban centers crave expansion into the plains beyond their walls, the traditional homeland of the proud, autonomous Ansion nomads. Should their demands be denied, secession could trigger a domino effect, provoking withdrawals and uprisings across other Republic worlds. At the Chancellor’s urging, the Jedi Council dispatches Kenobi and Luminara Unduli to broker peace and reach an accord with the elusive nomads. Undaunted by the task, Kenobi and Unduli—accompanied by their Padawans, Skywalker and Barriss Offee—press onward through the wilds. They face countless dangers, must earn the trust of wary strangers, and strive to persuade two vast armies to aid their mission, all while pursued by a foe determined to prevent any settlement and derail the entire operation.

Arundhatī is the eighth daughter of Ṛṣi Kardama and Devahūti, and is married to Vasiṣṭha, the eighth son of Brahmā. Brahmā assures the couple that they will have the Darśana (sight) of Rāma. The couple spends many years waiting for Rāma. Viśvaratha, the son of the king Gādhi, tries snatch celestial cow Kāmadhenu from Vasiṣṭha, but is unable to stand against the Brahmadaṇḍa of Vasiṣṭha. Viśvaratha undergoes penance and becomes the Ṛṣi Viśvāmitra. The revengeful Viśvāmitra curses all hundred sons of Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha to die. The forgiveness of the couple gives rise to a son Śakti, whom Viśvāmitra gets killed by a demon. Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha then head for Vānaprastha Āśrama, leaving their grandson Parāśara to look after their hermitage. Brahmā ordains them to re-enter Gārhasthya Āśrama, reassuring that they will have the Darśana of Rāma as a householder couple only. The couple starts living in an Āśrama near Ayodhyā. With the birth of Lord Rāma, a son named Suyajña is born to them. Lord Rāma and Suyajña study together in the Āśrama of Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha. After the marriage of Sītā and Rāma in Mithilā, Arundhatī meets Sītā for the first time when the newly-wed couple arrives in Ayodhyā. Sītā and Rāma spend fourteen years in exile. When they return home, they have their first meal after the exile which is prepared by Arundhatī, and the epic ends thereafter.

While Stephanie is looking for Kenny, his friend is fatally shot in the head, which complicates the case. Lula, the hooker introduced in the previous book, One For the Money, gets a job as a file clerk at Vinnie's Bail Bonds company, but decides that being Stephanie's sidekick is more interesting than filing. Stephanie talks to Spiro Stiva, the son of the owner of the local funeral home and a childhood friend of Mancuso. Stiva asks Stephanie to help him find the 24 bargain basement caskets that have mysteriously gone missing...along with various body parts. As the book continues, Stephanie begins finding embalmed body parts in her apartment along with threatening notes. Then, a number of weapons go missing from a military installation. Eventually, Stephanie and Grandma Mazur find themselves locked in the basement of Stiva's Funeral Home and end up setting the place on fire. Stephanie's Jeep Wrangler, Sahara model, stolen outside of the Eternal Slumber funeral home on Stark Street, and most likely wound up in a chop shop.

Set after All the Weyrs of Pern and drawing on elements from Dragonsdawn and The Dolphin's Bell (from The Chronicles of Pern: First Fall), the tale examines the current state of Pern’s dolphins—brought ashore by the original colonists—during the Ninth Pass. It weaves together the science-fiction origins of the Pern saga with the fantasy textures of the beloved early books, placing its events toward the end of the timeline and beyond. The narrative centers on two young protagonists and traces the founding of Dolphincrafthall and the first Dolphineer. Readis, heir to the Paradise River Lord Holder, survives a sea accident as a boy thanks to dolphins that spoke to him, an encounter that ignites his fervent fascination. Parallel to this, T'lion, a Bronze Gadareth dragonrider from Eastern Weyr, becomes intrigued after a preliminary dolphin meeting of his own. Their shared passion for dolphins drives them to form a friendship that transcends family, Hold, and Weyr, as they advocate for the dolphins’ intelligence and speech. While familiar Pern figures contend with ending the Thread era, Readis and T'lion—along with other allies—strive to usher in a new era in which humans and dolphins collaborate once more. The plot also brings back prominent characters from earlier Pern novels, including Lessa and F'lar, the Benden Weyrleaders, and Masterharpers Robinton and Menolly.

To settle his daughter Kitty Imber’s gambling debts, the widower Lord Theign plans to auction off his exquisite portrait Duchess of Waterbridge by Sir Joshua Reynolds to American magnate Breckinridge Bender. A young art critic named Hugh Crimble argues against the sale, insisting Britain’s artistic treasures belong at home. He finds support in Theign’s discerning daughter, Lady Grace. As news leaks about the possible Reynolds sale, newspapers whip up a patriotic furor, much to the cheerful, outspoken Bender’s amusement. In the meantime Crimble uncovers another piece within Theign’s holdings, a painting he suspects is a Mantovano rarity. Although James initially doubted the painter Mantovano existed, Crimble’s persistence proves him right. Ultimately, Theign chooses to donate the Mantovano to the National Gallery and aborts the Reynolds sale to Bender. Lady Sandgate, a close companion of Theign, also contributes her family’s Sir Thomas Lawrence to the Gallery, sealing a lasting bond between them.

Private detective Joe Leland begins a case for Norma MacIver, a recently widowed woman who asks him to uncover everything he can about her husband’s death. Norma seeks Leland personally because her husband had once spoken of knowing him. In a twist of coincidence, Leland and Colin MacIver had served in the same World War II unit, though not at the same time. His inquiries take him to Colin’s first wife and mother, and to the security guards at the racetrack where Colin is believed to have killed himself. Norma then introduces Leland to her neighbor, a former therapist named Dr. Wendell Roberts. During their talk, Wendell reveals a prior acquaintance with Leland’s wife, and it emerges that Wendell was friends with the man who had had an affair with Karen Leland. As Leland’s probe widens, signs of corruption and murder start to appear. Further revelations emerge: Colin MacIver is tied to a homicide from Leland’s own police-detective days. In the course of investigating Teddy Leikman’s death, a confession is obtained from Leikman’s roommate, Felix Tesla, who is later executed by electric chair. Eventually, it becomes clear that Colin MacIver was the actual killer. Meanwhile, Mike Petrakis, Leland’s partner, uncovers Colin’s coded notes, exposing a clandestine chain of corruption.”} } } }>

The narrative opens in the closing days of the Shaa era. For millennia, the Shaa, a formidable species, have dominated the Empire and enforced subjugation over humans and other umber alike. Their creed, Praxis, codifies absolute obedience within rigid hierarchy. The Empire’s collapse sparks civil conflict as the insectoid Naxids clash with humanity and allied races after the death of the last Great Master. Central to the tale are interstellar warfare and the evolving dynamic between two humans: a male naval officer and a female pilot. Lieutenant Gareth Martinez—a provincial noble—and Cadet Sula, leader of the Sula clan, cross paths during a rescue attempt for a yachtsman named Blitsharts. Martinez serves as the Fleet Commander Enderby’s communications officer and, upon recognizing Blitsharts’s peril, urges the captain of the ship Bombardment of Los Angeles to initiate a rescue operation. In response, the captain dispatches a pinnace, a single-seat craft piloted by Lady Sula. Throughout the rescue and the yacht’s lengthy retrieval—spanning more than a month due to vast distances—Martinez routinely conveys messages to Sula, peppered with humor and literary selections to sustain her on the long return voyage. He also reveals that the remaining Shaa plans to take his own life, thereby stepping aside and placing the empire under the convocation—a governing assembly made up of peers from every race.

Ramona Quimby’s neighborhood undergoes a reorganization of its schools, and she now commutes by bus to Cedarhurst Primary, where she and the other third graders will stand among the oldest students. She welcomes the changes at first, even as a bus passenger pilfers her new eraser. Undeterred, she confronts the challenge and grows to believe the so‑called Yard Ape isn’t necessarily terrible after all. The highlight of third grade, for Ramona, is Sustained Silent Reading; she cherishes daily in‑school reading time. Yet insecurity gnaws at her because she isn’t sure Mrs. Whaley, her teacher, likes her. A lunch mishap—cracking a hard-boiled egg on her head after discovering it wasn’t boiled—lands her in the secretary’s office with a head full of raw egg, and she overhears Mrs. Whaley describing her as a show-off and a nuisance. Even the Yard Ape can’t console her this time. Things deteriorate further when she vomits in class, forcing her mother to leave work to pick her up. Complications mount with the troublesome Willa Jean. Each day after school, Howie heads outside to ride bikes with friends, leaving Ramona to play infantile games. Beezus can always claim she’s busy with homework, but that excuse doesn’t satisfy Ramona. Nevertheless, she is maturing, using her imagination to devise ways to support her family and cope with the intricacies of growing up.

Anna Wulf, a writer, narrates The Golden Notebook, which centers on four distinct notebooks she uses to document her life and her effort to fuse them into a final, gold-hued volume. The narrative interweaves two strands: a seemingly realistic chronicle of Molly and Anna, their children, former spouses, and lovers—grouped under the banner Free Women—and selections from Anna’s own notebooks. The four colored sections—black, red, yellow, and blue—each represent a facet of experience: black chronicles Anna’s time in Southern Rhodesia and the wartime era that later inspired her bestselling novel; red recalls her days as a member of the Communist Party; yellow is a fictional ongoing work drawn from the painful end of Anna’s romantic relationship; blue serves as a private journal capturing her memories, dreams, and emotional life. Each notebook appears repeatedly, four times apiece, with episodes from Free Women woven between them, producing non-chronological, overlapping segments that converse with one another. This stylistic, postmodern approach—allowing space and playful interaction among characters and readers—is one of the work’s most celebrated features, even as Lessing urged readers and critics to heed the novel’s serious themes.

Centered loosely on Billy, a boy who longs to own a candy shop, the tale begins near an abandoned storefront known as The Grubber—the old confectionery landmark near his home. When the derelict building is suddenly refurbished, it becomes the head office for the Ladderless Window-Cleaning Company, introducing Billy to its quirky staff: a giraffe with an extendable neck, a pelican nicknamed Pelly who can retract his upper beak, and a monkey he befriends. The foursome unite after receiving a summons from the Duke of Hampshire to polish the windows of Hampshire House. Their mission proceeds without incident until, while cleaning the Duchess’s bedroom, the giraffe and the monkey notice a burglar attempting to steal the Duchess’s diamonds. Pelly swoops in, snatching the intruder with his beak and holding him suspended as the others panic. The Chief of Police later identifies the captured thief as “The Cobra,” one of the world’s most notorious cat burglars, and the authorities arrest him. In gratitude for recovering the diamonds, the Duke invites the L.W.C.C. to reside on his estate and serve as his personal helpers. Billy’s dream is fulfilled: the Grubber will no longer serve merely as a warehouse, thanks to the Duke’s aid, and will be transformed into the town’s most marvelous sweet shop—even carrying confections from Willy Wonka. The story closes on a note of harmonious celebration as they all live happily ever after.

Maerth asserted that the eating of brain produces an aphrodisiac effect (presumably due to the vast amount of hormones in it), and that this initially caused apes to become addicted to them, organizing brain hunts wherein the males of another tribe were eaten and the females raped in a frenzy of brain-induced sex and violence. However, this diet also inadvertently increased brain size and intelligence while triggering the loss both of body hair and of our innate psychic abilities. Thus man gradually came into being, remaining cannibalistic until 50,000 years ago. Modern humans, alienated from their surroundings now that they've no telepathic contact with nature and each other as animals do, suffering from a distorted sexuality resulting from hormonal imbalances, and driven insane from the constant pressure of their unnaturally large brains pressing on the inside of their skulls,Maerth (1974), page 53: are inevitably destroying themselves with pollution, overpopulation, racial integration and ultimately, nuclear war. He foresees a return to cannibalism in the near future,Maerth (1974), page 199: and suggests that the reader should drop out of society, embrace a vegetarian diet, steep himself in the wisdom of the East and perhaps employ various wooden frames and wire devices to alter the shape of his skull as some ancient cultures did, thus relieving the pressure on the brain and partially restoring psychic powers.

Narrated by a nameless mother who serves as the book’s voice, Jackson recounts roughly six years in her family’s life, concentrating on her efforts to preserve harmony and a well-run household as her brood grows. At the outset, the mother has two children and about five thousand books, and she foresees that before they move from their home the clan will number twenty children and easily half a million books. The two youngsters are Laurie and Jannie, characters largely modeled after Jackson’s own first two children. Laurie, about five, has just started kindergarten and is eager to gain a vote in domestic affairs; Jannie is nearly two. As the narrative unfolds, a third child, Sally, is introduced—also drawn from Jackson’s third child—adding to the prevailing chaos and comic chaos of daily life as the three children develop distinct, fiercely independent personalities. The book ends with the arrival of another infant, Barry, who again stands in for Jackson’s youngest child.

The narrative opens in Cordoba, where Aldonza, a girl with early sexual awareness, lives with her mother. After her mother dies, she relocates to her aunt’s home, only to flee with Diomedes, a merchant who sails the seas. The pair journey through various ports around the Mediterranean and into the Middle East, and Aldonza adopts the alias Lozana. Their travels lead them to Marseille, where Diomedes’ father, repulsed by his son, consigns him to prison and hires a sailor to erase Lozana from his life. Yet the sailor instead defies the order and transports Lozana to Livorno, from which she continues onward to Rome. Penniless, Lozana seeks aid in Rome’s Spanish Quarter, where women notice her talents in cooking, her medical knowledge, and her beauty—though a syphilitic blemish mars her face. A Neapolitan woman helps her by giving Lozana a servant named Rampin; Lozana agrees that Rampin will serve her and be her lover for a time. Heeding the advice of a postman and with the help of a Jew named Trigos who provides her a home, Lozana begins a new chapter as a prostitute. In the years that follow, she rises to the position of a brothel’s madam. Eventually Lozana and Rampin relocate to Lipari. The work concludes with a brief vignette recounting Rome’s sack.

Set within a fractured household, the drama centers on Beatrice, a single mother, and her two daughters, Ruth and Tillie, as they struggle with a grim, stagnant existence. The piece unfolds as a lyrical, Williams-esque meditation on family and fate. Tillie, the shy young scientist-in-waiting, plans a science-fair project: marigolds germinated from seeds tainted by radioactivity. Yet every step forward is obstructed. Beatrice, self-absorbed and abusive, blocks Tillie at every turn, while Ruth, loud and outgoing but unstable, capitulates to their mother’s will.Throughout the play, Beatrice relentlessly smothers Tillie’s chances, a reflection of her own unfulfilled life. As events unfold, the characters’ trajectories diverge: Tillie’s perseverance ultimately wins her the science fair; Ruth attempts to confront her mother, only to suffer a final nervous breakdown; and Beatrice, driven to madness by a deep-seated hostility toward everyone around her, murders the family’s pet rabbit, Peter, and sinks into a paralyzing sense of insignificance. Yet Tillie, embodying resilience much like her project’s marigolds—deformed, yet hardy and beautiful—retains a quiet conviction that every life has value, even when unseen by others.

Gemma and Alice have known each other all their lives, but when Gemma reads Alice's diary at a sleepover, it eventually leads her to discover Alice is moving. Because of their distance, Gemma and Alice struggle to stay friends, with the possibility of each other making new friends. The story's theme throughout the whole story is that true friends will be together until the end. Gemma and Alice have been best friends since birth. They were born on the same day, in the same hospital and have been inseparable ever since. Complete opposites (Gemma is athletic and messy, while Alice is graceful and tidy), they have a bond that is unbreakable and every year on their birthday they share the same wish: “We wish we stay friends forever and ever and ever.” Everything seems ruined when Alice's father gets a new job hundreds of miles away and the whole family has to move. Now Alice and Gemma have to navigate the rough waters of adjusting to life without each other. Alice has another friend Flora. Flora is really posh. Only Gemma hates Flora. Once Gemma visits Alice at the same time as Flora does. Gemma brings a cake and when she there she's there she throws it in Floras face. The book ends with a birthday card from Alice.

The wild young Viscount Sheringham is fast running through his considerable income through gambling and other extravagant pursuits; and he cannot as yet touch the principal, unless he marries. As the lady with whom he currently fancies himself in love, the beautiful Isabella Milborne, is also an heiress, he proposes. Isabella rejects him with contumely, citing his dissipated lifestyle. A lively quarrel then follows with his obnoxious widowed mother and her brother, who wish to retain control of his father's fortune themselves. The Viscount storms off in a fit of pique, vowing to marry the first female he meets. This turns out to be the pretty but orphaned and shy Hero Wantage, who has secretly loved him since they were children, and who now lives with one of his neighbours in the position of Cinderella, complete with Ugly Sisters. The rest of the novel, chronicling the Viscount's gradual transition to maturity and the realisation that the one he really loves is Hero (the "loving and giving" child of the title), is told with Miss Heyer's characteristic wit, and features some of her most memorable dialogue, plot twists and characters (such as the fiery but lovelorn George Wrotham, whose hobby is fighting duels).

In the wake of World War II, a clandestine Nazi submarine facility hid containers forged from pilfered wartime gold. The treasure wasn’t the solid ingots themselves, but the payload they concealed—an artifact so deadly that possession of what are called “Pandora’s Boxes” could unleash hell on Earth. While surveying Greenland’s stark wastes, geologist Philip Mercer stumbles upon a long-forgotten U.S. Army installation buried by ice, where a corpse still radiates. Before Mercer and his partner can delve deeper, a blazing flash destroys the base and forces an evacuation. Their aircraft then caroms to an emergency landing after a bomb is found aboard, sending them scrambling for shelter inside a clandestine icy cavern. There, the truth begins to surface. A formidable German conglomerate has initiated a covert campaign to eradicate evidence of its Nazi legacy. Among its hired guns, one mercenary understands the contents of the Pandora boxes and intends to seize world power unless Mercer can devise a way to stop him.

Penman’s 1985 novel Here Be Dragons inaugurates a trilogy tracing the medieval princes of Gwynedd alongside England’s rulers. To avert a broader war, King John of England leverages his illegitimate daughter Joanna by betrothing her to the Welsh king Llewelyn. The union, intended as a peacekeeping arrangement, becomes tense thanks to Llewelyn’s illegitimate son Gruffydd’s growing resentment. Joanna bears two legitimate children, Elen and Davydd, while English–Welsh tensions escalate. As Joanna serves as the diplomatic conduit between Llewelyn and her father, the conflict worsens when Gruffydd is seized as a hostage by John and narrowly spared execution. She becomes determined that her own son, Dafydd, should inherit Gwynedd, attempting to place him above Welsh customary inheritance, which prescribes equal division among sons. Internal family strife pushes Joanna toward an extramarital liaison with William de Braose, a former hostage she had encountered earlier in Llewelyn’s household. When their affair is exposed, William is put to death. Joanna is confined in seclusion, yet in the finale Llewelyn arrives to offer forgiveness and reconciliation.

Three pivotal events unfold in near simultaneity. First, Coruscant falls under occupation as the Empire leaves a wake of turmoil from a devastating bio-attack. The weapon, known as the Krytos virus, was engineered by General Evir Derricote and unleashed under Ysanne Isard’s orders. While humans appear immune, other species suffer severely. Coupled with the disruptive actions of Imperial Intelligence officer Kirtan Loor—carrying out orders from the Palpatine Counterinsurgency Front—the crisis plunges Coruscant and the New Republic into a state of emergency. Second, Rogue Squadron’s executive officer Tycho Celchu faces treason charges, accused of killing Rogue Squadron pilot Corran Horn, who had been captured during the invasion. Third, Corran Horn remains a prisoner in the Lusankya facility. His failed escape attempts lead him to uncover Rogue Squadron’s mole, turning the situation into a high-stakes race to exonerate the innocent and reveal the true traitor.

Opening the book, Rabo Karabekian, the narrator, apologizes to the arriving guests with a quip about promised autobiography gone awry in the kitchen. He presents himself as a museum guard who fields visitors’ questions about his priceless art collection. His solitary home is shared with his live-in cook and her daughter, Celeste. One afternoon, Circe Berman wanders onto Karabekian’s private beach, and when he approaches, she surprises him by asking, “Tell me how your parents died.” He recounts the tale and then invites her inside for a drink. After a drink and dinner, he asks her to stay, just as Paul Slazinger had done before. Over time, he begins to view her charm as manipulative, noting that she tends to get her way. Mrs. Berman shows little respect for Karabekian’s abstract holdings, including Pollock canvases, and she devotes herself to exploring every corner of the house while peppering him with questions. The only area forbidden to her is the potato barn, which houses Karabekian’s studio and his “secret.” The barn is windowless, with one end nailed shut and the other secured by six padlocks. This secret has drawn eager collectors who offer outrageous sums and fuel suspicions of stolen masterpieces, yet it will remain locked until Karabekian’s death.

Spanning nearly 17,000 years, Birthright opens with humanity expanding from Earth and closes with the extinction of the last of humanity. Across its arc, the tale portrays a gradual, sometimes hindered, but overarching conquest of a galaxy teeming with thousands of sentient alien civilizations who are consistently subdued—through economic leverage, deft diplomacy, or outright force. While some sections explore how humans treat aliens, others focus on the domestic politics that reshape the fledgling empire from a democratic system into a monarchy. Yet the central thread remains the quest to identify the elusive quality that lets mankind overpower every foe and achieve the monumental feat of galaxy-wide dominion. The answer never settles clearly, though it often surfaces in a moment when an audacious attempt to bridge the intergalactic void ends in failure. Once the galaxy is fully claimed, the momentum reverses: internecine strife and deep alien resentment corrode human supremacy, a decline that lasts nearly as long as the rise but receives far less narrative attention. In a twist of irony, one chapter even lampoons the very concept of a literary genre as yet another human oddity, unlike any alien race.”

April Lancaster, aged eighteen and the daughter of Janice and Hugh Lancaster, goes to the hospital for diagnostic tests after suffering headaches, blackouts, and a collapse in English class. There she meets Mark Gianni, a cystic fibrosis patient who has spent most of his life hospitalized. Mark becomes affectionate toward April, even telling her he plans to marry her, but she rejects his invitation to date because she already has a boyfriend, Chris. A physician reveals that April has an inoperable brain tumor—a recurrence from a condition she battled at age five—and that radiation therapy is required. After she informs Chris of the diagnosis, their relationship ends, and April starts seeing Mark. As their friendship deepens into love, Mark proposes; April accepts, though her parents initially disapprove before they come to terms with it. Not long after, Mark is racing in a car that flips and bursts into flames. He survives the crash but contracts pneumonia and dies. The narrative closes with April and her parents vacationing in St. Croix, where she releases a red balloon in Mark’s memory, a gesture he once made. The sequel, For Better, For Worse, Forever, opens with April still in St. Croix.

Scully Christopher Crockett La Cruz is an actor, a fortune hunter, and an adventurer hailing from the remote, self-contained orbital technocratic democracies of Circumluna and the Bubbles Congeries. He travels to what he believes is Canada to pursue family mining interests, only to find that Canada has become North Texas, and the remnants of North American civilization are governed by a boisterous, anti-intellectual, self-satisfied cohort of “good old boys” who view themselves as morally superior. In the skewed history familiar to the giant, hormonally boosted Anglo-Saxon rulers who dominate a small Mexican underclass, the original Texas — Texas — had secretly controlled the pre-nuclear United States since 1845. Texas dodged the nuclear devastation that wiped out the rest of the country thanks to the foresight of Lyndon the First. A vast bunker, once known as the Houston Carlsbad Caverns–Denver–Kansas City–Little Rock Pentagram and now simply called the Texas Bunker, safeguarded the heartland during a war that annihilated the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, as well as Europe, Russia, China, and Africa. In this narrative, Texas then subjugated the remainder of the continent, leaving Hawaii and Cuba defiant and unconquered.

On a mission in Bangkok, Parker, an American CIA operative, is captured. In response, another CIA agent, Sawyer, is dispatched solo under the codename Dragonfire to avert a fresh Southeast Asian conflict. Tracking Parker’s trail through Bangkok’s grim waterfront underworld and into the secluded hills of the Golden Triangle, Sawyer allies with Suong, a striking Eurasian resistance fighter, and Toonsang, a duplicitous opium trader who guides them to Bhun Sa, the most powerful kingpin in the narcotics trade. After Sawyer eliminates Bhun Sa, he and Suong flee to ruined temple sites in Cambodia. To prove she is loyal, Suong recounts how she survived the Khmer Rouge’s Killing Fields. Sawyer is taken prisoner by the Khmer Rouge, and it comes to light that Suong is a war criminal, the sister of Pranh, known as Brother Number Two of the Killing Fields. Vietnamese forces eventually assault the Khmer Rouge, freeing Sawyer, who then captures Suong. A confrontation on Bangkok’s waterfront culminates in Sawyer killing Vasnasong, the billionaire mastermind behind the plot, and delivering Suong to the Cambodian resistance. In the epilogue, the final fate of Suong—her brutal death aboard a ship at the hands of those she once harmed—is revealed.

Lauren Hartke and her film-director husband, Rey Robles, occupy a remote house near New York City. Their morning routine is minimal—a terse exchange at breakfast—before Rey departs for work. Not long afterward, news arrives: Rey has died by a self-inflicted gunshot at his first wife’s Manhattan apartment. An obituary follows, revealing Ré’s age of 64, a history of depression, and that Lauren had been his third wife. Bereaved and isolated, Lauren remains in the house despite pleas from friends and family to leave. She drifts out of sync with time and her own body, plagued by recurring, inexplicable déjà vu. Over the ensuing hours, days, and weeks, she grapples with this estrangement, continuing her signature practice of “bodywork”—the aerobic and stretching routines she devised to ready her body for performance pieces. Her life settles into a rhythm of daily rituals, including chopping wood and hours spent watching webcam footage of a road in Kotka, Finland. Then, one morning, a sound from the upper floor intrudes on her routine. She climbs the stairs to investigate, only to find no one present. The next day she returns upstairs; this time, a man is waiting in one of the bedrooms. His appearance shifts with each sighting, but in this first moment he is described as small, fine-boned, reminiscent of a child, with sandy hair and just awakened from a deep sleep.

Pine Cove suffers a major crisis when the town psychiatrist, Val Riordan — who has been haphazardly issuing prescriptions instead of dealing with the real mental problems of her patients — suffers a sudden bout of guilt and substitutes all of her patients' anti-depressants with placebos. At this same time, by coincidence, human-generated environmental activity stirs a prehistoric sea-beast from its underwater keep to come ashore. In addition to its ability to change form, the beast exudes a pheromone that inspires uncontrollable lust among the residents of Pine Cove and also lures some of them as prey. After mistakenly trying to mate with a fuel truck (causing an explosion), the beast hides in a trailer park, attracting the curiosity of local crazy lady and former B-movie star Molly Michon, who builds a rapport with the injured beast. Meanwhile, Theophilus Crowe, the town constable, investigates a strange suicide, the activities of his corrupt boss, and his adversely affected marijuana habit. When the beast (whom Molly has named "Steve") starts eating residents of Pine Cove and interfering with Theo's boss's meth business, Molly (who has become romantically involved with the beast) and Theo band together to make possible the beast's safe escape and to take down the boss at the same time.

Picking up directly from Exile, the narrative follows Ben as he returns to Jacen aboard the Sith Meditation Sphere discovered on Ziost. Jacen exerts control over political affairs, enacting a radical law that empowers him to rewrite existing statutes. Leveraging Cal Omas' betrayal of the Galactic Alliance, he and Admiral Niathal orchestrate a bloodless coup, capturing Omas and declaring themselves joint Chiefs of State. Concurrently, Jacen dispatches Ben to kill Dur Gejjen, plunging the Corellian-led Confederation into turmoil. Elsewhere, Boba Fett and Mirta Gev press on in search of a cure for Fett’s illness after encountering Kad Skirata, the clone’s son. Kad promises unity for the Mandalorians and, in return, cures Fett, granting him roughly thirty more years to live. During a overheard exchange between Lumiya and Jacen, Ben is horrified and confesses everything to his mother, Mara Jade Skywalker. Mara, furious at Jacen’s attempt to lure Ben to the dark side, resolves to kill him. The plan backfires when Jacen sacrifices Mara by killing her. That act completes a prophecy by destroying Ben’s love for Jacen. Believing Lumiya to be Mara’s killer, Luke goes after Lumiya and ultimately kills her. Ben then discloses that Lumiya could not have murdered Mara, since he was with Lumiya at the time. In the book’s finale, Jacen Solo appoints himself a new Sith name: Darth Caedus.

As the story opens, Tamis, a sorceress, is seeing the future. She discovers that only a mixed-blood Spartan called Parmenion can help her. Parmenion is a half-blood Spartan whose mother is from Macedon. He is an accomplished runner and a strategic genius, yet he is despised by the young Spartan nobles. He is forced to kill a love rival in duel, subsequently forcing him to flee to Thebes. There, Parmenion starts a new life as a professional runner, but also gets involved with Thebian rebels attempting to overthrow the Spartan garrison now residing in the city center. This ultimately leads to an extended war between to the two city states, ending with Parmenion crushing the Spartan army, destroying the Spartan legend in the process. Some years later Parmenion is a famous mercenary general, winning battles all around Asia. He is then offered a chance to rebuild the Macedonian army by Philip II of Macedon. Later on the story describes the rise of Macedon under Philip II of Macedon and the birth of Alexander the Great. fr:Le Lion de Macédoine pl:Lew Macedonii

Spock journeys to the era and setting of Here Come the Brides, a TV show inspired by Asa Mercer’s mission to bring civilization to 1860s Seattle by bringing in the Mercer Girls from the war-torn East Coast. The premise centers on Jason Bolt, the eldest Bolts’ brother, wagering his entire logging enterprise that he can lure one hundred marriageable women to Seattle, with the expectation that all will be wed or engaged within a year. Much of the drama and humor comes from Aaron Stemple, their benefactor, schemes to thwart the arrangement and seize control of the Bolts’ assets. In the course of the tale, Spock uncovers a Klingon plot aimed at destroying the Federation by killing Aaron Stemple before Stemple can foil a nineteenth-century alien invasion of Earth. For most of the narrative, Spock has amnesia and is—under Stemple’s care—presented as his nephew, “Ishmael,” while his true alien origins are concealed. Along the way, Spock identifies one of the women as a probable ancestor of his.

11-year-old Josie arrives in upstate New York to live with her great-aunt after her mother abandons her father for no apparent reason. There, she meets her 25-year-old cousin, Jared, who is studying to be a minister. Her stay is very unpleasant; she is physically and psychologically abused by both her mother and great-aunt. She is also bullied without mercy at her new school. Her mother turns her away for love and comfort. Feeling abandoned and unloved, she turns to Jared for the affection she longs for. However, Jared's intents are anything but to love and care for her. He uses false affection to get her to self-mutilate herself, drink her own blood, look at pornographic material, and endure verbal abuse from him. He soon begins sexually abusing her, which Josie mistakes to be him expressing true love to her, although she knows that what they are doing is wrong. Josie eventually discovers that her mother is incapable of love because she was always felt unimpressed by Josie's father and several other men. After staying there for an extended period of time, Josie starts to have a psychological breakdown within herself, probably from her taboo relationship with Jared. At one point in the novellette, she and Jared, after initiating sexual intercourse by a creek, sit together. Then, Jared cuts his chest with a stone, and Josie licks the blood off before he dies from blood loss. This is the climax of the novella. After, she leaves the mansion, breaking free of Jared's prison.

Tarzan, the king of the jungle, enters an isolated country called Minuni, inhabited by a people four times smaller than himself, the Minunians, who live in magnificent city-states which frequently wage war against each other. Tarzan befriends the king, Adendrohahkis, and the prince, Komodoflorensal, of one such city-state, called Trohanadalmakus, and joins them in war against the onslaught of the army of Veltopismakus, their warlike neighbours. He is captured on the battle-ground and taken prisoner by the Veltopismakusians, whose scientist Zoanthrohago conducts an experiment reducing him to the size of a Minunian, and the ape-man is imprisoned and enslaved among other Trohanadalmakusian prisoners of war. He meets, though, Komodoflorensal in the dungeons of Veltopismakus, and together they are able to make a daring escape. Spanish actor/Tarzan lookalike Esteban Miranda, who had been imprisoned in the village of Obebe, the cannibal, at the end of the previous novel, Tarzan and the Golden Lion, also appears in this adventure.

As a boy, Achak is separated from his family during the Second Sudanese Civil War when the Arab militia, referred to as murahaleen (which is Arabic for traveller), wipes out his Dinka village, Marial Bai. During the assault, he loses sight of his father and his childhood friends, Moses and William K. William K escapes, but Moses is believed to be dead after the assault. Achak seeks shelter in the house of his aunt with his mother, who is frequently identified throughout the book with a yellow dress. Before they are hidden, they hear the screaming of Achak's aunt, and his mother goes to investigate. Achak never sees her again afterward. He evades detection by hiding in a bag of grain, and credits God for helping him stay quiet. He flees on foot with a group of other young boys (the "Lost Boys"), encountering great danger and terrible hardship along the way to a refugee camp in Ethiopia . Their inflated expectations are shattered by the conditions at the camp, and eventually they are forced to flee to another refugee camp in Kakuma, after Ethiopian president Mengistu is overthrown and soldiers open fire on them. They make it to Kenya and finally, years later, he moves to the United States. The story is told in parallel to subsequent hardships in the United States.

In Cambridge, Bill—humble and penniless—finds himself nearly unable to finance his mother’s funeral, and thoughts of crime creep in. A friend warns him starkly that poverty can feel like a birthright of the aristocracy, and that if ever wealth comes, he will have abandoned that status forever. Helen, a literature undergraduate, moves through life with little steadiness, clinging instead to poetry, especially the romantic medieval verses of Tennyson. Her fixation on The Lady of Shalott and her self-identification with the poem’s heroine drive her toward a tragic end. Though she has dallied with Victorian-era medieval romances, she resists being charmed by Bill. Lance, a scientist hoping to rescue humanity, finds that his experiments cast a troubling shadow over Helen. Meanwhile, a notorious Cambridge rapist roams free. The scene is described as a world of bedsitter girls and the poets Auden, Betjeman, and Brian Patten. Bill’s purchase of aDonald Duck mask intended for bank robbery unintentionally links him to the rapist’s identity. Over one Michaelmas term week, the complex relations among the principal figures escalate into more than a robbery: ritual castration, cross-dressing, and a fatal car crash all unfold. The tension stretches from the Whipple Museum to the University Arms Hotel, leaving intellectuals and sightseers aghast at the catastrophic, unanswered question behind the noise. The novel interweaves lines from Tennyson and from poets such as Thomas Hood, William Thackeray, and W. H. Auden.

The story's narrator is a writer who works as a fact checker for a high-brow magazine—likely based on Harpers or The New Yorker, where McInerney himself once worked as a fact checker—for which he had once hoped to write. By night, he is a cocaine using party-goer seeking to lose himself in the hedonism of the 1980s yuppie party scene, often going to a nightclub called Heartbreak. His wife, Amanda, recently left him and he copes with this by pretending nothing happened and telling no one that she's gone. Initially hopeful that she will return someday, he eventually resorts to searching for her at a fashion event. He obsesses over every item she owned in his apartment, every modeling photo and every club she visited, even repeatedly visiting a mannequin based on her. Also, his partying is affecting his work and he appears to be on the verge of getting fired by his temperamental boss. The novel would go on to be the source material for the 1988 film Bright Lights, Big City, which was also written by McInerney. In 1999, an off Broadway stage musical was produced by the New York Theater Workshop, written by Paul Scott Goodman and directed by Michael Grief, with orchestrations and musical direction by Richard Barone.

The main content of the book describes the disease that would later cause a global catastrophe: H5N1, the bird flu. In parts of southeastern Asia, the bird flu is a deadly epidemic that is feared by many. The bird flu has already spread to parts of Africa and most of Europe, because of today's transportation methods. Pandemia illustrates the possibility that bird flu will possibly mutate and spread to the rest of the world, creating a global pandemic in a matter of weeks. This causes a global state of emergency, and eventually causes the collapse of society and many economies across the world. The book's full plot features a group of teens in Saline, Michigan that must try and escape the city and head to the countryside where they can hopefully stay alive long enough in their uncle's cabin to be rescued. But in doing so, the teens must use whatever weapons they can find to defend themselves against looters, insane killers, and contagious, potentially dangerous infected. In a world gone mad, can the group find the necessities: food, water and shelter to survive?

Bianca Barrett, the protagonist and daughter of a Welsh Surveyor and his Palestinian wife, becomes an "ambitious and mercenary" social climber and double murderess. Charming and well educated, Bianca marries four times and advances in wealth and social influence. With Bernardo, her first husband, Bianca has three children; they lose their son in a tragic car accident. After a divorce, she marries the rich Fredie whose family owns the Piedraplata commercial empire. Before it comes to a divorce, the second husband is shot and killed by a hitman who makes it look like a suicide. The killing is arranged by her lover, Phillipe Mahfud, and Bianca becomes the financial beneficiary. After a brief marriage to husband number three, - she had married him only to make Mahfud jealous-, she lastly marries Mahfud, a superrich Iraqi businessman and banker. When their relationship sours, the banker dies with his nurse in a mysterious fire in his apartment in the tax haven of Andorra. Bianca's lawyers pay off the police and investigators, and the only justice that remains is in the court of public opinion.

The central figure, Martin, is meant to be composing a book, yet an invitation to dinner draws him into the home of a repellent, quarrelsome couple whose land and possessions seem squandered. During the visit he discovers a painting he believes to be by Brueghel. Through meticulous inquiry and a thorough reevaluation of Brueghel’s The Months—specifically its five surviving panels—he concludes that the work is the long-mourning sixth image from the book of hours. At the same time, his wife, a genuine art historian, while Martin remains only tangential to the scholarly art world, and their infant daughter live in a cottage. He fears his wife’s growing scorn as his energy shifts from advancing his manuscript to pursuing Brueghel’s data. In order to obtain the painting, Martin has to simulate an affair with the house’s resident woman and engages in a sequence of improbable dealings with other pictures to maintain access to Brueghel’s image. Once the piece is finally within reach, misery follows. As he strains to transport it to a safe haven and secure his fortune, the old Landrover crashes, and the painting is consumed by flames. In the end, the truth about whether it is truly by Brueghel remains unresolved.

In the late 21st century life feels unusually serene. Earth enjoys lasting peace while humans wield self-replicating machines that manufacture engineering wonders on vast scales. Humanity builds artificial habitats across the solar system, and Valkyrie rockets powered by anti-matter carry explorers toward the stars at nearly light speed. For a time, everything seems orderly. Then from the indifferent void of space arrive swarms of relativistic missiles. Sized like boulders yet traveling at such speeds that their impact rivals many nuclear arsenals, they slip beyond tracking and evade any attempt at interception. The human race is almost annihilated by this merciless bombardment. (For a discussion of relativistic weapons and a sample of the assault, see Atomic Rockets: Relativistic Weapons.) A few survivors fight desperately to slip away from the alien mop-up fleet. They conceal themselves near the Sun, inside asteroids, beneath moon crusts, within icy rings, and deep in interstellar darkness. Still, most are hunted down and slaughtered. The last man and woman on Earth are finally captured to be put on display like zoo specimens. A squid‑like extraterrestrial aboard a vast alien starship explains the cruel rationale behind humanity’s execution: the moment we learned to travel at relativistic speeds, we gained the power to do to them what they did to us first. The assault was not personal; humanity simply proved themselves too dangerous a neighbor to keep around.

The novel opens in 54 BC, with Caesar in the middle of his epochal Gallic campaigns, having just invaded Britannia. The first half of the novel deals broadly with the conclusion of his conquests in Gaul, and the second half narrates the growing sense of unease in Rome concerning Caesar's intentions, the antagonism of the conservative 'boni' faction towards him, his crossing of the Rubicon, his invasion of Italy and his victory in the Civil War. Some of the pivotal moments include Caesar's return from Britannia; his narrow escape during the battle of Gergovia; his great victory at Alesia, which involved the complete circumvallation of the citadel, the repulse of a relief force, and the acceptance of the surrender of Vercingetorix; his final destruction of the Gallic resistance at Uxellodunum; the death of Julia and Marcus Licinius Crassus; his falling out with Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus and the final collapse of the First Triumvirate system; his failed negotiations concerning his re-election as consul; the opening of the Civil War; the Battle of Dyrrhachium and the Battle of Pharsalus; the flight of Pompey to Ptolemaic Egypt and his assassination there; and the scattering of the 'boni' leadership.

The third installment in Updike’s Rabbit saga follows Harry “Rabbit” Angstrom, a once-celebrated high school basketball star who has settled into a paunchy middle age in Brewer, Pennsylvania—the small, impoverished town where he was born. Harry and his wife, Janice, now twenty-two years into their marriage, enjoy a comfortable lifestyle after inheriting her late father’s Toyota dealership. Wealth aside, Harry’s life is unsettled by a string of problems: Janice’s drinking, his son Nelson’s troublesome schemes, his own restless libido, and echoes from the past that persistently surface. He has no real appetite for greed, yet contentment remains elusive. The narrative also follows Harry’s growing attraction to the wife of a friend from the country club and the challenges posed by Nelson’s indecision and irresponsibility as a Kent State student. Throughout, Harry grapples with lingering questions about his former lover Ruth and whether she ever bore his child.

Sixteen-year-old Miranda seeks practicality, while Cassandra, nearly ten, trusts in magic and marvels. They are outnumbered at home by Professor Aisling, who teaches mythology and legends at a university and shares a belief in the mysterious and magical. Yet some university colleagues doubt the value of mythic study, arguing that magical beings cannot be rationalized or measured. One skeptic in particular, Mr. Bilgewallow, enjoys tormenting Aisling, who longs for a ship that could carry him to realms where legendary creatures dwell. One evening, that dream comes true. While strolling by the river with his daughters, Aisling encounters a peculiar little vessel manned by dwarfs and gremlins. A dwarf introduces himself as Malachi, Captain of H.M.S. Basset, declaring the ship is Aisling’s conjured creation, ready to sail on the “tides of inspiration.” Astonishment and joy surge through Aisling, and he and Cassandra eagerly climb aboard, Miranda needing a touch more coaxing. The trio — the Aislings — set off on a magical voyage that brings a host of mythic beings aboard. Harpies seize control of the galley, followed by a Manticore, a Sphinx, a Minotaur, and a dryad rooted in a tree. Trouble arises when Aisling becomes fixated on obtaining tangible proof for Bilgewallow and his followers, and he even insists on taking aboard the dangerous Medusa, with dire consequences for one crew member. Yet, aided by his daughters and Medusa, he regains his purpose and steadiness, and all aboard must unite against the malevolent trolls who pursue them.

The story begins with Bernard, a laicised Catholic priest, escorting his unwilling father Jack to Hawaii at the request of his aunt Ursula, who is dying of cancer. On the day after arrival, Jack is hit by a car and sent to hospital. Bernard spends much time travelling between Jack's bedside and Ursula's nursing home, and through this, gets the opportunity to discover their past. Ursula, always portrayed as the selfish black sheep, had been sexually abused as a child by her oldest brother Sean, who was venerated as a hero by the family for his death in the war. Ursula explains to Bernard that the experience ruined her marriage and her life. She wants Jack's apology for Jack knew of the abuse but kept silent. In the midst of this, Bernard strikes up a tentative relationship with Yolande Miller, the driver of the car that hit his father. Bernard's gradual sexual awakening parallels Ursula's struggle with her illness. The narrative switches between third-person prose, Bernard's diary, a long letter from Bernard to Yolande, and postcards and notes sent from Hawaii by various characters encountered by Bernard and Jack on the plane journey from England, concluding with a letter from Yolande to Bernard. fr:Nouvelles du paradis

"The Owl and the Pussycat" features four anthropomorphic animals – an owl, a cat, a pig, and a turkey – and tells the story of the love between the title characters who marry in the land "where the Bong-tree grows". The Owl and the Pussycat set out to sea in a pea green boat with honey and "plenty of money" wrapped in a five pound note. The Owl serenades the Pussycat while gazing at the stars and strumming on a small guitar. He describes her as beautiful. The Pussycat responds by describing the Owl as an "elegant fowl" and compliments him on his singing. She urges they marry but they don't have a ring. They sail away for a year and a day to a land where Bong-trees grow and discover a pig with a ring in his nose in a wood. They buy the ring for a shilling and are married the next day by a turkey. They dine on mince and quince using a runcible spoon, then dance hand-in-hand on the sand in the moonlight. Portions of an unfinished sequel, "The Children of the Owl and the Pussycat", were first published posthumously in 1938.

Artemis Fowl enlists Mulch Diggums, a dwarf, to help him steal a tiara for a laser he’s constructing. Previously, a band of dwarfs under Sergei the Significant, disguising themselves as a circus troupe, has already taken the tiara. Their plan is to peddle it to a jewelry fence. While Captain Holly Short is taking a break pending a tribunal after the Fowl Manor Incident, Foaly informs her that Mulch Diggums’s stolen helmet has alerted the LEP to Artemis Fowl. Holly immediately flies to Ireland to confront the dwarfs. Once she has cataloged all the dwarfs in Sergei’s crew, she pursues Artemis and Mulch. The pair soon separate, with Artemis vowing to compensate Mulch with a check for the tiara. Holly intensifies her pursuit, demanding the tiara and the LEP helmet from Artemis. Artemis hands over the helmet but keeps the tiara for the moment. Holly compels him to relinquish the tiara, which he then does. In a later twist, it’s revealed that Artemis swapped the real gemstone in the tiara with a counterfeit. He then gives the genuine gem to his mother, a keepsake tied to Artemis’s father—the gem’s color reminding her of his eyes.

The novel is set in present-day [West Virginia]. The protagonist is Summer, an orphaned child who has been passed from one apathetic relative to another. At age six, she meets her Aunt May and Uncle Ob. The kindly old couple notices that, although Summer is not mistreated, she is virtually ignored by her caretakers and decide to take Summer home to their rickety trailer home in the hills of the Appalachian mountains. Summer thrives under their care, feeling that she finally has a home. Six years after Summer moves in, Aunt May dies suddenly in the garden. Summer must cope with her own grief while worrying about Uncle Ob, who is overwhelmed by the thought of living without his beloved wife. Uncle Ob decides to try contacting May's spirit, after he experiences the sensation that she has tried to communicate with him. He is assisted in this endeavor by Cletus Underwood, a classmate of Summer's, who provides information on a supposed spirit medium of some renown. Summer views his ideas with some skepticism, but is willing to try anything that might alleviate her uncle's sorrow. The three take a roadtrip to meet with the medium, only to discover that she had recently died. Uncle Ob is initially crushed by this news, and Summer fears that this disappointment was the last blow to his will to live. However, on the return trip, Uncle Ob suddenly snaps out of his depression, deciding to continue living on for Summer's sake.

This third novel of Updike's Rabbit series examines the life of Harry "Rabbit" Angstrom, a one-time high school basketball star, who has reached a paunchy middle-age without relocating from Brewer, Pennsylvania, the poor, fictional city of his birth. Harry and Janice, his wife of twenty-two years, live comfortably, having inherited her late father's Toyota dealership. He is indeed rich, but Harry's persistent problems — his wife's drinking, his troubled son's schemes, his libido, and spectres from his past — complicate life. Having achieved a lifestyle that would have embarrassed his working-class parents, Harry is not greedy, but neither is he ever quite satisfied. Harry has become somewhat enamored of a country-club friend's young wife. He also has to deal with the indecision and irresponsibility of Nelson, his son, who is a student at Kent State University. Throughout the book, Harry wonders about his former lover Ruth, and whether she had ever given birth to their child.

Five centuries after the conclusion of Earthfall, there is only one original colonist from Harmony: Shedemei, who now wears the Cloak of the Starmaster (a device that links her to the Oversoul). After hundreds of years, the descendants of Nafai and Elemak have built cities and towns - yet never forgetting the enmity between the two brothers. After hundreds of years, the Oversoul still has not achieved its original purpose: to find the Keeper of Earth, the central intelligence that alone can repair the Oversoul's damaged counterpart at Harmony. But now, the Keeper has once again begun to spread its influence. Heeding the dreams below, Shedemei has decided to return to Earth. The last book in the Homecoming saga marks a departure from the style and storyline of the previous four. All of the characters from the previous novels (except Shedemei) are long dead. The central conflict between Nafai and Elemak is represented in their descendants, but takes a back seat in this book. The focus is on the struggles within the descendants of those who followed Nafai.
