The king of Darakemba (an empire founded by the Nafaris), his children, and his advisers, along with the high priest of Darakemba, his children, and his converts, provide the main actions in the story.

The book is narrated from a distance by Arturo B. (probably Belano, Bolaño's frequent stand-in) and tells the story of Alberto Ruiz-Tagle, an aviator who exploits the 1973 Chilean coup d'état to launch his own version of the New Chilean Poetry: a multi-media enterprise involving sky-writing, torture, photography, murder, and verse. The narrator first encounters him in a college poetry workshop, where Ruiz-Tagle only has eyes for the beautiful Garmendia twins, Veronica and Angelica. As the novel progresses it becomes clear that Ruiz-Tagle is far more and far less than a mere poet through progressively darker and ironic twists and turns. The next sighting comes as the narrator stands in prison camp for political undesirables, gazing up at a WWII Messerchmitt skywriting over the Andes. The aviator is none other than Ruiz-Tagle, now serving in the Chilean force under his actual name, Carlos Wieder, and writing nationalist slogans in the sky. The narrator becomes obsessed with Ruiz-Tagle, suspecting that he is behind every evil act in Pinochet’s regime. After his release the narrator struggles to survive and make sense of his situation, but his destiny is eventually reconnected with that of Ruiz-Tagle/Wieder when a Chilean private detective seeks his help in tracking Wieder down by trying to identify the airforce pilot's hand behind various articles printed in neo-fascist publications.

From the realms of Dahomey to Mississippi’s slaveholding chaos, Flashman’s misbegotten gamble with Disraeli and Bentinck haunts him. His yearning for a Commons seat blows up into a grim stint in the West African slave trade, under the command of the erratic Captain John Charity Spring, a boastful Latin-speaker with a volatile temper. After a U.S. Navy capture, Flashman must talk his way out of confinement, inaugurating a long pattern of aliases in America. A sojourn in Washington, D.C., culminates in a troubling encounter with a young Abraham Lincoln, and, after slipping free from his naval guardians in New Orleans, he hides in a bordello presided over by Susie Willinck, a capricious madam. Re-arrest follows, this time by operators of the Underground Railroad. A journey upriver aboard a fugitive’s craft goes wrong again, and Flashman’s fate shifts toward life as a slave driver on a plantation, with danger of becoming a slave himself and of fleeing vigilantes who hunt him. Ultimately he returns to New Orleans to fall once more under Spring’s grasp. The tale continues in Flashman and the Redskins. Fraser, the editor, contends that Cassy and Flashman’s Ohio River flight inspired Uncle Tom’s Cabin, albeit with the protagonists’ names altered and the focus shifted to Cassy’s slave experience rather than Flashman’s. This echoes Flashman’s later boast that his Royal Flash adventures underpinned The Prisoner of Zenda.

In New York, journalist Blair Maynard, recently divorced, pursues a story about the mysterious vanishing of yachts and small boats across the Caribbean, aiming to challenge Bermuda Triangle theories. He has weekend custody of his preteen son, Justin, and decides to blend a vacation with investigation, bringing Justin along. Their journey departs from Miami aboard a flight to the Turks and Caicos archipelago, but a fishing excursion soon derails when a band of pirates seizes them. The pirates, astonishingly, have operated undetected since the establishment of their enclave by Jean-David Nau, formerly known as the infamous buccaneer L’Olonnais in 1671 (though historical records show L’Olonnais died four years earlier). They live under a rough, constitution-like system—the Covenant—that imposes brutal but functional order. The pirates abduct and raise any children they capture to sustain the colony, while executing anyone over thirteen. Before long, Justin is effectively brainwashed and groomed to lead the pirate crew, horrifying Maynard. Attempts at escape recur, and a chance sighting of the US Coast Guard cutter New Hope finally draws attention to their plight. The pirates assault the vessel, seize it, and Maynard wields a machine gun onboard to kill many of the attackers, securing freedom for himself and Justin.

The story starts with 10 year old Liza Barton accidentally shooting and killing her mother and shooting and injuring her stepfather Ted. She is acquitted of the crime and is later adopted by some distant relatives. Twenty-four years later, the story picks up with Liza determined to bury her past. She has changed her name to Celia Foster and married Alex Nolan after her first husband Larry's death. Alex, not aware of Celia's past, gifts her with a surprise birthday present—the keys to her own parents' home in a neighboring town Mendham. Alex, Celia and her 4 year old son, Jack, move into the home to find that it has been vandalized. Unsure of how Alex would react to her past, Celia decides to hide it from him for some more time. Flashes of the night her mom died come back to Celia as she sets out to find out more about what really happened that night. She discreetly tries to find information about her father's accident that led to his death a year before her mother's death. One by one, a few of the older residents of the town are murdered and some of the evidence leads to Celia being suspected. Celia finds her own life in danger, as the pursuit of the murderer's identity picks up pace.

The novel is set in a post-human future solar system. Jean le Flambeur is a legendary thief who has been imprisoned in a Dilemma Prison, a virtual jail of the Sobornost created by the Archons, themselves the creation of the Engineer-of-Souls. During an unsuccessful encounter with the All-Defector, he is sprung from his prison in the Neptunian Trojan belt by Mieli, a warrior from the Oort cloud, and taken to her ship, Perhonen. There, he finds out that his freedom comes at a price: he must return to his old criminal ways to steal something for Mieli's employer, the pellegrini. First, however, he has to retrieve his previous memories, which he had meticulously hidden in the Oubliette, one of the Moving Cities of Mars. In the Oubliette, Isidore Beautrelet is unraveling a gogol piracy case, brought to his attention by his tzaddik mentor, The Gentleman. Isidore is an architecture student and only ten Martian years old, but he has accumulated a reputation as a sharp detective. This case, however, exposes him to unwanted fame, which is extremely gauche in polite Oubliette society, where even people who share a flat remain discreetly behind a cloud of gevulot to avoid the faux pas of violating each other's privacy. Notoriety, however, brought him to the attention of a new client, the millenniaire Christian Unruh. Unruh is about to host a party to commemorate his early entry into Quiet, but a note has appeared under impossible circumstances in his mansion, which Unruh asks Isidore to investigate. The note announces an unlikely gate-crasher to the party: Jean le Flambeur.

The Romans have once again been humiliated by the Gauls. Felonius Caucus, right hand man of Centurion Nebulus Nimbus, head of the fortified camp of Totorum, suggests a Big Fight. This is a Gallic tradition where two Gallic chiefs fight and the winner becomes leader of both tribes. To fight Vitalstatistix, chief of Asterix’s tribe, the Romans enlist a Gallo-Roman Chief, Cassius Ceramix of Linoleum. Vitalstatistix would surely win with Getafix’ magic potion of invincibility, but the Romans plan to dispose of the druid long beforehand. In an effort to rescue him, Obelix accidentally puts Getafix out of action with a menhir, the impact of which causes amnesia and insanity. Cassius Ceramix' challenge therefore comes at the worst possible moment, and Asterix and Vitalstatistix desperately attempt to restore Getafix’s mind by consulting Psychoanalytix (original French name is Amnesix), a druid who specializes in mental disorders. But during an explanation of the cause of the problem, Obelix decides to physically demonstrate with a menhir, leaving Psychoanalytix in the same state. As the two crazed druids concoct a number of skin-coloring magic potions, Asterix tries to bring Vitalstatistix into good physical shape for the upcoming fight. Meanwhile the Romans plan to arrest Cassius after the Fight to stop him becoming too powerful. As the fight begins, Getafix accidentally makes a potion which restores his mind, despite Obelix throwing another menhir at him to try curing him, and quickly proceeds to brew a supply of magic potion. Cassius Ceramix looks sure to win, but Getafix' recovery gives Vitalstatistix the courage to win despite not having any potion. After another tussle with the Romans, who do not accept this victory, and Cassius Ceramix himself getting "menhired", Vitalstatistix returns home victorious to the inevitable feast. Psychoanalytix returns to business despite his current state, but he remains professionally successful (a wry comment on the state of psychiatry).

Gracie possesses the uncanny ability to sense looming danger—and sometimes to perceive events that have already occurred. She once pleaded with her mother to cancel a trip that culminated in her death after a truck delivering oranges struck her vehicle. Now living with her aunt Shay in Washington, Gracie’s visions increasingly involve her closest friend, Emily. Reluctant to have psychic powers at all, Gracie feels compelled to use every glimpse as a clue when Emily vanishes and a mystery unfolds. The core issue with Gracie’s gift is its ambiguity: visions blur the line between past and present, and she frequently misreads what she sees. With help from her cousin Diego, she pursues the clues her visions provide in hopes of locating Emily. After several missteps and a period of digging, Gracie discovers Emily’s trail only to be captured by the kidnapper. Confined within a dark, guarded house, Gracie begins to witness the kidnapper’s troubled childhood—and that of his relatives—through relentless visions. The kidnapper is a deranged man who regrets not saving his ailing sister Nell. Enraged, his father and most of his siblings perish in a blaze he setting off, including his cherished sister Lizbet. Disillusioned, the madman resolves to end things as he intends to die alongside his supposed foster family."

Arturo B. serves as a distant narrator, probably standing in for Bolaño’s recurring alter ego Belano, and the tale centers on Alberto Ruiz-Tagle, a pilot who hijacks the 1973 Chilean coup to push his own variant of New Chilean Poetry. His venture is a multimedia venture—skywriting, torture, photography, murder, and verse all fused together. In a college poetry workshop, Ruiz-Tagle initially catches the narrator’s attention only with his fixation on the stunning Garmendia twins, Veronica and Angelica. As the narrative unfolds, it becomes evident that Ruiz-Tagle embodies far more than a conventional poet, revealing darker, more ironic dimensions. The next glimpse occurs when the narrator is jailed in a political detention camp, looking up at a WWII Messerschmitt carving messages into the sky above the Andes. That aviator is none other than Ruiz-Tagle, now operating under his real name, Carlos Wieder, serving in the Chilean armed forces and inscribing nationalist slogans in the heavens. An obsession sprouts in the narrator, who grows convinced that Ruiz-Tagle/Wieder is the mastermind behind every atrocity of Pinochet’s regime. Upon release, the narrator fights to endure and to interpret his circumstances, yet his fate eventually intertwines again with Wieder’s when a Chilean private eye seeks him out. The detective hopes to locate Wieder by tracing the air force pilot’s signature behind a series of pieces appearing in neo-fascist publications.

The book follows the childhood memories of the narrator, illustrating various experiences in his life: fishing on the beach at dawn; his grandparents and how one grandfather went mad; a hunchback great-uncle; the betrayal of children by adults; fear of the unknown; an unwanted pregnancy, violence, possibly even murder. The general story is paralleled with the traditional story of the Mr. Punch show, 'The oldest, the wisest play'. The narrator is first introduced to Mr. Punch when fishing with his grandfather, but encounters it, and a mysterious 'professor' (Punch & Judy man), during various other activities. The story of Mr. Punch, is that he kills his baby, then his wife Judy and the police officer who comes to arrest him. He outwits a ghost, a crocodile and a doctor, convinces the hangman to be hanged in his place and, at the play's end, even defeats the devil himself. Like many of Gaiman's works, a major theme in this graphic novel is memory and the unreliability of one's own recollections.

Lauren Hartke and her film director husband, Rey Robles, are occupying an isolated house outside New York City. They have a sparse verbal exchange over breakfast before Rey leaves for work. Later that morning, Rey is found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in his first wife's Manhattan apartment. An obituary detailing the frequently ambiguous details of Rey's life ensues, where Rey's age (64) is revealed, along with his history of depression and the fact that Lauren had been Rey's third wife. A bereaved Lauren remains alone in the house against the advice of her friends and relatives. She becomes disconnected from the temporal world and from her own body, experiencing frequent and inexplicable déjà vu. Lauren spends the subsequent hours, days and weeks exploring this disconnection. She practices her trademark 'bodywork'-- aerobic and stretching techniques she has developed to prepare her body for performance pieces. Lauren also integrates a sequence of daily rituals, including chopping firewood and gazing for hours at webcam footage of a road in Kotka, Finland. One morning, Lauren hears a noise coming from the upper floor of the house. She goes upstairs to investigate but finds no one there. Lauren goes upstairs again the next day. This time, she finds a man sitting in one of the bedrooms. The man's appearance varies each time Lauren sees him, but in this first incarnation, he is described as "smallish and fine-boned [resembling] a kid, sandy-haired and roused from deep sleep" (43).

Fire in the Mist is the story of Faia Rissedote, who as the story begins is a shepherd from a small village. Faia returns from tending her sheep to find everyone in her village dead from the plague. In her anguish, she loses control of her magic and destroys the entire village. This act is felt even in the far away town of Ariss, where staff of the university that exists there to train mages travel to the village to see what happened. They find Faia and bring her back to their university. Faia does not fit in there, as she is a much stronger mage but has little control; the other mage students either don't believe in her power or dislike her for being from a humble background. She does meet and sleep with a young mage, which is expressly forbidden as sex is supposed to be harmful to magical talent. A series of murders occur; primarily targeting young mages with potential. The women at the university believe it to be the work of the men, as the murders resemble a much earlier legend which implicated the men. Faia's body is taken over by the spirit of the murderer, who it turns out was actually a woman (and is the same person from the legend) and proceeds to start killing the mages of the university. Faia defeats the murderer by surprising her with the fact that she (the murderer, in Faia's body) is pregnant, and regains her body. She escapes the university, the staff of which still bear a grudge against her, in spite of explanations, and begins to travel.

Audre Lorde’s upbringing unfolds in Harlem as the daughter of Black West Indian parents. Legally blind in childhood, she learns to read before starting school, a fact that provokes anger from the nuns and teachers at her Catholic school. The family endures hardship when their landlord commits suicide rather than continue renting to Black tenants. A later trip to Washington, D.C. exposes them to segregation firsthand through being refused ice cream. At 15, after menarche, Lorde forms a small circle of friendships with non-Black girls at Hunter College High School, known as “The Branded,” and she begins writing poetry, eventually earning the role of literary editor for the school’s arts magazine. After finishing school, she leaves home, sharing a flat with friends connected to Jean, one of The Branded, while also dating Peter, a white boy who abandons her on New Year’s Eve; she becomes pregnant and opts for an abortion. Her early years at Hunter College bring dissatisfaction, prompting a move to Stamford, Connecticut, where she works in a factory under brutal conditions. Following her father’s death, Lorde returns to New York City and enters a relationship with Bea, whom she later hurts by deciding to move to Mexico to escape McCarthyism. In Mexico, she attends university, works as a hospital secretary, and, in Cuernavaca, encounters numerous independent women—many of them lesbians—and begins a relationship with one named Eudora, while working in a library. Back in New York, she delves into the lesbian bar scene, cohabits with Muriel, then with Lynn who comes to live with them but ultimately departs abruptly, taking their money. Eventually, Lorde forms a bond with Afrekete, a mother who ultimately leaves to care for her child. The narrative closes with a tribute to Lorde’s mother.

Guy Openshaw, 44, lies on his deathbed as cancer tightens its grip. In his London flat, he cannot endure the flood of visitors who stop by, a burden on his waning strength. His wife, Gertrude, greets these callers—the same guests who once formed a lively after-hours circle for drinks and conversation. They leaned on Guy for both counsel and money, and with his illness approaching, the group begins to crack apart. Among the visitors is Tim Reede, a youngish, struggling artist who cannot sell his work and feels adrift without Guy’s backing. Tim has a girlfriend, Daisy, whose punk style, brash talk, and sailorlike drinking make them a matching pair of starving outcasts. After Guy dies, Daisy urges Tim to seek money from Gertrude, but she turns the encounter into something else: she questions his craft and reveals a wish to support him in other ways, offering him access to her country home in the French countryside. The romance between Tim and Gertrude—culminating in their marriage—constitutes the novel’s core, offering a sharp lens on class dynamics and the trope of a younger man with an older woman. Tim emerges as both flawed and admirable: capable of kindness, he endures the slings and arrows of Gertrude’s circle, which largely target him for what he can provide or what he represents, yet his relationship with Gertrude remains intact. While some of Gertrude’s friends show genuine concern, most are driven by love for her or by what she might yield from Guy’s inheritance. The narrative is rich with treachery and coincidence, yet Murdoch tempers these elements with consequences that unfold at a natural pace, letting time reveal their outcomes.

It is summer in Lake Eden, Minnesota and everyone is very excited with the family reunion that Hannah's partner Lisa has prepared coming up shortly. Lisa's Uncle Gus has made an unexpected return after a 30 year absence with expensive jewelry, clothes and a new car. Uncle Gus is immediately the center of attention at the reunion with no doubt. It is up to Hannah Swensen, the owner of The Cookie Jar bakery, to provide the treats. Hannah bakes one of her specialties, her carrot cake which is a big hit. Gus is impressed with Hannah's cake and asks her for another platter, but the next day as the pictures for the family reunion are being taken, everyone notices that there is one person missing. As Hannah goes out to search for Gus, she finds him over by the bar at the pavilion with two pieces of Hannah's carrot cake by his side, dead stabbed with an ice pick! It is up to Hannah to solve the mystery of the murder. It seems like Grandpa Jack might be blamed for killing Gus because of his Alzheimer's. Hannah thinks that he is not responsible for the murder, so she tries to prove that he is innocent. The book also has recipes.

The story follows the overlapping lives of three high school seniors, with the chapters alternating between their different points of view. Jason Carrillo, the jock, finds himself questioning his heterosexuality and decides to attend a meeting for gay youth. He does not expect to see his classmates Kyle Meeks and Nelson Glassman at the meeting. Afterwards, Kyle, the mostly-closeted swimmer, decides to help tutor Jason in math. It is revealed that Kyle has had a crush on Jason for the past three years of high school. They bond over their shared feelings towards coming out and their families. Which leads them to become more than friends.' Nelson, the flamboyant class clown, has conflicting feelings towards Kyle and their relationship. He's very close to his mother who claims to have always known about his homosexuality, but rarely sees his father. After getting into an argument with Kyle, he decides to hook up with an online stranger named Brick. He has sex for the first time, and fears he has contracted HIV. He becomes friends with HIV-positive Jeremy, and they begin a relationship.

A voyage begins with a family clinging to the ship’s hold amid a devastating gale. When the vessel strikes a reef, the crew evacuates into a lifeboat, leaving the family behind. Searches for any sign of the crew prove futile. Although the storm subsides and night passes, the ship remains visible only as the family nears a tropical island. Remarkably, the cargo endures: livestock, dogs, gunpowder and arms, carpentry tools, books, a dismantled pinnace, and provisions all survive the catastrophe. In response, the family fashions a raft, secures the most valuable supplies and the animals, and sets off toward shore, where they establish a provisional shelter. In the ensuing weeks, they repeatedly return to the wreck to clear the hold and salvage rigging, planks, and sails. A modest settlement takes shape on the island, and the hull of the ship eventually fractures in another storm and is lost to the sea. The middle portion of the novel unfolds through a sequence of vignettes spanning several years. The father and his elder sons venture beyond their camp to survey different parts of the island, encounter a variety of seemingly improbable flora and fauna, and construct a substantial treehouse that doubles as a library. Using the timber and other local resources, they also assemble a collection of mechanical devices. At last, while circumnavigating the island by the pinnace, they spot a European family concealing themselves from pirates. The siblings come to adopt the family’s daughter, who initially appears as a boy, and the daughter’s father returns later on a rescue mission, reestablishing contact with the outside world for the survivors who have endured isolation on the island.

When Carl's mother, Kerry, disappears, he and his brother, Harley, are sent to Wattle Beach to live with their aunt Beryl. During his stay at Wattle Beach, Carl works in a barge, an old colleague of Carl's grandfather. Carl does not know that his grandfather was involved in an accident that killed Skips 8-year-old son, Graham. Carl is initially withdrawn; he does not convey his worries about his missing mother, nor the anxiety that he feels over his rebellious younger brother, who is constantly in centrelink. However, during the course of the novel he learns to "open up" and share his feelings with those who care about him. In the end, it is discovered that Kerry Matt died in a bus accident when she was trying to get home to her children, Sarah, Harley and Carl. Once this is unearthed,Carl returns home to find that Aunt Beryl has run off in true Matt spirit to join her boyfriend, Bruce. Because Carl has nowhere else to stay, Joy Duncan invites him to come and live with them at Wiseman's Cove with his brother, Harley, who has already claimed the Duncans as his surrogate family. Their sister Sarah left them and flew to another country to get a chance at her own life.

Geoffrey Tempest, a penniless, famished writer, wanders through a life of near homelessness and unpaid rent, barely managing to light his room. Then three letters arrive, each shifting his fate in distinct ways. One, from an Australian friend who has risen financially, promises to set him up with a contact who could pull him from poverty. Another, from a solicitor, announces an unexpected fortune left by a dead relative. The third is an introduction from Lucio, a foreign nobleman who becomes Tempest’s companion and mentor in how to wield wealth. With this guidance, Tempest’s prospects brighten, yet he remains ignorant of Lucio’s true identity as the Devil in earthly disguise, despite warnings from others along the way. As the wealth accumulates, so does misery, culminating in Tempest’s realization of Lucio’s nature. He eventually rejects evil and reenters society destitute but spiritually hopeful, eager for a chance to purify his soul. While Tempest’s fall and eventual redemption frame the narrative, Lucio often stands as the more central figure, to the point that he eclipses Tempest in significance. The work’s title and much of its philosophical thrust hinge on Satan’s profound longing for salvation. Its principal contribution to Faustian lore lies in the provocative idea that, above all others, Satan alone clings to belief in the Gospel—yet is barred from partaking in it.

The novel follows the relationship between Irishwoman Adelia "Dee" Cunnane and American Travis Grant. As the story begins, the young and penniless Dee emigrates to the United States to live with her uncle, Paddy, who works on a large horse farm. Dee's love for animals is evident, and she is given a job working alongside her uncle. Dee has a fiery temper and often argues with Travis, the wealthy farm owner; many of their arguments lead to passionate embraces. Travis later rescues Dee from an attempted rape. When Paddy suffers a heart attack, he becomes very concerned about his mortality and Dee's future. He becomes overwrought and insists that Travis take care of Dee. After privately agreeing to a temporary marriage of convenience, Travis and Dee exchange vows in Paddy's hospital room. As the story progresses, the protagonists become increasingly unhappy, with neither willing to admit their love for the other. Although still unwilling to vocalize their feelings, Dee and Travis appear more confident in their relationship after they finally consummate their marriage. Soon, however, Dee's insecurities are exploited by Travis's sophisticated former girlfriend, Margot, who has returned to the area to win him back. Dee runs away. Travis follows, and the two confess their love and resolve to make their marriage work.

Seventeen-year-old Peter Collins McPhee, dubbed P.C. for his gaming passion, is summoned by his Uncle Cliff to Australia to unravel a mystery. When a young Aboriginal girl named Maruul learns that her brother—Maruul’s sibling—has vanished while seeking the tribe’s legendary treasure, she recalls a piercing screech and the sudden appearance of a boat just as his disappearance occurred. P.C. soon uncovers a predator beneath the reef, a creature that stalks the depths and ends up killing Uncle Cliff. Following this, the two youths consult Wally Wallygong, an Aboriginal shopkeeper who makes sense of the riddle. Returning to the reef’s site, they stage a simulated snake attack to lure the danger. A passing ship, appearing out of nowhere, takes them aboard. Their escape attempt nearly ends in disaster. It is revealed that the vessel’s captain—an on-board geologist—has long possessed the treasure, an intricately carved opal wall, and has been using a mechanical screech to summon the creature to strike. He also intends to destroy the treasure itself. P.C. manipulates the monster into feasting on the captain, while Maruul makes it back to her village with the prize. In the end, the community uses the treasure to acquire essential supplies they’ve needed for a long time.

The narrative begins in 54 BC, during Caesar’s peak Gallic campaigns, right after his invasion of Britannia. The opening portion surveys the tail end of his Gallic conquests, while the latter portion concentrates on Rome’s mounting anxiety over his aims, the hostile opposition of the conservative boni faction, and the decisive sequence that leads to Caesar crossing the Rubicon, marching into Italy, and triumphing in the Civil War. Among the key events are Caesar’s homeward return from Britannia, narrowly surviving the encounter at Gergovia, and a monumental triumph at Alesia, where he encircled the citadel, repelled a relief force, and compelled Vercingetorix to surrender. The narrative also covers the final subjugation of Gallic resistance at Uxellodunum, the deaths of Julia and Marcus Licinius Crassus, and Caesar’s rift with Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus that precipitates the unraveling of the First Triumvirate. It further recounts his unsuccessful efforts to secure re-election as consul, the outbreak of Civil War, and the battles of Dyrrhachium and Pharsalus. Pompey’s flight to Ptolemaic Egypt and his subsequent murder there mark the fall of the boni leadership, completing the book’s sweep through Caesar’s revolutionary trajectory.

Robert Lomax, a young Englishman, post–National Service opts to work on a plantation in British Malaya. While there, he privately experiments with a one-year detour into painting as a fresh career. Seeking inspiration for his canvases, Lomax travels to Hong Kong and checks into the Nam Kok Hotel. Initially unaware that the establishment operates as an informal brothel catering largely to British and American sailors, he nonetheless finds its atmosphere appealing and a rich source of material for his art. He quickly befriends many of the hotel’s bargirls, but his fascination centers on the archetype of the “hooker with a heart of gold”—Suzie Wong. Wong has introduced herself as Wong Mee-ling, a wealthy virgin whose father owns five houses and possesses more cars than she can count, and at first she pretends not to recognize Lomax at the hotel. Lomax had resolved not to sleep with any of the women there, intending to live with them for an extended period without straining their relationships. Yet it becomes clear that Suzie Wong is drawn to him not merely as a client but as a genuine sweetheart. Although Wong at one point becomes the kept woman of two other men, and Lomax briefly finds himself attracted to a young British nurse, their paths diverge and then converge once more, culminating in a joyful reunion and a hopeful, happy ending for the couple.

Jack Cull (a pun on the word "jackal") finds himself in a bizarre location called "Hell". A huge sphere with a sun in the center, Hell's population consists of deceased humans and demons; the humans have the same mind and body as when they died, there is no disease or famine, and deaths are reversed within hours. Earthquakes are frequent occurrences. Humans have taken control of Hell, and they have replaced the traditional inscription (as imagined by Dante), "Abandon all hope..." (written in Italian) with a new one: "Do not abandon hope" (written in Hebrew). Cull goes to his workplace, and hears that the mysterious "X", an analogue of Jesus Christ, has been killed by an unruly mob. Along with Phyllis and Fyodor, based on Fyodor Dostoevsky, Jack investigates his death. Travelling into a sewer, they find out that "Hell" is in fact a massive spacecraft, controlled by hyper-moral, ultra-powerful alien beings with the means of capturing many if not most of the souls they come upon, incorporating them in immortal bodies (provided they are fed regularly). However, the capturing of souls is an imperfect process, and many souls are lost to the void. Although the bodies are more or less immortal, there comes a time when the aliens destroy them when they feel the souls have progressed to an acceptable level. Even then, not all of the bodies are destroyed, and some continue on with the spaceship as it travels about the galaxy.

Danger is the name of the game when the Hardys agree to help their pen pal from Greece, Evangelos Pandropolos, search for a priceless, ancient Greek helmet. Years ago, Evan's uncle had loaned it to a Hollywood movie company for use in a silent motion picture, The Persian Glory, for a role in the movie, but the helmet was lost after the movie was done. At Hunt College, where Evan, Frank, Joe and Chet Morton are taking a summer course in film-making, the boys are harassed by Leon Saffel whose harassments get more and more vicious. All the while a gang is trying to force Mr. Hardy to give up his investigations of a national crime syndicate and also trying to find the helmet, which after speaking to Evan's billionaire uncle, may have belonged to King Agamemnon making the helmet even more valuable. The clues that the Hardys unearth keep them on the move-from their college campus to California and finally to Greece. In a sizzling climax, the Hardys, Evan and Chet match wits with their powerful enemies on the island of Corfu.

Princess Taramis of Shadizar promises to bring Conan's lost love Valeria back to life if the Cimmerian will procure two magical items that she hopes will gain her ultimate power, a wizard's gem and a horn that can awaken the dreaming god Dagoth. He undertakes the quest together with his thief partner Malak and Taramis' niece Jehnna and henchman Bombaata. On their journey they are joined by two additional allies whom Conan saves from dire fates; the magician Akiro and the female warrior Zula. At their goal, the castle of the wizard Amon-Rama, Jehnna is kidnapped. Thanks to Akiro's magic she is located in Amon-Rama's lair and a way in is discovered. Inside, Conan is separated from the others and forced to battle a Man-Ape in a hall of mirrors, which he is only able to defeat by destroying the mirrors. He also mortally wounds the wizard, who is hiding behind one of them. Jehnna, who is the only person who can safely handle the wizard's gem, retrieves the first magical item. Afterwards the group beats off an attack by Corinthian soldiers, and continues on to the fortress that holds the horn. It is retrieved at the cost of a battle with its Dagoth-worshipping keepers, whose leader Akiro defeats in a sorcerous duel. Bombaata and Jehnna escape through a tunnel, which the former closes to the others by starting a landslide. Back at Taramis' palace, the queen conducts a ritual to awaken Dagoth that entails the placing of the horn on the forehead of the sleeping deity, and ultimately the sacrifice of Jehnna. Conan, Akiro and Zula, having survived the landslide, interrupt the proceedings. Conan fights and defeats Bombaata while Zula rescues Jehnna. In the absence of the sacrifice, Dagoth is an uncontrollable monster on his revival, eating Taramis and threatening the destruction of everything else. On the advice of Akiro, Conan rips the horn from Dagoth's forehead, and the creature finally falls. In the aftermath, Jehnna succeeds to the throne of Shadazar and takes Zula, Akiro, and Malak as advisors. She offers Conan her hand and a place at her side as king, but the Cimmerian prefers to win his own kingdom.

During the Second Sudanese Civil War, Achak is torn from his family when murahaleen—Arabic for “traveller”—the Arab militia, attack his Dinka village, Marial Bai. In the assault, he loses track of his father and his childhood friends, Moses and William K. Though William K. escapes, Moses is presumed dead. Seeking safety, Achak and his mother take refuge at his aunt’s house, a woman repeatedly described in the book as wearing a yellow dress. Before they can be hidden, they hear the aunt scream, and Achak’s mother goes to investigate; after that moment, she vanishes from his sight forever. To stay hidden, he hides inside a grain bag and later credits divine aid for keeping him silent. Along with a band of other youths known as the “Lost Boys,” he ventures on foot, trudging through extreme peril and hardship toward a refugee camp in Ethiopia. The dream of safety he carries with him is crushed by the camp’s brutal conditions, forcing a subsequent withdrawal to another camp in Kakuma after Mengistu’s fall and soldiers’ gunfire. From there they cross into Kenya, and years later Achak finally relocates to the United States. The narrative unfolds in tandem with the new rounds of hardship he faces in America.

Rapp appears on the scene during a covert operation in Iran, where he uncovers intelligence about an impending terrorist attack aimed at the nation’s capital. Across the Atlantic, Washington, D.C. buzzes with the first day of NBC White House correspondent Anna Reilly. The same day, the terrorists breach the White House through a secret entry, seizing control and taking hostages. In the chaos, the president narrowly escapes a collapse into an unfinished bomb shelter, leaving him effectively trapped. Seizing the moment, the acting commander in chief, the vice president, seeks to polish his political image by yielding to the attackers’ demands, while Rapp conceals his own plan to combat the threat from inside the White House walls. Inside the mansion, Rapp rescues Anna Reilly from a brutal assault, birthing the partnership that will unfold in subsequent novels. As events unfold, a contingent of Navy SEALs infiltrates the White House, neutralizes the terrorists, frees the hostages, and rescues the president. Although the terrorist leader eludes capture by detonating carefully placed explosives, he ultimately flees to South America, where Rapp later locates and kills him.

Freshman Trixie Stone accuses her ex-boyfriend, Jason Underhill, of rape, but the crowd quickly takes Jason’s side, insisting their encounter was consensual. As the drama unfolds, Trixie’s parents—Daniel, a gentle, background-bruised comic-artist, and Laura, a college professor who carries on with one of her students—become entangled in the affair. Jason, whom many believed ruined, leaps from a bridge; what begins as an apparent suicide soon shifts to suspicion of Trixie’s involvement. To escape, Trixie flees to Alaska’s Yup’ik region—the place where her father grew up—and Daniel and Laura chase after her. In the book’s final turn, Laura admits to Daniel that she was present when Jason died. On the bridge, Jason, inebriated, lunges toward Laura, mistaking her for Trixie. Laura shoves him away, but he clings to the edge, and she hesitates before reaching for his hand and ultimately letting go, thereby exposing Laura’s guilt and Trixie’s innocence. The closing chapter features Daniel’s comic, The Tenth Circle, which depicts a father rescuing his daughter from hell and reuniting with her, mirroring the overarching narrative and its subplots. Throughout, Daniel’s latest graphic interweaves with the main storyline, drawing a parallel to his own life.

Opening with a prologue set at the 2009 FIRST Championship in Atlanta, the narrative captures the electrifying atmosphere there. It then moves backward to the January 2009 kickoff, detailing Dean Kamen’s founding of FIRST. The focus then shifts to the history of team 1717 and the Dos Pueblos Engineering Academy, the program they belong to. The account continues by tracing the 2009 team through a six-week build season, highlighting challenges ranging from mechanical failures to a spell of illness. A dedicated chapter spotlights team 217, the ThunderChickens, who strive for robot construction with military-grade precision, and team 395, 2TrainRobotics, whose students confront issues stemming from their position in a poor inner-city environment, as well as team 67, Heroes of Tomorrow. After the build, 1717 competes at two regional events, Los Angeles and Sacramento; they fall in the finals in Los Angeles but go undefeated in Sacramento, culminating in a victory there. The season concludes with 1717 at the FIRST Championship, where they are edged out in the division finals by a heavily favored rival.

Remy is an eighteen year old girl who is about to leave for college. Her father, a musician, had died before she was born. Before he died, he left a short song called "This Lullaby," which is now extremely popular. Remy's mother is getting married for the fifth time, with a car salesman. Consequently, love is something that Remy doesn't believe exists. In the past, she's been in many relationships with people she doesn't really care about, and they never last long. One day, she randomly meets Dexter. He claims to feel a connection with her the second he saw her. He is messy and a musician, two of her least favorite traits. But he is persistent. She slowly finds herself falling for him. She doesn't want to care about him, but somehow she just can't bring herself to get rid of him. Eventually they start dating and she is surprised by how open and honest and caring he is. When Dexter overhears Remy saying that she only wants him to be a summer fling, they break up. Remy begins to date another guy, but she finds herself always thinking about Dexter. Meanwhile, her brother is getting engaged, her mother's new husband is cheating, and her friends are all having problems of their own. But in the end, Remy realizes that she truly does love Dexter, and they get back together.

This story begins as Ender is made the commander of Dragon Army at Battle School, an institution designed to make young children into military commanders to fight in the next interstellar war against an unspecified enemy. Armies are groups of students that fight mock battles in the Battle Room, a null gravity environment, and are subdivided into squads known as "toons". Due to Ender's genius in leadership, Dragon Army goes on to dominate the competition, despite the teachers' attempts to put obstacles in their way. After his nineteenth consecutive victory, Ender is told that his Army is being broken up and his toon leaders promoted to be commanders in their turn, while he is being transferred to Command School for the next stage of his education. Here, a veteran named Mazer Rackham tutors him in the use of a space battle simulator. Eventually, many of his former toon leaders are brought along to serve under him once more. Once they are familiar with the simulator, they begin to fight a series of what Mazer tells them are mock battles against a computer-controlled enemy. Ender's team wins again and again, finally destroying a planet that the enemy fleet seems to be protecting. Once the battle is over, Mazer tells an exhausted Ender that all of the battles were in fact real, the children's commands having been relayed to the actual fleet, and that he just destroyed the enemy's home world and ended the war.

The book explores the aftermath of the crucifixion of Jesus through the experiences of the Roman tribune Marcellus Gallio and his Greek slave Demetrius. Prince Gaius, in an effort to rid Rome of Marcellus, banishes Marcellus to the command of the Roman garrison at Minoa, a port city in southern Palestine. In Jerusalem during Passover, Marcellus ends up carrying out the crucifixion of Jesus, but is troubled since he believes Jesus to be innocent of any crime. Marcellus and some other soldiers throw dice to see who will take Jesus' seamless robe. Marcellus wins and asks Demetrius to take care of the robe. Following the crucifixion, Marcellus takes part in a banquet attended by Pontius Pilate. During the banquet, a drunken centurion insists that Marcellus wear Jesus' robe; reluctantly wearing the garment, Marcellus apparently suffers a nervous breakdown and returns to Rome. Sent to Athens to recuperate, Marcellus finally gives in to Demetrius' urging and touches the robe; his mind is subsequently restored. Marcellus, now believing the robe has some sort of innate power, returns to Judea and follows the path Jesus took and meets many people whose lives Jesus had affected. Based upon their experiences first Demetrius and then Marcellus become followers of Jesus. Marcellus then returns to Rome where he must report his experiences to the emperor, Tiberius. Marcellus frees Demetrius who escapes, but later on because of his uncompromising stance regarding his Christian faith both Marcellus and his new wife Diana are executed by the new emperor, Caligula. Marcellus arranges that the robe be given to "The Big Fisherman."

Wolf contends that beauty, as a normative value, is entirely a social construction shaped by patriarchy to uphold its own dominance. In her opening remarks, she outlines an analysis in which she also introduces the concept of an “iron-maiden”—an inherently unattainable beauty ideal used to punish women both physically and psychologically for not meeting or conforming to it. While criticizing the fashion and beauty industries for exploiting women, she argues that the beauty myth permeates every sphere of human activity. She asserts that women must have the freedom to alter or abandon facial and bodily norms without being penalized by an ideology that uses attitudes, economic pressure, and even legal judgments about appearance to undermine them psychologically and politically. According to Wolf, the beauty myth targets women across five domains: work, religion, sexuality, violence, and hunger. In the end, she advocates softening rigid social standards of beauty.

On a honeymoon trip to Tunis with his new wife, the Parisian scholar Michel is struck by tuberculosis. As he recuperates, he rediscovers the joys of living and decides to abandon his past scholarly pursuits in order to seize the present—wanting the layers of learned knowledge to peel away from his mind like a cosmetic, revealing in patches the naked flesh beneath and the authentic self concealed there. Yet this is not the Michel his colleagues recognize, nor the Michel who will be readily accepted by conventional society, and he must mask his newly formed values beneath a veneer of the very attitudes he now despises. Disenchanted with Parisian society, he relocates to a family farm in Normandy, finding happiness there, especially in the company of the young Charles. Nevertheless, he soon returns to the city and to academic life. Michel remains unsettled until his first lecture, where he encounters Ménalque—a longtime provocateur of society who perceives in Michel a kindred torment. He then drifts further south, into the desert, until, as he tells his friends, he becomes lost in a sea of sand. Gide’s tale is rich with prose that vividly renders Michel’s outward voyage and his inner terrain: the African earth, awake after months of immersion, overflowing with water and new sap, laughing in a springtime frenzy whose echo he also senses within himself.

Canyons follows two boys, Coyote Runs (14) and Brennan Cole (15). The narrative initially presents Brennan recounting episodes from his own life, then repeatedly alternates with scenes featuring Coyote Runs. That back-and-forth narrative continues until a pivotal raid: during his first attempt to prove himself as a man within his Apache tribe, Coyote Runs is shot in the head by American soldiers and dies instantly. Nearly two centuries later, Brennan discovers the skull, noticing a bullet lodged in its forehead, and becomes consumed by the find. A mystical connection soon links Brennan’s thoughts to the dead boy’s spirit. Prompted by a conversation with his former biology teacher, Brennan undertakes an arduous sixty-mile journey that spans day and night to haul the skull to the top of a canyon—a place Coyote Runs once called his “medicine place.” After enduring a brutal run, with pursuers on their heels, Brennan returns Coyote Runs’ skull to its sanctified location, thereby breaking the bond and bringing the tale to a close.

In the fourth installment of the bestselling Children of the Lamp series, Djinn twins John and Philippa Gaunt embark on another globe-trotting adventure. As they race against time, they must rescue their mother, Layla Gaunt, from a foretold fate as the Blue Djinn of Babylon, and break the aging curse that binds their father, Edward Gaunt, a consequence of Layla’s own measures to keep the twins safe at home. Their mission expands to thwart a series of mysterious robberies and uncanny hauntings affecting museums around the world. Along their journey with friends, the twins discover a chilling anomaly: an ancient Chinese emperor’s terracotta soldiers have been awakened, and a spell now possesses the warriors with malevolent spirits. With the fate of the world at stake, John and Philippa must uncover the robberies, halt the haunted soldiers, and rescue their parents before time runs out.

A mysterious woman in black pursues Chinese Cinderella, and the tale opens with CC fleeing. After a fall, she ends up in hospital, where she overhears a famed painting, Along The River at Qing Ming, referenced in the ward. Suffering sudden, unpredictable blackouts, CC is tormented by dreams—vivid, strange, yet oddly familiar. An adventure unfolds, weaving threads of friendship, wealth and poverty, eunuchs, and an emperor who adored art. The narrative transports CC eight centuries back, to the Song Dynasty, as she drifts between wakefulness and slumber. Following another collapse, she is carried to medical care once more. As her consciousness ebbs and flows, these dreams persist, haunting her with their uncanny resonance. Thus begins CC’s emotional voyage back to a life of privilege imagined from a distant era. In her present, she is the daughter of a powerful, prosperous man, yet she finds herself drawn to a poor orphan boy who possesses a remarkable gift for capturing nature’s beauty. As their bond grows, art and tender love begin to clash with the stubborn, stratified codes of Chinese society.

Oakington is one of the lesser-known public schools in England, and Dr Roseveare, its headmaster, has been trying hard for seven years to improve its reputation. When, in the winter term of 1927-1928, one of the pupils is killed in his sleep by an old gas fitting falling down from the ceiling he contacts Colin Revell, an Old Boy, to discreetly investigate the matter. Not entirely convinced that there was no foul play involved but unable to pin down a motive on anyone, Revell leaves again after a few weeks, and most of the evidence is destroyed by the installation of electricity in the whole building. A few months later Revell is shocked to learn that the deceased boy's brother has also died under mysterious circumstances—he seems to have jumped into the school's indoor swimming pool late at night after the water had been drained—and travels to Oakington of his own accord. Now it turns out that the closest relative of the two brothers, who have been orphans for years, is actually a teacher at Oakington, and that he stands to inherit a small fortune. At the same time Revell falls in love with that teacher's beautiful young wife.

The year is 1985, and much of the action unfolds around the Russian River north of San Francisco. Bohemian Grove hosts a three-week retreat where successful businessmen from across the globe gather for male-bonding rituals. Downriver, Wimminwood—a lesbian music and arts festival—stirs trouble in the relationship between DeDe Halcyon-Day and D’orothea Wilson. Returning to the scene are Mary Ann Singleton, wrestling with balancing her duties as a local talk-show host, wife to Brian, and mother to Shawna—the daughter she cares for at Connie’s bequest on her deathbed; Michael Tolliver, the openly gay, romantically inclined longtime friend who has tested HIV-positive and is on AZT to shield his immune system; and Anna Madrigal, the transgender landlady who tends to her tenants at 28 Barbary Lane atop Russian Hill while striving to safeguard the lane’s historic wooden steps. Among the newcomers are Thack Sweeney, who encounters Michael during a guided Alcatraz tour, and Wren Douglas, a plus-size model whose influential self-help volume offers encouragement to women battling excess weight. The narrative also extends to a character previously seen in the background: Roger “Booter” Manigault, DeDe’s stepfather and a Bohemian Club member, who wanders into Wimminwood and is seized by one of the festival’s more militant organizers. Adding to the mix is Jed, Brian’s nephew and a college student who skews Reaganite—more interested in Harvard Law and wealth than carefree revelry."

Taylor Rusk stands out as a stellar college quarterback and a cannot-miss prospect for The League. North Texas lands an expansion franchise through undisclosed illicit means, as expected. The Pistols select Rusk with the first overall draft pick, embarking on a five-year mission to build a championship team with Rusk at its core. Yet he detects the corruption and refuses to be exploited. Guided by his former college coach and mentored by veteran players from the old league, Rusk plays by The League’s rules until he decides to strike a bold blow to dismantle the system. Betrayal shadows his path: a fellow player with a talent for scams ascends to become the Pistols’ general manager and ultimately betrays him, while another teammate endures a catastrophic knee injury that later turns darkly tragic. The botched surgery leaves him discarded; driven by steroid-fueled rage, he murders his family and ends his own life. Half a decade passes, and the Texas Pistols rise as world champions, but Rusk’s celebration is cut short. He must rescue the life of another person he loves—the mother of his child—before they can claim victory. In the end, the two of them seize control of the Pistols together.

The story begins in Santa Barbara, California. Travis Cornell, a former Delta Force operative, feels that his life has grown pointless, and is exploring a canyon near his home when he encounters two genetically engineered creatures that have escaped from a top-secret government lab. One, a golden retriever with extraordinarily enhanced intelligence, befriends Travis; the other, a terrifying creature known as the Outsider, appears to be trying to kill the dog. After eluding the Outsider, Travis takes the dog home and names him Einstein. Meanwhile, Nora Devon, an introverted young woman, whose abusive aunt recently has died, is attacked in her home by a man who attempts to rape her. Travis and Einstein intervene and the three quickly form a tight bond. Travis, Nora, and Einstein soon find themselves on the run not only from the Outsider, but from federal agents determined to track down the lab escapees, and Vince Nasco, a ruthless professional assassin, hired to kill the creatures and eliminate any witnesses he may encounter along the way.

From the hardcover jacket: An invasion of rabbits seems inevitable for Australia. Millions of creatures, now immune to the myxomatosis that had devastated them in the mid-20th century, flood the countryside. With an election looming, Prime Minister Kevin Fitzgerald—nickname Ella among his circle—must take action. The situation is framed as an emergency: the rabbits must be eradicated. Scientists mobilize and experiments commence. The outcomes are catastrophic. Suddenly Australia dominates as the planet’s most formidable power: in rapid succession, America, Russia, and the other major powers hand over their nuclear arsenals; Fitzgerald effectively governs the world. The Commonwealth Government, in an effort to secure lasting peace, enacts a global order in which only limited wars are permitted and conducted under strict Canberra-approved rules. Only two nations may engage in combat at a time, for instance. Yet, as this remarkable era of prosperity surges forward, a minor news brief slips through unnoticed: a rabbit—massive, as large as an Alsatian—shot by a Sunday-school teacher three miles north of Mudgee.

Birthright spans a timeline of nearly 17 millennia, beginning at a very early stage of expansion from Earth and ending with the death of the last humans. In between, it chronicles a slow but (despite some set-backs) steady conquest of the entire galaxy - inhabited by thousands of sentient alien races, which are overpowered and oppressed using whatever tool it takes: economic pressure, diplomatic finesse, or simple military power. Not all chapters deal with mankind's treatment of aliens; some also cover the "internal" politics that result in a development of the growing human empire from a democracy to a monarchy. But the biggest theme is undeniably the search for the elusive quality that allows mankind to overcome all opposition and manage the unique feat of conquering the entire galaxy. It is never clearly defined but manifests perhaps most succinctly when it also results in the failure of an attempt to cross the void between galaxies. Then, after there is no more room for conquest, the only way left is down: internal struggles as well as deep-seated resentment of aliens result in a decline of human power that takes nearly as long as the rise, but is described far less extensively. Somehow, despite whatever enabled humans to achieve total power, they were unable to keep it. Displaying a particular brand of irony, one of the chapters reveals the "literary genre of fiction" as another of mankind's peculiarities, not shared by any alien race.

A merchant family from a small Galician town unfolds the tale, a town that mirrors Drohobycz in numerous ways, much as the writer’s own hometown does. Mythic elements saturate the narrative, conveyed through a visionary, dreamlike style that often features a labyrinth as a recurring motif. Reality itself becomes mythologized, filtered through imagination, artistically warped and enriched with countless allusions to other literary works, great myths, and even more distant realms of experience. Among the work’s most pivotal figures is the Father, who serves not only as the family’s patriarch and the proprietor of a textile stall in the market, but also as a mad experimenter with extraordinary powers—a demiurge straddling life and death, the boundary between the real and the imagined. Yet Schulz’s literary fascination with the Father notwithstanding, Józef emerges as the central figure: the protagonist and, in effect, the narrator. Through this young boy’s eager exploration of the world around him, many of Schulz’s own characteristics become evident.

In the book, Oppenheimer supports the theory that modern humans first emerged in Africa and that modern human behavior emerged in Africa prior to the Out of Africa migration. Oppenheimer writes that there was only one migration out of Africa that contributed to the peopling of the rest of the world. Oppenheimer believes that anatomically modern humans crossed the Red Sea from the Horn of Africa and followed the "southern coastal route" once in Asia. Thus Oppenheimer is opposed to the theory that there was another out of Africa migration using northern route along the Nile and into the Levant as suggested by Lahr and Foley 1994. The book also supports the theory that modern humans were in South Asia during the Toba Castrophe. Oppenheimer uses familiar names to describe genetic lineages. The biblical analogies of Adam and Eve are used to describe the Most recent common ancestors via mitochondrial DNA and the y-chromosome. Other male lineages are described as Cain, Abel and Seth. Mitochondrial DNA haplogroups are frequently described with female names from regions where the haplogroups are common. For example haplogroup M is named Manju as it is frequent in India, and Haplogroup N is named "Nasreen" as it is predominant in Arabia.

The narrative follows the course of a man's life from his schoolboy days to his adulthood. The son of a north German merchant and an Italian artist, Tonio inherited qualities from both sides of his family. As a child, he experiences conflicting feelings for the bourgeois people around him. He feels both superior to them in his insights and envious of their innocent vitality. This conflict continues into Tonio's adulthood, when he becomes a famous writer living in southern Germany. "To be an artist," he comes to believe, "one has to die to everyday life." These issues are only partially resolved when Tonio travels north to visit his hometown. While there, Tonio is mistaken for an escaped criminal, thereby reinforcing his inner suspicion that the artist must be an outsider relative to "respectable" society. As Erich Heller –who knew Thomas Mann personally– observed, Tonio Kröger’s theme is that of the "artist as an exile from reality" (with Goethe’s Torquato Tasso (1790) and Grillparzer’s Sappho (1818) for company). Yet it was also Erich Heller who, earlier, in his own youth, had diagnosed the main theme of Tonio Kröger to be the infatuation and entanglements of a passionate heart, destined to give shape to, intellectualize, its feelings in artistic terms.

Odysseus leaves Ithaca once more, seeking fresh exploits after quickly tiring of domestic life. His first halt is Sparta, where he aims to rescue Helen, wife of Menelaus, whose abduction by Paris sparked the Trojan War. From there he proceeds to Crete, where a coup dethrones the king, and he abandons Helen along the way. His journey then carries him to Egypt, where another workers’ uprising erupts. He continues onward along the Nile, eventually reaching the lake-source, and there his companions erect camp while he ascends a mountain to commune with his god. Returning to the lake, he establishes a city guided by his religious commandments. An earthquake soon razes this settlement, and Odysseus mourns his failure to grasp the true divine meaning, sacrificing his companions in the process. His life shifts into asceticism. Along his path, he encounters Motherth, a figure representing the Buddha; Kapetan Enas, known in English as Captain Sole and, alias Don Quixote; and a fisherman from an African village who is identified with Jesus. He travels deeper into Africa, continually spreading his faith and resisting death’s advances. In time he reaches Antarctica, living for a year among villagers before an iceberg ends his life. His death is celebrated as glorious, signaling his rebirth and unity with the world.”

In 1938 Portugal, under Salazar’s regime, a crusty old journalist named Pereira, who toils at the Lisboa and dedicates his life to literature, reads an essay by a young hopeful named Monteiro Rossi about death. He invites Rossi and commissions him to craft “advanced obituaries” about eminent writers who might die at any moment. Pereira has long kept politics at arm’s length, but contact with Rossi—the distracted, left-leaning youth—shakes that stance and unsettles his insulated existence. The pieces Rossi sends, which Pereira pays for, are overtly leftist and entirely unsuitable for publication; yet something about Rossi persists in drawing Pereira in. Perhaps it is the memory of a wife who died before they could have children together. A hospital visit to soothe his failing heart leads Pereira to a physician, a man who soon becomes a trusted confidant with whom he debates the crisis in his apolitical life. Ultimately, fascist agents brutalize Rossi in front of Pereira. A breakthrough arrives when, aided by a phone call from his medical friend, Pereira manages to smuggle an article into the Lisboa that condemns the regime and exposes the murder.

The protagonist is a fifteen year old African American boy named Bobby who lives in an apartment in South Bronx with his mother and siblings. Despite his young age Bobby has intelligence that is advanced to most of the people around him. Bobby's Hispanic girlfriend Maria often spend time together and have plans for the upcoming summer. Bobby and Maria's lives are shattered when a vicious Hispanic street gang attack Bobby and Maria while the two were walking to school. Bobby and Maria are severely beaten and Maria is sent to the hospital suffering from near-fatal wounds. After Bobby is beaten he gets picked up by an old holocaust survivor named Moishe and an unlikely friendship between Bobby and Moishe begins. Maria, unable to cope with the mutilation of her face caused by the lye, commits suicide. We hear Moishe talking about his tragic story while he was in a concentration camp, while Bobby tells Moishe what has happened to him and Maria. Bobby states that deep in his mind, he still has a desperate need for revenge.

A crisis envelops Pine Cove when Val Riordan, the town psychiatrist who has been prescribing carelessly rather than addressing underlying mental illnesses, experiences a surge of guilt and substitutes placebos for all of her patients’ antidepressants. Coincidentally, human activity disturbs an ancient sea-beast sealed underwater, bringing it to shore. The creature can alter its form, and it releases a pheromone that arouses uncontrollable lust in Pine Cove’s residents, while also drawing some into prey. After an ill-fated attempt to mate with a fuel truck— which ends in an explosion—the beast sequesters itself in a trailer park, drawing the attention of Molly Michon, a local eccentric and former B-movie star. Molly forms a rapport with the wounded entity. At the same time, Theophilus Crowe, the town’s constable, delves into a mysterious suicide, probes his corrupt superior, and grapples with a worsening marijuana habit. When the beast, whom Molly nicknames “Steve,” begins devouring townspeople and disrupts the meth operation of Theo’s boss, Molly—now romantically entangled with the monster—and Theo join forces. Their goal: help the creature escape safely and simultaneously bring down the boss.

Kira Landon is a fifteen-year-old girl whose life has been completely normal until her friends talk her into being hypnotized. She finds herself revealing things about a past that she never knew, remembering her mother carrying her through war-torn cobblestone streets while speaking a foreign language. Kira's best friend Lynne pushes her to investigate, but before they can find out anything, Mrs. Landon disappears. That evening, a strange woman shows up at Kira's house, saying that she is her "Aunt Memory". "Aunt Memory" takes Kira to Crythe, a land where people are trained from childhood to remember everything that ever happens to them. Kira soon discovers that not only is her mother a prisoner in Crythe, but that many people are not who they claim to be. Mrs. Landon is actually Kira's real Aunt Memory, and the woman who had called herself "Aunt Memory" is actually Rona Cummins, an old enemy of Kira's parents who tries to obtain her parent's secrets. As Rona keeps raising the stakes, Kira must find a way to save Lynne, Mrs. Landon, and herself, as well as her parents' memories.

Soon, Christianity has come to saturate every facet of life—politics, television, the Internet, and cinema. At the top of a semi-theocratic regime sit Reverend Jimmy, a televangelist who serves as the President’s spiritual advisor, and Pastor Bob, a relaxed preacher who cannot resist golf and vies with Jimmy for spiritual primacy. Despite Jimmy’s claim of having spoken with God about nearly everything, his sermons run counter to Jesus’s ideals of peace, love, and universal forgiveness. On his program, Jimmy even asserts that bombing Europe would hasten the Second Coming. Meanwhile, a weary former journalist, Johnny Greco, grows hostile toward Jimmy and encounters Jay, an Irish-Hispanic Catholic whose healing miracles and message of peace, tolerance, and universal love challenge the current state of Christianity. At first skeptical, Johnny comes to suspect that Jay might truly be authentic. Yet tragedy strikes: Jay, several of his closest followers, and Reverend Jim (whom Jay has converted) are killed, as fate repeats the pattern of past losses. Undeterred, Jay’s remaining apostles persevere, spreading his deeds and teachings and establishing a new faith. The narrative closes with the line: THE END AND THE BEGINNING.

After Starfleet unveils a new android, its destruction sparks Lieutenant Commander Data’s investigation into the culprit. In the process, Data uncovers a truth: he may not be as solitary as he once believed. Throughout the original Star Trek series, audiences saw numerous robots and androids, yet Data is frequently portrayed as the sole android roaming the era of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Immortal Coil clarifies the fate of those other artificial beings and clarifies how Data’s story intertwines with theirs. The narrative nods to several previously introduced intelligences and characters, including: Exocomps from The Next Generation episode The Quality of Life; the androids from The Original Series episode What Are Little Girls Made Of?; the M5 computer from The Original Series episode The Ultimate Computer; Flint and Reyna from The Original Series episode Requiem for Methuselah; Doctor Ira Graves from The Next Generation episode The Schizoid Man; Commander Bruce Maddox from The Next Generation episode The Measure of a Man; and Dr. Noonien Soong, Data’s creator, first encountered in The Next Generation episode Brothers.

In a prosperous Scottish town dominated by industry, a church stands beside a notorious dance hall known as the Garden of Eden. The venue irks the innocent, otherworldly Father Malachy, who prays for God to close it down. After a dispute with a Protestant minister, the priest asserts that divinity could remove the Garden of Eden in an instant. The skeptic pastor laughs, and Malachy unexpectedly predicts a specific date when the miracle will occur. That date arrives, and the building, along with everyone inside, vanishes and then reappears on Bass Rock, a small island off the Firth of Forth. The astonishing event enthralls media, politicians, and scientists, all eager to propose rational explanations. Yet the Catholic Church hesitates to declare it a miracle, wary of losing influence over faith or of damage to its reputation if the disappearance proves to be a hoax. Believers from around the world begin pilgrimages to the former dance-hall site, transforming the locale into a bustling fairground. Local residents, merchants, and reporters seek profit from the phenomenon and the sudden influx of pilgrims, selling holy water and miniature Garden of Eden replicas. A young woman who was inside the hall the night of its disappearance rises to media prominence. Wealthy investors purchase the island’s reappearance site and erect a casino that soon draws large crowds. Meanwhile, Malachy endures a flood of requests from interviewers and a deluge of pilgrims pressing to meet the miracle-working priest. Isolated for most of his life in the monastery, he feels overwhelmed by modern excess and regrets having invoked the miracle at all. He travels to the island to plead for a second miracle to quell the frenzy, and God answers. The Garden of Eden is restored to its original position, and the town witnesses a return to normalcy.

Captain Jonathan Archer and the crew of the Starship Enterprise find their way forward blocked by a mysterious alien vessel, piloted by a race they will soon come to know as the Antianna. Unable to decipher the alien ship's transmissions, unwilling to risk a battle, Enterprise is forced to veer from its planned course. Almost immediately, they find themselves in the heart of space ruled by the Thelasian Trading Confederacy, who have also had dealings with the Antianna. The Thelasian leader, Governor Maxim Sen, is in fact in the middle of organising a war against the Antianna, to eliminate the threat they pose to the Confederacy's trading routes. Archer suspects Sen has other motives as well. He also suspects that there is a reason for the Antianna's seemingly hostile posture. But, with the assembled races of an entire sector against him, he needs more than just suspicions. He needs facts. And, only one woman can give them to him: Ensign Hoshi Sato. If she can translate the Antianna language, peace may just be possible. If not, war - a devastating sector-wide war - will soon result.

After having haughtily refused a number of suitors, under the pretext that they are not peers of France, Émilie de Fontaine falls in love with a mysterious young man who quietly appeared at the village dance at Sceaux. Despite his refined appearance and aristocratic bearing, the unknown (Maximilien Longueville) never tells his identity and seems interested in nobody but his sister, a sickly young girl. But he is not insensible to the attention Émilie gives him and he accepts the invitation of Émilie’s father, the Comte de Fontaine. Émilie and Maximilien soon fall in love. The Comte de Fontaine, concerned for his daughter, decides to investigate this mysterious young man, and he discovers him on the Rue du Sentier, a simple cloth merchant, which horrifies Émilie. Piqued, she marries a 70 year old uncle for his title of Vice Admiral, the Comte de Kergarouët. Several years after her marriage, Émilie discovers that Maximilien is not a clothier at all, but in fact a Vicomte de Longueville who has become a Peer of France. The young man finally explains why he secretly tended a store: he did it in order to support his family, sacrificing himself for his sick sister and for his brother, who had departed the country.

Laura Chant experiences one of her ominous forebodings yet must press on to school as if nothing is amiss. On the ride home, she and her younger brother Jacko cross paths with the menacing Carmody Braque, who teases by stamping Jacko’s hand, the mark oddly resembling Jacko’s own face. As illness tightens its grip on Jacko, Laura grows convinced that he has been taken over by a malign presence. She seeks out Sorensen “Sorry” Carlisle, whom she suspects as a hidden witch; to others he appears merely as an impeccably well-behaved school prefect with a sideline of bird photography. Through her investigations she learns Braque is an ancient life-drinker, sustained by siphoning others’ vitality. Winter, Sorensen’s grandmother and a veteran witch, urges Laura to embark on a “changeover”—to become a witch, a “woman of the moon”—so she can lure Braque into a trap and seize control of him. Though she is warned that the transformation carries danger, Laura’s determination to rescue Jacko—now nearing death—drives her forward. The changeover unfolds as a spirit journey that threads through a dark forest and also traverses Gardendale. The Carlisle witches assist her, though their motives are not pure, and Laura emerges with awakened powers of nature and imagination. With Sorensen by her side to conceal her new strength, she confronts Braque, gains dominion over him, and loosens his grip on Jacko. Initially intent on making the malevolent entity suffer, Laura resists the path of darkness and ultimately ends Braque’s unnatural life.

Dr. Roseveare, the headmaster of the relatively obscure English public school at Oakington, has spent seven years striving to elevate its standing. In the winter term of 1927–1928, a pupil dies in his sleep when an old gas fitting collapses from the ceiling, prompting Roseveare to enlist Colin Revell, an alumnus, to conduct a discreet inquiry. Although Revell harbors reservations about ruling out foul play, he cannot identify a clear motive, so he departs after a few weeks, and the investigation’s trail is largely erased by the building’s conversion to electricity. A few months later, Revell is startled by news that the dead boy’s brother, also an orphaned survivor, has perished under enigmatic circumstances—apparently leaping into the school’s indoor pool after the water had been drained—and he travels to Oakington of his own accord. There, he discovers that the brothers’ closest surviving relative is a teacher at the school, and that this teacher stands to inherit a modest fortune. Simultaneously, Revell finds himself falling in love with the teacher’s stunning young wife.

Eddie Coyle, an aging, low-tier gunrunner in Boston, awaits sentencing after being convicted of driving a hijacked truck in New Hampshire. He had been guiding the truck for Dillon, a convicted felon with extensive criminal connections to the syndicate. Refusing to betray Dillon for mercy, Coyle clings to silence. His final chance to avoid prison hinges on a sentencing recommendation from ATF Special Agent Dave Foley, who offers leniency only if Coyle agrees to become an informant. Meanwhile, a Scalise- and Van-led gang conducts bold daytime bank robberies, firearms supplied by Coyle at the center of these heists. One of Coyle’s sources for those pistols is a young bootlegger, Jackie Brown, who is entangled in a scheme to deliver military submachine guns to other clients. During a pistol handoff, Coyle uncovers the submachine guns and engineers a setup against Jackie for Foley. Foley and his team arrest Jackie, who discovers he’s been double-crossed by Coyle. Although Coyle believes he has fulfilled his obligation, Foley pressures him further for cooperation and information. Acting on a tip, Foley and colleagues seize Scalise and Van’s gang in the middle of a robbery. In a moment of desperation, Coyle offers Foley the only actionable lead remaining—the gang’s identity—but Foley has already made the arrest. Scalise suspects Eddie of betrayal, and the syndicate’s boss, enraged by the arrest of a relative within the gang, orders Coyle killed. Dillon receives a contract to eliminate Coyle and carries it out. Having lived with the fear that Coyle might have traded him for immunity, Dillon, who has been Foley’s informant, ultimately finger-points Scalise and Van instead of Coyle. When Foley asks Dillon for more information about Coyle’s murder, Dillon hesitates.

Reed Shelton is out to make the perfect camping trip with his wife, Beck. However, Beck is more of a stay-at-home kind of wife. But Reed manages to convince her to accompany him on the trip. As the couple makes camp for the night, they encounter a strange, unearthly wail accompanied by a set of glowing eyes. In a blur of action, Beck is snatched up by a creature and dragged into the night. Reed, with the combined efforts of a small town and a band of close friends, begins the investigation for his wife. In the meantime, Beck must fight for survival as she is forced to adapt not only to her surroundings, but also to the behavior of her frightening abductors. Realizing that there is little time, Reed and friends pour on the hunt for Beck, only to realize that they aren't the only ones doing the hunting. Something grave and terrifying—and definitely not human—is hunting them. As the net closes, the monster is revealed to be more real than originally imagined. In the midst of the horror, Michael Capella (or "Cap"), a friend of Reed's and a former scientist, investigates the DNA left at the monster's ravaging sites. As he researches further, he finds that it is some form of chimpanzee DNA "contaminated" with human DNA. This revelation leads him to suspect his former colleague, Adam Burkhardt, whom he discovers has indeed been doing some dangerous experiments.

Set in 18th‑century Japan, the tale centers on a quartet of distinctly different figures whose paths cross around Matari, a woman whose allure draws three men who each fall in love with her in their own way.
