Oboko, a wind‑loving poet and Buddhist monk (the name hints at Zen such as Obaku), Izzi, an outgoing court poet, Lord Arishi, a samurai and ruler, and Matari herself—beautiful, clever, and fleeing for her life—form the core ensemble. Although the narrative might be read as a love story, the protagonists’ divergent views on life, honor, and morality set up a fatal clash when their loyalties converge. The novel adheres to a comparatively traditional structure, unfolding linearly with a plot you could find in many books, yet Cockcroft’s deft incorporation of Zen philosophy provides a thoughtful, well‑rounded glimpse into Buddhist and samurai mindsets. Oboko survives the events and is later referenced in The Book of the Die, another work by the same author. The book has appeared in several editions under varying ISBNs: 0-246-10811-8 (Matari, hardcover, January 1975); 0-586-04116-8 (Matari, paperback, September 2, 1976); 1-4033-4796-4 (White Wind, Black Rider, hardcover, November 27, 2002); 1-4033-4795-6 (White Wind, Black Rider, paperback, November 27, 2002).

Chester W. Chester IV inherits a dilapidated mansion and a mountain of back taxes. To cover the debt, his first move is to auction off the house and its contents, including a colossal computer known as the Generalized Nonlinear Extrapolator, or “Genie.” While he and his ally Case Mulvihill survey the mansion and the machine, they discover Genie can tackle intricate problems rooted in historical fact and conjure vivid, lifelike images of those events. This sparks a plan: exploit Genie’s powers to stage an elaborate deception—a counterfeit time machine. He directs the computer to conjure a real, three-dimensional, life-size display of dinosaurs and to stage a four-wall presentation. The machine contemplates using a purely theoretical method that could yield total verisimilitude if feasible, and Chester tells it to proceed. The computer obliges, and in doing so, actually transports the pair through time. During their second voyage, before they realize they possess a time-travel device, they wander beyond their intended landing site and become stranded in the past. Even after they manage to return to the present, their past actions have reshaped history. Ultimately, they enlist the computer’s help to restore things—at least close to the way they were.

In 1857, after their attempt to smuggle contraband ends with a crushing fine from British Customs, Captain Illiam Quillian Kewley and his Manx crew must offer their vessel for charter. A swift hire follows, taken by a group of English travelers led by an offbeat clergyman, Reverend Geoffrey Wilson. He is convinced Tasmania hides the Garden of Eden and sets out on an expedition to locate it. Yet one among the travelers harbors a far different motive for the journey: Dr. Thomas Potter, a celebrated surgeon, is pursuing a thesis on human races and hopes to uncover intriguing specimens on the island. Running parallel to this narrative, but set roughly thirty years earlier, are the recollections of Peevay, a Tasmanian native. His account records the brutal disruption white settlers inflicted upon his people and the natives’ attempts to adapt to the sweeping cultural upheavals imposed upon them. The book alternates between these two timelines for many chapters, and when the Manx-flagged vessel finally reaches Tasmania, the two strands converge, guiding the story toward its ending.

The narrative unfolds by presenting Sal as a lively child, first pictured in her kitchen with her mother during the canning of blueberries. Rather than a pristine, dutiful perfect child, Sal amuses herself by slipping rings onto her wrist and fiddling with a spoon, a small, playful gesture that foreshadows the book’s portrayal of Sal’s genuine childlike behavior and mischievous moments that inevitably trouble her mother. When they set out for Blueberry Hill to gather berries, Sal’s carefree exploration leads to a minor mishap: she drops three berries into her bucket and then snaffles them, a pattern that repeats as mother and daughter become increasingly absorbed in picking and gradually become separated on the hill. Unbeknownst to them, a mother bear and her cub have also descended on Blueberry Hill to stock up for the winter. The story uses visual and verbal cues to draw parallels and contrasts between the human family and the bear family. Both groups appear in similar compositions, yet their paths diverge as they move toward the berry patch. Sal’s mother admonishes that there will be no overindulgence, explaining they must leave some berries to be canned for winter; in contrast, the bear mother urges her cub to eat deeply in order to build fat for the cold months. Sal gravitates toward the bear’s instinct, wandering off to eat. In the ensuing mix‑up, Sal and the bear cub end up following the other family by mistake. It takes several minutes for the two mothers to notice the wrong child is tailing them, a realization sparked when the bear cub attempts to sample from Sal’s mother’s bucket and the distinctive clinking sounds—“ku-plink, ku-plank, ku-plunk”—announce Sal’s berry-dropped tin pail. Ultimately each youngster is correctly paired with its proper mother, and both families depart Blueberry Hill. Just before the departure, Sal drops one last berry into her now-empty pail. The epilogue images Sal back in the kitchen, again at play as her mother cans berries, closing the circle of the opening scene.

In an isolated realm called Minuni, Tarzan—the jungle’s ruler—arrives to a land whose inhabitants are a quarter of his own size: the Minunians. They dwell in impressive city-states that frequently clash in wars with one another. Tarzan forms an alliance with Adendrohahkis, the ruling king, and with Komodoflorensal, the prince of Trohanadalmakus, a city-state caught in the fray against its aggressive neighbors, the Veltopismakusians. Joining their cause, Tarzan fights beside them as they resist the invaders. During the conflict, he is captured on the battlefield and becomes a prisoner of the Veltopismakusians. There, Zoanthrohago, a scientist among their ranks, conducts an experiment that shrinks Tarzan to Minunian size, leading to his imprisonment among Trohanadalmakusian POWs. While confined in the dungeons of Veltopismakus, Tarzan encounters Komodoflorensal, and the two hatch and execute a bold escape plan. Making a further appearance in this tale is Esteban Miranda—Spanish actor and Tarzan lookalike—who had previously been confined in the village of Obebe, the cannibal, at the end of Tarzan and the Golden Lion.

The novel concerns a doctor who develops a mechanical method of eradicating painful memories from people's brains so that they can feel good about life again. The protagonist persuades his lover to try the process after she has been seduced by a rival. She is transformed until the protagonist awakes and realizes that he has dreamt of the doctor and his process and that his lover has committed suicide. The book is notable for its vivid description of small-town American life and mores in the period (1880). The 'Process' mentioned in the title is a plot mechanism to introduce a long discussion of the meaning of guilt. If one loses ones memory of the deed, is one still guilty? If one has changed of time since the deed, is one still guilty? The argument also emphasises the difference between guilt (in the eyes of others) and remorse (one's own judgement), and suggests that forgiveness can remove guilt but not remorse. (Information in this paragraph based on my recent reading of the book).

The play revolves around the dysfunctional family consisting of single mother Beatrice and her two daughters, Ruth and Tillie, who try to cope with their abysmal status in life. The play is a lyrical drama, reminiscent of Tennessee Williams' style. Shy Matilda "Tillie" Hunsdorfer prepares her experiment, involving marigolds raised from seeds exposed to radioactivity, for the science fair. She is, however, constantly thwarted by her mother Beatrice, who is self-centered and abusive, and by her extroverted and unstable sister Ruth, who submits to her mother's will. Over the course of the play, Beatrice constantly tries to stamp out any opportunities Tillie has of succeeding, due to her own lack of success in life. As the play progresses, the paths of the three characters diverge: Tillie wins the science fair through perseverance; Ruth attempts to stand up to her mother but has a nervous collapse at the end of the play, and Beatrice—driven to the verge of insanity by her deep-seated enmity towards everyone—kills the girls' pet rabbit Peter and ends up wallowing in her own perceived insignificance. Despite this, Tillie (who is much like her project's deformed but beautiful and hardy marigolds) secretly continues to believe that everyone is valuable.

The Gauls again humiliate the Romans as Felonius Caucus, Nebulus Nimbus’s right-hand man and commander of Totorum’s fortified camp, proposes a grand duel. In this Gallic tradition, two chiefs from Gallic tribes battle, and the victor leads both peoples. To test Vitalstatistix, the chief of Asterix’s clan, the Romans recruit Cassius Ceramix of Linoleum, a Gallo-Roman chief, to challenge him. Although Getafix’s invincibility potion would likely ensure Vitalstatistix’s triumph, the Romans intend to neutralize the druid well before the fight. Desperate to save Getafix, Obelix accidentally knocks him out with a menhir, causing amnesia and insanity. The looming clash therefore comes at the worst possible moment, and Asterix and Vitalstatistix scramble to cure Getafix by consulting Psychoanalytix (Amnesix in the original French), a druid who specializes in mental disorders. During Psychoanalytix’s attempt to explain the root cause, Obelix interrupts with a dramatic menhir demonstration, leaving the druid in a delirious state. While the two frenzied healers experiment with a series of color-altering magic potions, Asterix focuses on rebuilding Vitalstatistix’s strength for the imminent fight. The Romans, meanwhile, intend to arrest Cassius to curb his growing power. As the battle commences, Getafix unexpectedly formulates a potion that restores his own mind, even as Obelix hurls another menhir at him in a futile bid to cure him, and Getafix quickly begins brewing a fresh supply of magical potion. Though Cassius Ceramix appears poised to prevail, Getafix’s revival emboldens Vitalstatistix to win without any potion. After another clash with the Romans, who resist the outcome, and with Cassius himself knocked “menhir-ed,” Vitalstatistix returns to his village victorious for the feast. Psychoanalytix resumes practice despite his altered condition, yet remains professionally successful, a wry jab at the state of psychiatry.

Camilla is facing significant problems at home. Her mother, Rose, has begun an affair with a man named Jacques. Her mother begs Camilla to keep it a secret, while Camilla's father, Rafferty, asks her to be honest and tell him the truth. Camilla is torn between her loyalty to both parents and begins to realize they are very imperfect people. To cope with the struggle, Camilla befriends Frank, her best friend's older brother. He is understanding of her problems and assists her in accepting her parents flaws. Frank encourages Camilla to define herself not by her family but to define herself as who she truly is. The pair share ideas on life, religion and philosophy and begin to form a romantic attachment. Their happiness is cut short when their families problems get worse. Frank's parents break up and he is forced to suddenly move away with his father. Camilla's parents decide to work on their marriage and go on a European Vacation together. Unfortunately, while her parents are traveling, Camilla is going to be sent to a Swiss boarding school. While Camilla is heartbroken by the loss of Frank, she uses the inner strength she has gained in the past weeks to deal with the changes in her life.

In Fort Weakling, Texas, the year 1878 finds the town gripped by fear of Billy the Kid, a bully whose notorious reputation unsettles the citizens. When Lucky Luke, passing through, fails to bring Billy to justice by normal means, he opts to expose the desperados’ fearsome image for what it is. He takes on the persona of a desperado himself, enlisting the town’s lone brave defender—the editor of the local newspaper—as his ally. To Billy’s growing irritation, the townspeople begin to see him not as an unbearable menace but as someone who might liberate them from that menace. The story culminates in a scene akin to the cover illustration: Lucky Luke administering a stern spanking to Billy and then escorting him to jail. This bold move inspires Fort Weakling’s residents to face future incursions with wit and a smile, a realization that Jesse James quickly recognizes.

The novel opens as an experimental star ship tests a deadly weapon on an uninhabited world, devastating the surface. From here the story essentially follows the two main characters as they are recruited by the Sutherlin Alliance in their bid to overthrow the Alcon Empire. The junior of the two opens the story as a pilot in the Empire’s prestigious Devil Squadron. The senior recruit had also once served in this fighter group only to resign years early and take up the life of a mercenary and bounty hunter. With these two skilled men added to their backbone of ex-Imperial soldiers and raw youth from around the galaxy the Alliance takes the fight to the Empire. With the threat of the Alliance growing the Empire learns of their location and decides to unleash the power of their world killing star ship. The two recruited men learn of the ship’s existence and its target just days before its use and develop a plan of attack to cripple both the ship and the sizable force escorting it. One of the themes that is expressed throughout the story is attachment and the human need to belong; both main characters fight with these needs in their own ways. The elder of the two battles the desire with his own wishes to stay separate from the needs of the others while the younger fights to keep his distance, not wanting to feel the loss of war.

In the book, Wolf argues that "beauty" as a normative value is entirely socially constructed, and that the patriarchy determines the content of that construction with the goal of reproducing its own hegemony. In her introduction, Wolf offers the following analysis: Wolf also posits the idea of an "iron-maiden," an intrinsically unattainable standard of beauty that is then used to punish women physically and psychologically for their failure to achieve and conform to it. Wolf criticizes the fashion and beauty industries as exploitative of women, but claims the beauty myth extends into all areas of human functioning. Wolf writes that women should have "the choice to do whatever we want with our faces and bodies without being punished by an ideology that is using attitudes, economic pressure, and even legal judgments regarding women's appearance to undermine us psychologically and politically". Wolf argued that women were under assault by the "beauty myth" in five areas: work, religion, sex, violence, and hunger. Ultimately, Wolf argues for a relaxation of normative standards of beauty.

The book tells two separate but related tales: first, the romance between Nacib Saad, a respectable bar owner of Syrian origin, and Gabriela, an innocent and captivating migrant worker from the impoverished interior. And second, the political struggle between the old guard of Cacao growers, led by the Bastos clan, and the forces of modernization, in the person of Mundinho Falcão, a wealthy young man from Rio de Janeiro. It can be read simultaneously as an unusual, charming love story, a description of the political and social forces at work in 1920s Brazil, a somewhat satirical depiction of Latin American aspirations to "modernity", and a celebration of the local culture and pleasures of Bahia. The book was made into series for Brazilian television in 1960, in 1976 and again in 2012. A feature film of the novel was directed by Bruno Barreto in 1983. The feature version starred Sonia Braga as Gabriela and Marcello Mastroianni as Nacib, and featured original music by Antonio Carlos Jobim.

Here Be Dragons (1985) is the first of Penman's trilogy about the medieval princes of Gwynedd and the monarchs of England. England's King John uses his out-of-wedlock daughter Joanna as a negotiating tool by marrying her to the Welsh king Llewelyn to avoid war between England and Wales. Joanna and Llewelyn's marriage is marred by resentment from Llewelyn's illegitimate son, Gruffydd. Joanna gives birth to two legitimate children, Elen and Davydd. Growing animosity between the English and Welsh results in Joanna having to act as a diplomatic intermediary between her husband and her father, and the situation deteriorates when Gruffydd is taken hostage by John and narrowly escapes execution. Joanna becomes determined that her own son, Dafydd, will be his father's heir as ruler of Gwynedd, disregarding the Welsh law that all sons should receive equal shares of their father's inheritance. Family disagreements lead Joanna into an affair with William de Braose, whom she has met earlier in the story when he was a hostage in Llewelyn's household. Their affair is discovered and William is executed. Joanna is placed in secluded captivity, but at the end of the book Llewelyn comes to find her and offers her forgiveness.

One day in the Cretaceous Period as a Tyrannosaurus is about to devour a smaller dino he captured, a flying saucer piloted by an alien named Vorb arrives. He recruits him and several other dinos he's found for a trial of a special "vitamin" he's developed, which, upon feeding it to the dinos, causes them to become sapient. Vorb takes them aboard his saucer and they travel to the present, dropping them off in New York City, which at that moment is celebrating the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The dinos pretend to be inflatable balloons to sneak along with the parade, but Rex mistakes one of the real dino balloons to be his friend Allosaurus. The ruse is broken as a result of him accidentally popping "Allosaurus" and the dinos flee as the crowd panics in sight of them. The police come to capture the dinos soon after, but the helpful curator of the American Museum of Natural History, Dr. Bleeb, takes the dinos in, and hides them from the cops by having them pretend to be life-size model dinosaurs. This satisfies the police, who leave to search for the dinosaurs elsewhere, and the curator lets them stay for the night. She reads them a bedtime story about a trilobite who wanted to walk on land, while the dinos watch out the window, unsure about their future. ru:Мы вернулись! История динозавра

In 2010 Denver, a man named Thomas Hunter experiences a head wound from a gunshot that leaves him unconscious. When he awakens, he finds himself amid a bizarre landscape of black, twisted trees. After being attacked by bat-like beings called Shataiki, and then led out of the Black Forest by a white bat, he inexplicably slips back into unconsciousness from blood loss and later wakes again in Denver. He is startled by the abrupt shift and cannot determine which world is real. Soon he realizes a troubling pattern: every time he drifts to sleep, he regresses to the other realm, and only returns when he dozes there again. Beyond the Black Forest lies the Colored Forest, a utopian region inhabited by immortal yet innocent humans and overseen by Elyon, a god-like figure. Roush, pure white and bat-like, accompanies Elyon as a servant, acting as a foil to the Shataiki. Thomas uncovers the shocking truth that the alternate world is actually our future, thousands of years ahead, and that a virus—deriving from a mutated vaccine—will devastate his present-day Earth later that same year. He is compelled to confront evil across both realities, a daunting task since each realm depicts malevolence differently, yet both are equally formidable. Ultimately, stopping a catastrophic event proves to be an arduous challenge for him.

The tale resumes at the moment Cugel the Clever is found, after The Eyes of the Overworld, moping on a desolate northern beach far from Almery. His aim remains to reach home and to strike back at Iucounu, the Laughing Magician, whom he blames—albeit indirectly—for a second exile. Departing on a new course, he come(s) into possession of a lethal relic from the Overworld, Sadlark, and signs on as worminger aboard a worm-powered merchant vessel. He proceeds to steal both the ship and its owner’s wife, along with his three attractive daughters. Aware of his schemes, the wife outwits him, forcing him to abandon the vessel and the women. What follows are a string of adventures and misfortunes, until, with the help of newfound allies, he manages to defeat Iucounu. The narrative, like its precursor, embraces a picaresque structure, and Cugel remains as morally ambiguous and appealing as ever. The original edition is currently out of print, but it is reprinted together with The Eyes of the Overworld in the omnibus Tales of the Dying Earth. In the Vance Integral Edition, the work appears as volume 35 under the title Cugel: The Skybreak Spatterlight, as curated by its editor. An earlier follow-up, Michael Shea’s A Quest for Simbilis, appeared in 1974.

The story of the novel follows the life and career of Henry Coningsby, the orphan grandson of a wealthy marquess, called Lord Monmouth. Lord Monmouth initially disapproved of Coningsby's parents' marriage, but on their death he relents and sends the boy to be educated at Eton College. At Eton Coningsby meets and befriends Oswald Millbank, the son of a rich cotton manufacturer who is a bitter enemy of Lord Monmouth. The two older men represent old and new wealth in society. As Coningsby grows up he begins to develop his own liberal political views and he falls in love with Oswald's sister Edith. When Lord Monmouth discovers these developments he is furious and secretly disinherits his grandson. On his death, Coningsby is left penniless, and is forced to work for his living. He decides to study law and to become a barrister. This proof of his character impresses Edith's father (who had previously also been hostile) and he consents to their marriage at last. By the end of the novel Coningsby is elected to Parliament for his new father-in-law's constituency and his fortune is restored. The character of Coningsby himself is based on George Smythe. The themes, and some of the characters, reappear in Disraeli's later novels Sybil, and Tancred.

Francis Petrel, recently released from an asylum faces his own inner demons as he recounts his memories of a murderer in the asylum during his time there. The story tells itself in two parallel parts: one of the stories is during his time in the asylum, all a memory slowly bringing itself back to life; the other story takes place after he is released, and he feels compelled to author a book on the events surrounding that murder. He has no paper, so he writes his story on the wall and is constantly challenged with tedious interruptions. At the same time, he forgoes his medication, and the tension of continuing with his work becomes threatened by his struggle with his own madness. It is currently being turned into a movie and it was supposed to be filmed from November 26th, 2007 until approximately January 20th, 2008 at Fairfield State Hospital in Newtown, Connecticut. Filming has not yet taken place due to personal issues of Jonathan Rhys Meyers, the films star, according to an article in the Newtown Beehttp://www.newtownbee.com/. Trivia: Descriptions in the text suggest that the central hospital, "Western State Hospital", is actually modeled on the Northampton State Hospital, which operated in Northampton, MA from 1856 - 1996.

The book is divided into two parts. The first attempts a complete diagnosis of the totality of modern capitalist civilization, moving through what the Invisible Committee identify as the "seven circles" of alienation: "self, social relations, work, the economy, urbanity, the environment, and to close civilization". The latter part of the book begins to offer a prescription for revolutionary struggle based on the formation of communes, or affinity group-style units, in an underground network that will build its forces outside of mainstream politics, and attack in moments of crisis – political, social, environmental – to push towards anti-capitalist revolution. The insurrection envisioned by the Invisible Committee will revolve around "the local appropriation of power by the people, of the physical blocking of the economy and of the annihilation of police forces". The book points to the late 2000s financial crisis, and environmental degradation as symptoms of capitalism's decline. Also discussed are the Argentine economic crisis (1999-2002) and the piquetero movement which emerged from it, the 2005 riots and 2006 student protests in France, the 2006 Oaxaca protests and the grassroots relief work in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina as examples of breakdown in the modern social order which can give rise to partial insurrectionary situations.

A second Raman vessel enters our solar system seventy years after Rendezvous with Rama. Its arrival is anticipated, and a mission is dispatched to uncover more of Rama’s secrets, yet the crew confronts unforeseen discoveries and internal conflicts. Rama II introduces new characters into a fresh narrative that largely stands apart from the first work and mainly serves to lay groundwork for its own sequels. The tale concludes with three of the twelve astronauts—Nicole des Jardins Wakefield, Richard Wakefield, and Michael O’Toole—left stranded inside Rama as it drifts beyond the solar system. In contrast to Rendezvous with Rama, which portrayed a utopian future and concentrated on hard-science marvels of the alien craft, Rama II and its successors undermine Clarke’s optimistic view of solar-system colonization by depicting a global economic collapse that nearly extinguishes human activity. The series then pivots to a markedly different storytelling approach, foregrounding contemporary issues such as abortion, racism, drug abuse, and organized crime.

On a hiking holiday following Harriet Vane’s acquittal in Strong Poison, she comes upon a man’s body on a secluded shoreline rock, his throat slit and the blood still liquid. Only the man’s footprints and Harriet’s disturb the otherwise empty sand. She documents the scene, saves some evidence, but the corpse is carried away by the tide before help can arrive. Lord Peter Wimsey joins the investigation alongside the police. The victim, Paul Alexis, is a professional dance partner at the local hotel, of Russian extraction, and engaged to a wealthy, older widow. Although the death appears to be a suicide, Wimsey and Harriet uncover a carefully crafted murder plot. Alexis, a romantic who fancied himself a descendant of Russian royalty, becomes the target of the widow’s son. The young man, irritated by his mother’s prospective remarriage to a gigolo and the potential loss of his inheritance, collaborates with a friend and that friend’s wife to exploit Alexis’s fantasies. They lure Alexis to the rock with the belief that he’ll return to Russia in triumph as the rightful Tsar, and there he is murdered by the son, who rides a horse along the beach against the incoming tide to avoid leaving tracks, while the others furnish him with an alibi. The plan is to pass the death off as suicide. Yet haemophilia cripples the victim’s ability for normal blood clotting, so his unclotted blood clouds the timing of death and ultimately helps expose the conspirators.

The plot concerns four college students who discover a manuscript, The Book of Skulls, dealing with an order of monks living in a monastery in the Arizona desert, whose members have the power to bestow immortality on those who complete their bizarre initiation rite. The boys travel to the monastery, where they are accepted as a "Receptacle," and told that for each group of four who agree to undergo the ritual, two must die in order for the others to succeed - one must sacrifice himself, and the other must be sacrificed. The narrative switches back and forth between the viewpoints of the four students as each confronts his personal demons on the way to completing the ritual. Ned, who is openly homosexual, must face his guilt over the tragic aftermath of one of his affairs; Eli, the gifted (but socially inept) young man who discovered the manuscript, makes a confession that could destroy his academic career; Timothy, star athlete and prodigal son of a wealthy family, confronts a terrible sin from his past involving his younger sister; and Oliver, the farm kid from the wrong side of the tracks, comes face to face with his own true innermost nature. The Book of Skulls has been republished as part of the series SF Masterworks.

A playwright called Ashenden is recruited by Colonel R., a British Intelligence officer. He is sent to Switzerland where he becomes involved in a series of adventures. In one he accompanies a man called the Hairless Mexican to Italy, where a Greek agent of the Germans is to be assassinated. In another he must get an Italian dancer to induce her Indian lover, a German agent, to cross the border into Switzerland to see her, so that Ashenden can arrest him. # R. # A Domiciliary Visit # Miss King # The Hairless Mexican # The Dark Woman # The Greek # A Trip to Paris # Giulia Lazzari # Gustav # The Traitor # Behind the Scenes # His Excellency # The Flip of a Coin # A Chance Acquaintance # Love and Russian Literature # Mr. Harrington's Washing The chapters are collected in later collections under different titles, as below. It is unknown whether they were rewritten slightly from original publication. * "A Domiciliary Visit" & "Miss King" as Miss King * "The Hairless Mexican", "The Dark Woman", "The Greek" as The Hairless Mexican * "A Trip to Paris, "Giulia Lazzari" as Giulia Lazzari * "Gustav", "The Traitor" as The Traitor * "Behind the Scenes", "His Excellency", as His Excellency * "A Chance Acquaintance", "Love and Russian Literature", "Mr. Harrington's Washing" as Mr. Harrington's Washing

Sandry, a Lord from Tep’s Town, is one of the central figures, alongside his cousin Regapisk—also a Lord—and Burning Tower, Whandall’s daughter and the book’s protagonist in the previous volume. Regapisk proves imprudently deficient as a lord, prompting his relatives to arrange a shoreward voyage that ends with him being pressed into service as an oarsman aboard a coastal vessel. Throughout the narrative, Sandry and Burning Tower sustain a romantic bond. When a flock of large, flightless birds assaults a caravan, Sandry defeats them and is then dispatched by the Lords to aid the caravan—which Burning Tower accompanies—to uncover the birds’ origin. Their trek takes them first to Condigeo, a southern metropolis, and then to Crescent City, fending off terror-bird assaults along the way. In Crescent City, Regapisk reappears, having escaped confinement on his ship, and joins the trio. The trio presses on to Aztlan, a city famed for its high magic, where Regapisk at last earns redemption. The authors state that they conducted research into Aztec culture for this work, and many cultural elements depicted stem from that inquiry, a note that appears in a brief closing section of the book. Additionally, the note observes that within the book’s timeline, terror birds persisted well beyond the arrival of humans in the Americas, a fact linked to Titanis walleri, a North American phorusrhacid, with a caveat directing readers to McFadden et al. 2007 for further context.

The book begins in the lead-up to the declaration of hostilities between Germany and Britain, whereas Massie's previous work ended with the beginning of the war. All the significant naval strategies and battles of World War I are covered, including the Battle of Coronel, where a German squadron led by Admiral Maximilian von Spee destroyed a weaker British cruiser squadron under the command of Admiral Sir Christopher Cradock; the ensuing Battle of the Falkland Islands where von Spee's force was annihilated by a superior British squadron; the Battle of Dogger Bank (1915); Naval operations in the Dardanelles Campaign; and a detailed multichapter narrative of the Battle of Jutland and its aftermath. Other chapters describe German submarine warfare and events triggering America's entry into the war. There are also chapters dedicated to central personalities such as British Admirals John Jellicoe and David Beatty and the German Admirals Franz von Hipper and Reinhard Scheer. The book ends with an account of the scuttling of the German High Seas Fleet in Scapa Flow. A number of maps and photographs are included.

After Misha's father kills a prominent businessman from Oklahoma, the INS bars the entire Vainberg family entry to the United States, trapping Misha in his native Saint Petersburg, which he nostalgically refers to as "St. Leninsburg." Misha, a.k.a. "Snack Daddy" from his days at Accidental College, somewhere in the Midwestern U.S. (the college resembles Oberlin College, which Shteyngart attended, while the name is a play on Occidental College), is desperate to return to his true love, Rouenna, whom he met while she was working at a "titty bar" and who now attends Hunter College, at Misha's expense. Misha's father is killed by a fellow oligarch. Soon after, Misha is given an opportunity to buy a Belgian passport from a corrupt diplomat in the fictitious ex-Soviet republic of Absurdsvanϊ (also known as Absurdistan). Absurdistan's reputation for oil riches got it the title "Norway of the Caspian." Divided between two major ethnic groups, the Sevo and Svanϊ, whose mutual hatred stems from a dispute over which way the "footrest" of the Orthodox cross should be tilted, Absurdistan soon finds itself ensconced in civil war and Misha is forced to take sides on behalf of a new love. Appointed "Minister of Multiculturalism," he is asked to petition Israel for funds, but he soon finds he is being played by the Sevo leader, who has, in fact, been in league with the Svanϊ leader all along.

The story takes place entirely aboard an Emergency Dispatch Ship (EDS) headed for the frontier planet Woden with a load of desperately needed medical supplies. The pilot, Barton, discovers a stowaway: an eighteen-year-old girl. By law, all EDS stowaways are to be jettisoned because EDS vessels carry no more fuel than is absolutely necessary to land safely at their destination. The girl, Marilyn, merely wants to see her brother, Gerry, and is not aware of the law. When boarding the EDS, Marilyn sees the "UNAUTHORIZED PERSONNEL KEEP OUT!" sign, but thinks she will simply have to pay a fine if she is caught. Barton explains that her presence dooms the mission by exceeding the weight limit, and will result in the deaths of the colonists. No cargo can be jettisoned, and the presence of the captain is required on ship, so Barton cannot sacrifice himself. After contacting her brother, Marilyn willingly walks out of the airlock and is ejected into space. The story, first published in the August 1954 issue of Astounding, has been widely anthologized and even dramatized.

This novel follows Dragonsdawn and the short story The Dolphin's Bell (short story contained in The Chronicles of Pern: First Fall) by discussing the present state (Ninth Pass) of the dolphins that were brought to Pern by the colonists. Set near the end and after the events of All the Weyrs of Pern it further integrates the science fiction aspects of the origins of the Pern series with the fantastical aspects presented by the original books. The plot focuses primarily on two young characters and chronicles the birth of the Dolphincrafthall and its first Dolphineer. Readis, the Paradise River Lord Holder's son, is saved by talking dolphins ("shipfish") as a young boy after falling into the sea and subsequently develops a strong fascination with the dolphins. T'lion, the young Eastern Weyr dragonrider of Bronze Gadareth, also develops an interest after being involved in an early dolphin encounter. The two befriend each other due to their shared interest and, in their own ways, defy family, Hold and Weyr to maintain their friendships with dolphins and convince others of the dolphins' intelligence and ability to speak. While familiar characters struggle to end the era of Thread, Readis, T'lion and others struggle to begin a new era in which dolphin and human work together again. Well-known characters from previous Pern novels are also involved in the plot, including Benden Weyrleaders Lessa and F'lar, and Masterharpers Robinton and Menolly.

Eleven-year-old Jamie Reardon’s cat dies, his father leaves home; and his aunt Sapphy has an accident at work that causes her memory to skip. Jamie is a boy who is teased at school and, on the other hand, has a memory he'd give anything to be able to forget. He is performing badly at school and has Miss Miller,an unsympathetic teacher. A visiting author, or as Jamie hears the name - 'Arthur', recognises that the boy is troubled, but the two do not have a chance to really communicate. Jamie has to sort out his problems himself. He tries to find the magic trigger that will help Sapphy's memory jump the scratch, like the needle on a record, but in the end it's Audrey Krouch, a neighborhood girl who hypnotises him. Under hypnosis, when he is hoping to learn how to forget, Jamie recalls his recent sexual abuse by Old Gray, a paedophile caretaker at the trailer park where he lives in Traverse City, Michigan. Jamie's emotional reaction to the incident he was trying to suppress returns Sapphy’s memory, and the boy is finally able to tell her everything. The actual abuse is not described in the book. Sarah Weeks has said that, "I felt like I wanted to protect Jamie’s privacy... Jamie didn’t want anybody to know what had happened to him in Old Gray’s office on Christmas Eve, so it didn’t feel right for me to tell all the details either."

Rather than retrace Napoleonic-era events to place his hero anew, Cornwell chooses a prequel approach, venturing into the British Army’s colonial campaigns in India. The tale opens with Richard Sharpe, serving as a private, as British forces invade Mysore and advance toward Seringapatam, the capital of the Tippoo Sultan. Sharpe contemplates desertion with his lover, Mary Bickerstaff, a widow. In a staged cruelty, the sadistic company sergeant Obadiah Hakeswill goads Sharpe into attacking him, setting in motion a death sentence of two thousand lashes for the private. Yet, after only 200 lashes, Lieutenant William Lawford rescues him to enable a covert mission behind the Sultan’s lines. Ordered to pose as deserters, Lawford and Sharpe undertake a rescue of Colonel Hector McCandless, the head of the East India Company’s intelligence service. Although Lawford leads in name, Sharpe’s forceful personality quickly eclipses him, and, without authorization, he brings Mary along on the mission. Disguised within the Tippoo’s army, they uncover a trap: the British are lured into Seringapatam by mines planted at the city’s weakest walls. Before they can transmit a warning to their comrades, Hakeswill betrays them. Having been captured in battle, Hakeswill faces the Sultan’s mercy only if he exposes Sharpe’s and Lawford’s identities as spies. Consequently, Sharpe and Lawford are imprisoned as the British army prepares to assault the booby-trapped fortress. Mary helps Sharpe escape, and he detonates the mine just before the main force can breach the trap. When the Tippoo attempts a retreat through a dark tunnel, Sharpe confronts him, kills him, and seizes the sultan’s luxurious jewels. In the aftermath, Sharpe consigns Hakeswill to the sultan’s tigers; however, the creatures, recently fed, ignore him, leaving the formidable foe alive to trouble Sharpe in future adventures.

The narrative begins in 2021, inside a nation ruled by a tyrant named Jeeva. His regime enforces population control: aging citizens are allowed to live only up to a fixed age and are killed once they surpass it. Every person must bear a government-assigned two-letter name, and all citizens are compelled to follow Jeeva’s dictates while publicly worshiping him. A vast network of robots pervades society, and identities are reduced to social security numbers stored and managed by a master computer in the capital. On New Year’s Eve, Nila, a homemaker, celebrates receiving government approval to bear a son from the Population Control Board. She shares the news with her husband, Sibi. Meanwhile, the state designates Nila’s home for a man named Ravi and his robotic pet, Jeano. Government rules cap the number of occupants at three, so Sibi leaves to confirm Ravi’s allotment but never returns. Desperate, Nila searches for him using his social security number, only to discover that no such person exists. Frustrated and fearful, she continues the search without success. What happened to Sibi? What role does Ravi play in his disappearance? How will Nila uncover the truth about Jeeva’s dictatorship with Jeano’s help? The remainder of the story unravels as these questions are answered.

Julian, Dick and Anne arrive in Cornwall to stay with George for the holidays. They plan to spend time exploring Kirrin Island but their happiness is spoilt when Aunt Fanny falls ill and has to leave with Uncle Quentin to be treated in a far-off hospital. They are cared for by Aunt Fanny's temporary cook, Mrs Stick, who is accompanied by her husband and their ghastly son Edgar. The Sticks and the children come to hate each other. When Mrs Stick tries to poison George's dog Timmy, George can take it no more. She hatches a secret plan to run away to Kirrin island and look after herself but when Julian catches her leaving she decides to allow the other children to go with her. While on the island, they find evidence of smugglers on an old wreck. A scream in the night and the discovery of a young girl's clothes alert the Five that there could be something very sinister going on. They discover that the Sticks have kidnapped and imprisoned a little girl on the island, the daughter of a very rich man. Having tormented the Sticks into a retreat they rescue the girl, taking her to the police who are amazed to see the child "the whole country is looking for!!" The police accompany them back to the island in time to trap and arrest the Sticks. The kidnapped girl's father allows her to spend a week with her new friends on Kirrin Island.

Four Polish scientists and a private detective join forces as “Flame Breathers” and perish; a car and a plane shatter speed records before they’re destroyed; the driver, the pilot, and a reporter are slain; explosions rock a Montreal police laboratory, Singer’s mansion, and a bathtub clutching financier Henderlin. A NJ residence, heated and illuminated without any conventional power source, blows apart as well. A striking woman with black hair repeatedly thwarts Justice Inc. A diminutive, enigmatic man appears to be tied to the scheme. Benson cannot initially pin down any chemical cause for the flames and blasts. His pursuit unfolds with his aides playing minor, supporting roles. Benson carries the burden of a betrayed, aging appearance—paralyzed features and white hair—while the plot complicates itself through rival factions. Two syndicates, each under the influence of a financier, vie to control a covert process uncovered by the four researchers, a method that could convert water into energy. The black-haired heroine aims for vengeance for her brother, the murdered reporter, and, with Benson’s intervention, sees the two gangs wreck each other. The lab assistant who served the scientists dies, and with him the secret of extracting energy from water perishes as well.

The book seems to begin as memoir or an autobiography, but rapidly devolves into numerous fragmented accounts of Thompson's exploits which could be termed as a type of Gonzo biography. There is a rough adherence to actual chronology though many events in the book are not in order. However, some continuity does exist throughout the work, for example, the "Witness" segments, dealing with Gail Palmer's trial against him, appearing once every section in roughly the same area. In addition to these larger narratives, there are also several sections which hold no connection to each other in any way, with the exception of some of the same people or places from a previous section being mentioned. Among the events, the ones which seem to be as closely related to Thompson's life are listed below: *An early incident involving the FBI attempting to arrest a then nine-year-old Thompson for an action which apparently resulted in the destruction of a federal mailbox. *The "Witness" sections *Various exploits of Thompson's either at or involving the Mitchell Brothers O'Farrell Theatre in San Francisco, an infamous pornographic theater where he claims to have worked throughout the mid eighties. *A possibly fictionalized account of how Thompson met his assistant and later wife Anita.

Set in the early 1980s, Liza Normal goes on numerous theater and commercial auditions, at the behest of her mother Peppy, who costumes the child in a strapless evening gowns, heavy make-up, and false eyelashes. Humiliations repeat for Liza, as she and her family encounter endless degradation, after opening a dinner theater in Marin County, California. Throughout the first half of the novel, Liza is forced to perform in a dilapidated firehouse, which functions as the theater, as well as the family's home, attend school where she is constantly ridiculed and tormented, and at one point, raped. After this, Liza undergoes several phases, the first of which is a gravitation toward the punk rock aesthetic, specifically embracing and cultivating the look of Plasmatics performer, Wendy O. Williams. Liza eventually becomes involved with a drug pusher, and at one point becomes addicted herself during her stint at "Elf House," which Wilson describes as a commune of hippies who have a fetish with elves and speaking in "Quenya, the J.R.R. Tolkien version of High Elf language." It is during this time, that Liza, while working for Centaur Productions—a company that creates and distributes Slash fiction, that she concocts an "alter ego, Venal de Minus, into a phone sex phenomenon and Las Vegas stage act," achieving a new definition of success that is a spin-off of the earlier theater ambitions initially sought by her mother.

The text surveys a range of threats—environmental degradation, famine, overpopulation, climate shifts, floods, tornadoes, and the hothouse/greenhouse effect among them—and projects them as intensifying toward the end of the 20th century. Berlitz compiles an extensive roster of predicted doomsdays, beginning with December 31, 999, when many anticipated Christ’s return, and continuing through numerous forecasts by scientists, prophets, astrologers, and other voices. In chapter 8, he questions whether the world has ever truly ended, invoking Atlantis as an example—a notion he revisits later in The Mystery of Atlantis and Atlantis: The Lost Continent Revealed. He entertains the possibility that a flood may have occurred, a theory he examines further in The Lost Ship of Noah: In Search of the Ark at Ararat (1987). In chapter 9, he cites flood legends from the Bible and the Torah, alongside accounts from Sumerian, Babylonian, Assyrian, Greek, Indian, Persian, Welsh, Norse, Lithuanian, Irish, Chinese, Aztec-Toltec, Mayan, and Chibcha sources."

Lief, Barda, and Jasmine have already recovered the topaz in The Forests of Silence. Pressed on toward the Lake of Tears to claim the ruby, they discover that Thaegan, a sorceress of evil, dominates the land around the lake and commands thirteen monstrous offspring. Along their trek, they rescue Manus, a man from Raladin, from Grey Guards—the Shadow Lord’s enforcers. A century ago, Thaegan cursed Raladin and its entire line so that none could speak. They also learn that Thaegan transformed D’Or into the Lake of Tears. After a narrow escape from the Grey Guards, Manus joins them briefly but soon they are captured by Jin and Jod, two of Thaegan’s children. The group eventually defeats Jin and Jod and continues to Raladin, where Manus hopes to reconnect with his people. Upon arrival, the city appears deserted; when the Ralads hear the visitors, they emerge from hiding. Lief, Barda, and Jasmine urge them to embark for the Lake of Tears, though they withhold the fact that the party is seeking one of the gems of the Belt of Deltora. Manus agrees to serve as their guide. At the lake, the monster Soldeen—a fearsome, speech-capable, fish-like behemoth—attacks. With the topaz, Lief convinces Soldeen to surrender the ruby. As the exchange nears completion, Thaegan materializes and menaces them. The ruby slips from Lief’s grasp into the lake’s depths as Thaegan’s magic wounds them. Just as doom seems certain, Jasmine’s bird Kree slays Thaegan, breaking all of her spells. The Ralads regain their speech, and the Lake of Tears reverts to the city of D’Or. Nanion, the man behind Soldeen, reveals himself, grants the ruby and the topaz to the trio, and wishes them success on their quest. With both gems reclaimed—the topaz and the ruby—the party then turns toward the City of the Rats to continue their journey.

Frisk is narrated by Dennis, who had a troubled childhood. In 1969, aged 13, he was regularly allowed to read pornographic magazines and was particularly affected by snuff pornography, even though he later learns that the pictures were faked. He recognises that Henry, now aged 17, was the 13/14-year-old boy portrayed in the pictures. Dennis is gay and a drug-taker and is devastated when his boyfriend Julian leaves him to go off to France. Dennis takes up with Julian’s younger brother Kevin. The boy is psychologically troubled, yet 18-year-old Dennis involves him in drugs and starts a sexual relationship. In 1989, Julian receives a letter from Dennis describing how he embarked on a sadistic killing spree in Amsterdam. The descriptions in the letter are explicit and the torture and sadism are described in graphic terms. Dennis then meets up with two Germans, tells them what he has done, and they join forces to commit a series of random, motiveless murders. One of the serial killer’s most recent victims was an 11-year-old boy, whom they tortured before mutilating and murdering in Dennis’ home, a converted windmill, two weeks before the letter was written. Julian travels to Amsterdam with Kevin to find out if the murders in the letters are true or just a cruel fantasy.

Julian, Dick, and Anne arrive in Cornwall to spend the holidays at George’s house. They intend to explore Kirrin Island, but their joy is dampened when Aunt Fanny falls ill and must depart with Uncle Quentin for treatment at a distant hospital. In their absence, Mrs Stick—Aunt Fanny’s temporary cook—arrives with her husband and their ominous son, Edgar. Tensions soon emerge as the Sticks and the children come to despise one another. When Mrs Stick attempts to poison George’s dog Timmy, George can endure it no longer. She hatches a plan to flee to Kirrin Island to look after herself, but Julian catches her in the act and she decides to let the other children accompany her. On the island, the friends stumble upon evidence of smugglers aboard an old wreck. A night-time scream and the sighting of a young girl’s clothes raise the Five’s suspicions that something sinister is afoot. They uncover that the Sticks have kidnapped and imprisoned a little girl on the island, the daughter of a wealthy man. After pressuring the Sticks into retreat, they rescue the girl and escort her to the police, who are astonished to see the child for whom “the whole country is looking!!” The police then accompany the group back to Kirrin Island to set a trap and arrest the Sticks. The kidnapped girl’s father permits her to spend a week with her new friends on Kirrin Island.

Barton Royal is an overweight man in his 40s who is obsessed with boys. He lives in Los Angeles but travels out of state to find and abduct a suitable young boy so he can be his "father". When he spots 12-year-old Billy Neary in an Iowa shopping mall, he follows the boy home, abducts him late that night, and drives back to California with Billy strapped into the back of his Aerostar minivan. The narrative includes glimpses of Barton's miserable childhood, especially the physical and sexual abuse he suffered at the hands of his father and his recollections of what he has done to other boys before Billy. Billy tries to escape and also manages to make a few telephone calls, both on the road to and from Barton's home. Barton's behaviour switches between extreme violence and interludes of self-delusion. Billy finds his way into Barton's dungeon, his "black room", and discovers the remains of many other young boys. Billy’s father beats the police to Billy's location, just barely preventing Barton from torturing and killing him.

The Praxis begins with the last days of the Shaa. The Shaa are a powerful race that have ruled the Empire for thousands of years, having subjugated humans and other races. The Praxis is their philosophy, founded on total obedience and hierarchy. The end of the Empire brings civil war, as an insectoid race, the Naxids, battle humans and the other races following the death of the last of the 'Great Masters'. The plot revolves around interstellar battles and the relationship between two humans, a male naval officer and a female pilot. Lieutenant Gareth Martinez, a provincial peer, and Cadet Sula, head of the Sula clan, meet after participating in the rescue attempt of a yachtsman named Blitsharts. Martinez, the communications officer to Fleet Commander Enderby, realising that Blitsharts is in distress, requests that the captain of the 'Bombardment of Los Angeles' launch a rescue. The captain in turn launches a pinnace, a small single seater spacecraft, piloted by Lady Sula. Over the course of the rescue and subsequent recovery of the yacht, a period of over a month due the distances involved, Martinez sends Sula regular messages which include comedy and literature to entertain her during the long journey home. Martinez also informs Sula that the last remaining Shaa intends to commit suicide leaving the convocation, a committee consisting of peers of all races, in charge of the empire.

The story picks up where the protagonist, Cugel the Clever, had been left at the end of The Eyes of the Overworld: sitting disconsolately on a barren beach far to the north of his homeland of Almery. As in The Eyes, Cugel's goal is to return home and avenge himself upon Iucounu, the Laughing Magician, whom Cugel regards as indirectly responsible for his second banishment. Taking a different route this time, Cugel obtains a deadly relic of an Overworld being, Sadlark; takes service as worminger (a crewmember responsible for the maintenance of huge marine worms) aboard a worm-propelled merchant ship, which he steals along with its owner's wife and his three comely daughters. Cugel is outwitted by the owner's wife and forced to abandon ship and females; and has various other adventures and setbacks, until with the aid of some new friends, he encompasses the defeat of Iucounu. Like its predecessor, the structure of the story is picaresque, and Cugel remains as ambiguously appealing a character as before. The book is currently out of print in its original form, but is included (with The Eyes of the Overworld) in the omnibus collection, Tales of the Dying Earth. In the Vance Integral Edition, it is volume 35, retitled by its editor as Cugel: The Skybreak Spatterlight. An earlier sequel, A Quest for Simbilis by author Michael Shea, was published in 1974.

The Shepherd’s Paradise presents a mythical pastoral realm devoted to Platonic affection, serving as a sanctuary for unrequited lovers of both sexes—a tranquil haven for troubled minds. Its ruler is Bellesa, symbolizing beauty, who was almost certainly portrayed by Henrietta Maria. Fidamira is the play’s central heroine. Much of Montagu’s plot revolves around Basilino, a prince, and his close companion Agenor, who share a tendency to fall for the same women. The drama complicates itself with disguise: Basilino operates under the name Moramente, while Agenor assumes Genorio. By the play’s end, Agenor/Genorio is unmasked as Prince Palante, the Navarre king’s long-lost son. A prominent masque within also hosts a lengthy inquiry into the essence of love, featuring Martiro advocating the Platonic ideal, contrasted with Moramente and Melidoro who defend marriage. The finale aligns with conventional comic marriages: Basilino, now Moramente, weds Bellesa—who is in fact Sapphira, Princess of Navarre and his original betrothed—while Agenor/Genorio/Palante weds Basilino’s sister. This ending invites readings that celebrate marital union over Platonic affection. Fidamira is revealed to be sister to both Bellesa/Sapphira and Agenor/Genorio/Palante, the lost Miranda, remaining a virgin yet attaining queenship of the Shepherd’s Paradise in the conclusion.

In the prologue, Watarai leads his team of Cobalt Knights to an area inaccessible to normal players. They attempt to delete a vagrant AI in the form of a little girl in a red dress, but their attempt fails and she escapes. In the first chapter, we are introduced to Albireo. He cheats his way into the lowest level of the dungeon and meets the Vagrant AI. Through text chat, she reveals her name to be Lycoris. The end-of-dungeon treasure was an item named "eciov.cyl", which Albiero traded to Lycoris by her request. In the game, she gains her voice. Lycoris teleports them without warning to his home, where there was currently a massive monster attack. A newbie player, Hokuto, appeals to Albireo to help her. He is forced to help her and finish the event involuntarily, gaining an item "rae.cyl". This is also traded to Lycoris. Hokuto manages to blackmail him into letting her into his empty friend's list, and then into forming a party of the two of them. Due to this, Hokuto was able to see Lycoris. Albireo was also approached by Orca and Balmung to ask for assistance in resolving the "One Sin", an event considered unbeatable. He declined however. He was unable to log out from The World, but was able to continue with his normal life (unlike infected characters later in the .hack series, who fell into comas). Upon returning, he headed to the "One Sin" location. Hokuto met him there, and they witnessed Orca and Balmung defeat the boss character there. Upon its defeat, an angel appeared, trailing feathers. Lycoris requested that Albireo find a red feather, which turned out to be "eye.cyl". This restored Lycoris' sight. Lycoris brought them to another zone. She entered a phantom spring, and Albireo gained "yromem.cyl". Returning to the area in the prologue, Albireo gives Lycoris the item. She regains her memory and realizes that Albireo is none other than Watarai, the Cobalt Knight who had first tried to delete her. Watarai had attempted to complete the event in order to delete the previously fragmented Lycoris. She informs him of the existence of Morganna Mode Gone and the fact that she was a failed prototype of Aura, and reveals the last fragment of herself, hidden in Albireo's spear: "etaf.cyl". She then chose to delete herself, impaling herself onto Albireo's spear.

Fresh from the Bacta War on Thyferra, Wedge Antilles sets his sights on forming a new fighter squadron—this time a hybrid of combat commandos with pilots as a secondary consideration. While presenting the plan to Admiral Ackbar, he outlines a cost-free approach for the New Republic: recruit the misfits, the washouts, and those pilots barely clinging to Fighter Command status—those no one else will take. In contrast to Rogue Squadron, built from elite pilots who also had ground-fighting chops, this unit would consist of seasoned ground fighters whose piloting ability would be secondary. With Wes Janson's aid, Antilles assembles a crew that becomes known as Wraith Squadron, featuring: Jesmin Ackbar, a communications specialist and Admiral Ackbar’s niece; Hohass “Runt” Ekwesh, a Thakwaash with multiple personalities; Garik “Face” Loran, once a child actor recruited by the Empire; Voort “Piggy” SaBinring, a Gamorrean who pilots; Kell Tainer, a demolitions expert and the son of a Rebel pilot Antilles was forced to kill; Myn Donos, the sole survivor of an Imperial ambush against his Talon squadron; Ton Phanan, a former doctor with some mechanical augmentation; Falynn Sandskimmer, a Tatooine vehicle expert known for insolence; Tyria Sarkin, a former Antari Ranger with minor Force sensitivity; and Eurrsk “Grinder” Thri’ag, an accomplished code slicer and prankster. The story centers on Wraith Squadron’s misadventures as they go undercover aboard Night Caller, an Imperial blockade runner hired by Warlord Zsinj, to accompany the crew on a covert mission.

Reed Shelton longs to orchestrate a flawless camping adventure for himself and his wife, Beck. Yet Beck prefers the security of home, a preference Reed manages to override for the sake of the trip. Once darkness falls and the campsite is set, a chilling, otherworldly wail pierces the night, its source marked by a cluster of glowing eyes. In a sudden burst of action, a creature seizes Beck and vanishes into the darkness. Determined, Reed—backed by a small-town chorus and a circle of trusted friends—sets out to locate his missing spouse. Meanwhile, Beck fights to survive, adapting not only to her surroundings but to the unnerving behavior of her abductors. With dwindling time, Reed and his allies intensify the search, only to discover they are being hunted as well. The threat proves to be far more tangible—and terrifying—than they imagined. As danger closes in, Michael Capella, known as Cap and a former scientist, begins examining the DNA traces left at the sites of the monster’s rampages. His investigation reveals something extraordinary: a chimpanzee DNA sequence tainted with human genetic material. This clue points toward his former colleague, Adam Burkhardt, whom Cap believes is conducting perilous experiments beyond the pale of ethics.

To cover the gambling debts of his daughter Kitty Imber, the widowed Lord Theign is planning to sell his beautiful painting Duchess of Waterbridge by Sir Joshua Reynolds to American billionaire Breckinridge Bender. Hugh Crimble, a young art critic, argues against the sale, saying that Britain's art treasures should stay in the country. He is supported by Theign's perceptive daughter, Lady Grace. When the newspapers get wind of the potential sale of the Reynolds, they raise a patriotic stink, which delights the bumptious, good-humored Bender. Meanwhile, Crimble has found another painting in Theign's collection that he suspects is a rarity by Mantovano. (James thought this was a completely fictitious name, but it turned out there really had been an obscure painter called Mantovano.) Eventually, Crimble's hunch about the Mantovano turns out to be correct. Theign decides to donate the Mantovano to the National Gallery and not to sell the Reynolds to Breckinridge. His woman friend Lady Sandgate also donates her family's Sir Thomas Lawrence painting to the Gallery, which unites her and Theign forever.

In The Forests of Silence, the topaz had been retrieved by Lief, Barda, and Jasmine. They continue on their way to the Lake of Tears, to retrieve the ruby. They learn that the land surrounding the Lake of Tears is controlled by the evil sorceress Thaegan, who has 13 monster children. As the companions travel through the countryside they rescue a man named Manus from the Shadow Lord's servants, Grey Guards. Manus is from the city of Raladin. 100 years ago, Thaegan put a spell on Raladin that caused them and all of their offspring to never be able to speak. Lief, Barda, and Jasmine also learn that Thaegan put a spell on the city of D'Or and turned it into the Lake of Tears. The companions, with Manus, escape from the Grey Guards only to be captured by Jin and Jod, two of Thaegan's children. They eventually defeat Jin and Jod and journey to the city of Raladin, where Manus hopes to find his people. Upon arrival, they find the city empty. Only when the Ralad people hear the companions, they come out of hiding. Lief, Barda, and Jasmine tell the Ralads that they must journey to the Lake of Tears, despite the Ralads pleas, but they do not tell them they are going in quest of one of the gems of the Belt of Deltora. Manus agrees to be their guide. When they get to the Lake of Tears, the monster Soldeen attacks them. Soldeen is a giant fish-like creature who is very deadly and has the ability to speak. Using the power of the topaz, Lief persuades Soldeen to give them the ruby. As Soldeen agrees, Thaegan appears and threatens to kill them all. The ruby flies out of Lief's hand and into the depths of the Lake as Thaegan uses her magic to harm them. Just as Thaegan is about to kill them all, Jasmine's bird Kree comes and kills Thaegan by drawing blood. All of Thaegan's spells are broken: the Ralads can now speak and the Lake of Tears turns back into the city of D'Or. Soldeen is a man named Nanion and gives the three companions the gem and wishes them well on their quest. The Belt now holds the topaz and ruby and now they journey towards the City of the Rats.

Detective Chief Inspector Alan Banks’s career has lately seemed stalled, nearly ruined by the petty squabbles of his politically driven superior, Chief Constable Riddle. The turning point comes when nude images of Riddle’s runaway teenage daughter appear on a porn site, forcing Riddle to seek Banks’s aid. Banks traces the trail first to Soho in London—an enclave of strip clubs and sex shops—and then to the refined district of Little Venice, where Emily Riddle resides with a dangerous gangster connected to the rock world. Initially, Emily resists returning home, but she later reappears at Banks’s hotel, battered and frightened, pleading for help. She eventually goes back to her family in Yorkshire, and Banks believes his involvement is finished. Yet other matters demand his attention. Eastvale Regional Headquarters undergoes a sweeping reorganization and expansion, bringing Detective Sergeant Annie Cabbot back into Banks’s orbit, where she confronts her own inner struggles. As they start investigating the murder of Charlie Courage, a petty criminal, a new homicide erupts at an Eastvale nightclub, fueling tabloid headlines about scandal, sex, and high-level corruption. The brutal killing deeply unsettles Banks and eventually unveils connections that tie it to the Charlie Courage case. The investigation’s grim findings push Banks toward an unwanted path, forcing him to confront the past and the private life of his most formidable adversary, Chief Constable Riddle.

A white male is picked up by the New York Police after being found bending over the victim of a mugging at Grand Central Terminal in midtown Manhattan. After having responded to the police questions with somewhat strange answers, he is transferred to Bellevue Hospital for evaluation. Although not physically ill, he is found to harbour a strange delusion: That he is from a planet called K-PAX in the constellation of Lyra. The patient, who calls himself "prot" (intentionally lower-case to reflect the insignificance of an individual life form in the universe), is eventually transferred to the Manhattan Psychiatric Institute (MPI), where he becomes the patient of Dr. Gene Brewer. Dr. Brewer, with the help of a journalist named Giselle, discovers that prot may simply be an alter ego (the result of Multiple Personality Disorder) of Robert Porter, whose life has been devastated by the murder of his wife and child and his subsequent killing of the perpetrator. When prot returns to his own planet, Robert Porter is left in a catatonic state. However, Bess (another patient prot had promised to take with him) disappears along with a box of souvenirs prot has been collecting. Prot promises to return in "about five of your years".

Amanda McCready disappeared from a Boston neighborhood in 1997 when she was just four. Desperate appeals from her aunt drew in the shrewd, stubborn sleuths Patrick Kenzie and Angie Gennaro, who took on the case with everything at stake. They chased her down only to arrange her return to a neglectful mother and a fractured home. Now, at sixteen, Amanda is gone again. An exceptional student, bright yet distant, she seemed fated to break free from her upbringing. Her aunt returns to Kenzie’s door, worried about the girl who has blossomed into a striking, intelligent young woman and has vanished for two weeks. Carrying the weight of the past, Kenzie and Gennaro reopen the case that haunted them most, tracing a twelve-year web of secrets and lies through Boston’s rough, blue-collar streets. They persuade themselves that this time will be different, determined to locate Amanda and ensure her safety. Yet their resolve to do the right thing carries dark stakes—stakes that could claim Amanda’s life and their own. In the interval since Prayers for Rain, Kenzie and Gennaro have married and started a family.

Ranald Sigmundson, a native of Orkney, embarks for Vinland as a young man, fights at Clontarf, and accumulates further exploits along the way. In later years he tends a farm and cautions his kin and friends against letting themselves become absorbed in worldly affairs. The novel’s prose is spare and vivid, channeling the cadence of an ancient Norse saga, and Brown’s work frequently revives that very literary form. Composed during a period when Brown’s health waned, Vinland offers a rare autobiographical glimpse into the author’s reflections on mortality. Much like Ranald, Brown adopts a Christian mindset. Within the narrative, Ranald longs for one final voyage to Vinland, but the journey is symbolic: he dies on Easter Monday, making the passage spiritual rather than corporeal. Across Brown’s body of work, Vinland resonates with the pursuit of “silence”—a longing for Christian peace, unity, meaning, and order. The author situates Viking notions of fate (wyrd) as a backdrop to his argument for Christian order. As Ranald grows to loathe the Viking way of life, he becomes deeply introspective and isolated, probing life’s meaning through the lens of emerging Christian ideals. Put plainly, his ultimate trip westward is really a journey toward heaven, toward an Eden-like harmony that is struck down when the mythic apocalyptic hound Fenrir’s Wolf slays a native American, shattering any hope of reconciliation.

Ten-year-old Liza Barton accidentally killed her mother and wounded her stepfather, Ted. Though acquitted, she is later adopted by distant relatives. Fast-forward twenty-four years, Liza—now living as Celia Foster—strives to erase her past and begins a new life with Alex Nolan, following the death of her first husband, Larry. Unbeknownst to Alex, Celia’s history runs deeper. He gifts her a birthday surprise: the keys to her own parents’ house in the neighboring town of Mendham. The threesome—Celia, Alex, and their four-year-old son, Jack—move in only to discover the home has been vandalized. To avoid upsetting Alex, Celia decides to conceal her history for the time being. Memories of the fatal night flood Celia’s mind as she starts to uncover the truth about what happened that evening. She also quietly seeks information about the accident that claimed her father’s life a year before her mother’s death. As several elderly townspeople are murdered one by one, clues increasingly point toward Celia. With the killer’s pursuit accelerating, Celia’s own life becomes imperiled while the mystery of her past closes in.

The second book follows Becker Drane on another mission. At the end of the first book, The Glitch in Sleep, it was revealed 50 trays of Frozen Moments were stolen. With that, a Time Bomb could be constructed causing great damage to The World. When news show the Time Bomb has been found in the Department of Time, Lucien Chiappa is sent in to Fix it, until the bomb explodes and Becker is called in to repair the mess by bringing the two parts of the bomb together so no Essence (liquid that everything to age much faster) can enter the World. To Fix the Second, Becker must bring both halves of the Second together again to prevent any more Essence from dripping out. The first is found in a basement and the second is found to be trapped by the Tide, the organization who created the bomb and wants to overthrow the current order of the Seems and create a new world. A legendary Fixer thought to be dead, Tom Jackal arrives to help Becker and manages to capture the Second and put it together, but the Essence has soaked through their Sleeves (lightweight bodysuits) and causes him to age. Tom dies from overexposure, but saves the World. At the end, Becker breaks the Golden Rule which prevents him from meeting with Jenifer Kaley, whose Case File (documents on her private life) was given to Becker after the Mission. However, in the epilogue, the Time Being, a powerful founder of the Seems agrees to join The Tide.

In Harstad's novel, Albert is 42 years old and still lives with his father in the same apartment. When his father suddenly dies, Albert sees it as an opportunity to finally create the life for himself that he longed for all these years he was taking care of his father. A large part of the novel is made up of a flashback to 1985-86 when Albert traveled around Europe with his friend Viktor, and by coincidence ends up in Hong Kong and later Paris, where he meets a girl and almost decides to stay for good, before ending up returning to his father in Hässelby. The novel starts as a traditional novel exploring themes such as the relationship between father and son, growing up in suburbia, friendship and politics, but throughout the novel the tone gradually gets darker and darker as more surreal elements are introduced. The novel ends as a nightmarish tale where Albert discovers that someone have been following him for over twenty years, all over the world, and that the world is coming to an end.

Act I finds Elyot and Sybil honeymooning at a Deauville hotel, their courtship brief and tense; her curiosity about Elyot’s first marriage sours the mood. Next door, Amanda and Victor embark on married life, while Victor remains preoccupied by the cruelty Amanda endured from her ex-husband. Elyot and Amanda, once married for three tempestuous years and divorced five years ago, unexpectedly discover they are sharing a terrace on their separate honeymoons with younger spouses. Each begs the other’s new mate to leave the hotel immediately, but both spouses refuse and retreat to dine alone. Realizing they still love one another and regretting the divorce, Elyot and Amanda abandon their companions and flee to Amanda’s Paris flat. Act II unfolds after a Paris dinner, as Elyot and Amanda adopt the code word Sollocks to curb their quarrels. A fierce kiss follows, yet the idyll proves unsustainable: neither can live with nor without the other. Their relationship devolves into blistering arguments, reminiscent of their former marriage, as they try to outwit each other and re-create old patterns. The conflicts escalate into violence when Amanda cracks a record over Elyot’s head and he slaps her in retaliation, sealing a repetitive cycle of ardor and hostility that consumes them. At the peak of their fiercest clash, Sybil and Victor stage an entrance. Act III opens the next morning with Amanda attempting a discreet departure, only to encounter Sybil and Victor. Elyot arrives, reviving their familiar bickering. A mutual agreement emerges: neither Elyot nor Amanda’s new spouse will permit a divorce for one year, allowing time to determine if their reunion is truly desired. Tempers flare as Sybil and Victor defend their partners, and Amanda and Elyot recognize that Sybil and Victor may be equally well-matched for one another. They forgive one another and slip away, leaving the younger couple to fend for themselves. As Elyot and Amanda quietly exit, Victor and Sybil reach a tipping point of mutual hostility.

La Vendetta is a short work relating the tragic fate of Ginevra Piombo, the daughter of proud Corsican immigrants, who has the misfortune of falling in love with another Corsican Luigi Porta. When it becomes known that Luigi is the sole survivor of a massacre in which the rest of his family were the victims of a bloody vendetta with Ginevra's family, Ginevra's father Bartolomeo is determined to complete the act of vengeance by having him killed. But Ginevra refuses to yield to her father's demands and she and Luigi are married. Over the following years the pair eke out a miserable existence, dogged by hunger and poverty, while Ginevra's wealthy father refuses to lift a hand to support her: it is as much as he can do to refrain from murdering Luigi. Ginevra gives birth to a child, but she and the child die on the very day that Monsieur Piombo finally relents and decides to assist the impoverished couple. Before he can act, however, Luigi visits him and gives him the tresses of his deceased daughter. "Dead! Our two families were doomed to exterminate each other. Here is all that remains of her," he says, laying Ginevra's long black hair upon the table. Ginevra's parents are shaken, as though a stroke of lightning has blasted them. Luigi departs. "He has spared me a shot, for he is dead," says Bartolomeo, slowly, gazing on the ground at his feet.

Kang In-ho, a teacher who has been driven from his family after the suicide of a former student with whom he had an affair, relocates to Mujin, a fictional city. There he takes a job at a school for the hearing-impaired. On his very first day, a boy is fatally struck by a train, the latest tragedy in a troubling string of accidents he soon uncovers. Rumors point to a girl who recently killed herself by leaping from a cliff. As Kang investigates, he becomes convinced that something darker is at play and discovers that the students—both boys and girls—are subjected to abuse by the school’s leadership: the principal, a powerful and esteemed figure in the community; the administrative head; and the dormitory superintendent. His attempts to reveal the crimes to the public are thwarted by entrenched corruption among police, physicians, and local business leaders. The defense lawyers attempt to undercut him by revealing past transgressions, including his relationship with the deceased student. Compounding the ordeal, moneyed parents press for silence in exchange for financial compensation. In the conclusion, the three accused receive probation and are released back to the school. Overcome with humiliation because his personal failures have been exposed and with justice elusive, Kang chooses to leave Mujin and return to his family in Seoul.

A Romance of Two Worlds starts with a young heroine, in first person, telling her story of a debilitating illnesses that includes depression and thoughts of suicide. Her doctor is unable to help her and sends her off on a holiday where she meets a mystical character by the name of Raffello Cellini, a famous Italian artist. Cellini offers her a strange potion which immediately puts her into a tranquil slumber, in which she experiences divine visions. Upon wakening, she craves more.
