Later, she meets her guardian angel named Heliobas, the hero of the story, who whisks her through infinite solar systems faster than a shooting star while human spirits fly by like gossamer silk. He shares the truth of religion and the secret of human destiny, but still she longs for more. She comes to understand God as pure light and pure love, but it's not enough that she should see and hear these things from the touch of an angel. She wants to master this ability on her own and seeks a oneness with God through a series of meditative disciplines while locked away in a monastery.

The book is written in the form of a false document. It opens with a foreword by Meyer, who states that the manuscript was brought to his attention by a woman with some familial connection to Horace Vernet, also an ancestor of Holmes. The woman had read The Seven-Per-Cent Solution and thought Meyer might be interested. Although damaged by water, the manuscript proved authentic. Dr. Watson explains in his own preface that he did not publish the story because of the number of well-known persons who would be affected - persons whose identity would be impossible to disguise. Holmes had for a long time refused Watson permission to write the story on these very grounds, but Watson eventually persuaded him by promising to place the manuscript in Holmes' hands, the only condition being that he not destroy it. The story involves many well-known people, including George Bernard Shaw, who hires Holmes to look into the death of an unpleasant theatre critic; Sir Arthur Sullivan, one of whose singers at the D'Oyly Carte Opera Company was another victim of the murderer; and others including W. S. Gilbert, Oscar Wilde, Bram Stoker, Henry Irving, Ellen Terry and Frank Harris. In the novel, Holmes clears the name of a shy Parsee Indian wrongfully accused of murder; in real life Conan Doyle played a significant part in helping George Edalji, a Parsee victim of injustice in the English court.

A decade ago, Charles MacKenzie, Jr.—known as Mack—vanished from his apartment without a word, and no trace of him has ever reappeared. He still contacts his mother every Mother’s Day, calling to assure her he is well, then ends the call, leaving her with unanswered questions and growing dread. Even the death of his father in the 9/11 attacks failed to bring him back or interrupt the pattern. Now, Carolyn MacKenzie resolves that moving forward means seeking closure and solving the mystery of her brother’s disappearance. When Mack’s annual Mother’s Day call arrives this year, she announces her plan to find him, no matter the risks. The next day, a note arrives for Monsignor Devon Mackenzie: Uncle Devon, tell Carolyn not to search for me. Despite the anger and disapproval of those who love her, Carolyn presses on, diving into a perilous mystery whose edges widen with each turn. What secrets hide behind the superintendent’s door at Mack’s former building? What do his former roommates know about what happened? Could he have ties to the girls who have vanished over the past decade? Might he be linked to the brutal murder of his drama teacher—and for what motive? Carolyn’s relentless pursuit of truth draws her into a deadly clash with someone close to her, whose secrets they refuse to let her expose.

In the year 2363, Cadet Larry Stark—twenty years old and a fresh graduate of the Space Patrol Academy, hailing from a lineage of Space Patrol commanders—begins his journey aboard the interstellar vessel Carden for the customary final training cruise. Upon completion, he is to receive his commission as an officer of the Space Patrol. The Carden traverses four and a half light-years to Alpha Centauri in just fifteen days, propelled by faster-than-light overdrive. Alpha Centauri’s fourth planet, an Earth-like world once home to dinosaurs, had been colonized 125 years earlier. Stark, raised to follow orders and to trust Earth and the Space Patrol’s infallibility, arrives on planet IV of Alpha C after colonists have begun voting to declare—and perhaps fight for—independence from Earth. The presence of the Carden and its crew could sway the unfolding revolution. For Stark, this is the first time he faces a choice between a right and a wrong when the stakes are ambiguous. His actions may jeopardize his Space Patrol career and his relationship with his father. The narrative, rooted in a metaphor for the American Revolution, casts Earth as England and Alpha Centauri as the United States. In the end, Stark aligns with the Alpha C colonists, yet he remains convinced his father would be proud that he stayed true to himself. Notable aspects of the 1955 novel include: 1) the overdrive—grounded in spacetime warping; 2) the use of “electronic guitar” for electric guitar and “wristchron” for wristwatch; and 3) a vacuum-tube radio aboard the ship. The character Harl Ellison bears his name in homage to science-fiction writer Harlan Ellison, a neighbor of Silverberg in New York during the period of writing. This tribute was verified in a special edition celebrating Silverberg’s thirty-fifth year in the field.

The book questions the U.S. government version of the events and raises a large number of questions on the details of the events which, according to many observers, marked the beginning of the 21st century and changed the geopolitical world order. It makes the following claims: The actions that provoked the collapse of the Twin Towers in the heart of New York and damaged part of the Pentagon building were not the result of attempts by foreign suicide pilots, but were rather an action organized by a group within the U.S. administration; an internal plot aimed at driving opinion and forcing the course of events. The war on Afghanistan was not a response to the September 11 events, since it was prepared long before in coordination with the British. President Bush found support in evangelical groups to launch a crusade against Islam, according to the strategy known as “Clash of Civilizations”. The “war on terror” was a pretext to cut individual liberties in the United States and later in allied countries in order to impose a military regime. Osama bin Laden was a CIA fabrication and never stopped working for the U.S. secret service. The bin Laden and the Bush families jointly manage their wealth by means of the Carlyle Group. The U.S. administration was taken over by some industrial groups (weapons, oil, pharmaceuticals) whose interests would be defended by the government in detriment of others. The CIA would develop a program of interference at all levels, which would include the resource of torture and political assassination.

Eric Packer, a 28-year-old billionaire asset manager, grinds a peculiar odyssey through midtown Manhattan to reach a haircut. His stretch limo, described in exquisite detail as luxurious, expansive, and technologically equipped, glides with blocked-out street noise courtesy of cork lining, bulletproofing, Carrara marble floors, and a wall of television screens and computer monitors. Packer’s progress is repeatedly impeded by a presidential visit, a vociferous anti-capitalist riot, and a funeral procession for a Sufi rap star. Along this journey, he has several chance exchanges with his wife and engages in extramarital affairs. He is tailed by two men: a comically inept “pastry assassin” and a volatile, self-styled “credible threat.” As the day unfolds, Packer watches enormous sums vanish from his clients’ accounts due to bets against the yen’s ascent, a loss that mirrors his own financial and personal unraveling. He appears to take grim pleasure in relinquishing wealth, even ensuring his wife’s fortune is squandered to seal his ruin. In the end, the second stalker—a former employee who views Packer’s murder as the only meaningful act left—shoots him to death.

Critique of Dialectical Reason is the product of a later stage in Sartre's thinking, during which he no longer identified Marxism with the Soviet Union or French Communism but came closer to identifying as a Marxist. It puts forward a revision of Existentialism, and an interpretation of Marxism as a contemporary philosophy par excellence, one that can be criticized only from a reactionary pre-Marxist standpoint. Sartre argues that while the free fusion of many human projects may possibly constitute a Communist society, there is no guarantee of this. Conscious human acts are not projections of freedom that produce human 'temporality', but movements toward 'totalization', their sense being co-determined by existing social conditions. People are thus neither absolutely free to determine the meaning of their acts nor slaves to the circumstances in which they find themselve. Social life does not consist only of individual acts rooted in freedom, since it is also a sedimentation of history by which we are limited and a fight with nature, which imposes further obstacles and causes social relationships to be dominated by scarcity. Every satisfaction of a need can cause antagonism and make it more difficult for people to accept each other as human beings. Scarcity deprives people of the ability to make particular choices and diminishes their humanity. Communism will restore the freedom of the individual and his ability to recognize the freedom of others.

A tale unfolds around Lancelot, who has endured into the present through magical means and now must aid Morgana le Fay against a destabilized Merlin. Appearing as an old man yet retaining his vigor and prowess, Lancelot has wandered the land since Camelot fell, chasing the Holy Grail under the belief that his immortality is a punishment for his sins and that attaining the Grail could lift the curse. Morgana reveals a harsher truth: Merlin, not fate, is the source of his condition. Though Merlin has slept for centuries, he is on the verge of awakening and intends to recruit Lancelot as a champion and guardian for his own schemes. Morgana warns that Merlin’s misguided attempts to fix the modern world will wreak havoc, and that he must be stopped. In a confrontation with Merlin, Lancelot uses a magical elixir to awaken him, hoping to convince him to abandon his plans. Merlin, in response, strips away the spell of immortality. Sensing the danger, Lancelot drinks what remains of the elixir to restore his youth. Merlin retaliates by summoning a hollow knight—an armor-clad specter animated by a spirit—to kill Lancelot. Morgana defeats Merlin, and Lancelot defeats the summoned spirit, yet the battle leaves him mortally wounded. As he nears his end, Lancelot finally beholds a vision of the Holy Grail.

When Nita's sister Dairine signs up for an intragalactic exchange program without permission, their local advisors transfer the mission to Nita and Kit. The destination seems to be an ideal planet, and they are hoping for a vacation. Meanwhile, the aliens who arrive at Dairine's house appear to be very "alien". However, Nita's dreams become nightmarish and the planet Alaalu turns out to be hiding a dark secret: an avatar of the Lone Power has been trapped in this dystopia since their people refused Its gift of entropy. While this may have prevented deterioration to war, crime and natural disasters, among other things, it also prevented such change as evolution, and the Alaalu people are trapped in their current stage of existence when they have the potential to be free of it. It becomes the young wizards' job to convince the Alaalu wizard and her people to accept this change, inevitably setting the Lone Power free. On Earth, the wizards at Dairine's place have become aware that their Sun is in danger of flaring up to the point of scorching their planet. However, one of the visitors comes from a planet where he is a guardian against the recurrence of such a disaster, and recognizes it in time for them to save the Earth.

Four Polish scientists and a private detective become "Flame Breathers" and die; a car and a plane set speed records and are destroyed, the driver, pilot, and a reporter, killed; a Montreal police lab, the financier Singer's home, a bathtub with financier Henderlin in it all explode; a house in NJ, heated and lit without using electricity, gas, or oil, explodes. A beautiful woman with black hair thwarts the Justice Inc. team repeatedly. A small strange man seems to be implicated in the scheme. Benson initially finds no chemical explanation for the flames and explosions. He investigates, his aides playing relatively small roles. Benson is betrayed by his paralyzed face and his white hair. The plot is complex: two gangs, each backed by a financier, fight for control of a secret process, discovered by the four scientists, that can turn water into an energy source. The black-haired woman seeks justice for the death of the reporter, her brother, and gets it as Benson causes the gangs destroy one another. The small man, lab assistant to the four scientists, dies, taking the secret of getting energy from water to the grave with him.

The Hardys embark on a perilous quest to help their Greek pen pal, Evangelos Pandropolos, track down a priceless ancient helmet. Years earlier, Evan’s uncle lent the artifact to a Hollywood studio for a silent film, The Persian Glory, but it vanished after filming wrapped. At Hunt College, where Evan, Frank, Joe, and Chet Morton are enrolled in a summer film-making program, they face escalating harassment from Leon Saffel. Meanwhile, a criminal syndicate pressures Mr. Hardy to halt his investigations and simultaneously hunts for the helmet, which may have belonged to King Agamemnon, increasing its value after a conversation with Evan’s wealthy uncle. The clues the Hardys uncover propel them across continents—from their campus to California, and ultimately to Greece. In a tense climax on the island of Corfu, Evan, Chet, and the brothers outwit their formidable enemies.

Chelsea’s family resolution keeps her from hosting a birthday party because of the expected cost. Meanwhile, her envy grows as Geneva and Warwick, her siblings, receive more money from their parents. In the Stomping Ground nightclub, she forms a friendship with Bex, which deepens a few weeks later after Fee’s friend Eddie tries to assault Chelsea; Bex intervenes to protect her. Separately, Barry Gee launches his own restaurant venture, christening it Gee Zone. Jemma longs to pursue acting, but her parents object when she sacrifices schoolwork for acting and dancing lessons. She disregards their concerns, placing faith in Ms. Olivia Ockley, the owner of the acting school, who praises her abilities. Friction arises, however, when Alexa Browning lands a lead role ahead of Jemma. Jemma’s romance with Rob strains her bond with Chelsea, though they repair their relationship following Chelsea’s confrontation with Eddie. Jon begins to like Sumitha, but she has lost interest. He is also irritated by his busy parents. After Laura is injured during one of his mother’s animal-rights demonstrations, he realizes his feelings for her and asks her out. Laura’s mother is pregnant, while her boyfriend Melvyn resents Laura’s participation in demonstrations with her neighbor Daniel. Laura’s brother arrives prematurely, and, at Laura’s suggestion, is named Charlie. Sumitha turns into a diligent student—an admirer of her new science teacher, Paul Sharpe—yet, at term’s end, she reveals her crush only to learn that Paul is engaged to Mrs. McConnell. When Sandeep asks her to return home with him, Sumitha dismisses him, and later feels remorse upon discovering that he is being bullied by Kevin and Matthew.

Mr. Plumbean occupies a home on a street described as “neat,” where every dwelling shares the same look. A seagull swoops above and drops a can of vivid orange paint onto his roof. Rather than conforming to the uniform appearance of the block, he uses the paint to sculpt the house into a reflection of his own dreams. Neighbors pressure him to repaint it to match theirs, yet every person he speaks with ends up transforming their own houses to mirror the dreams they harbor. Ultimately, the consensus among the neighbors crystallizes: “Our street is us and we are it. Our street is where we want to be, and it mirrors all our dreams.” The artwork on the walls is done with markers, and a careful observer can discern the marker lines upon close inspection. In a 1978 interview, Daniel Manus Pinkwater acknowledged explicit hallucinogenic undertones threaded throughout the tale. This disclosure led to the book being withdrawn from most Missouri libraries in the early 1980s. A common interpretation links the seagull to Pinkwater’s older brother, Steven, nicknamed “Seagull.”

The Maasai people become aware that a global crisis is approaching. Malevolent, unearthly creatures called shetani, which inhabit another dimension the Maasai know as the “Out Of” (because all things, such as humans, animals and plants, originally came "out of" it), are finding their way into the world. They are fomenting trouble between the superpowers, intent on causing mischief up to and including war. If not prevented, the barriers between the two dimensions will be breached and uncountable hordes of shetani will overrun the world, destroying all life. Olkeloki, a Maasai elder, comes to Washington DC to warn the US President and seek help. He encounters Joshua Oak, a disenchanted FBI agent, and Merry Sharrow, a shy and unfulfilled call centre worker. He is convinced that they are the key people he has been seeking, and his persuasion, coupled with several dangerous encounters with shetani, convince them to return with him to Africa, where they join in Maasai attempts to hold back the shetani. Eventually Olkeloki takes Merry and Oak into the Out Of, where, with their help, he performs a ritual which seals the breach between dimensions, sacrificing his own supernatural powers in the process. All three return to this world, where the shetani’s tricks have ended and the diplomatic crisis is receding, and Oak and Merry realise they have found what they have been looking for in each other.

In the book, environment, famine, overpopulation, climate changes, floods, tornadoes, hothouse effect (now commonly referred to as greenhouse effect), etc. are generally predicted to worsen and become acute by the end of the 20th century. Berlitz lists of doomsday years is long. He starts with the year 999, December 31 when many expected Jesus to return, and goes through a great many doomsday prophecies by scientists, prophets, astrologers and others. In chapter 8, he asks whether the world has ended before, mentioning Atlantis, an idea which he revisits later in his books The Mystery of Atlantis and Atlantis: The Lost Continent Revealed. Berlitz suggests that there may have been a flood, an idea which he explores further in his book The Lost Ship of Noah: In Search of the Ark at Ararat (1987) and in chapter 9 where he cites the tales of a great flood from the Bible and the Torah, Sumerian, Babylonian, Assyrian, Greek, Indian, Persian, Welsh, Norse, Lithuanian, Irish, Chinese, Aztec-Toltec, Maya records and Chibcha tales.

Lenny, recently released from prison, looms large but carries scars from repeated sexual violence endured during incarceration, and he struggles to reassert his manhood once free. His girlfriend Daisy, who drinks too much, longs for a genuine life with a real partner and deserts him at a shabby Times Square bar—an area still haunted by pre-Giuliani days—in search of inexpensive Chinese takeout. Inside the bar, Skank—a once-promising actor turned heroin addict—fights to endure the downpour and to salvage a buyback from the Irish bartender who vanished long ago as he descends into withdrawal. There, Sammy, an old man plagued by guilt and near death, drifts between waking life and an afterlife-like haze. Seventeen-year-old DeMaris, a gun-toting single mother, aspires to learn the art of sex work. She seeks help from Chickie, Skank’s girlfriend, who, in turn, hovers near a naïve day bartender named Charlie. Charlie believes himself a Jedi and showers Chickie with meals, cherishing the day they might someday go out together “as friends.” The bar’s owner, Jake, inherited the place from his father and, after three decades, longs to escape this sewer and reinvent himself in Florida. The booming real estate market, the city’s gentrification, and Disney’s arrival in Times Square could grant him that escape. Unbeknownst to them, their last anchor of home is about to be yanked away, yet the patrons persist. Their humor, unrealized hopes, and stubborn refusal to wallow define them, etched as tattoos on their souls. Before the final act, each character will seize the opportunity to confront their intricate, painful truths head-on.

In Baltimore’s predominantly Eastern European enclave, December 1941 frames the meeting of Michael Anton and Pauline Barclay as he tends to her bloodied brow in his family’s grocery store. Their bond leads to marriage after Michael leaves the Army with a permanent injury inflicted by a deliberate shot from a man he had attacked. The couple sets up residence in a small flat above the shop, yet their starkly contrasting temperaments—his repressed, controlling, and reticent nature versus her loud, emotional, and romantic disposition—soon sow discord. At Pauline’s urging, they relocate to the suburbs and raise three children: Lindy, George, and Karen. Lindy flees to San Francisco in 1960, drawn into the emergent drug scene. Eight years afterward, her parents reclaim Pagan, their three-year-old grandchild, as Lindy undergoes rehabilitation. The marriage gradually unravels, culminating in Michael abandoning Pauline on their thirtieth anniversary. For him, the sense that they were utterly unprepared for marriage, “amateurs” in the domestic domain, makes divorce a form of salvation; for Pauline, it becomes a tragedy that leaves her engulfed in despair.

Opening with a retrospective glance at Koestler’s childhood, the author lays out his worldview. He frames his perception of the world with the lens of ancient Babylon, then traces the lineage from Babylon and Egypt to the emergence of Greek philosophy. “Homer’s world is another, more colorful oyster, a floating disc surrounded by Oceanus.” A central thread running through The Sleepwalkers is how faith and reason shift in their relationship to one another. Koestler shows that, despite appearing at odds today, the greatest minds of the West once unified spirituality with intellectual rigor. A second major motif is the disruption of established paradigms to forge new ones, highlighting how even scientists cling to cherished, outdated beliefs and resist recognizing the flaws in their own ideas while embracing those that will replace them. In Koestler’s closing argument, he contends that modern science overemphasizes rationality. He argues that science reaches its peak when researchers permit themselves to act like sleepwalkers rather than forcing every deduction through exhaustive syllogistic scrutiny.

The narrator of the story, a somewhat naive American admirer of English novelist Mark Ambient, visits the writer at his home in Surrey. The narrator is very enthusiastic about Ambient's work, especially his latest novel Beltraffio. He meets Ambient's beautiful but chilly wife, his sickly seven-year-old son Dolcino, and his strange sister Gwendolyn. He also learns that Ambient's wife strongly dislikes her husband's novels and considers them corrupt and pagan. Dolcino eventually becomes much more ill. In order to "protect" him from what she sees as the baleful influence of his father, Ambient's wife withholds the boy's medicine. Dolcino dies, and the details of his mother's conduct are told to the narrator by Gwendolyn. The mother, grief-stricken over her role in Dolcino's final illness, dies herself after a few months. In a grimly ironic note to conclude the story, the narrator says Ambient later revealed that his wife had become partially reconciled to his novels and even read Beltraffio in the weeks before her death.

Snow Country is a stark tale of a love affair between a Tokyo dilettante and a provincial geisha that takes place in the remote hot spring (onsen) town of Yuzawa (Kawabata himself did not mention the name of the town in his novel). The hot springs in that region were home to inns, visited by men traveling alone and in groups, where paid female companionship had become a staple of the economy. The geisha of the hot springs enjoyed nothing like the social status of their more artistically trained sisters in Kyoto and Tokyo and were usually little more than prostitutes whose brief careers inevitably ended in a downward spiral. The liaison between the geisha, Komako, and the male protagonist, a wealthy loner who is a self-appointed expert on Western ballet, is thus doomed to failure. The nature of that failure and the parts played by others form the theme of the book. As his most potent symbol of this "counter-Western modernity", the rural geisha, Komako, of his novel Snow Country embodies Kawabata's conception of traditional Japanese beauty by taking Western influence and subverting it to traditional Japanese forms. Having no teacher available, she hones her technique on the traditional samisen instrument by untraditionally relying on sheet music and radio broadcasts. Her lover, Shimamura, comments that, “the publishing gentleman would be happy if he knew he had a real geisha—not just an ordinary amateur—practicing from his scores way off here in the mountains.” But on his way to the town, Shimamura is fascinated with a girl he sees on the train, a young girl named Yoko who is caring to a sick man traveling with her. He wants to see more of her, even though he is with Komako during his stay. Already a married man, it doesn't faze him that he is thinking about Yoko while being public with Komako.

Ray Smith's story is driven by Japhy, whose penchant for the simple life and Zen Buddhism greatly influenced Kerouac on the eve of the sudden and unpredicted success of On the Road. The action shifts between the events of Smith and Ryder's "city life," such as three-day parties and enactments of the Buddhist "Yab-Yum" rituals, to the sublime and peaceful imagery where Kerouac seeks a type of transcendence. The novel concludes with a change in narrative style, with Kerouac working alone as a fire lookout on Desolation Peak (adjacent to Hozomeen Mountain), in what would soon be declared North Cascades National Park (see also Desolation Angels). These elements place The Dharma Bums at a critical junction foreshadowing the consciousness-probing works of several authors in the 1960s such as Timothy Leary and Ken Kesey. One episode in the book features Smith, Ryder and Henry Morley (based on real-life friend John Montgomery) climbing Matterhorn Peak in California. It tells the story of Kerouac's first introduction to this type of mountaineering and would serve as inspiration for him to spend the following summer as a fire lookout for the United States Forest Service on Desolation Peak in Washington. The novel also gives an account of the legendary 1955 Six Gallery reading, where Allen Ginsberg gave a debut presentation of his poem "Howl" (changed to "Wail" in the book), and other authors such as Snyder, Kenneth Rexroth, Michael McClure, and Philip Whalen performed.
